title: ‘Yes, Dear’ star Anthony Clark dies at 62, co-star announces
text:
(Gray Media) – Actor and comedian Anthony Clark died Tuesday at the age of 62. He was best known for his roles in “Yes Dear” and “Boston Common.”
Friend and castmate Mike O’Malley announced his death in a post on social media, saying Clark was a “hilarious guy.”
“He was so unique—one of those comics who is laughing along with you at the absurdity of his stories and observations. I was a fan before I was a friend,” O’Malley said, adding they had just spoken on the phone three weeks ago.
Clark played the role of Greg Warner on “Yes Dear,” a sitcom that ran on CBS for six seasons, and Boyd Pritchett in “Boston Common.”
“Anthony Clark was one of my first clients,” manager Barry Katz said on Instagram. “Arguably one of the funniest people that I have ever met in my lifetime.”
A cause of death was not released.

title: Portland celebrates grand opening of new Longfellow Playground
text:
City of Portland celebrates grand opening of new Longfellow Playground
The Portland Parks, Recreation and Facilities Department celebrated the grand opening of the new Longfellow Playground on Thursday.
A ribbon-cutting ceremony was held at 12 p.m. at Longfellow Elementary School on Stevens Avenue. After the ribbon was cut, students cheered and sprinted to test out the swings, slides and timber climbing structures.
"This one was really outdated. We had some old equipment. Things were rusting apart. Things had to be removed for safety reasons, and so we've been working for the past two years getting the funding from the City Council to make this thing happen," said Ethan Hipple, director of the Parks, Recreation and Facilities Department.
While the roughly 30,000-square-foot playground is on school property, the space is open to the whole neighborhood.
The new playground boasts on-site drainage to keep the play area dry and accessible, along with paved walkways and natural landscaping.
Last week, the city celebrated the renovations made to the Reiche School Playground in the West End.

title: What men need to know after a major update to prostate cancer guidelines
text:
What men need to know after a major update to prostate cancer guidelines
Middle-aged men should undergo regular screening for prostate cancer, the American Cancer Society said Thursday in a major change to its guidelines.
The screening involves a simple blood test, and men at average risk of getting prostate cancer should receive that PSA test every two years between the ages of 50 and 69, the cancer society advised.
Men at high risk, including Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer, should get yearly PSA checks and start earlier, at age 45.
Thursday’s guideline update marks a shift in thinking about routine blood tests for PSA, or prostate-specific antigen.
Since 2010, the cancer society has recommended that men at average risk talk with their doctors about whether and how often to get PSA tests. That’s a protein produced by both normal and cancerous prostate cells, meaning a high level might signal a tumor but also could be from a benign enlarged prostate or be a temporary spike from vigorous exercise.
Catching prostate cancer early without overtreating
Prostate cancer is highly survivable if caught early, but widespread PSA testing in the past was blamed for overtreatment of slow-growing tumors and unnecessary follow-up testing in men who turned out to not have cancer.
The updated advice comes after advances in understanding how regular PSA testing can help catch prostate cancer before it spreads and becomes harder to treat, as well as how to reduce potential harms from screening, according to the cancer society. That includes steps such as repeating a PSA test to be sure it’s truly high or adding an MRI scan to help identify who needs a biopsy, as well as monitoring rather than aggressively treating low-risk tumors.
A prostate cancer specialist not involved with the guideline said the change will be especially helpful for primary care doctors who introduce cancer screenings to patients but may be less familiar with the complexities.
“This has taken ambiguity out of it. They are basically saying, ‘Do it,’” said Dr. Ash Tewari, who leads the urology department at Mount Sinai's Icahn School of Medicine in New York. “This guideline will only make things easier for men, and hopefully it will have more grandfathers eating dinner with their family 10 years from now.”
Still talk with your doctor about your prostate cancer risk
There still needs to be a doctor-patient conversation about the pros and cons, the cancer society guideline stresses.
“We want to find the right balance,” Tewari agreed. “Patients need to understand that their risk of prostate cancer differs,” which explains why the recommendations aren't one-size-fits-all.
What is a strong family history?
The cancer society says that means having one close relative — a father, brother or son — diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or multiple close relatives diagnosed at any age. That puts them in the high-risk category for yearly PSA checks starting at 45. But if men have just one close relative with prostate cancer diagnosed after 65, they should still start screening at 45 but can go two years between testing.
How long should screening continue?
It's not for men of any age whose health is so poor that they aren't expected to live another 10 years. For everyone else, the guideline advises talking with a doctor at age 70 about the choice, saying benefits are less clear. The cancer society no longer recommends screening at 75 — while acknowledging that particularly healthy 75- to 79-year-olds may choose to continue — and discourages it once men turn 80.
Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men. The cancer society estimates more than 333,000 men in the U.S. will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2026, and about 36,000 will die of it.

title: Five questions every business should ask before plugging into AI
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The state is putting money into AI literacy and adoption this year. The Maine State Library is building a statewide AI literacy plan, and the Maine Technology Institute offers eligible small businesses free AI courses through one of its programs.
What gets less attention is the step before you sign up for a new AI tool. A free account takes two minutes, and by lunch someone has pasted a customer list, a patient note or a draft contract into the platform. The questions come later, like where that information went and whether you just broke a promise to a client.
I spent years on the vendor side, selling AI and cybersecurity products to regulated buyers, and the careful ones asked some version of these five questions. None require a technical background, and you can work through them in an afternoon.
Where does our data go, and is it used to train the model? Read the privacy policy and terms for the plan you’re buying, not the marketing page. Some free and consumer plans let the vendor use what you type to improve its models, while business plans often turn that off. Find out how long your prompts and files are kept, where they are stored and whether an administrator can delete them. If the answers aren’t in writing, keep sensitive information out.
Can the vendor prove its security? Ask for an independent audit of whether security controls worked over several months or for a certificate that certifies a formal information security program. Ask whether it covers the AI product you’re buying and which outside companies handle your data.
What do our contracts and regulators already require? This is the one owners skip. When I was selling threat intelligence, a Canadian company asked me what U.S. regulators would expect of them. The question built trust and made them more comfortable with the deal. It taught me that once a buyer knows they can stay compliant, the conversation becomes about the business and not red tape. If you handle patient information, federal law requires a business associate agreement with any vendor that stores or processes it, even when the data is encrypted.
Client contracts often carry confidentiality clauses that reach the tools your staff uses. Under Maine law, a vendor holding your customers’ personal information must tell you immediately about a breach, and you generally have 30 days to notify affected Maine residents. A 2025 law also requires a business that uses a chatbot with consumers to disclose clearly that it isn’t a person if a reasonable customer could be fooled.
How will we check its work? AI tools give confident answers that are sometimes wrong. Decide up front who reviews output, what gets checked every time (numbers, names, legal or medical language) and what never goes out without a person signing off. Put it in a one-page policy so new staff know the rules.
What does it cost, and can we leave? Per-seat prices look small until the whole team uses it, and usage-based plans can climb fast. Ask what happens to your data if you cancel, whether you can export it in a usable format and who owns what the tool produces.
Next steps
Once a tool clears those questions, run a small pilot. Pick one task, such as drafting quotes or summarizing meeting notes. Give it to two or three people for 30 days and use only information that wouldn’t hurt anyone if it leaked. Track the time saved and the mistakes caught. At the end you’ll have a real answer instead of a sales demo.
None of this is meant to slow anyone down. Free training is a great place to start, and these five questions are what can transform another free account into a trustworthy tool.

title: New Wiscasset Massage and Healing Arts Studio Encourages Self-Care
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Wiscasset studio offering massages and wellness sessions opened its doors on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Kindred Kneads Massage and Healing Arts Studio, owned by Shannon McAuliffe and Chelsea Edgar, offers services that seek to improve their customers’ physical and mental health. The studio’s primarily offers massages, in addition to stretching sessions, foot reflexology, a pressure point-based therapeutic technique, and Reiki, a Japanese energy-based relaxation practice.
“We wholeheartedly support modern medicine and we very much believe in all facets of healthcare, but I feel like somewhere along the way, we kind of lost that magnitude and importance of human touch as a healing facilitator,” Edgar said. “That’s what is beautiful about massage therapy is that it can facilitate so many elements of healing for another person.”

title: Hospitality with a purpose in the heart of the county
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
COURTESY OF LERAE KINNEY, IGNITE PRESQUE ISLE
In downtown Presque Isle, a hotel stay, a shared meal, or an evening of trivia can do more than make a good memory. Each helps support a bigger idea: that hospitality can be an engine for community growth.
Ignite Presque Isle, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, owns and operates The Northeastland Hotel and Rodney’s at 436 Main. This locally rooted model connects the work of welcoming guests with a mission of investing in people, businesses, and the future of rural downtown.
The newly renovated, 49-room historical hotel offers visitors a home base for discovering Aroostook County. Fully renovated event spaces and a conference room welcome weddings, business meetings, and community gatherings. The Innovation Center’s coworking space gives entrepreneurs, remote workers, and small businesses a professional place to work and connect.
At Rodney’s at 436 Main, farm-to-table dining brings another layer of local investment to the table. Every meal helps support local farmers while offering guests a taste of The County. As a premier downtown restaurant, Rodney’s helps make Main Street a destination for residents and travelers alike.
With 54 team members, Ignite is also a significant local employer. Those jobs support households, build hospitality careers, and help sustain the businesses where employees shop. Without a national hotel or restaurant brand behind it, Ignite keeps the focus on local ownership and reinvestment. Dollars spent here help circulate through the community, supporting wages, local purchasing, and Ignite’s mission.
All proceeds support that mission and are invested back into the community. Through Ignite You, workshops and workforce development initiatives help business owners, managers, and employees strengthen their skills. Programs have covered leadership, workplace culture, digital marketing, and collaboration, creating access to professional development close to home.
Constructive Cocktails networking events bring people together to exchange ideas, build relationships, and discuss opportunities for the region. The Aroostook Women’s Network creates space for connection, learning, and leadership. These investments recognize that a healthy downtown needs both thriving businesses and people equipped to lead them.
Community also grows through shared experiences. Trivia, music bingo, game nights, and murder mystery dinners give neighbors reasons to gather, laugh, and spend time downtown. For visitors, they offer something valuable: a chance to experience the people and personality of The County.
Partnerships make this work stronger. Collaboration with the Central Aroostook Chamber of Commerce, workforce development organizations, educators, local businesses, and community leaders expands what Ignite can accomplish. Its nonprofit structure also opens opportunities to apply for grants that support training, business resources, and community development.
That structure comes with a commitment: Ignite pays property and other applicable taxes, contributing to the public services and infrastructure its community depends on.
The guiding belief is simple: a rising tide lifts all boats. When visitors choose The Northeastland, diners gather at Rodney’s, or businesses come together to learn, they become part of an investment in Aroostook County’s future.
Here, hospitality is more than a welcome. It is a way to help a rural downtown thrive, one stay, one meal, and one connection at a time.

title: Judge allows Trump defamation case against BBC to proceed but tosses 1 claim
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation case against the BBC remains on track, for the moment.
A federal judge in Florida ruled late Tuesday that Trump’s defamation claim could go forward, though he did not rule on the merits. The publicly funded British broadcaster had sought to dismiss the case.
Judge Jeffrey Kuntz did dismiss part of the lawsuit, tossing out a Trump claim that the BBC’s actions violated a Florida law concerning unfair business practices.
Trump filed his lawsuit against the BBC in December. The Republican president accused the BBC of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, “Trump: A Second Chance?” The 33-page lawsuit accused the BBC of broadcasting a “false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump,” calling it “a brazen attempt to interfere in and influence” the 2024 U.S. presidential election.
The BBC apologized about the editing of Trump footage
The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers had spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021, before the storming of the U.S. Capitol, to make it seem that Trump was directly urging violence.
The broadcaster apologized over the editing, and that was something the judge made note of in his ruling Wednesday allowing the case to go forward. The head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But the broadcaster denies Trump’s claims that it defamed him.
In October, a different judge in Florida ordered Trump to sit for a deposition in the case by Dec. 11. Lawyers for the BBC had complained that Trump was delaying his appearance in his own lawsuit. Charles Tobin, an attorney for the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”
The BBC said in a statement after Tuesday’s ruling that it was “surprised by this decision but respect the court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage.”
“We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process,” the broadcaster said.
Trump called Kuntz’s latest ruling a major victory.
“A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth, just handed down by highly respected District Court Judge, Jeffrey T. Kuntz, of the Southern District of Florida,” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.
“We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” Trump wrote Tuesday evening.
Judge said that BBC editing was ‘creating something different’
In his ruling, Kuntz described the editing done in the documentary, splicing together two parts of the speech, as more egregious than mere routine editing.
“Editing is often required,” the judge wrote. “However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement. This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech. BBC also had the entire speech available to them for nearly three years by the time of the documentary.”
The judge also wrote that Trump might have a plausible argument to demonstrate malice — whether or not he can ultimately prove this at trial — given past BBC reporting about him.
“Trump paints a picture that demonstrates the BBC has a record of allowing the publication of false statements in their portrayal of Trump,” the ruling said. “BBC asks the Court to put on blinders and treat the Panorama team as if they were blocked off from the rest of the organization, ignorant of everything else going on at BBC.”
The lawsuit is one of several skirmishes between Trump and the news media during his second term. Through administrative and executive action and sometimes through lawsuits, he has chosen to take a more aggressive approach toward the press and toward coverage he dislikes.

title: Electric vehicle owners could soon face annual federal fee under proposed bill
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) - Owning an electric vehicle may soon cost more.
A surface transportation bill moving through Congress would require electric vehicle owners to pay an annual federal fee beginning at $130.
The fee could then increase by $5 each year, with a maximum of $150, according to the proposed legislation.
Owners of plug-in hybrids would have to pay $35.
Current funding for surface transportation is set to expire next month. The electric vehicle fees could take effect as soon as December if approved by Congress.
The government uses money it collects from gasoline taxes to help pay for road projects. Electric vehicles do not require gasoline, so those drivers do not pay that tax.
Supporters of the measure said it ensures electric vehicle drivers help pay for the roads they use.

title: CMH welcomes triple board-certified hip, knee, trauma surgeon
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON, ME – Central Maine Healthcare (CMH) is pleased to welcome Zafar Ahmad, MD, FRCS, FRCSC, to its orthopedic surgery team, expanding access to advanced joint replacement, sports knee surgery and fracture care for patients throughout central Maine.
Dr. Ahmad is a fellowship-trained orthopedic surgeon whose career spans the United Kingdom, Canada and the United States. His practice covers the full range of hip and knee surgery, including partial, total and revision knee replacement, soft-tissue knee surgery, including ligament reconstruction and the treatment of sports-related knee injuries, primary and revision hip replacement, hip resurfacing and the surgical treatment of fractures of the hip, pelvis and lower extremity.
Before joining CMH, Dr. Ahmad served as an orthopedic surgeon at Down East Community Hospital in Machias and previously practiced at St. Mary’s Regional Medical Center in Lewiston. Prior to relocating to the United States, he held a consultant orthopedic trauma surgeon post at a Level I Major Trauma Centre in England.
Dr. Ahmad is triple board-certified in orthopedic surgery, holding certification from the Royal College of Surgeons in the United Kingdom (FRCS Tr&Orth), the European Board of Orthopaedics and Traumatology (EBOT) and the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada (FRCSC), the last of which he achieved in 2025.
He earned his medical degree from St George’s, University of London, graduating with merit in the top 10 percent of his class, and holds a Doctor of Medicine (MD) research degree from the University of Cambridge, where his doctoral work focused on tissue engineering for tendon repair. He completed advanced fellowship training in sports knee surgery, hip surgery, adult reconstruction and orthopedic trauma, and has authored more than 25 peer-reviewed publications.
Before medicine, Dr. Ahmad earned a bachelor’s degree in computer science and business studies from Queen Mary University of London, and he maintains an active interest in the application of artificial intelligence to surgical care.
“Throughout my career, I have been committed to helping patients restore mobility, reduce pain and return to the activities they enjoy most,” Dr. Ahmad said. “I am excited to join Central Maine Healthcare and look forward to providing compassionate, evidence-based orthopedic care to the people of central Maine.”
Patients seeking joint replacement, knee ligament surgery, revision surgery or fracture care can schedule an appointment with Dr. Ahmad through Central Maine Healthcare’s orthopedic services.

Dignified transfer underway for Clinton firefighter after her unexpected death
text:
Dignified transfer held for Clinton firefighter after her unexpected death
Members of Clinton Fire Rescue are mourning the "sudden and unexpected" death of firefighter-EMT Becky Stuart
Dignified transfer held for Clinton firefighter after her unexpected death
Members of Clinton Fire Rescue are mourning the "sudden and unexpected" death of firefighter-EMT Becky Stuart
Members of Clinton Fire Rescue are mourning the "sudden and unexpected" death of firefighter-EMT Becky Stuart, whose colleagues held a procession Thursday from Waterville to the medical examiner’s office in Augusta.
The procession was scheduled to begin at 9:45 a.m. at Veilleux Funeral Home on Elm Street in Waterville. The route continued to Silver Street, crossed the Carter Memorial Bridge toward Winslow and traveled south on Route 201 to Augusta.
Waterville Fire Rescue said Elm Street would be closed between Western Avenue and Silver Street for about an hour starting at 9 a.m. on Thursday. Drivers were advised to expect delays and find another route if possible.
Clinton Fire Chief Rick Barton asked the community to keep Stuart’s family, friends and fellow firefighters in their thoughts. The department has not announced a cause of death but shared mental health resources, including the National Suicide Prevention Hotline.
West Forks Volunteer Fire and Rescue also confirmed Stuart was a member of its department. The Clinton Police Department offered condolences to Stuart’s family, friends and colleagues, saying her loss was felt throughout the public safety community.
Among those mourning Stuart's death is Republican State Rep. Amanda Collamore, who wrote on Facebook that she is "truly missed."
Jason Mills, co-owner of the Resilient Responder Wellness Center, told WABI-TV that mental healthcare is part of first responders’ occupational readiness. Wally Fraser, co-founder of the Toned Out Project, said treatment programs designed for first responders are available.
People in Maine who need crisis support can call or text 988.

title: Oklahoma man executed for killing of girlfriend’s husband
text:
McALESTER, Okla. (AP) — An Oklahoma man was put to death Thursday for the fatal shooting of his girlfriend’s estranged husband as he arrived to pick up his two young children before Thanksgiving. It was the first in a pair of executions in the U.S. scheduled for Thursday.
James Pavatt, 73, received a lethal injection at the state penitentiary in McAlester. His breathing did not appear labored during the execution, and he was declared unconscious about six minutes before being pronounced dead at 10:12 a.m. CST.
In Texas, John Allen Rubio was set to be put to death Thursday evening. The 46-year-old was convicted of fatally stabbing and beheading three young children in 2003 in Brownsville, a border city with Mexico.
Although the death penalty is getting renewed attention after the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September, the U.S. is on track to surpass 40 executions for a second consecutive year — a pace driven by Florida.
Last week, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office, which experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.
On Thursday, former Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of being an accessory in a 1997 murder and awaits sentencing in December. Glossip, who had been on the brink of execution three times, was released on bond in May after spending nearly 30 years in prison. The U.S. Supreme Court had overturned his conviction and he was awaiting a retrial.
Oklahoma advertising executive killed in garage
When Pavatt was asked if he had any last words, he shook his head no. As a chaplain read to him from a Bible, he appeared to be mouthing some words, but they could not be heard.
Pavatt was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder in the 2001 death of Rob Andrew, a 39-year-old advertising executive. Pavatt attended the same church as the Andrew family and had been having an affair with Rob Andrew’s wife, Brenda Andrew. She was convicted at a separate trial and is currently the only woman on death row in Oklahoma.
Weeks before the shooting, Rob Andrew told police someone was trying to kill him after the brake lines on his car were cut. Brenda Andrew told police after her husband was killed that masked intruders shot her in the arm and fatally shot him.
Pavatt and Brenda Andrew went to Mexico with her two children after the shooting and were arrested three months later while reentering the U.S.
At a clemency hearing last month, Pavatt said he was “not guilty of shooting anyone,” and that he’d fallen in love with Brenda Andrew and believed “everything she told me.”
“It was not until my trial that I began to see the extent to which I had been manipulated by Brenda,” Pavatt told the board. “I can see why the jury believed that we were both involved in Rob’s murder.”
Prosecutors have said that Pavatt and Brenda Andrew plotted to kill her husband, and that no matter who fired the shots, both were equally guilty.
No family members of Rob Andrew or Pavatt witnessed the execution, although his daughter and her husband visited him the night before, a prison spokesperson said.
3 young children beheaded in Texas
Rubio and his girlfriend, Angela Camacho, were accused in the killings of 3-year-old Julissa Quesada, 14-month-old John E. Rubio and 2-month-old Mary Jane Rubio in the squalid, windowless apartment they shared in Brownsville, located on Texas’ border with Mexico.
Camacho pleaded guilty and is serving a life sentence.
Rubio’s first capital murder conviction in the killings was overturned by an appeals court, which ruled that statements by Camacho were wrongly allowed as evidence in his trial. Rubio again pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity for his second trial but he was once again convicted and sentenced to death.
Rubio, according to court records, wasn’t the biological father of the two older children but treated them as if they were his own.
At various points, Rubio claimed the children were possessed and that he was the “chosen one” intended to save the world. Defense experts diagnosed Rubio as suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, a determination rejected by prosecution experts.
Defense experts testified his childhood — filled with violence at home, “toxic” parents, drug use and prostitution — damaged him developmentally.
The apartment building where the children were killed was later demolished and the land was turned into a park and a community garden.
Rubio was set to be executed Thursday evening at the state prison in Huntsville.
____
Graczyk reported from Huntsville, Texas.

title: Maine State Library limits ICE access under new policy
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine — Public libraries across the country are determining how to respond to potential encounters with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement as the agency ramps up deportation enforcement this year.
The Maine Legislature passed three laws in 2026 restricting federal immigration actions: ICE Out of Policing, ICE Out of Our Homes and ICE Out of Schools and State Health Care.
All three took effect July 29. ICE Out of Schools and State Health Care covers Maine’s public libraries.
The Maine Library Commission unanimously adopted a policy Monday prohibiting anyone “acting on behalf of the state library” from voluntarily granting law enforcement officers access to nonpublic library areas for immigration enforcement.
If a law enforcement officer demands access to nonpublic areas, the policy instructs staff members to first ask why the officer needs entry.
The policy calls for library staff members to contact the designated administrator on duty if the officer possesses a court-issued warrant or any other official documents authorizing immigration enforcement activity.
The administrator would then review the documents or orders and, if necessary, consult with legal counsel before advising library staff members on how to respond.
The policy also instructs library staff members not to physically interfere with a law enforcement officer who attempts to access nonpublic library areas before this review process occurs.
The guidelines also address access to library records. Staff members cannot voluntarily offer protected patron records to officers seeking information for immigration enforcement.
As with nonpublic space access, library staff members must ask law enforcement officers requesting patron records for immigration purposes to produce a court-issued warrant or official authorization.
An administrator would then review the documents and consult legal counsel.
The policy also sets mandatory compliance guidelines if federal statutes authorize ICE or other law enforcement officers to interview noncitizens frequenting the library or access records as part of an official investigation.
Under these circumstances, the library must designate a nonpublic area where interviews or record reviews can take place.
The Maine Library Commission adopted a second policy Monday providing free notary services by appointment when the Maine State Library reopens.
The commission also unanimously reaffirmed policies on computer use, internet safety, photocopying and bulletin boards.
Commissioners approved the new guidelines as the state prepares to reopen the Maine State Library inside the Cultural Building in Augusta. The building, which also houses the Maine State Museum and the Maine State Archives, closed in early 2020 for a $3 million renovation.
Delays in elevator repairs and public computer deliveries forced the commission to push back the reopening to mid-December. The Maine State Museum reopened Oct. 24.

Executions in Oklahoma and Texas include a father who beheaded 3 children
text:

Gavin Newsom announced he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office, which experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.
Pavatt, 73, was set to be put to death at Oklahoma’s state penitentiary in McAlester. John Allen Rubio, 46, was set to be put to death later in Texas at the state prison in Huntsville.
3 young children beheaded in Texas
Rubio and his girlfriend Angela Camacho were accused in the killings of 3-year-old Julissa Quesada, 14-month-old John E. Rubio and 2-month-old Mary Jane Rubio in the squalid, windowless apartment they shared in Brownsville, located on Texas’ border with Mexico.
Camacho pleaded guilty and is serving a life sentence.
Rubio’s first capital murder conviction in the killings was overturned by an appeals court, which ruled that statements by Camacho were wrongly allowed as evidence in his trial. Rubio again pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity for his second trial but he was once again convicted and sentenced to death.
Rubio, according to court records, wasn’t the biological father of the two older children but treated them as if they were his own.
At various points, Rubio claimed the children were possessed and that he was the “chosen one” intended to save the world. Defense experts diagnosed Rubio as suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, a determination rejected by prosecution experts.
Defense experts testified his childhood — filled with violence at home, “toxic” parents, drug use and prostitution — damaged him developmentally.
The apartment building where the children were killed was later demolished and the land was turned into a park and a community garden.
Oklahoma advertising executive killed in garage
Pavatt was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder in the 2001 death of Rob Andrew, a 39-year-old advertising executive. Andrew was fatally shot in the garage of the Oklahoma City home he’d previously shared with his wife as he picked up their two young children before Thanksgiving.
Pavatt, who attended the same church as the Andrew family, had been having an affair with Andrew’s wife, Brenda Andrew. They were convicted at separate trials and each was sentenced to death.
Weeks earlier before the shooting, Rob Andrew had told police someone was trying to kill him after the brake lines on his car were cut. Brenda Andrew told police after her husband was killed that masked intruders shot her in the arm and fatally shot him.
Pavatt and Brenda Andrew went to Mexico with her two children after the shooting and were arrested three months later while reentering the U.S.
At a clemency hearing last month, Pavatt said he was “not guilty of shooting anyone,” and that he’d fallen in love with Brenda Andrew and believed “everything she told me.”
“It was not until my trial that I began to see the extent to which I had been manipulated by Brenda,” Pavatt told the board. “I can see why the jury believed that we were both involved in Rob’s murder.”
Prosecutors have said that Pavatt and Andrew plotted to kill Rob Andrew, and that no matter who fired the shots, both were equally guilty.

title: Lobstermen weigh in on study of baby lobster decline
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WINTER HARBOR — Area lobstermen shared their take on the recently released UMaine study, which found a steep drop in baby lobsters provided an early warning of the sharp decline in adult lobsters along Maine’s midcoast.
The midcoast area, which ranges from Brunswick to the Schoodic Peninsula, is where researchers recorded the steepest declines in lobster population in the Gulf of Maine. Those losses followed a period of growth, when the number of lobsters sampled doubled from the 2000s to the 2010s. Researchers linked the region’s boom and subsequent decline to warmer water temperatures.
Overall, the report stated that researchers found an 80% decline in baby lobster sampled from 2010 to 2022, followed by a 70% decline in young lobsters since 2015, and a 50% decline in adults large enough for lobstermen to catch.
Curt Brown, lobsterman and president of Bold Coast Seafood, a company that processes and sells lobster at its waterfront facility in Prospect Harbor, said he did not see the report as a cause of serious concern.
“Last year, we were in the 80 to 90 million-pound range for overall landings,” Brown said. “Had we landed that 20 years ago, everyone would be over the moon. It’s a wild-caught fishery, so we are going to see some ups and downs.”
He said Bold Coast Seafood conducts its own separate study alongside UMaine researchers to look at how lobster settlement varies by depth. Brown said every spring Bold Coast and UMaine researchers set out about 400 cages full of rocks at varying depths to test the prevalence of baby lobsters who tend to hide in rocky crevices for shelter. This is similar to the methods referenced by the UMaine-released study, published in the journal Marine Ecology Progress Series, in which scientists analyzed state surveys that used traps and trawls at different depths.
“It gives us an annual indicator of how the population in this area is doing,” Brown said. “The last two years have looked pretty good for us.” However, Brown said that colder water coming into the Gulf of Maine in the last few years has caused lobster populations to drop off at depth, where the environment can be too cold for the crustaceans. In shallower waters, he asserted, numbers still look strong.
According to the UMaine study findings for Southern Maine, where cold water doesn’t circulate from the depths to the surface, the number of lobsters sampled across all life stages has remained relatively stable since 2010. Deeper waters remain too cold for lobsters even as water temperatures rise, and the territory in which they can reside remains unchanged.
Winter Harbor-based lobsterman Jeremy Holmes Norton says the study results for the midcoast area don’t match his experience on the water.
“There are tons of eggers [female lobsters carrying eggs] and snappers [small lobsters] around,” Norton said. “I think, personally, that you’ll see an excellent season next year and in 2028.”
He said he and other lobster fishermen are worried about further restrictions based on the study.
“The question that looms overhead is if or when the state will drop us from 800 tags to 600,” Norton said. “I think there are advantages and disadvantages to that myself, and it’d be a while before the catch would even out for fishermen again with 600, but it’s a huge fear for us lobster fishermen.”
Regulations or not, the outlook from the UMaine study can spell concern for the industry that generated more than $461 million in Maine landings in 2025. Conducting studies of populations has become increasingly difficult as warming waters are changing where lobsters live. Previous UMaine research found that lobster population density declined as the animals became more dispersed and shifted habitats.
Differences along the coast are part of the reason UMaine and the Maine Department of Resources are focusing on studies of broad areas, according to Kathleen Reardon, senior lobster fishery scientist with DMR.
“Maine DMR is invested in a comprehensive, coastwide lobster monitoring approach and leads multiple surveys to study lobsters across their full life cycle,” Reardon said.
Researchers said differences in survey methodology, coupled with lobster behavior and habitat preferences, can also influence the results and hamper scientists’ efforts to track and interpret population changes.
“American lobster may be one of the most data-rich fisheries in the world; however, even with the abundant data, we are continuing to expand sampling efforts to effectively support our sustainable fishery and understand how it will be impacted by future environmental changes,” said the study’s lead researcher Robert Jarrett II.
According to the study, baby lobsters serve as an indicator for the industry, as their decline preceded decreases in adolescent lobster populations in the midcoast. It follows another recent study that examined a preferred food source for baby lobster amid declines in young lobster survival and the availability of that food source.

Police: 1 killed, 4 injured in D.C. shooting; Suspect shot himself after police standoff
text:
1 killed, four injured in D.C. shooting that began at gym; suspect dead
A gunman killed a man inside a busy gym during morning workouts on Thursday before fleeing and shooting four more people, shocking a popular capital neighborhood and attracting a swarm of police officers who ascended to the roof of a building during the search and chaos.
He fatally shot himself while holed up in his penthouse apartment, where he had been speaking by phone with police negotiators, said Jeffery Carroll, interim chief with the Metropolitan Police Department.
The gunman was identified as a doctor locked in a dispute with building management over mold and moisture problems in his seventh-floor unit, court records show.
Mayor Muriel Bowser said she was "devastated" at the loss of life in a "senseless act of gun violence."
The shootings occurred around 8 a.m. in Logan Circle, about a mile north of the White House. Much of the block on 15th Street Northwest was cordoned off as police urged people to avoid the area, which includes the VIDA Fitness center, St. Luke's Episcopal Church, residences and a Whole Foods store. Schools were locked down.
Law enforcement SWAT teams and other officers had their guns drawn on the roof of an apartment building and on the ground below.
Carroll said one man died at VIDA and another victim was in critical condition.
James Spellman, who was at the gym, said there were about 50 people there when the shooting began.
"Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," he said. "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck."
Anthony Mirones was in the gym's cardio area when he heard a loud bang and thought something fell off the wall. He said someone was trying to help the wounded man but then a fire alarm went off and many people ran.
"The people in cardio had to step over the body," Mirones said.
Another witness, Ryan Dubicki, said he was in his nearby apartment around the same time when he "heard about five bangs."
"They were really spread out so I thought it was construction," said Dubicki, an AP employee on the elections team. A short time later "there were cops everywhere."
Authorities have preliminarily identified the shooter as Matt Lambert, according to two law enforcement officials and another person familiar with the matter who spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to publicly discuss the investigation.
Lambert was deeply upset with his condo building's management. He filed a lawsuit last year, alleging that he hadn't been able to use his penthouse since 2024 because of mold, moisture and water problems. He claimed the problems began after a contractor had worked on the building's exterior.
The litigation was ongoing, with mediation scheduled for next March, according to court filings. Lambert appeared to share his condo woes, including photos and an engineering report, on an X site titled OfMiceandMold.
The Logan Circle neighborhood has seen violence before. In early August 2025, a onetime member of President Donald Trump's Department of Government Efficiency was assaulted early on a Sunday morning in the neighborhood by a group of teenagers attempting to carjack him and a woman, authorities said.
Days later, Trump fulfilled his threat to bypass local authority and imposed direct federal control over the city, sending in hundreds of National Guard members to reduce crime. That deployment continues today.
___
Associated Press writers Rebecca Santana and Gary Fields in Washington and Dave Collins in Hartford, Conn., contributed to this report.

title: Good 4 ME: Honey Buffalo Chicken & Broccoli Sheet Pan Supper
text:
Hannaford dietician Mary Lavanway has a sheet pan recipe for you to try.
Honey Buffalo Chicken & Broccoli Sheet Pan Supper
Serves: 5
Ingredients:
- 2 lbs. chicken breasts, cut into cubes
- 1/2 tsp. McCormick® Paprika
- 1/2 to 1 tsp. McCormick® Onion Powder
- 1/2 to 1 tsp. McCormick® Garlic Powder
- Kosher salt, to taste
- Kosher black pepper, to taste
- 1/4 cup flour
- 4 Tbsp. olive oil, divided
- 3 cups broccoli florets
- 1/4 cup Frank’s RedHot® Original Cayenne Pepper Hot Sauce
- 3 Tbsp. butter
- 2-3 Tbsp. honey
- 1 cup Stonyfield® Organic Nonfat Plain Greek Yogurt
- 1 Hannaford Ranch Dressing & Dip Mix Packet
Directions
- Preheat oven to 450°F. Line a baking sheet with parchment paper or rub it with oil.
- On the sheet pan, toss together chicken, paprika, onion powder, garlic powder, salt and pepper. Add flour and toss again. Add 2 tablespoons olive oil, tossing to coat. Arrange chicken on one side of the baking sheet. Add broccoli to other side. Toss with remaining 2 tablespoons olive oil, salt and pepper. Bake 15-20 minutes, until chicken is cooked through.
- Meanwhile, make the sauce. In a saucepan set over medium heat, melt together hot sauce and butter. Stir until melted and combined. Remove from heat and mix in honey.
- Remove broccoli from sheet pan. Then pour sauce over chicken and toss to coat. Bake another 5 minutes, until the sauce is baked onto the chicken.
- In a medium bowl, combine Greek yogurt and packet of ranch dressing seasoning; mix well.
- Serve chicken and broccoli with ranch dressing mixture. Serve over steamed brown rice.
Nutritional Information (not including brown rice)

title: Fiber artist displays her ‘Wild Threads’ at Center for Maine Craft
text:
For more than 35 years, quilter Betsy Dorr has explored the expressive possibilities of fabric, color and thread. A lifelong lover of sewing, Dorr illustrates landscapes, textural flora and fauna, and vibrant animal forms with colorful fabrics and threads. Her work will be on display in “Wild Threads: The Nature of Quilts” at the Center for Maine Craft from Nov. 13 through Dec. 31.
Dorr’s relationship with sewing began in childhood, influenced by a family of makers that included her mother, both grandmothers and three sisters. After two careers, she followed her passion by opening Quiltessentials in Auburn, where she spent 27 years surrounded by beautiful fabrics and the creativity of fellow quilters. Teaching machine quilting and sharing her expertise with students throughout Maine have remained important parts of her practice.
Nature is a constant source of inspiration. Time spent hiking and wandering through the woods informs Dorr’s attention to the textures, colors and patterns of the landscape, from the intricate forms of mushrooms to the changing character of trees. Working with cotton fabrics, including hand-painted textiles, she builds compositions through thoughtful combinations of color, pattern and material.
Dorr utilizes machine quilting to create her intricate line details. Using free-motion stitching on a domestic sewing machine, Dorr approaches thread as a drawing tool, adding lines and textures that reinforce a composition or bring particular details into focus.
After decades of running a quilt shop and creating work for others, Dorr found new freedom in retirement to follow her own ideas and explore the subjects that inspire her most. Her quilts reflect both the technical mastery developed over a lifetime and the pleasure of making something entirely her own.
Dorr was featured in Better Homes and Gardens in 2015, recognizing Quiltessentials among the top 10 quilt shops in the United States. Dorr continues to share her work through exhibitions, teaching from her home studio in Auburn and displaying her work at the Center for Maine Craft.
In “Wild Threads: The Nature of Quilts,” Dorr invites viewers to look beyond the familiar function of a quilt and discover its potential as an art object, where fabric becomes landscape, thread becomes line and the natural world finds new expression through the art of stitching.
The Center for Maine Craft is a retail gallery and exhibition space showcasing the work of hundreds of Maine Crafts Association members. Located within the West Gardiner Service Plaza, find handmade craft in a broad range of media, along with rotating exhibitions, pop-ups and artist demonstrations throughout the year.
The center is open daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. at 288 Lewiston Road in West Gardiner.

title: Maine residents can adopt a letter to Santa
text:
Every year, Maine post offices receive letters from children addressed to Santa. Many will receive the presents on their wish list from loved ones, but some will not.
The USPS Operation Santa program was created in 1912 to ensure children’s and families’ wishes are heard each holiday season.
I am proud to share that last year, the residents of Maine joined thousands of Americans across the country who took on the responsibility of helping Santa make these children’s wishes come true.
We continue to receive letters every year and ask readers to give back this holiday season by visiting uspsoperationsanta.com to adopt a letter and donate presents to these children.
Letter adoption begins on Nov. 16; registration to participate is already underway. Presents need to be shipped no later than Dec. 12 to arrive by Dec. 25.
Adopters can also join forces with friends, family, co-workers or community groups to divide up the wish list from an individual child or an entire household with multiple children in need.
I am so thankful to the Maine community for their generosity and hope we can continue to deliver to those who might otherwise go without this holiday season.
Judy K. Ferriera
United States Postal Service (ME, N.H., VT District)
Smithfield, R.I.

title: Longtime NBC Sports broadcaster Dan Hicks dies at 64, his family says
text:
(AP) - Sportscaster Dan Hicks, who was the voice of golf, Olympic swimming and Notre Dame football during a 35-year career at NBC Sports, has died, his family and NBC announced Thursday. He was 64.
Hicks died late Wednesday in Connecticut. He died of an acute illness, according to his wife, Hannah Storm. He had been scheduled to call Notre Dame’s game Saturday.
“Our family is heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected passing of Dan,” Storm said in a statement. “He was a devoted husband of over 30 years, loving father to our three daughters, and cherished friend to so many. His loss is immeasurable.
“Dan was truly one of a kind and, quite simply, the person everyone wanted to be around. When he walked into a room, he brought the energy, the laughter and the people together. He was endlessly kind, thoughtful and funny, and he made everyone feel like they mattered.”
Hicks was best known as the lead announcer for golf, as well as swimming and skiing at the Olympics and Notre Dame football. He joined NBC in 1992 following three years at CNN.
“I’m incredibly lucky to stay at one place this long. It takes a lot of things going your way as far as NBC continuing to have the properties that I’ve been a part of through the years,” he said during an Associated Press interview in September. “So lots of variables, lots of things that can happen in your career. But I think I appreciate it more and more the longer it’s been.”
Hicks’ favorite sport was golf
Hicks was on the call for 27 tournament victories by Tiger Woods, including three at the U.S. Open. His most famous was 2008, when Woods, playing with shredded ligaments in his left knee and a double stress fracture in his leg, faced a 12-foot birdie putt on the 18th hole at Torrey Pines to force a playoff.
“He asked what it was like on the 18th,” Roger Maltbie, who was on the ground for NBC at Torrey Pines, said Thursday. “I said Tiger expected to make it. Everyone expected him to make it. He had that invincible aura at the time.”
The putt curled in the right side and Hicks said, “Expect anything different?”
Hicks was a tower announcer from 1995-99 before taking over as the main voice in 2000.
“He was a great quarterback, a point guard. If you listen to his broadcast, to me he was terrific at passing the ball around,” Maltbie said. ”He always had a question. He always got you engaged. That’s a big part of the job.”
Hicks called 27 U.S. Opens and 23 U.S. Women’s Opens. USGA CEO Mike Whan said in a statement that Hicks “was a true friend to the game and to the USGA, but more importantly, a wonderful person whose warmth, generosity, and friendship touched everyone fortunate enough to know him.”
Hicks also called the Ryder Cup, British Open and PGA Tour events, including The Players Championship.
“Dan’s voice filled our living rooms with his steady narration of countless golf broadcasts, calling some of the game’s biggest moments,” the PGA Tour said in a statement. “The sound of his voice is woven into our memories of the game, and the warmth he brought to the broadcast was matched only by the kindness he showed those around him.”
One of NBC’s most versatile Olympic announcers
Hicks worked a total of 16 Olympics — nine Summer, seven Winter — with his first being the 1992 Barcelona Games as a host for the Olympic triplecast.
“Dan Hicks was an extraordinary colleague, friend and person,” NBC Sports’ Rick Cordella, Sam Flood and Molly Solomon said in a statement. “He was an exceptional storyteller and caller of games and events who elevated some of the biggest moments in sports history.”
Hicks called swimming at the Olympics eight times with Rowdy Gaines. The duo chronicled Michael Phelps’ eight gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Games and Katie Ledecky’s 14 medals across four Olympics (2012-24).
“My heart is broken. Danny wasn’t just my partner in the booth for eight Olympics. He was one of my closest friends, someone I trusted with everything, both in and out of that arena. He was the glue that held us all together at all of those Games,” Gaines posted on social media. “He made me laugh like no other person ever has. We shared thousands of races and a friendship that went way beyond the pool deck. I’ll miss his voice, his steadiness, and just having him next to me.”
Hicks was on the call for alpine skiing for the last four Winter Games as well as speed skating in 2002, ’06 and ’10.
Two-time Olympic champion Ted Ligety, who was NBC’s alpine skiing analyst the last two Olympics, said Hicks excelled at calling races but also telling athletes’ stories.
“I was always in awe of his ability to know so much about so many sports so fluidly. And his curiosity, he didn’t come in ever with this idea that he knew what was up — he asked a million questions and was really curious. He was able to instantly bring that into the broadcast,” Ligety said. “It’s fun to sit there next to somebody and watch them at their craft at such a high level. Beyond that, just fun to sit next to him and be with him and after a call, share a beer. Just a genuinely fun and awesome dude. The amazing part is his on-air personality and likeableness was only greater in real life.”
Two stints calling Notre Dame football
This was Hicks’ seventh season calling games for Notre Dame, from which his wife graduated in 1983. He did it from 2013-16 before returning in 2024.
Fighting Irish athletic director and former NBC Sports president Pete Bevacqua said Hicks “was a fixture here on campus and in the broadcast booth as one of the great voices for Notre Dame Football. ... More importantly, a dear friend over the course of the last quarter century.”
Hicks also called regional NFL games on NBC from 1992-97, five French Opens and some NBA coverage from 1992-2000.
Hicks is survived by Storm — his wife of 32 years — and their three daughters Hannah, Ellery and Riley.
___
AP Sports Writer Pat Graham in Denver and AP Golf Writer Doug Ferguson in Jacksonville, Florida, contributed to this report.
___

title: One man’s search for a hiking partner became a 5,000-member group honoring history
text:
RICHMOND, Va. (Aging Untold) — Dennis Bussey was looking for someone to go hiking with. Now he has thousands of people, and they also volunteer in the community.
How the group started
Bussey, who now lives in Lexington, Virginia, founded James River Hikers, which describes itself as “hiking with history.”
He had walked along the river by himself for a year and a half before starting the group.
“I thought, gosh, I wish I could find someone who would go hiking with me,” Bussey said.
After searching online, he found people to join him. The first meetup drew about seven people, and that was 14 years ago.
“Today we have 5,000 people,” Bussey said.
“We do hikes. We do history. We do social things. We do all kinds of things,” Bussey said.
Cleaning headstones
One of the hikers’ volunteer projects is cleaning gravestones at Shockoe Hill Cemetery.
The cemetery is the final resting place for some of Virginia’s historic figures:
- James Marshall, the nation’s fourth chief justice.
- Elizabeth Van Lew, a Civil War Union spy and abolitionist.
- Dr. William Foushee, the first mayor of Richmond.
When the group first started cleaning at the cemetery, headstones were not legible.
They started the work after they received permission from the city.
Bussey said Foushee was buried 201 years ago and that his headstone was “completely black.”
“Today is the 65th time we were out here cleaning these graves,” Bussey said. “We have cleaned probably 70% of all the stones in this cemetery.”
How the work is funded
Volunteers meet at the cemetery twice a month and scrub the stones.
The work is not cheap. Without donations and grants, the group would not be able to do it.
“Let’s go out and honor these folks and do this thing in a right way,” Bussey said. “And it’s a win-win for everybody.”

title: During a crisis, Orono’s football coach gave players his best. Then they gave him theirs.
text:
The day after his world was shaken, Orono head football coach Bob Sinclair came to a Thursday evening practice with a straightforward message for his players.
“You’re going to get the best of me, not the rest of me,” Sinclair told his Red Riots football team on Oct. 1. “I can promise you that.”
Less than 24 hours prior, Sinclair’s youngest son, Tyler, felt a peculiar numbness in his right leg while coaching Orono Middle School’s football team. Tyler called his father over on the sidelines during the game. The pain came to Tyler suddenly, without warning.
“He told me he didn’t feel well, that he couldn’t feel his foot,” Bob said. “At first, we didn’t know if it was anything serious. Then, hours later, he was in critical care at the cardiac ward. It all happened so fast.”
The problem was far worse than expected. Tyler, 37, had suffered a tear in his aorta, causing restricted blood flow to his numb leg. As his symptoms quickly grew harsher, he was rushed to the hospital.
That evening, Tyler was coaching middle school football.
By nightfall, he was receiving emergency open-heart surgery.
“He’s 37 years old, and for three weeks, he had tubes coming out of him every which way,” Bob said. “We truly weren’t sure if he was going to live.”
Tyler spent weeks on end at a rehabilitation facility, regaining the ability to walk and function. The Orono and greater Maine community organized donations and meal trains to help the family through the process.
Since then, Bob has spent many days fulfilling his assistant principal and coaching duties at Orono, only able to visit Tyler at night.
Bob credits the doctors and his wife, Sally, for taking care of Tyler during the day so he could be there for his players.
His players have been there for them, too.
“The kids love [Tyler], they really do,” Bob said. “It’s been incredible to see. They even showed up before last week’s game with T-shirts that said ‘Tyler Strong.’ They’ve all rallied around him and been there for us.”
Orono’s senior captains — Gabe Brewer, Audi Baker, Richie Watson and Josh Wood — even came to visit Tyler in the hospital as he recovered from surgery. Tyler had taken on a large role with Orono’s high school team this year, helping film during games and consistently pouring into the players.
On the morning of Nov. 6, before Orono’s 8-man Small North Regional Championship game at Stearns, Tyler briefly left his rehabilitation facility to come to campus and wish the team luck before the road trip.
“He couldn’t make the trip to [Stearns] for the game, but he really wanted to be here for the kids,” Bob said. “Wheeling him in the building, everyone was waiting for him there. They loved it. They were so happy to see him.”
With Tyler watching from back home, Orono pulled off a wild 55-52 upset win over Stearns to clinch the North Regional title.
“All year, coach has said, ‘Believe, believe, believe.’ That’s what we all did,” said senior running back Richie Watson, who had six touchdowns in the win. “The program has been through so much adversity this year, and we haven’t stopped for anything. We just keep believing.”
Bob also has a renewed belief, he said, in the power of football to bring people together. He’s seen it more than ever this season.
The beloved coach has, admittedly, struggled not to be distracted by his son’s medical issues. But he’s done exactly what he promised his players, who now sit one game away from capturing a state title: He’s given them his absolute best.
They’ve been there, every step of the way, to fill in the rest.
“This is a very close community. It’s a very close team,” Bob said. “But as a dad, to see those captains come down to the hospital, to see [Tyler’s] middle school players come down to visit him, it really lifted my spirit. It lifted his, too.”
Tyler Sinclair is set to return home Friday. Orono will take on Old Orchard Beach at 2:30 p.m. Saturday at Edward Little High School in Auburn for the 8-Man Small State Championship.

title: 5 people are shot in a trendy DC neighborhood, including 1 killed at a gym, then suspect kills self
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A man in a long-running dispute over the conditions of his penthouse condo shot and killed the building manager in a busy gym Thursday before fleeing and shooting four more people from his patio in just minutes, shocking a popular capital neighborhood and attracting a swarm of police officers.
Matt Lambert, a 55-year-old doctor, then fatally shot himself while holed up in his apartment, where he had been speaking by phone with police negotiators, said Jeffery Carroll, interim chief with the Metropolitan Police Department.
Lambert was locked in rancorous litigation with management over mold and moisture problems in his seventh-floor unit, court records show.
Mayor Muriel Bowser said she was “devastated” at the loss of life in a “senseless act of gun violence.”
The shootings occurred around 8 a.m. in Logan Circle, about a mile (1.6 kilometers) north of the White House. Much of the block on 15th Street Northwest was cordoned off as police urged people to avoid the area, which includes a VIDA Fitness center, St. Luke’s Episcopal Church, residences and a Whole Foods store. Schools were locked down.
Chaos in less than 5 minutes
Law enforcement SWAT teams and other officers had their guns drawn on the roof of a building and on the ground below. Carroll said Lambert, armed with three guns, shot and wounded four people from his condo patio. Three sustained non-life-threatening injuries and the fourth remained in critical condition by late afternoon.
“This whole incident took place in less than five minutes. ... I can only imagine being in that area and hearing the gunshots or being inside the gym,” he said.
The man killed at VIDA gym on the ground floor was identified as James Stuart, 46, the building manager, the police chief said.
“There has been an ongoing dispute between the suspect in this case” and management “regarding maintenance issues, mold and the like. We believe it’s related to that,” Carroll said.
Lambert had filed a lawsuit, alleging that he hadn’t been able to enjoy his penthouse since 2024 because of mold, moisture and water problems, records show. He claimed the problems began after a contractor had worked on the building’s exterior.
The litigation was ongoing, according to court filings. Lambert appeared to share his condo woes, including photos and an engineering report, on an X site titled OfMiceandMold. The report was described online as “my manifesto.”
Speaking to reporters, Lambert’s lawyer, Joel Braithwaite, said he was “deeply shaken and saddened” by the violence. He said the condo resembled a “war zone” because of its conditions and said Lambert had spent more than $300,000 in pressing the lawsuit.
“I don’t think there’s any sense to be made,” Braithwaite said of the shootings. “I can’t give you that closure.”
Braithwaite said Lambert had lived in the unit since 2017. Online property records show he bought it in September 2016 for nearly $1.1 million.
Gym members scrambled when they heard shots
James Spellman, who was at the gym, said there were about 50 people there when the shootings began.
“Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out,” he said. “One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck.”
Anthony Mirones was in the gym’s cardio area when he heard a loud bang and thought something fell off the wall. He said someone was trying to help the wounded man but then a fire alarm went off and many people ran.
“The people in cardio had to step over the body,” Mirones said.
Another witness, Ryan Dubicki, said he was in his nearby apartment around the same time when he “heard about five bangs.”
“They were really spread out so I thought it was construction,” said Dubicki, an AP employee on the elections team. A short time later “there were cops everywhere.”
While inside his condo, Lambert also cut a natural gas line to the fireplace and started a fire, triggering the sprinkler system, which quickly contained the flames, Carroll said.
The Washington Sun posted an online story by Michael Brice-Saddler, who said he had interviewed Lambert last year about his condo problems. Lambert had told another resident that he knew Stuart’s morning routine at the VIDA gym.
“If you want to see the building manager,” Brice-Saddler quoted Lambert as saying, “he comes in the gym about 8 o’clock.”
___
This story has been corrected to show the interim police chief’s name is Jeffery, not Jeffrey.
___
Associated Press writers Ed White in Detroit, Rebecca Santana and Gary Fields in Washington, Dave Collins in Hartford, Conn., and Christopher Weber in Los Angeles contributed to this report.
