title: Cargo ship strikes bridge between New Jersey and Philadelphia, causing traffic backup
text:
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — A cargo ship struck a bridge across the Delaware River on Thursday, disrupting traffic between Palmyra, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, according to a Pennsylvania lawmaker.
The collision left the 3,659-foot-long (1,115-meter-long) Tacony-Palmyra Bridge unable to close, causing a major backup on the Philadelphia side, state Rep. Ed Neilson said in a news release. No injuries have been reported, he said.
The U.S. Coast Guard said the cargo vessel is currently moored at a Kinder Morgan facility in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where an inspection team is on site. The Coast Guard has not yet released further information on the ship’s owner or operator.
The drawbridge was open for ships to pass through at the time of the collision around 1:15 p.m., according to the Coast Guard. It remained open afterward because another vessel needed to pass through, and has since come back down.
The steel bridge carries vehicles along Route 73 between Palmyra and the Tacony neighborhood in northeast Philadelphia. It has three lanes of vehicular traffic, two into Philadelphia and one into New Jersey. Estimates from 2025 show the bridge can carry as many as 76,200 vehicles each day.
No one answered the phone Thursday afternoon at the Burlington County Bridge Commission, which owns, operates and maintains the bridge. A recorded message said the bridge is closed to vehicular and pedestrian traffic until further notice, and that an update would be provided in time for evening rush hour.
Opened in 1929, the Tacony-Palmyra toll bridge was found to be in “fair” condition, according to the Federal Highway Administration’s 2026 National Bridge Inventory data released this fall.
Inspectors rated the deck of the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge as in good condition, the substructure as in fair condition and the superstructure — the component that absorbs the live traffic load — as fair.
___
Associated Press journalists Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City, Julie Carr Smyth in Columbus, Ohio, and Christopher L. Keller in Albuquerque, New Mexico, contributed.

title: Pope Leo XIV declares Peru his homeland
text:
Pope Leo XIV declares Peru his homeland as he arrives in Lima on a historic visit
Pope Leo XIV seems omnipresent in Chiclayo. His image is painted in colorful murals, emblazoned on baseball hats and bobbleheads, and celebrated with signs across this city in northern Peru that read: “Welcome home.”
Video above: Pope Leo's cancer diagnosis sparks push for more screenings
Lima is the culinary epicenter of South America. Cusco is the historic capital of the Inca Empire and the gateway to Machu Picchu. But Chiclayo has a special claim as home to the Peruvian American pope, who returns there on Friday.
The first U.S.-born pontiff, Pope Leo, spent about two decades in Peru as a missionary and church leader, obtaining Peruvian citizenship shortly before he served as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023. He remains beloved here for championing social justice issues and for his closeness to the people, especially the poor.
Many remember how the bishop — then known as Robert Prevost — led the life-saving purchase of oxygen production plants during the COVID-19 pandemic; how he waded through mud after torrential rains to bring help to the needy; how he celebrated Mass at the local prison. Others recall how he’d drive his pickup truck to remote villages to hand out blankets and sing Christmas songs, and his love of regional dishes like duck with rice and goat stew.
The love is reciprocal
In his first words as the leader of 1.4 billion Catholics, Pope Leo gave a special shoutout in Spanish to his “beloved Diocese of Chiclayo” from the balcony of St. Peter’s Basilica. His return reaffirms his affection for Chiclayo's churches, schools and sanctuaries and is widely viewed as the emotional highlight of his South American trip.
“People aren’t saying: ‘The pope is Peruvian.’ They’re saying, ’The pope is Chiclayano!’” said the Rev. Jasson Sempertegui, who was his secretary when he led the diocese. “In Chiclayo we like to say: ‘The pope is returning home.’”
It is, Sempertegui said, the most important moment in Chiclayo’s history since it was settled in the 16th century by Spanish Franciscan priests as an Indigenous village about 13 kilometers (8 miles) from the Pacific Ocean.
Chiclayo and its people, he said, might have been more influential to the pope than his native Chicago and the Vatican.
The torrent of crises he confronted in Chiclayo — including the COVID pandemic, assisting newly arrived Venezuelan migrants, and the devastating floods — helped form his pastoral identity.
“He’s Chiclayano because he faced the biggest challenges of his pastoral life here,” Sempertegui said. “This helped him to connect with people’s pain.”
From Chicago to Chiclayo
During his time in the city, Leo often repeated a joke: “Chicago, Chiclayo, what difference is there? Only one letter.”
A city of about 700,000 people, Chiclayo is the commercial hub of Peru’s northern Pacific coast, with highways linking it to the Andes and the Amazon region. Chiclayanos take pride in the city's nickname, “Capital of Friendship,” and its proximity to major archeological sites.
“Before, we were an unnoticed, low-profile city," said Zuly Castillo, who worked for Leo when he was bishop. Across from her office, a life-size cardboard cutout of the pope now welcomes visitors to his former residence. "Now we see that he has given us so much — and we have become known worldwide.”
In Chiclayo, the pope would wake before dawn to pray, then walk to the cathedral in the city center. He listened to confession and was moved by stories of adversity in a city where 20% of residents live in poverty.
He became known as an efficient problem solver, even fixing diocesan cars with YouTube tutorials. He learned local jargon and humor, and sometimes invited priests to join him for a lunch of his lomo saltado (Peru’s classic beef and tomato stir-fry) or ceviche (raw fish marinated in lime juice).
A pope who binge-watched ‘Prison Break’
In the breaks between prayers, theology classes and chores, the aspiring priests at the city’s seminary of Santo Toribio de Mogrovejo remembered how Leo would visit them — offering encouragement, sharing a meal, playing tennis.
The Rev. Marcos Ballena, a seminary leader, recalled the glee of seminarians watching TV in the common room when Cardinal Prevost was elected pope. “Everyone jumped as if they had won a World Cup!”
Seminarian Jose Miguel Teran agreed: “There are some funny videos where we’re all euphoric ... and even more when he said, ‘My beloved diocese of Chiclayo’, we understood very clearly that this is his home, and we feel him as part of our family."
Darwin Sanchez first met Leo while serving as an altar boy. Soon, he’ll have the honor to carry the miter that Leo will wear when celebrating Masses.
“In our youth ministries, with the altar boys there’s a surging interest in the vocation because the pope is deemed to be Chiclayano," Sanchez said.
On his breaks in Chiclayo, he liked to watch his beloved Chicago White Sox baseball games and binge-watch American TV series, like “24” and “Prison Break.”
In the working-class neighborhood of San Antonio, people remember him sharing a meal with the needy at a soup kitchen that he inaugurated.
Video below: Pope Leo XIV leads Sunday prayers as he recovers from lung surgery
“He told immigrants at the time that we welcomed vulnerable people,” said Daria Chavarry, a volunteer at a soup kitchen that has been renamed “Papa Leon XIV.”
After a meal near a large poster of the pope, 78-year-old Maria Teresa Santa Cruz said she paid 25 soles (about $3) in three installments to buy a T-shirt of Leo.
“I bought it because we have one more representative here on Earth,” she said about Leo’s mission to protect the dignity of the poor.
A pope who waded through mud in rubber boots
Leo helped deliver donations in 2017 when hundreds lost their homes as rivers overflooded. He also welcomed Venezuelan migrants escaping their country’s political and economic crises and oversaw construction of a temporary shelter and 13 homes.
“This is the place that he gave us for us to build a home again,” said Betania Marina Rodriguez, who worked closely with Leo on projects and lives in one of the homes.
She recalled how Leo delivered live chickens to her home during the COVID pandemic, to share with other migrants.
“In him we saw the feeling of hope,” Rodriguez said. “He always said that human dignity has no borders.”
Rocio Zeña lost her home to flooding in 2023 and remembers fondly how Leo took off his priestly robes and waded through the mud in rubber boots to reach the needy.
“He was the first person who came with help and cared about us when everything was flooded and the water reached our necks,” said Zeña. “It’s surreal to think that the person who’s been there for you is now the pope – the most important person on Earth after God.”
Video below: Chicago students send Pope Leo XIV a care package and heartfelt messages as he receives treatment for cancer.
He grew so fond of Chiclayo that he hoped to stay put “and even to be buried alongside the diocese’s other bishops,” Daniel Burke and Scott Detrow write in their book, “American Pope.”
But then Pope Francis asked him to return to Rome for an important Vatican job. He teared up in his final Mass with his parishioners.
Prisoners at Chiclayo penitentiary gathered at the carpentry workshop to carve a papal staff before his visit — their gift to the missionary who visited them to celebrate Mass and who became the pope.
“There’s so much joy over his visit,” said the Rev. Elmer Uchofen, the prison chaplain. “We knew he’d come back; Chiclayo is in his heart.”

title: Only one person is to blame for the blue wave
Six Waldo County Fire Departments Makes Important Updates After Mill Fire
text:
Officials Suspend Fines And Support Waldo County Fire & Rescue Departments To Fix Citations Issued After Robbins Mills Fire
More efficient processes and safety procedures are being implemented in several Fire Departments across Maine following the conclusion of the investigation into the Robbins Lumber mill fire and explosion that took place in Waldo County this past May.
Read More: Bangor Firefighters Contain Early Morning Center Street Blaze
The Maine Department of Labor and the Maine Occupational Safety and Health program looked into the Fire and Rescue Departments in Appleton, Belmont, Lincolnville, Montville, Morrill, and Searsmont and issued citations for the areas in which those departments needed improvements to meet state or federal standards.
"MEOSH issued citations related to the lack of an effective accountability system for tracking the location of firefighters on scene on May 15 to all six fire departments. As a result of the lessons learned that day, all of the fire departments have augmented their accountability systems. MEOSH also issued citations to five departments related to the use of personal protective equipment (PPE), including firefighting gear and breathing apparatus, to keep personnel safe from the hazards of a fire scene. "
Each department mentioned has already started to make changes and update their protocol, policies, or equipment to move towards compliance with the expected standards.
All five departments resolved the immediate deficiencies and have committed to attending Respiratory Protection Program training delivered by SafetyWorks! in Waldo County in January.
The Maine Fire Chiefs' Association and Maine Fire Service Institutes will help the departments in their efforts to improve by holding special training sessions in the area over the winter.
Read More: Two Fires Strike Belfast Area Over One October Weekend
To support the departments' efforts to improve internal operations as well as coordination and incident command of major mutual aid emergencies, the Bureau is coordinating with the Maine Fire Chiefs' Association and Maine Fire Service Institute to provide training for these departments' chiefs and officers in Belmont in February.
Bureau Director Kate Burkhart says there were civil penalties attached to the citations that added up to $108,000, but the bureau suspended almost all of the fines so that the small-town departments could put their efforts and money into the much-needed improvements instead.

title: Angus King, are you listening?
text:
I hope that the Maine election results have registered with Sen. Angus King.
The people of Maine do not want someone working across the aisle. The last two years have shown that this strategy was not going to save the country from the oligarchy trying to control it. Speeches on the floor and strongly worded letters are not what we voted for this year. Even the people in the 2nd District voted for someone to fight for them. The state wants representatives who will stand up, not make nice.
We are expecting legislation to help ease the suffering that thousands of Mainers are already feeling with the passage of the big ugly bill. At the same time, we expect that the administration and the president will be investigated for crimes they have committed. We expect Congress to get this country back on the path we have so clearly articulated we want taken.
Fight the good fight, let Trump veto the efforts and make the 2028 election a clear choice once again.
Karen Heck
Waterville

title: Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman Listed Among Writers of ‘Avengers: Doomsday’
text:
Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman Listed Among Writers of ‘Avengers: Doomsday’
Well, well, well. This is an interesting (and potentially spoiler-y) development.
All movies written by members of the Writers Guild of America are listed in the organization’s online database. A few years ago, that database was expanded to include writers whose contributions to a film were not significant enough to be granted the main “Written By” onscreen title. These writers now receive an “Additional Literary Material” credit in the WGA directory — and the listing for Avengers: Doomsday (via Variety) includes some very intriguing names.
Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman both earned two of these “Additional Literary Material” credits on Doomsday, strongly suggesting they will show up somewhere in the film as Deadpool and Wolverine. After all, why else would they by writing stuff for the movie?
READ MORE: The Best Performances Ever in Marvel Movies
The final credited screenwriters of Avengers: Doomsday are Stephen McFeely (who co-wrote Captain America: Civil War, Avengers: Infinity War, and Avengers: Endgame) and Michael Waldron (who created Loki and wrote Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness).
Others writers to receive “Additional Literary Material” on Doomsday also include Jeff Loveness (writer of Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania and the original writer on the film back when it was known as Avengers: The Kang Dynasty), Andrew Lanham (co-writer on Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings), Destin Daniel Cretton (director of Shang-Chi, the intended director of The Kang Dynasty, and the eventual director of Spider-Man: Brand New Day), and Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers, who have written all four of Tom Holland’s Spider-Man movies.
If you want to speculate that increases the chances that Tom Holland’s Spider-Man shows up in Doomsday as well ... I wouldn’t disagree. In fact, I’d be inclined to agree with you.
Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters on December 18.

title: Maine voters rarely have a choice for this obscure office. They still won’t give it up.
text:
Maine voters rarely get more than one name to pick from when they elect county treasurers. But voters in three counties want to keep picking anyway.
York, Franklin and Washington county voters appear to have rejected referendums on Nov. 3 that would have let county commissioners appoint treasurers instead. Some small towns have still not reported results, but roughly 70% of voters in each county were poised to vote the change down.
The proposals were meant to professionalize an office that oversees the finances of each of Maine’s 16 counties. State law does not require treasurers to be accountants or have any financial background. These obscure offices have drawn scrutiny of late amid local tax revolts and major governance issues in a handful of counties.
Both have happened in Washington County. A multimillion-dollar budget shortfall last year left the county scrambling to pay its debts and narrowly avoiding an unprecedented default.
Commissioners weighed a 40% tax increase and asked voters to approve $11 million in borrowing to dig out. They placed much of the blame on longtime Treasurer Jill Holmes, who they said mismanaged funds and moved $400,000 from the Unorganized Territory fund into the general fund in violation of state law.
Holmes retired last fall as the scope of the crisis became clear. She had run unopposed since the late 1990s. The county’s last contested treasurer’s race was in 1992, when Holmes lost.
Treasurers have long been elected in most of Maine’s counties, but state law allows counties to hold referendums to allow commissioners to appoint them. Three counties have made this change. Knox County voters were the first to allow commissioners to appoint treasurers after a 2004 vote. In 2012, voters in Cumberland and Androscoggin County did the same.
After Washington’s crisis, county commissioners decided to ask voters whether to begin appointing treasurers.
After the crisis, commissioners decided to ask again.
“Anybody who’s going to be running the finance department needs to have a lot of qualifications in this day and age, and we wanted to make sure that that person was not just elected because of name recognition,” Washington County Commissioner David Burns, a former Republican state senator from Whiting, said.
But commissioners said recent steps to professionalize the county’s finance department have taken some of the burden off the treasurer, making it less essential that the person in the role be a qualified hire. Commissioner Courtney Hammond said he ultimately voted against the referendum he helped put on the ballot.
“We don’t really need a full time, you know, hands-on day-to-day treasurer,” Hammond said.
York County commissioners put the question forward even though voters there rejected abolishing the elected position in 2018. The job is largely symbolic in York, which cut its treasurer’s salary to $500 a year after setting up a county finance office.
Commissioner Justin Chenette, a former Democratic state senator from Saco, said he opposed the change for reasons similar to Hammond’s.
“The role of the elected treasurer has been diminished because of a strengthened financial management operation and full-time staff,” Chenette said. “From my perspective, the public should still be able to pick that individual if we’re going to keep the role.”
Few people seek the job anywhere in Maine. Only three of the 13 counties that still elect treasurers had more than one candidate on the ballot this year, and that was an improvement. In 2014 and 2022, only one county had a contested treasurer’s race.
Kennebec County had two candidates for treasurer this year for the first time this century. Aroostook County hasn’t had a contested race for the job since 1994, and Piscataquis County hasn’t had one since before 1986.
Washington County voters may want to keep picking their treasurer, but they won’t get to anytime soon. Nobody ran for the job this year. Commissioners say the process for filling the spot is unclear, but the governor may have to appoint someone.
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: The climate majority doesn’t know its own strength
text:
Thomas S. Bateman is professor emeritus of organizational behavior and leadership at the University of Virginia. He lives in Rockport.
Around many Thanksgiving tables this year, climate change will be on people’s minds but rarely in the conversation. Two-thirds of Americans are worried about global warming, and a majority of voters want Congress and corporations to do more about it. Yet most underestimate how many others share their concern. That mistake holds back climate action.
In an April survey by Yale and George Mason researchers, 77% of registered voters supported regulating carbon dioxide as a pollutant, and nearly two-thirds supported moving the U.S. economy to 100% clean energy by 2050.
Americans underestimate public support for major climate policies by nearly half. Psychologists call this pluralistic ignorance. People who want climate action stay quiet when they assume others don’t share their view, and their silence keeps the false belief alive.
Learning the truth can change minds. In one experiment, economists told Americans that most of their fellow citizens try to fight global warming. Participants, especially climate skeptics, became more willing to act and to support climate policies.
But people misjudge others’ climate actions in the opposite direction. A study published this summer in Nature Climate Change found that people overestimate how many others donate to climate causes or engage in climate politics. In the Yale-George Mason survey, only one registered voter in 10 had contacted a government official about climate change in the past year. The climate majority is both larger and quieter than people think.
We can’t assume enough others are speaking up. New voices speed progress toward tipping points. In online experiments, once about a quarter of a group committed to a new norm, the rest quickly followed.
Maine shows how quickly climate solutions spread when neighbors talk to neighbors. The state hit its goal of 100,000 new heat pumps two years early, and Efficiency Maine’s registered installers have grown from 30 or 40 a decade ago to 585 today. “Most referrals are word of mouth,” Bridget Gifford of Efficiency Maine told me. “Maine is a small town.”
My research has focused on proactive behavior: acting early to head off problems before the damage arrives. Climate change is my Exhibit A for the cost of waiting. Speaking up takes some nerve and is among the most proactive things anyone can do.
The holiday table is one place to start. Ask what others think and what worries them most, listen seriously, then share your perspective. Climate change touches so much of life, from heating bills and severe weather to the fishing and farming so many Maine families depend on, that almost anyone can find a reason to care.
If the moment is right, mention that nearly all climate scientists agree humans are warming the planet; learning this tends to raise concern.
Staying quiet cedes the debate to a determined, well-funded minority. In February, the Trump administration repealed the EPA finding that greenhouse gases endanger public health. Officials will keep treating climate as a losing issue until the majority tells and shows them otherwise.
This month’s elections changed control of Congress and several statehouses, and newly elected officials are setting priorities and hiring staff. In a 2016 survey, senior congressional staffers in both parties underestimated their constituents’ support for climate action. Staffs have turned over since, but the bias probably persists. After Thanksgiving, write or call your state legislators and members of Congress and tell them you want more and smarter climate action.
We need far more climate leaders, and they don’t need titles. Starting a climate conversation, contacting officials and showing neighbors your heat pump or solar panels are acts of leadership.
We understand climate science, we know what to do and majorities want more action. The climate majority holds a stronger hand than most realize. This holiday season, let’s start playing our cards.

title: Why days of rain barely budged Maine's extreme drought
text:
Why days of rain barely budged Maine's extreme drought
Topsoil is wetter after days of rain, but Maine still faces a steep deficit to recharge dry wells before the ground freezes
Why days of rain barely budged Maine's extreme drought
Topsoil is wetter after days of rain, but Maine still faces a steep deficit to recharge dry wells before the ground freezes
Despite several days of substantial rainfall across Maine, roughly 8.5% of the state remains locked in extreme drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. While the recent wet weather soaked dry topsoil and helped shrink the footprint of moderate and severe drought across several counties, a single multi-day storm system is not enough to erase deep, long-term water deficits.
The weekly drought map by the U.S. Drought Monitor evaluates more than just recent rainfall, factoring in streamflow, deeper soil moisture and depleted groundwater levels that have built up since 2025. Maine still needs roughly 12 to 15 inches of rain to meaningfully replenish dry wells and record-low water tables, making the next few weeks a critical race against time before the ground freezes for winter. Once frozen soil seals the surface, rain and melting snow will run off into rivers and streams instead of soaking down to recharge aquifers.

title: Maine caregivers report confusion over DEA medical cannabis reclassification
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MILO, Maine (WABI) - The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration is implementing a reclassification of medical cannabis under the federal Controlled Substances Act, and the change has caused confusion and uncertainty for Maine caregivers.
The Justice Department said the change is intended to support state-regulated medical marijuana programs while maintaining federal controls.
Caregivers say communication is lacking
Shannon Lord, owner of Triple Goddess Wellness in Milo, is one of many Maine caregivers who say communication is lacking from the DEA about registration for medicinal cannabis.
“A couple of our vendors, a couple of other stores had gotten a hold of us and said, ‘are you applying for the registration?’ And we said, ‘we don’t even know what’s going on,’” Lord said.
The reclassification gives caregivers the option to register with the DEA in addition to registering with the states where they sell.
“What was the point? I have no idea,” Lord said.
Supplier losses
Suppliers and businesses that registered with the DEA are no longer allowed to conduct business with those who did not register. The change is causing Lord to lose 90% of her suppliers.
“It’s business as usual for us, other than not being able to do business with people who registered,” Lord said.
Not being permitted to do business with registered suppliers will in turn affect Lord’s customers.
“Our patients have come to rely on what we carry. They like what we carry. They ask specifically for what we carry. And now they have to start all over again,” Lord said.
Federal registration concerns
Medical cannabis is still federally illegal. With the new registration, business owners would be registering an illegal business with the federal government, even though it is legal in Maine.
“There is not much of a trust factor here. Like I said, it’s like going back to 2010, when we had the federal marshals come to our house, pull up our driveway. We never knew if they were going to come back. We did not know if we were going to be the ones that got raided,” said Catherine Lewis, director of education for Medical Marijuana Caregivers of Maine.
Lewis also owns a small business and said the change will affect her customers as well.
“We are on a month-to-month basis as it is now, and it has been for so many of the small caregivers. There is an abundance of businesses out there. There’s only so many patients we can serve,” Lewis said. “I’ve heard so many people say, well, just let the free market determine what the free market can handle. Make no mistake, this is so far from a free market. This is a heavily regulated and skewed market.”
Letter to congressional delegation
Lord wrote to Maine’s congressional delegation asking for clarification on the change. She said Rep. Jared Golden responded and connected Lord with a hemp and agriculture aid.
“I did more than write a letter. I drafted a proposal to amend the Controlled Substance Act to allow Congress to have states continue to operate the same as they have been,” Lord said. “it clearly states in the rule that they did in April that the states are doing a great job and they’re doing what the feds would require anyway. So why duplicate a program that’s already working?”
Kristi Shaw, vice chair of Medical Marijuana Caregivers of Maine, supports the letter.
“Nobody knows what to expect. They’re not really laying out their vision of what this looks like other than, you know, making it easier for the bigger companies to succeed and us to go away,” Shaw said.
State and federal responses
The Maine Office of Cannabis Policy has been releasing guidance documents for caregivers across the state. They also provided the following statement from Alexis Soucy, director of media & stakeholder relations, Office of Cannabis Policy:
“The administration and enforcement of federal cannabis law is outside of OCP’s purview and jurisdiction, and we have not received any guidance from federal agencies regarding these changes.”
The DEA has not responded to a request for comment.

title: Man accused of running over and killing mother after argument about borrowed car, police say
text:
TULSA, OKLA. (Gray News) - An Oklahoma man is accused of running over and killing his mother after an argument about a borrowed car, according to authorities.
John Tiffin, 31, was arrested on charges of second-degree murder, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, reckless driving and obstructing an officer, a press release said.
Tiffin allegedly borrowed his mother’s silver car on Oct. 7 to run errands but never returned it. His mother was identified as 69-year-old Karen Curthoys.
Police said Curthoys wanted her car back and contacted her other son, Timothy Curthoys, who agreed to help her recover the vehicle.
Tulsa police said Curthoys and her son tracked down the car.
According to court documents, they found the car in a driveway. An argument followed as Timothy attempted to recover it.
Tiffin allegedly put the car in reverse and hit his mother, who was standing outside between two vehicles. Timothy was in the front passenger seat.
Karen Curthoys was taken to a hospital, where she died from her injuries on Oct. 12.

title: Broadway After Dark brings ‘Come From Away’ to Presque Isle
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Broadway After Dark is bringing the musical “Come From Away” to the University of Maine at Presque Isle, with the first performance set for Nov. 13.
The production follows passengers stranded in Gander, Newfoundland, after American airspace closed on Sept. 11, 2001, and the residents who welcomed them. Dozens of planes were diverted to the small Canadian town, and people living there opened their doors to thousands of strangers.
A story based on real people
Shelby Pelletier, producer of “Come From Away,” said the characters in the show are based on actual people from Gander or from the planes. That includes Captain Beverly Bass.
“A lot of shows are based on a true story, but this is literally the true story,” Pelletier said.
Pelletier plays Beverly Bass along with several other roles. Across the production, a cast of 12 portrays more than 100 characters.
Director saw early presentation
Director Darci Faye said bringing the musical to Aroostook County has been years in the making. Faye first saw a 45-minute presentation of the show while it was still being developed.
“I knew it was going to be something incredibly special from that,” Faye said.
The production features a live band. Organizers recommend it for audiences ages 13 and older, noting some mild swearing and the subject matter.
Faye said that while Sept. 11 provides the backdrop, the show also offers younger audiences a way to understand the uncertainty people experienced.
“Even though it’s never really explicitly talked about, it’s still that confusion and that fear and a lot of things that we felt on that day,” Faye said.
In the story, that uncertainty is met with meals, places to sleep and ways for passengers to reach their families.
Performances recognize community members
The local production will also recognize people serving in the community. Each performance has a theme: first responders, community helpers, health care workers and paying it forward. A portion of ticket sales will benefit first responders in Aroostook County.
“‘Come From Away,’ obviously it’s an amazing story of community and kindness, but also especially a display of kindness during a dark time,” Pelletier said. “And I think that that’s what also makes it incredibly powerful.”
Show dates and times
“Come From Away” opens Nov. 13, with additional performances Nov. 14, 20 and 21. Each show begins at 7 p.m. at UMPI.

title: Star Wars Drops ‘A New Hope’ Subtitle For 50th Anniversary Re-Release
text:
Star Wars Is Dumping ‘A New Hope’ Subtitle For 50th Anniversary Re-Release
Star Wars takes place a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away. But now the film itself comes from a long time ago. 2027 marks the 50th anniversary of the original Star Wars’ first release in theaters, and now that very first version of the film — one that has been held back from public view for decades — is returning to theaters.
Disney and Lucasfilm confirmed today that a “restored version of the original Star Wars” will play in theaters around the world next February. They said the movie “will be released in digital and film formats, including IMAX 70mm, Digital IMAX, 4DX and D-BOX, with the presentation including an added celebratory logo in advance of the film featuring a newly orchestrated score by John Williams.”
READ MORE: Every Star Wars Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best
Lucasfilm also unveiled a new poster for Star Wars’ 50th re-release, designed by Matt Ferguson — one that, tellingly, does not contain the longer title (Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope) that writer/director George Lucas retroactively gave to it when he began making Star Wars sequels. When Star Wars first played in theaters in 1977 it was just called Star Wars. And now it’s just called Star Wars again.
The title tweak was among the first of many changes Lucas made to Star Wars through the years. In 1997, he added new scenes and new digital effects to the film for its 20th anniversary, and re-released it in theaters as the “Special Edition.” The re-release was a massive box-office hit, and helped pave the way for the Star Wars prequels a few years later.
The Special Editions were initially greeted warmly by fans. But as Lucas continued to tweak Star Wars through the decades, they began to demand both cuts of the film. Instead, Lucas kept the 1977 cut locked away and only put the Special Editions (and later, further edits that added more weird stuff like Greedo shouting “Maclunkey!” to the infamous Cantina scene) on home video. So this 50th anniversary release really is a big deal from a historical perspective.
Lucasfilm’s plans for the 50th anniversary of Star Wars also include Star Wars screenings in the Cosm immersive movie format, Star Wars in Concert: The Skywalker Saga at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles in April, which will coincide with the latest installment of the Star Wars Celebration convention as well.
On May the 4th (Be With You), they will also release a new documentary called The Hero Awakens about the making of Star Wars. What there is left to say after countless documentaries about books about the making of the film I do not know, but the press release claims it “features archival footage and audio captured during and around the making of the historic film in 1977.”
The 50th anniversary re-release of Star Wars hits theaters on February 19, 2027.

title: Maranacook standouts make college commitments official
UMaine hockey’s Lipinski making significant strides after ‘tough end’ to freshman season
text:
ORONO, Maine — Jaden Lipinski couldn’t have gotten off to a better start during his freshman season at the University of Maine last year, notching two goals and three assists in his first three games.
But he only managed to score one goal and hand out six assists over the next 28 games and his playing time dwindled.
And he didn’t dress for the Black Bears’ lone playoff game, a 5-0 loss to Boston College in the Hockey East quarterfinals.
It would have been understandable if he decided to transfer like three of his fellow freshman forwards: Justin Poirier (Penn State), Miguel Marques (Northeastern) and Nick Peluso (RIT).
But Lipinski decided to work on his game and return and he has made significant strides while earning a regular shift centering the team’s power forward line between Robert Morris (PA) transfer Tanner Klimpke and Arizona State transfer Sam Alfano.
Lipinski and Alfano each stand 6-foot-4 and weigh 210 pounds while Klimpke is 6-2, 182.
Lipinkski will enter this weekend’s two-game road series against Hockey East leader Vermont on a three-game points streak with a goal and two assists after going scoreless in his first seven games.
He didn’t play in the 5-3 win over Quinnipiac.
He leads the team in plus-minus at plus-six.
Players get a plus-one if they are on the ice when their team scores an even-strength or shorthanded goal and a minus-one if the opponent scores one.
Lipinski admitted that it was a “tough” end to the season for him a year ago.
“But the coaches really do want what’s the best for us. To (succeed), it’s going to be hard and uncomfortable. They’re going to push you. I believe in the way they do it,” said Lipinski. “If you listen to them and accept it and handle it like a man, good things will happen.”
It was one of the most challenging things he has had to deal with but he said “there are always ebbs and flows with hockey. But growing is uncomfortable so I know I’m in the right place.”
He has been happy with his start including his current points streak, his first such streak since the first three games of the 2025-26 campaign.
“After last year, I was in a position where I had to prove myself,” said the fourth round draft pick (112th overall) of the Calgary Flames. “Good things happen when you do the little things. I’ve been working hard and playing to our identity and have been rewarded for it.
“The theme was we all had more to give, especially me. It’s a great place and I couldn’t be happier that I stayed,” he added.
All three of his goals last season were game-winners and he tied for the team lead in that category. He also won 60.8% of his faceoffs and he is at 55.6% this season, second only to Max Scott (58.2%) among players who have taken at least 20 faceoffs.
“He has made a real conscious effort to become a 200-foot player,” said UMaine head coach Ben Barr. “We all get hit in the face by reality at some point in our careers. For him, I think last year was a little bit of that. It was hard. But he made the decision to come back and put himself back in that environment of wanting to become a more complete player.
“And, so far, he is putting the work in and it’s happening. It isn’t perfect or anything like that but it’s great to see the work pay off with the little things on the ice,” Barr added.
Breaking down Lipinski’s game, Barr said he is “holding onto pucks and staying on his feet more. He is is 6-foot-4 so his game is below the tops of the circles in the offensive zone. He can make plays on the rush and all that kind of stuff. That’s great. Most players can at this level but the real good ones, especially when you are as big and strong as he is, have to be good down low and in one-on-on battles and in holding onto pucks.
“That’s been the one thing that has really improved this year.”
“That has been the process ever since coming here. Being a bigger guy, sometimes it takes a little bit just with the coordination and all that. They have hammered that into me and so the challenge now for me is to do it every day,” said Lipinski, a Scottsdale, Arizona native who tallied 68 goals and 124 assists in 260 games over four seasons for the Vancouver Giants in the Western Hockey League which is one of the Canadian Hockey League’s three Major Junior leagues.
He acknowledged that playing college hockey was an adjustment.
“I wasn’t used to playing this way. The CHL (Major Junior Hockey) is a little more open so I fell into that category but it has been great ever since,” said Lipinski, who appeared in three games for the American Hockey League’s Calgary Wranglers.
UMaine graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler said Lipinski has been “awesome so far this year.
“You get happy for guys when they come back and you see the strides they’ve taken over the summer because they’ve put the work in. He is not going to be denied of anything,” said Fowler. “He has a great work ethic and you’re happy when you see someone like that succeed.”
The Black Bears are 5-5 overall, 1-3 in Hockey East, and will be taking on a surprising Vermont team that is leading the league with a 4-1-1 league mark and a 5-3-1 overall record.
The games at the Gutterson Fieldhouse in Burlington, Vt. will start at 7 on Friday and 5 on Saturday.
“They’re playing great hockey,” said Barr. “They have a lot more depth than they’ve had. They don’t beat themselves and they have a lot of belief. They have some guys who have been there a long time and some real good new players. Their goalie (Jacob Oster) is playing really well.”
Oster, a former OHL Goaltender of the Year, is 5-2-1 with a 1.96 goals-against average and a .930 save percentage.
Defenseman and Boston College transfer Michael Hagens is the Catamounts’ leading scorer with three goals and five assists followed by right wing Ethan Burroughs (3 & 4) and center Cedrick Guindon (2 & 4), who are linemates with Colin Kessler (3 & 2).
Right wing Lee Parks (5 & 3), left wing Klimpke (5 & 3) and center Scott (2 & 6) lead the Black Bears with Isa Parekh (2 & 4) being the top-scoring defenseman. Goalie Albin Boija is 4-3 with a 1.78 GAA and .921 save percentage.

title: Teen who spent years building lawn business has nearly $20,000 worth of equipment stolen
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRAIRIE VILLAGE, Kan. (KCTV/Gray News) - A Kansas teen who spent years building a lawn care business says he had about $20,000 worth of equipment stolen the night before Halloween.
Sonny Gallardo is the owner of Sunnyside Jobs LLC. He started as a sixth grader knocking on doors and raking leaves with his grandfather.
Those small jobs grew into mowing lawns.
Four years later, the business was big enough for a five-person crew.
“I just like doing it; it gives people joy and gives me joy. I love making people happy,” Gallardo said.
Ring doorbell video appeared to show someone stealing Gallardo’s trailer.
The stolen items included five mowers, two weed eaters and two blowers that were on the trailer.
Gallardo’s family said the work vehicle was also emptied.
“It was $20,000 worth of equipment. It took me three years to get that equipment, and it’s a bummer,” Gallardo said.
The equipment was stolen before Gallardo had a chance to get the business insured.
Gallardo’s mother started a GoFundMe to help him rebuild that has already raised thousands of dollars.
“I really was speechless. I didn’t believe it. I still can’t believe it right now. I’m just thankful to God for all these people who are donating money,” Gallardo said.
According to Prairie Village police, an investigation remains ongoing despite not having any immediate leads in the case.
Police are asking people to watch for large amounts of lawn equipment in yards or being sold online.
“Nothing is going to put me down. I mean, you can try your best, but I’m never going to go down. I love this stuff too much. It’s been my dream since I was little,” Gallardo said.
Gallardo said he remains working and available for lawn care work.

title: Newburgh house fire caused by electrical failure, officials say
text:
NEWBURGH, Maine (WABI) - The cause of a fire that heavily damaged a home in Newburgh has been ruled accidental, according to the Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office.
Several departments responded to the fire on Western Ave. just before 11 a.m. on Tuesday. While the fire was quickly suppressed, officials say the flames, heat, and water used to put out the fire caused significant damage. No residents were injured, but WABI was told by firefighters at the scene that one firefighter suffered minor injuries.
Investigators from the FMO determined the fire originated under the residence, and was caused by an electrical failure. It has been deemed accidental. Officials say the home was insured.
Crews on scene said ongoing training happening at Hermon Mountain at the time of the call aided in their speedy response.

title: Obituary: Peter Arthur LaVerdiere
LePage confirmed as winner of Maine’s 2nd District race
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WAGM) - Republican Paul LePage has won Maine’s 2nd Congressional District race, defeating Democrat Matt Dunlap following ranked-choice tabulation. The Associated Press called the race Thursday, nine days after the Nov. 3 election.
The tabulation process began Monday, Nov. 9, at the Maine Department of Public Safety headquarters in Augusta. Election workers continued Tuesday before pausing Wednesday for Veterans Day and resuming Thursday, the third day of counting.
The additional count was required after neither candidate received more than 50% of the total ballots cast in the initial tally. LePage initially received 170,263 votes, or 49.894%, while Dunlap received 164,845 votes, or 48.307%, according to the secretary of state’s office.
Dunlap conceded Nov. 5, a week before the result was confirmed.
LePage, a former two-term Maine governor, will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden.

title: Letter: Maine should not object to permitting reform bill
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I was disappointed to see Attorney General Aaron Frey sign a letter opposing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA).
Mainers pay some of the highest electricity rates in the country, driven largely by our dependence on out-of-state fossil fuels, particularly natural gas. Lowering electricity costs and meeting our climate goals can go hand in hand. Maine has abundant, low-cost clean energy waiting to come online, but transmission and other infrastructure upgrades are needed to deliver it.
The New England Clean Energy Connect (NECEC) is now delivering clean Canadian hydropower to New England, displacing fossil fuel generation. Its completion should be a point of pride. Instead, years of lawsuits and political battles added more than $500 million to its cost — a burden that ultimately falls on ratepayers.
I believe BAAJA would help prevent such delays without weakening environmental protections. It establishes reasonable timelines for project reviews and legal challenges while preserving the authority of courts to send inadequate reviews back for correction. It also limits arbitrary permit revocations that have stalled offshore wind and other renewable energy projects.
The bill further ensures that data centers pay for the grid upgrades they require, rather than passing those costs to Maine families. Faster connections for clean energy will also help reduce the pollution warming the Gulf of Maine.
Maine has a proud tradition of putting results ahead of party politics. I hope Sen. Susan Collins makes BAAJA a priority before the end of her term and that Sen. Angus King supports it when the Senate considers the bill this month. I hope Attorney General Frey takes another look as well.
Mainers cannot afford another NECEC.
Don Parent
Cumberland

title: These 25 Maine areas could see more investment under federal program
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than two dozen communities across the state are readying for what could be a tidal wave of investment over the next decade. It could also just be a trickle. Or it might not come at all.
State and federal officials this week announced the 25 “tracts” that have been selected as the next federal Qualified Opportunity Zones, a designation designed to help draw private, long-term investment to low-income areas.
Maine’s current 32 Opportunity Zones have been in place since 2018 and are set to expire.
Gov. Janet Mills announced Tuesday that she selected the 25 areas from a list of 78 options.
Eight of the 25 tracts — including parts of Westbrook, Brunswick, Augusta and East Millinocket — were also designated in the previous round.
But areas that missed out a decade ago, like Sanford, Biddeford, Houlton, Machias, Skowhegan and Dover-Foxcroft, will get their shot at attracting some needed investment.
A lack of reporting requirements makes it impossible to tell how successful the program is. There’s no way to know whether a project used Opportunity Zone funds unless a developer volunteers the information.
The program appears to have been used successfully at least a handful of times in Maine, including for projects in South Portland, Brunswick, Waterville and Augusta.
Data from elsewhere in the country, however, suggests mixed results.
Opportunity knocks
The Opportunity Zone incentive program was established in 2017 by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act to encourage long-term investments in low-income urban and rural communities nationwide. It was made permanent last year and reintroduced as the Opportunity Zone 2.0 program, which offers additional incentives for selections in rural areas, has tighter qualifying criteria and new reporting requirements.
Eligible communities are determined based on income and poverty thresholds.
It has been hard for municipalities to track the success of the program because there has not been a requirement to report whether a project is using the incentive. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, however, Opportunity Zones attracted more than $100 billion in the last 10 years. Another $100 billion is expected in the next decade.
The program allows investors to create or invest in so-called “opportunity funds” through which they can reinvest capital gains — profits from the sale of investments — into designated areas tax-free for at least five years, then get a 10% tax break on the initial investment. That increases to 30% in designated rural areas. Any profits they make annually through the investment after 10 years are tax-free.
Governors nominated eligible communities for the designation, which were then certified by the U.S. Department of the Treasury.
Maine’s 32 current zones were selected by former Gov. Paul LePage and will expire at the end of 2028. The new zones will take effect Jan. 1, 2027, so there will be a roughly two-year overlap.
‘Transformative impact’
Mike Duguay, commissioner of the Maine Department of Economic and Community Development, said state officials spent the last year consulting with developers, local leaders and financial professionals to determine where investment “can have the most transformative impact.”
“We did not approach these designations lightly,” he said in a statement. “This was a bottom-up effort to ensure that these federal tools are working hard for Maine’s specific needs.”
Tony Armstrong, a commercial real estate broker and adviser, was thrilled to see Dover-Foxcroft make the cut this time around.
He has been working to redevelop Browns Mill, the former Maine Leathers Tannery, in the Piscataquis County town.
The project has the potential to see the same kind of transformation as mill projects in Lewiston and Biddeford, if on a smaller scale, Armstrong said, but hasn’t had the necessary “oomph” to draw the kind of attention needed.
At the same time, the Piscataquis County Economic Development Council has been trying for years to recruit a developer to build an 80-room hotel.
That, too, hasn’t quite made it over the finish line.
“This kind of program … is going to make the difference,” Armstrong said.
Wasted opportunity?
But other parts of the state that could desperately use an infusion of investment, like large swaths of northern and western Maine, were passed over, despite being some of the most rural parts of the state.
According to Brady Meixell, a senior research associate at the Urban Institute who is studying opportunity zones and their impact, that may not be a bad call.
The Urban Institute found that in Ohio, more than two-thirds of the state’s opportunity zones did not receive a single dollar of investment from 2020-24. The vast majority of money flowed into metropolitan centers like Cleveland and Columbus.
Ohio is the only state with Opportunity Zone data because of reporting requirements to get a matching state-level credit, so the Urban Institute views the Midwestern state as a sort of case-study of the program’s efficacy.
Governors in other states, Meixell said, took a lesson from those results: “There are going to be some very disinvested tracts that are eligible that it would feel good to select because you want to drive capital into them, but Opportunity Zones just are not the program that’s going to do that,” he said. “To some degree, some of those might be wasted picks.”
Only 39% of tracts selected for the Opportunity Zone 2.0 program were in rural areas, despite the added incentives.
There are “Goldilocks tracts” he said, in areas that could be poised for greater development but need an extra push to get there.
But in many cases, governors overcorrected and prioritized areas that already had a large number of jobs and a higher percentage of multifamily housing (which is the most common use for Opportunity Zones).
“A meaningful number of zones were already ascending rapidly before designation,” Meixell said.
Based on the data from Ohio, those are the zones most likely to see significant investment —those that were already experiencing greater income and home value growth in the years before the program launched.
Essentially, the zones receiving the most money from investors were the ones that didn’t need an incentive to court development in the first place.
A boon for Bayside
According to the Urban Institute, Portland’s Bayside is one of those communities.
The neighborhood already has hundreds of units in the pipeline and hundreds more in pre-development.
Portland officials initially tried to decline Bayside’s potential designation.
In a March meeting, members of the Housing Economic Development Committee feared the city could face another Urban Renewal by welcoming in a developer without any control over what is built in the neighborhood while investors line their pockets at the expense of longtime residents.
But Duguay sent a letter to Mayor Mark Dion, outlining how the program works.
“Being designated as an Opportunity Zone does not take away local control over land use, zoning, or project approvals. It is merely a federal tax incentive program, not a land-use or permitting regime,” he wrote. “In a nutshell, the program changes who might provide capital, not who makes the decision on whether a project gets approved.”
Chris Marshall, co-founder of GreenMars Real Estate in Portland, has plans for a more than 300-unit housing development in Bayside. The Opportunity Zone will be crucial in bringing in the investors that project needs, he said.
While Marshall is primarily focused on Bayside, he was excited to see the city’s other tract, which includes Riverside Street and the Riverton neighborhood.
The area has more commercial and industrial space than the kind of high-density multifamily housing that often draws opportunity zone investors, but it’s a prime location near the highway with access to highly skilled workers, making it ripe for economic development, he said.
“You need economic activity to boost wages,” he said. “If we can get more supply in one zone (in Bayside) and increased wages in another zone, that’s a win/win and work both sides of the equation on housing affordability,” he said.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Hannah LaClaire can be reached at hlaclaire@pressherald.com.

title: Black voters view Scott Colom's historic US Senate win through lens of Mississippi's racial legacy
text:
Black voters view Scott Colom's historic US Senate win through lens of Mississippi's racial legacy
It's been nearly 150 years since a Black man has represented Deep South and deep red Mississippi in the U.S. Senate.
That changed Wednesday evening as Democrat Scott Colom was declared the winner over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, who had been endorsed by President Donald Trump. For many in the state and for Black Americans across the nation, Colom's victory reflects the ambitions that were thwarted by generations of systemic oppression and violence.
Janice Johnson, who lives in Greenville in the Mississippi Delta, says having a Black senator has been a long time coming. “In the last few years we have seen great strides,” she said.
Out of all the southern states, Mississippi has a special place in the struggle over Black Americans’ exclusion from the nation’s promises of freedom and justice. There's Ida B. Wells-Barnett, the Mississippi-born journalist who investigated 19th century lynching across the South, and Emmett Till, the 14-year-old whose 1955 kidnapping and murder by white men in Mississippi reinvigorated the Civil Rights Movement.
There's Medgar Evers, the NAACP's first Mississippi field secretary who fought at Normandy in World War II and organized Black voter registration until his 1963 assassination. And Fannie Lou Hamer, the civil rights leader who challenged Mississippi's all-white delegation at the 1964 Democratic National Convention.
Rep. Bennie Thompson, who represents Mississippi’s 2nd District, was a student organizer for Hamer while studying at Tougaloo College, where Colom’s victory celebration was held Wednesday night. And now, Thompson is watching his mentee, Sen.-elect Colom, fill a more than 145-year gap of Black leadership in statewide office.
“From my perspective, I now have a partner in Washington,” Thompson said before introducing Colom.
"I can't help but think about Medgar Evers on Veterans Day," Colom said during a victory speech. “A moment like this, where he served his country and came home to Mississippi, when they wouldn't let him vote. But he had the faith that Mississippi could make progress. ... He had faith that a day like this was possible.”
He added, “All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this.”
Johnson, who watched part of Colom's victory speech from home, says she understands that Black voters, alone, aren't responsible for Colom's win. White voters, too, had to be fed up with the state's economy, school systems and crumbling health care infrastructure for the poor — Black and white — under Republican rule.
“The most important part is we've got to have faith that Mississippi is ready to do the right thing,” an elated Johnson told The Associated Press on Thursday. “We as a people — and Mississippi as whole — are ready to show the nation. We have to work together, and that was his message. He wants to help pull us together.”
Jerome Dunn, a barber in Jackson, echoed Johnson's sentiment.
“It takes everybody to vote, not one single race,” said Dunn, 59, who is Black and also voted for Colom. “I think people are looking for him to work for everybody. People are tired of Republicans and what they believe."
Two came before Colom
Blanche K. Bruce, a Republican, was the second Black man in the Senate from Mississippi after that state's legislature elected him to a six-year term. He served from 1875 to 1881. Hiram Revels, another Republican, was the first after the Senate voted to seat him in 1870 to fill a vacancy left empty since the start of the Civil War. Revels' term expired about a year later.
Bruce and Revels were among 16 Black men from southern states who served in Congress during the period of Reconstruction, which aimed to address the inequities experienced by Black people during enslavement, while preparing re-entry for the 11 Southern states that seceded from the union at the start of the U.S. Civil War.
Once Reconstruction ended and federal troops were withdrawn, freed slaves in the South lost many of the freedoms gained following the war as Southern states enforced racial segregation through Jim Crow-era laws.
White conservatives have dominated Mississippi’s Statehouse and congressional delegation ever since. Nearly all were white Democrats as laws restricted where Black people could live, work and go to school. That weight carried on through the Civil Rights era, but during the late 1960s white elected leaders in Mississippi switched political parties and became Republicans.
Colom's win represents “a pretty significant change in Mississippi politics," said Brian Shoup, head of political science and public administration at Mississippi State University.
“We haven't seen a Democrat win the Senate since the 1980s and even then that was a traditional kind of more southern conservative Democrat,” the professor said. “We haven't had an African American senator since the era of Reconstruction, so this is obviously a very significant and important election in Mississippi history.”
Mississippi has been burdened by its racial legacy
Black voters in Mississippi and across the South were faced with the reality of redistricting efforts designed to reduce Black representation in elected positions, set off in late April by a Supreme Court decision that gutted the landmark Voting Rights Act of 1965. The ruling helped fuel increased voter turnout.
But it's difficult for many to ignore Mississippi's troubling past involving race relations, from the lynching of Black people by the Ku Klux Klan and other mobs to the killings of Evers and Till.
In his 1963 “I Have a Dream” speech, civil rights icon the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. referred to Mississippi as a state “sweltering with the heat of injustice, sweltering with the heat of oppression.”
Colom’s election is historic and means things are changing in parts of the South, said Elnora Fisher, 68, of Greenville, who was born and raised in Mississippi where she remembers that simply living often didn’t seem fair to Black people.
“As I understood, my grandparents always tried to save up to vote," Fisher said. “They had to pay a tax to vote.”
As a child during the 1960s, Fisher said her mother took her to an NAACP meeting. “While we were there the white police stopped the meeting and made us leave,” she said.
Black people in Mississippi should be ecstatic with Colom as a U.S. senator, Fisher added.
“Here in Mississippi, so much has been taken from the poor people and given to the rich people,” she said. “I hope Colom will give back to the people who helped get him where he is.”
Good may come of it all with so many eyes on the results of the contest between Colom and Hyde-Smith, said Shoup, the professor. Mississippians, along with the rest of the nation, may be ready to begin healing from the past.
“This race, the fact that it has been so close, and it has activated so much turnout, might portend the prospects of maybe being able to talk about these things in a more civil and open fashion,” he said.

title: Computers in the Classroom
text:
WASHBURN, Maine (WAGM) - Computers are a regular part of the classroom today, but decades ago, some students in Washburn were getting an early start on skills that would eventually become part of everyday life. It’s the focus of this week’s Throwback Thursday with Brian Bouchard.
For students today, learning how to use a computer starts pretty early, but there was a time when computer programming was something only a handful of kids had access to. In this week’s Throwback Thursday, we dial the time machine back to 1981 where WAGM Reporter Peter McHugh met a group of students learning the basics of programming.
Here at the Foster Building in Washburn, some elementary school students are learning computer programming. These students are doing exceptionally well in their classes, and they’ve been specially chosen to work with the computers. This experience allows the children to be ahead going into high school, and by the time they go on to college, their training could be very advanced.
“Well, if I ever do, you know, work at it, I’ll know how to do it. I’d be able to teach other people how to do it.”
The students range from 5th grade to 8th grade. The training that they learn now is basic, but as time goes on, they’ll go on to higher levels. Computer programming teacher Bud Myers explains how this training will help the youngsters.
“It teaches them logical thinking. It teaches them task organization. It teaches them division of tasks into smaller tasks. If the original task seems to be insurmountable, then they can divide it into smaller tasks and take each one at a time. And of course it teaches them the technology that they’re going to need in their future because these things are going to become part of everyone’s lives.”
If they haven’t already.
The only problem with the program is when they go on to high school, computers are not that available to the students and they could lose interest in what could prove to be an exciting and rewarding career.
For Newsline 8, I’m Peter McHugh

title: Americans said ‘no’ to one-man rule
text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 42 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
In one of his greatest poems, “Easter, 1916,” W.B. Yeats intones, “All changed, changed utterly.” One might say the same about Washington, D.C., after the 2026 midterm elections.
Yeats was commemorating the Easter Rising in Dublin, which eventually resulted in a new Irish nation after more than two centuries of British rule — though not without civil war and extensive bloodshed. Our own uprising, one hopes, will not spark similar violence.
But make no mistake: this was no ordinary election. It represents not only a repudiation of the policies of President Trump, but a rejection of Trumpism — the insidious movement, encouraged by the Supreme Court and abetted by a supine Congress, toward one-man rule.
If continued, this would have produced an autocracy alien to our Constitution and the rule of law that’s served us well for two and a half centuries. It wasn’t just about Iran and gas prices. Americans said “no” to a dangerous departure from democratic governance.
Consider the new senators-elect: A pediatrician from South Carolina. A former wheelchair basketball star from Iowa. A Methodist megachurch pastor from Kansas. An epidemiologist and professor from Michigan, the first Muslim senator. A family restaurant owner from New Hampshire, the first openly gay man elected.
If present trends hold, a district attorney will become the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction, and the first tribal member will be elected from Alaska. And of course, a professional logger-turned-state Senate president from Maine. Even for a party that thrives on diversity, this is stunning.
The spotlight now turns to Senate leaders, with now-minority Republicans grumbling, but sticking with John Thune. Chuck Schumer, however, faces obstacles in an attempted return as majority leader. A half dozen new Democrats, including Troy Jackson, have strong reservations, and several current senators share them.
That’s no surprise. In his previous two-year stint as majority leader during the Biden administration, Schumer was by any standard a weak leader. The first and primary duty of a Senate leader is to keep the caucus together — just ask Schumer’s opposite number for six years, Mitch McConnell — and in this task Schumer failed utterly.
Schumer allowed two marginal members, Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema, to effectively run the caucus by vetoing Democratic plans. Neither even ran for reelection, and Manchin’s role was particularly significant. His refusal to end the filibuster rule prevented Democrats from enacting strong legislation on healthcare and labor rights.
If Schumer survives, he may have to emulate House Speaker Nancy Pelosi in 2021 and, much earlier, Senate Leader Robert Byrd in 1987, pledging to serve only two more years. That led first to the elevation of Sen. George Mitchell and now, Hakeem Jeffries as speaker-apparent. Many will be vying to succeed the 75-year-old Schumer.
Through it all, Democrats have to remain focused on the reasons voters provided them the keys to Congress. While “affordability” remains an elusive concept, organizing a national health system, reviving labor organizing and providing true tax reform — not just surcharges on the wealthiest — provide the means to that end. Working people want better jobs, fairer taxes and guaranteed access to healthcare, not handouts. All are achievable.
These bills may not become law in the next Congress — Trump retains the veto — but they’ll make a much stronger platform for 2028 than anything Democrats have offered since the 1960s.
One issue where Republicans may be willing, perhaps even eager to cooperate, is ending the war with Iran, a millstone around the party’s neck. Trump’s inability to face reality over a war he launched himself and has no idea how to “win” requires bipartisan congressional action.
It wasn’t possible through the impeachment resolution offered by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie. That was just for show, but it will be top priority in the new Congress. Republicans must insist, as a first step, that Trump fire Pete Hegseth, who fancies himself leading a “Department of War,” and demand a highly qualified, experienced and even-handed successor — all the things Hegseth isn’t.
Here’s a subtle local indication: in Kennebec and Oxford counties, Democrats narrowly ousted Republican incumbents for commissioner and sheriff based on the “overseas vote,” primarily from military families.
It’s not surprising young voters are feeling empowered, even giddy. They made a big difference, and will continue to do so. Yet elections are only a first step; governing is harder.
A cautionary note. Yeats’ final line in “Easter, 1916” repeats, “A terrible beauty is born.” The road ahead will not be smooth, but reclaiming our nationhood is well worth the price.

title: Whipped cream sold at Costco recalled in a dozen states ahead of Thanksgiving

The 15-ounce cans of Kirkland Signature Real Heavy Whipped Cream were sold in 12 states across the Midwest and Southeast between Oct. 11 and Oct. 31 of this year.
Manufacturer Alamance Foods says one batch of the whipped cream may contain a small amount of a cleaning chemical. There have been reports of a chemical smell and taste but no serious issues requiring medical care.

title: Maine wants dam operator to pay $120K for Penobscot River fish kills
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine wildlife officials want a subsidiary of energy giant Brookfield Renewable to pay $120,000 for a series of mass fish strandings caused by malfunctions at the Ripogenus Dam near Baxter State Park.
The Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife proposed the payments to compensate for the hundreds of landlocked salmon and brook trout that were killed when water flows from the dam were abruptly reduced in 2023, 2025 and 2026. The dam on the west branch of the Penobscot River is owned by Brookfield affiliate Great Lakes Hydro America.
“I wouldn’t characterize this as a warning, we have a responsibility to the resources so what this is attempting to do, is make this whole again,” James Bruce, deputy director of the department’s fisheries and hatcheries division, said in an interview.
The department calculated the cost of dead fish and future recreational value at $40,000 per stranding, according to a filing with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which is responsible for approving the proposed payments. The money would go to support fisheries restoration and improvement in the region.
The department also wants Brookfield to install a river gauge to provide more data about river flows and accelerate replacement of electrical infrastructure to prevent future malfunctions.
The dam has automatic protective systems that shut down generators if there is an electrical or mechanical fault. When that happens, the dam defaults to a minimum-flow that is often much less than the amount of water that was flowing through the dam immediately before, which can expose shallow areas downstream.
A lightning strike in 2023 caused such a “trip event” but the other two strandings resulted from failing transmission line crossarms, according to the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife.
In a statement, Brookfield said it has supported the concept of mitigation payments associated with flow interruptions.
“We are continuing to review MDIFW’s recent filing and the department’s other recommendations and intend to respond directly in the FERC docket,” spokesperson David Heidrich said.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Camden Hills completes perfect season with Class A state girls soccer championship
text:
CAMDEN, Maine (WABI) - Camden Hills captured the Class A state girls soccer title after a dominant, undefeated season.
The Windjammers outlasted Scarborough, 1-0 in double-overtime, in the state championship match on Saturday.

“It feels amazing. It is the perfect ending. I’ve been wanting a win since freshman year, and the whole team wanted the win, so it feels great. We definitely went into it knowing it was going to be a really tough game and the toughest game we’ve played all season. The Windjammers’ goal differential across the regular season and state tournament was 130-4.
It’s their first state championship since they won four straight from 2016-2019 for the program total of five.

title: Witnesses felt helpless amid the chaos while watching a Brooklyn building come crashing down
text:
Witnesses who watched a building come crashing down in Brooklyn felt helpless amid the chaos
Before the screams started, Dervie Mapp heard loud popping noises outside her Brooklyn apartment. She bolted out of bed to the kitchen window and watched as a neighboring building came crashing down, raining three stories of bricks and twisted metal.
Stunned survivors cried out amid thick dust and piles of rubble that moments earlier had been people’s homes.
Related video above: Witness captures moments after Brooklyn building collapses
“I saw the whole thing come down,” Mapp, a 67-year-old retiree, told The Associated Press on Thursday. “People were running up out of the pit, screaming and hollering. I couldn’t believe it — I froze.”
The deadly collapse that occurred without warning Wednesday afternoon took down a building that housed a store selling medical uniforms on the ground level and four apartments on the floors above.
At least eight people died, including two children. The dead included two men from Ecuador, José Luis Caguana Cosquillo and Gabriel Ariolfo Siguencia Yupa, according to the Ecuadorian consulate in New York. Officials said 18 others suffered injuries.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Thursday described the victims as “parents and children, young families building their lives in our city and immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Trinidad and beyond.”
Among those hurt were four firefighters assisting with rescue efforts, which continued Thursday as crews searched for survivors through heaps of debris that included mattresses, a broken sink and a refrigerator with its door missing and food jumbled inside. Vinyl records, shoes and other personal belongings littered the rubble.
James Williams said he heard loud banging at the construction site all day Wednesday as he worked at a deli across the street. He said he noticed bricks falling from a building next to the site. Then the whole building fell down.
Video below: Brooklyn building collapse witness Anthony Griggs describes what he saw and heard
The collapse ripped away a wall shared with an adjacent building, which remained standing with the interiors of its apartments exposed — closets crammed with clothing, a stuffed bear sitting atop a pile of shoes and laundry heaped on a pink bedspread.
Security camera video from the building showed an interior stairway shaking as the wall beside it fell in a loud crash and a cloud of dust. The camera later recorded a firefighter helping a resident descend the same stairs above a yawning abyss of debris.
“Nice and easy,” the firefighter said as the person clutched both his hand and the railing.
Despite the chaos, construction workers who had barely escaped with their lives turned around and began clawing through the wreckage to free survivors, said Mamdani. He said their swift actions saved lives.
The mayor said Thursday that two construction workers were among the dead.
Related video below: Brooklyn building collapse Thursday afternoon news conference update
They included Caguana Cosquillo, a 26-year-old immigrant from Ecuador who had a young child and pregnant wife, his brother, Carlos Caguana, told WNBC-TV.
“He was the sole provider for the family,” Caguana said, adding that his brother's wife was devastated.
“She’s completely overwhelmed,” he said, “and can’t even find the words to speak.”
Rico reported from Atlanta. AP journalists Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia; Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa; and Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, contributed.

title: ‘General Hospital’ actor Randall England dies at 75
text:
(Gray News) - Actor Randall England, known for his role as Jack Slater on the popular soap opera “General Hospital,” has died. He was 75.
England died on Sept. 25 surrounded by loved ones, according to an obituary shared by his family. He died following a battle with esophageal cancer, according to Deadline.
“An actor, model, writer, producer and musician, Randall lived a life full of interesting people and stories. Of all his roles, being a father and ‘Pappaw’ to his grandchildren meant the most to him,” the obituary read.
England appeared on “General Hospital” from November 1984 through June 1985 as the villainous jewel thief Jack Slater, according to the Hollywood Reporter.
His other television appearances include “The Young and the Restless,” “Dallas” and “Baywatch.”
England also starred in the films “Beverly Hills Chihuahuas” and “Cat City,” as well as Maroon 5’s music video, “Sugar.”
“Charming, loving, and generous with his time and energy, Randall was someone people could count on. Friends, family, and former students have remembered his authenticity and the steady presence he offered in their lives. He offered encouragement and advice freely. His legacy lives on in the people he loved, taught, and supported,” his obituary read.
England is survived by his daughter Micaela Reed and his son-in-law Sam Reed, as well as his sister Linda Baker, grandchildren Katherine and Julian, and his mother Catherine Burgess.
The family asked for donations to be made to the Esophageal Cancer Action Network in lieu of flowers.
