title: Roma Cafe and Bramhall to close in Portland
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Roma Cafe and Bramhall announced on Wednesday their plans to close later this month.
The historic Congress Street properties are owned by restaurateur Michael Fraser, who could not be reached immediately for details on the decision.
“It’s hard to find the right words for this, but after so many years of good food, strong drinks, familiar faces and nights that turned into mornings, Bramhall and Roma will be closing their doors on November 21st,” a post on Roma’s Instagram page reads in part.
Bramhall was a speakeasy in the 1920s, located in the basement beneath Roma Cafe. It later became Bramhall Pub before closing in 2009. Fraser reopened Bramhall in 2014.
Roma Cafe opened in 1924 at 489 Congress St., then moved to its current location at 769 Congress St. in 1935. Before it closed in 2009, it was considered one of Portland’s best special occasion, romantic restaurants.
Fraser reopened Roma along with partners Guy Streitburger and Anders Tallberg in 2017.

title: 14-year-old volleyball player loses part of her leg after collapsing during practice
text:
CASA GRANDE, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - A 14-year-old volleyball player needed the lower half of her leg amputated after she collapsed during practice because of a heart condition she didn’t know she had. She is now determined to walk and play volleyball again with a prosthetic.
Delilah Mendez, a 14-year-old student-athlete at Casa Grande Union High School, loves playing volleyball. She had big dreams of getting a college scholarship, but two months ago, everything changed when she had a health crisis during practice and collapsed on the court.
“I couldn’t catch my breath, and then, I felt dizzy at the same time,” Delilah said.
Her mother, Rosie Mendez, received a call that her daughter had passed out.
“I thought maybe she was just dehydrated or something small, so I didn’t think anything serious until they told me she didn’t have a pulse,” Mendez said.
‘She is a fighter’
Delilah was rushed to a local hospital then flown to Phoenix Children’s Hospital, where she was placed on a heart and lung machine to keep her alive. Doctors determined she had an underlying heart condition and needed surgery right away.
But complications led to blood clots and circulation issues, and doctors had to amputate the lower half of Delilah’s left leg.
“She is a fighter. She went through a lot. She even surprised me with how strong she was with everything, especially her leg. That was really hard for me to tell her about that,” Mendez said.
Mendez says Delilah is trying to stay positive.
“She’s a very independent person. She always likes to do everything on her own. That’s the part where I think she might be struggling a little bit,” Mendez said.
Goal to return to volleyball
After two months in the hospital, Delilah is home, playing video games and spending time with her younger brothers. She knows the road to recovery will be long, but she is determined to walk and play volleyball again with a prosthetic.
“It’s gonna be pretty hard, but I think I can get through it,” Delilah said. “I want to get through this and learn how to walk again with a prosthetic and do all the things I used to do.”
Mendez believes her daughter will one day return to the court.
“I believe she is strong, and she’s shown us she is strong. I believe she’s gonna be back out there, and I will be very proud of her,” she said.
Delilah is currently walking with crutches and getting stronger every day. She says support from friends, family and teammates has made a difference.
“My volleyball team has sent cards, and they’ve been really supportive. My best friend has been visiting me. She’s on the volleyball team, too,” she said.
Classmates have made signs and T-shirts to raise money for Delilah and her family as they deal with rising medical bills. A GoFundMe has also been set up to help the family.

title: Brooklyn building collapse killed 2 children and 6 adults, mayor says
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Investigators began what could be a long search for the cause of a Brooklyn apartment building collapse that killed eight people as the fire department ended rescue operations Thursday after the last victim was freed from the wreckage.
The three-story building gave way while construction workers were digging Wednesday afternoon at an adjacent lot, causing New York City’s mayor to order inspections at about 100 building sites involving companies related to the project.
“If there is anyone, or any entity, operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said during a news conference.
Investigators have not determined what caused the collapse. Two children were among those killed and 18 others were injured, including four firefighters, Mamdani said.
One witness said he watched bricks fall minutes before the disaster while a woman in a neighboring building said she and fellow residents blamed vibrations from the construction for cracks that appeared in their apartment walls.
Emergency workers used power saws and pickaxes to get through the debris, pulling four victims out of the rubble in the early hours of Thursday. Hours later, excavators removed larger chunks of the wreckage so searchers could get deeper into the construction pit, said New York Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore.
Witnesses describe the aftermath and destruction
James Williams, who works at a deli across the street, said he heard loud banging at the site all day Wednesday and looked outside to see bricks falling. “Two minutes later, the building collapsed,” he said.
As the building crumbled and exposed the neighboring building, Williams spotted a woman on a staircase. “There wasn’t anything I could do,” he said, his voice cracking.
Customers and stylists at a nearby hair salon jumped up and ran onto the sidewalk as the building fell.
“We heard the boom and we all rushed outside and saw smoke and dust everywhere,” said hairstylist Brigitte Anama.
She saw emergency workers pulling people from the rubble, including what appeared to be a child. “People were saying, ‘Pray for the baby, pray for the baby,’” Anama said.
Dervie Mapp, who lives along the construction site, said she and others complained for months about the project. Her landlord brought engineers into the building, but residents never received an inspection report, she said.
Determining cause of Brooklyn collapse will take time, expert says
Construction safety expert Glenn Corbett of John Jay College in New York said it’s way too early to know what caused the accident.
“It could be a design flaw, it could be a construction flaw, or it could be some kind of work that was going on,” he said.
It appeared that the shoring of the excavation work failed, but finding out why will take more investigating, he said.
The one-story building previously on the site was demolished earlier this year. Records show a contractor, Mordechai “Marty” Waisbrod, notified the city that excavation would begin in September and include rock blasting.
Permit applications indicated plans to dig below 15 feet (4.5 meters). Phone and email messages were left at one of Waisbrod’s Brooklyn-based businesses.
Engineering drawings submitted with the applications show various plans to brace walls at the edge of the site. Messages were left Thursday for the engineer, Jieming Wang, and for an inspector who’s listed as being involved with the project.
Rescuers faced a massive pile of rubble
This was the second high-profile structural problem with a building in New York in the past five months. In July, several buildings in Manhattan were evacuated after support columns buckled inside a skyscraper that once was the headquarters of Pfizer.
First responders in Brooklyn worked to clear a massive heap that included mattresses, a broken sink and a refrigerator tossed on its side. Scattered in the debris were vinyl records, clothes and shoes.
Firefighters pulled a pregnant woman from the rubble Wednesday, hoisted her up on a stretcher and rushed her to a waiting ambulance. Others were rescued as the night wore on.
Building records show there were four apartments on the upper two floors and a commercial unit on the ground floor of the collapsed building.
Victims were from multiple countries
Among those killed and injured were people from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador and Trinidad, New York’s mayor said. Two of the dead were construction workers, Mamdani said.
Some workers who survived joined firefighters in digging out survivors, he said.
The Consulate of Ecuador in New York said José Luis Caguana Cosquillo and Gabriel Ariolfo Siguencia Yupa, both from Ecuador, were among those killed.
Carlos Caguana said his brother, José, was working at the construction site and had a pregnant wife and a young child.
“He was the sole provider for the family,” Caguana told WNBC-TV.
Two Colombian children and an adult were also killed in the collapse, according to the country’s consulate in New York. Another Colombian woman was injured and is receiving medial assistance.
The surrounding blocks along Flatbush Avenue, a busy thoroughfare in Brooklyn, are tightly packed with older brick buildings and a few newly built apartment complexes. A mix of Caribbean and Mexican restaurants reflects the diversity of the neighborhood.
Inspectors reported violations earlier this year
New York City’s buildings commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, said Wednesday that construction workers were excavating the empty lot next door when the building buckled. The city’s Department of Buildings is investigating.
City officials said a stop work order was issued in March after inspectors concluded the building next door was being demolished without adequate overhead protection such as netting to shield neighboring buildings, the department said in an emailed statement.
In April, inspectors found that the demolition work had resumed in violation of the stop work order, the department said. Work was allowed to continue after the problems were corrected, it said.

title: ‘Help us’: Kids rescued after holding handwritten note against home’s window
text:
KISSIMMEE, Fla. (Gray News) - Police in Florida are praising the bravery of a child who held a handwritten note that read “Help us” against a window while hiding during a domestic disturbance.
Kissimmee Police say they responded Oct. 26 to a domestic disturbance involving 33-year-old Andre Janard Smithson at the Florida Ridge Condos. A woman inside the home told her sister that Smithson was “beating” her, WTSP reports, citing an arrest affidavit.
Family members told police that children were in the home, and they feared for their safety.
Using a drone, police found three kids hiding in a guest room. Meanwhile, Smithson and the victim were in the master bedroom with their 5-month-old daughter, according to WTSP.
One of the kids held a handwritten note against the window that read “Help us.” Police later praised the child’s bravery in a Facebook post about the incident.
WTSP reports that Smithson spoke to officers by phone and refused repeated requests to let the victim and kids leave the home. Police say the kids were able to safely escape while Smithson was distracted.
With help from a SWAT team and crisis negotiators, police say Smithson eventually surrendered peacefully. He was arrested on charges of false imprisonment and an outstanding active warrant.
Smithson reportedly told investigators he wanted to spend time with his infant daughter before going to jail, according to WTSP.

title: Paul LePage’s victory confirmed after ranked-choice count, state says
text:
Former Gov. Paul LePage won the race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District after a ranked-choice vote tabulation this week, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said Thursday, confirming the 78-year-old Republican’s remarkable, against-the-grain victory.
LePage entered the ranked-choice tabulation Monday just 362 votes shy of the majority threshold and more than 5,000 votes ahead of his Democratic opponent, State Auditor Matt Dunlap. The tabulation, which reallocates blank and write-in votes and confirms the validity of all ballots cast, confirmed that LePage won 50.8% of the vote, to Dunlap’s 49.2%.
In the end, LePage’s margin of victory was just 40 votes larger than before the tabulation. He won by 5,458 votes.
The competitive race was all but decided last week: LePage declared victory in a Bangor press conference the day after the election, and Dunlap conceded to him a day later. Each acknowledged there was no mathematical way back for Dunlap.
Regardless, the election went to a ranked-choice runoff because neither candidate received more than 50% of the total first-choice vote. That’s required by state law, no matter what the candidates say.
State law also stipulates that all ballots cast are counted toward the total, including those left blank. More than 6,000 blank ballots — those that did not rank LePage, Dunlap or the declared write-in candidate first — were reallocated to their second choice, or removed from the total vote count if they were left completely blank.
More than 3,600 ballots were left totally blank for this race, according to the state’s official tally. After eliminating those, LePage had secured more than 50% of the vote.
Another 258 people “overvoted,” or voted for multiple candidates as their first choice, and 434 people voted for only a write-in and did not rank LePage or Dunlap as their second choice.
After the ballot review and ranked-choice tabulation, LePage gained 627 votes and Dunlap gained 587. They ended with 170,890 and 165,432 votes, respectively.
The Department of the Secretary of State conducted the tedious process of verifying the validity and accuracy of the ballots over three days, with each day livestreamed for the public. Observers and members of the media watched Thursday afternoon as election officials manually reconciled hundreds of auxiliary ballots — or those that could not be read by vote-tabulator machines last week.
The ranked-choice tabulation itself was very quick: Maine Director of Elections Heidi Peckham ran the numbers at about 1:30 p.m. on a massive spreadsheet that indicated all first- and second-choice votes for each ballot cast in the 2nd District. That spreadsheet is now posted to the state’s website.
Bellows said last week that it was unprecedented for a Maine election to go to ranked-choice tabulation with a candidate so close to a majority of votes.
In 2024, the 2nd District race between incumbent Democratic Rep. Jared Golden and Republican Austin Theriault went to a runoff after 3% of voters did not select either candidate. That runoff began a week after the election and finished three days later, with Golden declared the winner. A subsequent recount confirmed his win.
In that case, Golden’s lead was much slimmer and his gap to secure a majority much larger than LePage’s in this year’s race.
The former governor’s return to elected office is especially remarkable in the context of this election cycle: LePage would become just the third Republican so far in this “blue wave” midterm to flip a Democratic-held U.S. House seat, and the only one to do so in a district that hadn’t been gerrymandered in Republicans’ favor in the past two years.
All of Maine’s other elections heavily favored Democrats, with Troy Jackson defeating incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Hannah Pingree easily winning the governor’s race. Democrats expanded their majorities in both chambers of the Maine Legislature.
But by running up the margins in deep-red, rural areas, LePage completed his political comeback.
LePage, who will be 80 years old by his first reelection opportunity, will be one of the oldest freshman congressmen in American history — a back-bencher with little individual lawmaking power in a heavily Democratic House. He’ll be the only Republican from New England in Congress.
LePage has already been in Washington this week for congressional freshman orientation, where he has met with Golden and other incoming members of Congress. Meanwhile, members of his team were present during the ranked-choice tabulation in Augusta this week.
“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” LePage adviser Brent Littlefield said in a social media statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

title: Ex-Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip pleads guilty to lesser charge in 1997 murder
text:
Former Oklahoma death row prisoner Richard Glossip, who spent nearly 30 years incarcerated and was on the brink of execution three times for a 1997 murder, pleaded guilty to a lesser charge, his attorney said Thursday.
Glossip had been sentenced to death over the killing in Oklahoma City of his former boss, motel owner Barry Van Treese. Van Treese was beaten with a baseball bat in what prosecutors have alleged was a murder-for-hire scheme.
The U.S. Supreme Court previously threw out Glossip’s conviction, and he was released on bond in May to await retrial. His longstanding claims of innocence have drawn support from Kim Kardashian and other prominent figures.
Glossip pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of being an accessory, and the murder charge was dismissed, according to Don Knight, Glossip’s attorney. He said Glossip will be sentenced in December.

title: Death Notice: Ruth Ida Seigars-Herrick
Midcoast town still contending with toxic carpet pile 25 years later
text:
Officials with the state and the town of Warren continue to map a strategy for cleaning up the rifle range off Route 90 that was turned into a massive illegal waste site in the 1990s.
On Nov. 6, representatives from the Maine Department of Environmental Protection’s Land Bureau and the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife visited the site with town officials.
Town Manager Sherry Howard said the visit was to review existing wetlands and natural resources on the property and discuss how the proposed cleanup and potential redevelopment activities may affect these environmental features.
“This coordination is an important part of the planning process, helping the project team identify environmental considerations and applicable permitting requirements as cleanup plans continue to develop,” the town stated in a notice to residents on its website.
The town was notified in May 2025 that it will receive a $4 million Brownfields grant to help in the cleanup of the estimated 27,000 tons of waste.
Howard said the town hopes to begin a community engagement in the next month to hear from residents about what they want done with the property.
“We’re still in the ideas mode,” the manager said.
The money will be used to clean up the former Steamship Navigation Site at 2287 Camden Road (Route 90). The 71-acre site had been used for multiple purposes including a firing range, firearms retail store, and photographic laboratory. The site has been vacant and unused since the 1990s and is contaminated with metals and inorganic contaminants. Grant funds also will be used to support community engagement activities, according to the EPA in its news release.
In 1997, Chester and Kathleen Dunican bought land off Route 90 in Warren under the corporate name of Steamship Navigation Co. The property had been the Oyster River Rifle Range, used for many years, including by local police departments for training.
In meetings with the Warren Planning Board in 1997, Dunican said the rifle range would become the largest on the East Coast. His plans called for a new retail store, a new lodge for club members and a 7,000-square-foot indoor shooting range. He said the range would create many new jobs for local residents.
Dunican said, however, it needed to accept polyester fiber scraps from the former Gates Formed-Fibre Products Inc. of Auburn to create berms for the rifle range.
The Dunicans were paid an estimated $1 million from Gates Formed-Fibre to accept the material that had been largely used as linings for the trunks of motor vehicles. Opponents to the range questioned whether the owners were simply using the property as an unlicensed dump to make money by accepting the material.
The owners abandoned the property after accepting more than 27,000 tons of waste, leaving the property covered with huge mounds of uncovered materials as far as the eye can see. The plans for the massive rifle range did not materialize. The owners failed to pay their property taxes, which forced residents to vote each year for the past 23 years on whether to foreclose on the property. The town had balked at foreclosing on the property out of concern of being liable for the environmental cleanup.
On Dec. 7, 2022, Warren residents finally agreed to foreclose and take ownership of the land after reaching an agreement with the Maine DEP that the town would not be liable.
The town and Maine Department of Environmental Protection had tried several projects that would reuse the material including being burned at the Dragon cement plant in nearby Thomaston. The Penobscot Energy Recovery Co. trash incinerator in Orrington had also considered accepting the wastes but that did not come to pass. A Massachusetts company also had considered using the material to manufacture composite materials, but the expense was exorbitant and the proposal was dropped.

title: Maine Man Who Picks Up Litter While Running Finds Wallet Full of Cash
text:
Maine Man Who Picks Up Litter While Running Finds Wallet Full of Cash
We often drive down our local roads and notice the trash, but one young Portland man is doing something to try to make it disappear. His name is Ben, and his Instagram, ploggarun, is all about picking up one piece of trash at a time.
Why? To make the world more beautiful.
Ben practices something called “plogging,” which comes from a swedish word and is a combo of running, jogging and picking up litter. Instead of passing trash on his runs, he now stops to collect it and dispose of it properly.
And believe it or not, this whole thing started with a conversation with his wife.
Ben pitched her an idea: What if he started grabbing the bottles he saw along his running route? He decided to give it a try, and on his first run, he counted 63 bottles. At five cents each, that was $3.15.
The next time, he brought bags and started collecting them.
Since then, Ben has turned those bottle deposits into more than $550, this is all while making his city a little cleaner. He is a South Portland native, and he invests in his community with this.
He's been doing this since January 2025, and what started as a simple idea has turned into something much bigger.
Ben describes the feeling as a mix of frustration and appreciation. He doesn't want to see all the trash, but he also realizes that if nobody else is going to pick it up, he'll do it.
And apparently, a whole lot of people are here for it. Ben now has more than 130,000 followers supporting his “trashfluencing” journey.
But Ben's impact goes far beyond picking up litter.
During one of his plogging runs, he came across a wallet filled with cash. And I'm talking a thick stack of cash sitting inside a zip-up wallet.
Rather than walking away or keeping what he found, Ben immediately turned it over to a nearby police officer.
It's a small moment, but one that says an awful lot about the kind of person he is.
In a world where it's easy to focus on everything going wrong, stories like this are a refreshing reminder that good people are still out there.
Babes, the next time you're driving, walking or plogging around Portland and spot someone in a bright yellow shirt jogging with a bag of collected trash, give Ben a wave or even a thank-you.
He’s cleaning up our community, inspiring others to do a little better, and proving that sometimes the biggest difference starts with simply stopping to pick something up.

title: Eddington school board member held without bail following new drug charges
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - An Eddington mother and school board member was ordered held without bail Thursday after pleading not guilty to new drug-related charges.
Brittany Wood, 36, turned herself in to Penobscot County sheriff’s deputies Wednesday night after a multiday search. She pleaded not guilty to drug possession, falsifying physical evidence, and violating conditions of release.
New charges
Deputies allege they found Wood with what turned out to be illegal drugs during a traffic stop over the weekend. Wood said in court Thursday that she had a prescription for the drugs.
The judge ordered Wood held without bail because she was already out on bail on aggravated assault charges. Those charges stem from allegations that her then-9-month-old baby nearly died from exposure to drugs, including fentanyl and cocaine, in May.
Despite the judge’s caution, Wood addressed the court.
“I don’t know why the state feels that I would need to be held away from my children, my family, my responsibilities. I’m doing everything right. I have extreme circumstances. I’m cooperating. I’m working. I’m doing everything that everybody’s asking — DHHS, law enforcement, everyone in the whole world. And I’m doing the best I can,” she said.
School board status
Wood remains an elected member of the RSU 63 school board. Under board policy, she could be removed if she misses three consecutive meetings.

title: New guideline urges routine prostate cancer screening for middle-aged men
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Middle-aged men should undergo regular screening for prostate cancer, the American Cancer Society said Thursday in a major change to its guidelines.
The screening involves a simple blood test, and men at average risk of getting prostate cancer should get that PSA test every two years between the ages of 50 and 69, the cancer society advised.
Men at high risk, including Black men and those with a strong family history of prostate cancer, should get yearly PSA checks and start earlier, at age 45.
Thursday’s guideline update marks a shift in thinking about routine blood tests for PSA, or prostate-specific antigen.
Since 2010, the cancer society has recommended that men at average risk talk with their doctors about whether to get regular PSA tests. That’s a protein produced by both normal and cancerous prostate cells, meaning a high level might signal a tumor but also could be from a benign enlarged prostate or be a temporary spike from vigorous exercise.
Widespread PSA testing in the past was blamed for overtreatment of slow-growing tumors and unnecessary follow-up testing in men who turned out to not have cancer.
The updated advice comes after advances in understanding PSA’s benefits and how to reduce potential harms, according to the cancer society. That includes steps such as repeating a PSA test to be sure it’s really high or adding an MRI scan to help identify who needs a biopsy.
How long should men continue screening? Starting at 70, men should talk with their doctors about whether it’s beneficial to continue the routine PSA checks, the guideline says. But it discourages screening for men 80 and older and those of any age who aren’t expected to live another 10 years because of other health problems.
Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men. The cancer society estimates more than 333,000 men in the U.S. will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2026, and about 36,000 will die of it.

title: 'Blatant criminality': White House warns Democrats over proposed investigations in letter
text:
'Blatant criminality': White House warns Democrats on proposed investigations in letter
The White House criticized Democrats' planned investigations into the Trump administration in a letter directed at one top lawmaker.
'Blatant criminality': White House warns Democrats on proposed investigations in letter
The White House criticized Democrats' planned investigations into the Trump administration in a letter directed at one top lawmaker.
In a newly released letter, the White House issued a stark warning to Democrats about their planned investigations into the Trump administration, accusing them of pushing a process driven by "pettiness, hatred and an unlawful motive to intimidate" rather than pursuing a legitimate legislative purpose.
The letter, dated Nov. 9, was directed to Rep. Robert Garcia, D-California, the incoming Chairman of the House Oversight Committee.
Garcia previously suggested looking into several possible cases, including President Donald Trump and his family's business dealings in crypto and minerals, the Trump administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case, Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations, and construction projects like the White House ballroom.
In the letter, the administration said it was "monitoring abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators," citing public statements such as Garcia's election night warning to Trump officials to "lawyer up."
On Thursday, Garcia doubled down on his previous statement.
"Our job is to ensure that there are checks and balances, and the idea that the president, the attorney general, the White House legal team is trying to intimidate us is not going to work," Garcia said in a TV interview. "They're going to be investigated because we want to stop corruption and we want to pass laws to ensure it doesn't happen again."
Attorney General Todd Blanche previously warned that the Justice Department could investigate if Democrats' rhetoric turned threatening. He later acknowledged that Congress does have oversight authority and said the DOJ would cooperate to answer lawmaker inquiries.
Separately, the Associated Press declared Democratic candidate Scott Colom the winner of Mississippi's Senate race over incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by a razor-thin margin.
Colom's victory increases Democrats' majority in the Senate from 54 to 55 seats, adding more leverage for Democrats to pass legislation and issue subpoenas and investigations.
The win also marks a major shift in Mississippi, which has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since the 1980s.

title: Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree hires chief of staff
text:
Maine Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree is tapping her mother’s longtime chief of staff to take on the top role in her incoming administration.
Pingree, a 50-year-old North Haven Democrat, announced Thursday that she’s hiring Jesse Connolly as her chief of staff, where he will be tasked with managing the governor’s inner circle, policy agenda and messaging.
Connolly has served in the same role for U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, since 2012. He has prior experience working in the state Legislature, as well as on gubernatorial and presidential campaigns.
“Jesse is one of the most capable, strategic, and trusted leaders I have ever worked with, and I am grateful he is joining my administration,” Hannah Pingree said in a written statement.
The announcement marks the governor-elect’s first major staffing decision. This week, she assembled a 22-member transition team to recruit and vet 15 Cabinet positions — roles she hopes to have mostly filled before being inaugurated on Jan. 6.
Connolly served as Hannah Pingree’s chief of staff for four years when she was majority leader from 2006 to 2008 and the speaker of the Maine House of Representatives from 2008 to 2010.
“Governor-elect Pingree has a bold vision for Maine and the experience to deliver it,” Connolly said in a written statement. “This administration has a real opportunity to make a difference in people’s lives, from making Maine more affordable to building a stronger economy and a government that works for every community. It will be meaningful to be part of that work.
“Our job now is to build the strongest team and get to work for Mainers.”
During the campaign, Pingree said she planned to tackle the state’s affordable housing crisis, improve public education and support small businesses. She also vowed to pass a bill within the first 100 days of her administration to recognize the inherent sovereignty of tribes in Maine.
Pingree must also address a structural budget gap. A four-year budget forecast released by the Mills administration in September projected a structural deficit of roughly $1.3 billion by the 2028-29 biennium.
Connolly is a Portland native and holds a political science degree from Bates College. He lives in South Portland with his wife, Nicole Clegg, who is CEO of Planned Parenthood of Northern New England, and their son, Finn.

title: Only one person is to blame for the blue wave
text:
Jacob Posik is the political director of Maine Civic Action and the director of legislative affairs for the Maine Policy Institute. He lives in Biddeford.
Dear Mr. President,
I hope you or someone from your team reads this.
I’m a 32-year-old libertarian who leans conservative. In November 2024, I voted for you. Two years later, I regret that decision. I wouldn’t have voted for Kamala Harris, but in hindsight, I would have left that office blank on my ballot.
Your second presidency has been a tremendous disappointment so far to me and millions of other Americans, and if you don’t understand why, it will continue to be one.
When I voted for you, I was voting for the “America First” idea you championed.
To me, that meant exactly what you told voters it meant: prioritizing the problems facing Americans rather than endlessly involving ourselves in other parts of the globe. It meant putting Americans first by getting our own house in order before assuming responsibility for the rest of the world.
Apparently, I misunderstood. Or perhaps, you lied. Regardless, it’s clear today the term “America First” is nebulous. It means whatever you want it to mean on any given day.
That’s not a real political movement, that’s narcissism.
Like most Americans, I’ve seen energy costs increase in recent years more than any other line item in my family budget. In 2024, I voted for the candidate who promised affordable energy. That promise was especially appealing because the boneheads in Augusta enacted policies that enrich their friends in the solar industry and hurt Mainers to the tune of $220 million per year.
I voted for lower prices, not foreign policy decisions that would send them skyrocketing. Now home heating oil is above $6 per gallon and it costs more than $50 to fill my SUV. That’s to say nothing of the cost increases from tariffs or the budgetary mismanagement that is bankrupting our country as quickly as the Biden administration.
As someone who considers themself a free-speech absolutist, I was horrified by the Biden administration’s efforts to pressure social media companies into suppressing speech, especially dissenting opinions surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic and the ensuing government interventions.
I voted for you because you promised to restore free speech, not weaponize the federal government against people who express opinions you dislike. Then I watched your administration threaten, deport and take other action against college students who dared protest violence against Palestinians paid for with our tax dollars.
After the Biden administration let anyone with a pulse come here illegally for four years, I voted to restore our borders and deport law-breaking criminals who didn’t belong.
Then one morning while making breakfast, I heard one of my neighbors down the street — Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero — get gunned down just blocks from where I live. A law-abiding man with no criminal record.
I’m part of the generation that watched the 9/11 attacks unfold on a box television that was wheeled into my second-grade classroom. I’ve spent most my life watching American politicians squander trillions of dollars and countless American lives fighting pointless wars in the Middle East.
I voted for you because you promised to end those wars, not to prolong old wars like the one in Ukraine or start new ones like the one in Iran.
On these issues and others, your administration has repeatedly placed the interests of foreign governments, political allies and your own ego ahead of the American people.
Two years into your second presidency, the America First agenda I voted for is nowhere to be found. Instead, those words have been perverted into a meaningless political slogan.
You cannot sell Americans a bill of goods, immediately renege on virtually every promise you made and then expect voters to remain loyal to you.
The trouncing Republicans experienced across the country on Nov. 3 should make that abundantly clear. You are the person most chiefly responsible for that disastrous showing.
Republicans didn’t lose because your name wasn’t on the ballot. They lost because you are the sitting president and have not delivered on your promises to the American people. In fact, in many ways, we’ve gotten the opposite.
You promised economic relief and pursued policies that make everyday life more expensive for everyone. You promised free speech and delivered government intimidation. You promised to deport criminals and masked ICE agents are shooting legal immigrants in the streets. You promised peace and delivered more war.
This election wasn’t about socialism or any other nonsense the conservative talking heads keep droning on about. It was about your failure to deliver on your promises to the American people.
Unless something changes quickly, your administration’s inability to put America first will be the defining betrayal of your presidency.

title: Hunt for clues in deadly Brooklyn building collapse will take time
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Investigators began what could be a long search for the cause of a Brooklyn apartment building collapse that killed eight people as the fire department ended rescue operations Thursday after the last victim was freed from the wreckage.
The three-story building gave way while construction workers were digging Wednesday afternoon at an adjacent lot, causing New York City’s mayor to order inspections at about 100 building sites involving companies related to the project.
“If there is anyone, or any entity, operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said during a news conference.
Investigators have not determined what caused the collapse. Two children were among those killed and 18 others were injured, including four firefighters, Mamdani said.
One witness said he watched bricks fall minutes before the disaster while a woman in a neighboring building said she and fellow residents blamed vibrations from the construction for cracks that appeared in their apartment walls.
Emergency workers used power saws and pickaxes to get through the debris, pulling four victims out of the rubble in the early hours of Thursday. Hours later, excavators removed larger chunks of the wreckage so searchers could get deeper into the construction pit, said New York Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore.
Witnesses describe the aftermath and destruction
James Williams, who works at a deli across the street, said he heard loud banging at the site all day Wednesday and looked outside to see bricks falling. “Two minutes later, the building collapsed,” he said.
As the building crumbled and exposed the neighboring building, Williams spotted a woman on a staircase. “There wasn’t anything I could do,” he said, his voice cracking.
Customers and stylists at a nearby hair salon jumped up and ran onto the sidewalk as the building fell.
“We heard the boom and we all rushed outside and saw smoke and dust everywhere,” said hairstylist Brigitte Anama.
She saw emergency workers pulling people from the rubble, including what appeared to be a child. “People were saying, ‘Pray for the baby, pray for the baby,’” Anama said.
Dervie Mapp, who lives along the construction site, said she and others complained for months about the project. Her landlord brought engineers into the building, but residents never received an inspection report, she said.
Determining cause of Brooklyn collapse will take time, expert says
Construction safety expert Glenn Corbett of John Jay College in New York said it’s way too early to know what caused the accident.
“It could be a design flaw, it could be a construction flaw, or it could be some kind of work that was going on,” he said.
It appeared that the shoring of the excavation work failed, but finding out why will take more investigating, he said.
The one-story building previously on the site was demolished earlier this year. Records show a contractor, Mordechai “Marty” Waisbrod, notified the city that excavation would begin in September and include rock blasting.
Permit applications indicated plans to dig below 15 feet (4.5 meters). Phone and email messages were left at one of Waisbrod’s Brooklyn-based businesses.
Engineering drawings submitted with the applications show various plans to brace walls at the edge of the site. Messages were left Thursday for the engineer, Jieming Wang, and for an inspector who’s listed as being involved with the project.
Rescuers faced a massive pile of rubble
This was the second high-profile structural problem with a building in New York in the past five months. In July, several buildings in Manhattan were evacuated after support columns buckled inside a skyscraper that once was the headquarters of Pfizer.
First responders in Brooklyn worked to clear a massive heap that included mattresses, a broken sink and a refrigerator tossed on its side. Scattered in the debris were vinyl records, clothes and shoes.
Firefighters pulled a pregnant woman from the rubble Wednesday, hoisted her up on a stretcher and rushed her to a waiting ambulance. Others were rescued as the night wore on.
Building records show there were four apartments on the upper two floors and a commercial unit on the ground floor of the collapsed building.
Victims were from multiple countries
Among those killed and injured were people from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador and Trinidad, New York’s mayor said. Two of the dead were construction workers, Mamdani said.
Some workers who survived joined firefighters in digging out survivors, he said.
The Consulate of Ecuador in New York said José Luis Caguana Cosquillo and Gabriel Ariolfo Siguencia Yupa, both from Ecuador, were among those killed.
Carlos Caguana said his brother, José, was working at the construction site and had a pregnant wife and a young child.
“He was the sole provider for the family,” Caguana told WNBC-TV.
Two Colombian children and an adult were also killed in the collapse, according to the country’s consulate in New York. Another Colombian woman was injured and is receiving medial assistance.
The surrounding blocks along Flatbush Avenue, a busy thoroughfare in Brooklyn, are tightly packed with older brick buildings and a few newly built apartment complexes. A mix of Caribbean and Mexican restaurants reflects the diversity of the neighborhood.
Inspectors reported violations earlier this year
New York City’s buildings commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, said Wednesday that construction workers were excavating the empty lot next door when the building buckled. The city’s Department of Buildings is investigating.
City officials said a stop work order was issued in March after inspectors concluded the building next door was being demolished without adequate overhead protection such as netting to shield neighboring buildings, the department said in an emailed statement.
In April, inspectors found that the demolition work had resumed in violation of the stop work order, the department said. Work was allowed to continue after the problems were corrected, it said.

title: Orono, Old Town set to compete in separate state football championships on Saturday
text:
ORONO, OLD TOWN, Maine (WABI) - The Orono Red Riots are up against Old Orchard Beach in the 8-Man Small School State Football Championship.
The Red Riots pulled the No. 2 over No. 1 upset against Stearns in the North title game, 55-52, after starting their playoff run with a 64-22 triumph over Washington Academy.
“We’ve been improving all year. That’s what Coach has been saying. Every single day, we’re using it to get better. I think we’ve gotten better every single day until now. title: US returns over $12 billion in oil proceeds to Venezuela since Maduro's ouster, report says
text:
US returns over $12 billion in oil proceeds to Venezuela since Maduro's ouster, report says
The Trump administration says it has returned more than $12 billion, or almost 99%, of the revenue obtained from the sales of Venezuelan oil since it ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro in January.
In a report released Thursday by the State Department, the accounting firm KPMG said the sales of Venezuelan crude, along with minor amounts of gold, minerals and fertilizer, produced $12.26 billion. Almost all of the money has been returned to Venezuela under the terms of a broad energy deal reached with the country's interim authorities, according to the report.
As of Sept. 30, the end of the 2026 budget year, $168.6 million remained in an escrow account managed by the U.S. Treasury Department, the report said.
Under the terms of the deal, Venezuelan crude is sold on the open market, with proceeds going into the U.S.-managed account. Venezuelan officials then seek approval for those funds to be returned to the country to pay for infrastructure and humanitarian needs.
The report offers a window into the Venezuelan government’s finances since the U.S. captured Maduro — bringing him to New York to face drug-trafficking charges — and took effective control of the country’s dilapidated oil industry.
The bulk of the more than $12 billion in oil revenue collected by the U.S. through September was disbursed to individuals and businesses in Venezuela through foreign exchange transactions with commercial banks in the country.
However, some $133 million was channeled to directly pay for services or supplies needed by the Venezuelan government, the report showed.
U.S.-approved transactions include $5 million for Miami-based law firm Greenberg Traurig, nearly $24 million for dialysis and coal-mining equipment, and $8.7 million to settle Venezuela’s debts for vaccine procurements with the Pan-American Health Organization, it said.
The report redacts the names of the 20 companies that purchased oil and gold during the first nine months of 2026.
Still, each had to go through vetting by the U.S. government for compliance with sanctions and money-laundering controls — a sharp break from past practice when Venezuela’s government faced little scrutiny in the management of its oil funds.

title: Three UMaine football storylines to follow against Albany
text:
The University of Maine football team outgained Rhode Island 352-212 on Oct. 31 but still couldn’t pick up a win. The Black Bears lost 14-13 in overtime to head into their bye week on an eight-game losing streak.
After a week off, the Black Bears (1-8, 1-5 Coastal Athletic Association) will try to end their skid when they face Albany (6-4, 4-2 CAA) on the road at noon Saturday (FloSports). Here are three storylines to watch ahead of that contest.
Kicking-game woes?
Sam Tremblay was 10 for 10 on field goals over the first seven games. In the last two games, though, the sophomore is 0 of 2 on field goals and 1 of 3 on extra points.
Those misses were especially costly against Rhode Island. First, he was unsuccessful on 34-yard attempt in the first half. Then, after Maine scored first in overtime, the Rams blocked Tremblay’s extra point. A touchdown and extra point by Rhode Island ended the game.
“I don’t know (if it’s a mental thing),” said Maine coach Jordan Stevens. “We’ve had full confidence in Sam, and he’s just been so terrific for us over the last year. … We’re continuing to work with him, and creating competition within our kickers as well is really important. We’ve got to put the best guy out there.”
Streaks of infamy
The calendar hadn’t even hit September the last time Maine won a game. The eight-game losing streak, though, isn’t the longest in program history, although it’s unclear what the record actually is.
The official Maine football media guide cites a 10-game losing streak from 1967-68 as the Black Bears’ longest-ever skid. Yet a closer look at that guide shows Maine once lost 11 straight, dropping the final game of 1944, all five in 1945 and the first five in 1946.
Want to get technical? Maine forfeited its three wins from 1993 as a result of ineligible players, bringing its official mark to 0-11. Tack on a loss to end 1992 and four straight to begin 1994, and you get a losing streak of 16.
Albany’s pass-rushing phenom
From Stony Brook’s Khalid Bueno (No. 1 in the Football Championship Subdivision with 14 sacks) and Lance Byndon (eight sacks) to Delaware State’s Carl Nesmith (nine), Maine has largely avoided the CAA’s top pass-rushers this season, thanks to its schedule. That changes Saturday.
Meet Shawan Lewis, who is fourth in FCS with 9 1/2 sacks. His success this season includes a 3 1/2-sack performance Oct. 31 against a Campbell team that hammered Maine the week before.

American Cancer Society announces major change to its prostate cancer screening recommendations
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Middle-aged men should undergo regular screening for prostate cancer, the American Cancer Society said Thursday in a major change to its guidelines.
The screening involves a simple blood test, and men at average risk of getting prostate cancer should get that PSA test every two years between the ages of 50 and 69, the cancer society advised.
Men at high risk, including Black men and those with a strong family history of prostate cancer, should get yearly PSA checks and start earlier, at age 45.
Thursday’s guideline update marks a shift in thinking about routine blood tests for PSA, or prostate-specific antigen.
Since 2010, the cancer society has recommended that men at average risk talk with their doctors about whether to get regular PSA tests. That’s a protein produced by both normal and cancerous prostate cells, meaning a high level might signal a tumor but also could be from a benign enlarged prostate or be a temporary spike from vigorous exercise.
Widespread PSA testing in the past was blamed for overtreatment of slow-growing tumors and unnecessary follow-up testing in men who turned out to not have cancer.
The updated advice comes after advances in understanding PSA’s benefits and how to reduce potential harms, according to the cancer society. That includes steps such as repeating a PSA test to be sure it’s really high or adding an MRI scan to help identify who needs a biopsy.
How long should men continue screening? Starting at 70, men should talk with their doctors about whether it’s beneficial to continue the routine PSA checks, the guideline says. But it discourages screening for men 80 and older and those of any age who aren’t expected to live another 10 years because of other health problems.
Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men. The cancer society estimates more than 333,000 men in the U.S. will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2026, and about 36,000 will die of it.

title: InvestigateTV+: Printers carry hacker risks
text:
(InvestigateTV) — An outdated setting on an office printer can give hackers easy access to sensitive information, and InvestigateTV+ uncovers how it could put doctors, schools, even police at risk.
Then, we go inside one company’s bid to pause death to buy time for science, and why some see it as a bold step.
Plus, we decode the colors of the underground utility system and explain the free step that can help homeowners avoid disaster.
Network Nightmares
InvestigateTV found possible printer problems across the country after receiving a confidential audit of several agencies’ machines.
Humming in the corner of offices across America, many modern office printers and multifunction devices do more than scan and copy documents. Depending on the model and settings, they may store documents, scan histories, address books, network settings or other sensitive information. Modern office printers can also have hard drives, firmware and default passwords that may never get changed.
Cryonics and the questions that remain
People frozen for years then thawed out and awake in a different time. It’s a common scene in popular science fiction movies.
But this isn’t the script of a blockbuster, a nonprofit in Arizona is attempting to make it a reality. Since the 1970s, Alcor has specialized in cryonics, defined as the practice of preserving life by pausing the dying process using subfreezing temperatures.
Alcor is betting on future science to do what today’s cannot.
Call before you dig
As the weather warms up, many homeowners are getting ready for landscaping and other yard projects. But before you dig, experts say one phone call could prevent disaster.
“You can’t assume you know what’s underground. You have to assume that you don’t,” said Sarah Magruder Lyle, president and CEO of Common Ground Alliance.
A jam band for mental health
A group of veterans has turned their shared experiences into a mission, using country music to address mental health stigma in the military community.
Vet Jams, a band that performs at bars around the New Orleans metro area, combines live music with open conversations about therapy and mental health support for veterans.

title: ‘What I actually did was split the Republican vote’: Independent Mississippi Senate candidate shares why he stayed in the race
text:
TUPELO, Miss. (WTVA/Gray News) – Independent Mississippi Senate candidate Ty Pinkins says his goal was to elect Mississippi’s first Black U.S. Senator since Reconstruction.
Pinkins was the third and independent option on the ballot, alongside Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic candidate Scott Colom.
About 20,000 votes went to Pinkins, enough to have swayed the election in either direction. His campaign drew attention as the close Senate race went over a week without a clear winner.
Colom ultimately won the seat, with the results officially announced just over a week after Election Day. He will be Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.
Pinkins told WTVA he knew he had no chance of winning the election but remained in the race.
In an interview on the day after the election, Pinkins said the beautiful thing about a democracy is that voters have freedom of speech to vote for whomever they want.
He said a poll showed that if he ran, 70% of his voters would be disgruntled Republican supporters. Pinkins said he believed he drew votes from Republicans and purposely did not campaign in majority-Black areas.
“Here is what needs to be shared. The portion of the vote that I drew – and people were concerned about splitting the Black vote – what I actually did was split the Republican vote,” Pinkins said. “Most of my votes came from Harrison County, DeSoto County, Rankin County, Jackson County, Hancock County, Madison County, Jones County, Pearl River County, Lamar County. All those counties have 13 percent Black population. Sixteen percent Black population. Ten percent Black population because I did not go to the Mississippi Delta. While Scott Colom was going all over this state.”
Pinkins has made national headlines, even as one of the losing candidates.

title: Buried alive: 911 call reveals fear, panic of family members notifying authorities of missing baby
text:
LEXINGTON, S.C. (WRDW/Gray News) - A newly released 911 call captures the panic and confusion as a grandmother reported her grandbaby had gone missing along with his father, who had been making threats about possibly taking his son.
Michael Comer, 25, was charged with attempted murder this week after authorities said he buried his 11-month-old son Koah alive in a dog crate, with the child miraculously surviving.
Comer had vanished earlier in the week with Koah, according to family members.
“My son was supposed to be watching his son today,” the boy’s grandmother could be heard telling the dispatcher. “He don’t have custody. The mother has custody. And I was supposed to take the baby home tonight.”
She explained that Comer had recently been released from jail and was on probation, and that he had been making disturbing statements.
“He kept making comments that he’s going to take off to New York, which he cannot because he’s on probation,” she said. “He just got out of jail last month. And we have not been able to get a hold of him all day.”
The grandmother said in the call that she had left work after relatives couldn’t reach Comer and they were growing concerned he hadn’t come home the previous night.
Koah was found alive Tuesday afternoon just over 24 hours after he was last seen with Comer.
Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said Koah was found buried in a dog crate wrapped in a towel at Comer’s father’s house. Investigators noted finding a pine straw and “freshly disturbed dirt.” Once they started digging, they heard the boy crying.
“So, as you imagine, the race was on,” Koon said. “Everybody’s getting down there trying to get him out. By the grace of God, [it] probably provided enough air for him to survive an estimated 24 hours under that dirt.”
Comer appeared in court Thursday in Lexington County, where a judge refused to set bond on the most serious charges.
Although news cameras were in the courtroom, Comer was hidden from view, behind a door that the judge could see beyond but others in the courtroom could not.
Prosecutors said that even after Comer was told Koah was found alive, he showed no remorse. They also told the judge that Comer did nothing to help investigators during the search.
His next court appearance is scheduled for Dec. 10.

title: Master carver to engrave crystals from last year's New Year's Eve ball sold as mementos
text:
Dropped in Times Square on New Year’s Eve, the Constellation Ball was created with 5,280 Waterford crystals that incorporated three different designs to represent life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness in honor of the nation’s 250th birthday in 2026.
On Thursday, people can buy one of those crystals and get their names engraved on it as a memento. They will be replaced with new crystals to ring in 2027 with a theme yet to be announced.
It takes about three days to make each crystal by hand for the roughly 12-foot (3.7-meter) geodesic sphere that weighs 12,350 pounds (5,602 kilograms). The process involves the design, molding, kilning and the finishing of each crystal. Waterford, a longtime luxury crystal brand from Ireland, has designed the New Year’s Eve ball’s crystals for over 25 years. Some new crystals are swapped in every year.
Richard White, a master cutter for Waterford, flew to New York City to engrave the crystals that vary in size from 1.5 to 4 inches in diameter. White will use a small electronic pen with a diamond tip to engrave names on the small crystal pieces Thursday.
“To be actually here and to be up close, personal with it, is a real excitement for me,” White said of seeing the completed ball.
Delfin Ortiz, general manager and senior vice president of One Times Square, the 26-story building from which the annual ball drops, said the crystals are part of “tomorrow’s history.”
A New Year’s Eve ball was first dropped in Times Square in 1907. Built by a young immigrant metalworker named Jacob Starr, the 700-pound (318-kilogram), 5-foot (1.52-meter) diameter ball was made of iron and wood and featured 100 25-watt light bulbs. Nine versions of the ball have been featured in the century-plus since that first celebration.
The only years no ball drop occurred were 1942 and 1943, when the city instituted a nightly “dimout” during World War II to protect itself from attacks. Crowds instead celebrated the new year with a moment of silence followed by chimes rung from the base of One Times Square.
One Times Square began offering crystals for purchase last year, though Thursday marks the first time they will be engraved.
The prices of the crystals range between $140 and $195, depending on the size.

title: Fire that significantly damaged Newburgh home ruled accidental
text:
Fire that significantly damaged Newburgh home ruled accidental by Maine investigators
The Maine State Fire Marshal's Office has determined a fire that significantly damaged a home in Newburgh was accidental.
The fire at 2628 Western Ave. was called in to the Newburgh Fire Department shortly after 10:50 a.m. Tuesday.
Firefighters were able to quickly knock down the flames, and no injuries were reported.
Members of the State Fire Marshal's Office were called to the scene to investigate the origin and cause of the fire.
Investigators determined that the fire started under the house and was caused by an electrical failure.
Officials said Newburgh firefighters received assistance at the scene from members of the Hermon, Carmel, Hampden and Dixmont fire departments.

title: Greater Portland Metro hopes to fill a bus with donations from food drive
text:
Greater Portland Metro hopes to fill a bus with donations from holiday food drive
The Greater Portland Metro, Maine's largest public transit system, is hoping to fill a bus with donations collected during its annual holiday food drive.
Now through Dec. 11, Greater Portland Metro will be collecting donations for Wayside Food Programs.
"Once we have closed out the campaign in December, we're going to bring all the boxes onto a bus and bring it over to Wayside," said Megan Hannan, Greater Portland Metro's director of government affairs and community engagement.
Requested items include kids' snacks, peanut butter, cereal, flour, sugar, cooking oil, rice, dried beans, canned vegetables, soup, pasta and macaroni and cheese.
Organizers said the holiday season can be a tough time for many people, and that the food drive is a great way to give back to the community.
"It's a great partnership and it's a great opportunity for us to get more in for our warehouse and to share it with our partner agencies," said Don Morrison, operations manager for Wayside Food Programs.
In-person donations will be accepted on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. at 114 Valley St., which is the address for Greater Portland Metro's administrative headquarters.
Donations will not be accepted on Greater Portland Metro buses, but people can donate online by making a purchase through an Amazon wish list.

Cargo ship strikes bridge between New Jersey and Philadelphia, lawmaker says, causing major backups
text:
Cargo ship strikes bridge between New Jersey and Philadelphia, lawmaker says, causing major backups
A cargo ship struck a bridge across the Delaware River on Thursday, disrupting traffic between Palmyra, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, according to a Pennsylvania lawmaker.
The collision left the 3,659-foot-long (1,115-meter-long) Tacony-Palmyra Bridge unable to close, causing a major backup on the Philadelphia side, state Rep. Ed Neilson said in a news release. No injuries have been reported, he said.
The U.S. Coast Guard said the cargo vessel is currently moored at a Kinder Morgan facility in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where an inspection team is on site. The Coast Guard has not yet released further information on the ship’s owner or operator.
The drawbridge was open for ships to pass through at the time of the collision around 1:15 p.m., according to the Coast Guard. It remained open afterward because another vessel needed to pass through, and has since come back down.
The steel bridge carries vehicles along Route 73 between Palmyra and the Tacony neighborhood in northeast Philadelphia. It has three lanes of vehicular traffic, two into Philadelphia and one into New Jersey. Estimates from 2025 show the bridge can carry as many as 76,200 vehicles each day.
No one answered the phone Thursday afternoon at the Burlington County Bridge Commission, which owns, operates and maintains the bridge. A recorded message said the bridge is closed to vehicular and pedestrian traffic until further notice, and that an update would be provided in time for evening rush hour.
Opened in 1929, the Tacony-Palmyra toll bridge was found to be in “fair” condition, according to the Federal Highway Administration’s 2026 National Bridge Inventory data released this fall.
Inspectors rated the deck of the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge as in good condition, the substructure as in fair condition and the superstructure — the component that absorbs the live traffic load — as fair.

title: Grandfather of baby found buried alive details the dramatic rescue
text:
Grandfather of South Carolina baby found buried alive details the dramatic rescue
An 11-month-old South Carolina boy who authorities say was buried alive in a dog crate by his father was found by rescuers after about 24 hours, crying and covered in dirt, his grandfather said about the dramatic rescue.
But soon after, little Koah Sharp stopped crying, John Comer told The Associated Press on Wednesday night as he recalled the events that played out the day before in the woods on his neighbor's property. The infant was put on the back of a truck and sat up, Comer said.
“I became ecstatic, my hands straight in the air. I’m looking in the sky, jumping up and down, praising God,” Comer said. “And at the same time I hit my knees and I’m just crying.”
Koah was released from a hospital Tuesday night and is expected to make a full recovery, Sheriff Jay Koon said.
The boy’s father, Michael Comer, 25, has been charged with attempted murder. John Comer said he'd opened his home to his son and grandson on Monday after Michael Comer said they needed a place to stay.
Michael Comer has been in custody since Monday, when Koah disappeared. Authorities haven’t revealed anything about Comer’s motive. He was sentenced to probation in October after pleading guilty to domestic violence.
Koah’s parents “have had some situations,” the sheriff said.
“Children,” he said, “sometimes get caught in the middle.”
Survival was helped by cool temperatures and a towel
Dozens of first responders scoured the countryside looking for the boy with reddish blond hair. After a full day of searching, authorities found freshly disturbed soil and heard cries from below ground, the sheriff said.
“As you can imagine, the race was on. Everyone was trying to get him out,” Koon said.
The boy likely survived because of cool temperatures and an air pocket created by a towel that was wrapped around the crate below ground, he said.
Koah was soon freed and “clinging to life,” the sheriff told reporters.
Comer was arrested while hiding in a building in Batesburg-Leesville. It wasn’t immediately known if he has a lawyer who could respond to the charges. A court hearing was planned for Thursday.
“We’re better now that we know that Koah is safe,” his great-aunt, Amber Hammond, told The Associated Press. She was watching as he was freed from the crate.
The boy's father took him before a caregiver arrived
Authorities said Koah had been in the care of Michael Comer’s mother. She had to run an errand and left the boy in Comer’s care while another caregiver was on the way.
“By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone, and Koah was gone with him,” the sheriff said.
Surveillance video from several businesses in the area showed Comer without the baby on Monday afternoon, Koon said.
John Comer said he feels like he was taken advantage of by his son when he asked for a place to stay. But, he said, he is also thankful that he agreed because if they had gone somewhere else they may not have found the boy in time.
“It just seems like he already had this planned out, and he knew what he was doing,” Comer said. “And he took the opportunity to do what he did. And if it hadn’t have been here, I don’t think anybody would have known where he would have went, and this would be a completely different story.”
Michael Comer had talked of taking the boy out of state
Hammond said her nephew had talked about taking the baby to New York because “he didn’t want to be in the same state as the mom.” When Koah vanished, she and others assumed that Comer had given the boy to someone.
“We had no idea something like this would happen at all,” Hammond said.
Comer was sentenced to probation in October after pleading guilty to domestic violence and aggravated breach-of-peace charges related to an arrest in July, Lexington County online court records show. Prosecutors dropped a gun charge as part of the plea deal. He also got credit for spending more than two months in jail.
At nearly a year old, Koah has been trying to stand on his own, said Hammond, who cared for him last weekend. And he loves watching Mickey Mouse cartoons.
John Comer said he'd never heard his grandson cry before he was found underground.
“He's always been happy,” he said. “The kid's always got a smile on his face.”

title: How Trump’s latest food assistance cuts could affect Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
President Donald Trump’s administration is seeking to once again limit how many people automatically qualify for a federal food assistance program that covers about 1 in 10 Americans and about 150,000 Mainers.
A proposed rule that the U.S. Department of Agriculture published Tuesday is meant to close what the Republican administration views as a loophole. The rule would no longer allow certain people who receive benefits under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program to automatically qualify for the separate Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
The proposed rule, if implemented, would not take effect until 2029, when Trump will leave office at the end of his second term. His administration sought to make a similar SNAP rule change in 2019, but former President Joe Biden withdrew the proposal upon taking office in 2021.
Still, hunger prevention groups in Maine and elected officials are warning that the latest proposed changes would make it even harder for low-income Mainers to receive food assistance.
“At a time when so many Americans are struggling to afford high prices, the last thing they need is government making it even harder to put food on the table,” U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, D-2nd District, said in a statement. Golden, who also opposed the 2019 proposal, is leaving office in January.
The department is accepting public comments on the proposed change until Dec. 10. U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, mentioned in a Thursday statement how her party will have control of Congress come January as the result of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
“Last week, the American people made clear they’re fed up with Republicans’ failure to bring down costs. Maine families are already stretching every dollar to buy groceries and fill their tanks,” Pingree said. “Now, Trump’s USDA wants to take food assistance away from millions of people. It is the definition of tone-deaf — and unbelievably cruel.”
Good Shepherd Food Bank, which works on hunger relief throughout Maine, said the change could affect people in households earning between $21,000 and $31,000 annually who currently qualify for SNAP through expanded categorical eligibility, despite having incomes above the federal SNAP eligibility threshold. Those people typically receive benefits averaging about $25 per month, the food bank added in a statement.
“The proposed rule could push more working households into food insecurity and place additional pressure on food pantries and a statewide emergency food network that is already facing sustained, elevated demand,” Good Shepherd Food Bank said Thursday.
If the Trump administration’s rule change affecting SNAP and TANF takes effect in two years, then it will represent “another attempt by the federal administration to make it harder for struggling Mainers to get and keep food assistance,” said Anna Korsen, co-executive director of Full Plates Full Potential, a nonprofit that seeks to end childhood food insecurity in Maine.
“Not only will eliminating broad-based categorical eligibility increase bureaucratic paperwork and administrative costs, it will also hurt household budgets, school budgets and our state budget,” Korsen said Thursday. “Ultimately, more Maine kids will go hungry because of this decision, which isn’t what anyone here wants.”
It is not immediately clear how many Mainers would lose SNAP eligibility if the rule takes effect in 2029, but the Department of Agriculture said about 6.3 million people nationally could lose eligibility for the program that, as of this summer, was serving 36 million people.
That would be on top of the 5.5 million people who have lost SNAP benefits over the past year, per the Agriculture Department, after the GOP-controlled Congress and Trump approved the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that expanded SNAP work requirements to those ages 55 to 64 and to parents whose youngest children are at least 14 years old. The sweeping legislation also required states to start shouldering about three-fourths of the cost of running SNAP, up from half.
Children whose families receive SNAP benefits are also eligible for free school meals. The Agriculture Department says that nearly 1.8 million children would lose eligibility if their families lose SNAP benefits, although 97% of them would still qualify for free or reduced price school meals through another process. However, the government said some children would not get the lunches if their families don’t apply.
The TANF program provides federal grants to states, which set their own eligibility rules for distributing cash and other benefits meant to help cover various needs to low-income families with children. TANF covers about 4,500 households in Maine that include 8,662 kids, according to state data. SNAP covers food and groceries, and Maine has 88,650 households with 148,810 people in the program, according to the latest state data as of September.
The Trump administration’s rule is focused on what it views as a loophole, as some states have used the automatic eligibility to expand SNAP benefits to people who might not otherwise qualify. Federal guidelines generally limit SNAP benefits to those earning less than 130% of the poverty level, or more than $1,700 monthly for an individual or nearly $3,600 for a family of four. To reduce duplicative paperwork, the federal government allows people who already receive TANF benefits to automatically qualify for SNAP — though they still have to apply.
In its new rule, the Department of Agriculture “acknowledges these revisions may result in some level of increased administrative burden on states, a reduction in SNAP benefit spending and associated effects on school meals eligibility.” Still, it said the change would emphasize providing Americans with benefits “that directly encourage self-sufficiency.”
U.S. Sen. Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, and his office are “in the process of reviewing” the proposed change, spokesperson Matt Felling said Thursday.
A spokesperson for U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, said the proposed change would not go into effect until after she leaves office, and deferred comment to King and U.S. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, who beat Collins in the Nov. 3 election. Jackson’s transition team did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday.
State government leaders are in a period of transition right now, with Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree taking office in January after winning the election this month to succeed Gov. Janet Mills, a fellow Democrat termed out of office.
States can currently base SNAP eligibility on TANF-funded benefits such as job counseling or one-time vouchers for vehicle repairs so that people can get to work, David Super, a Georgetown University law professor who has studied the food aid program, told The Associated Press.
“The administration here is basically proposing to eliminate the flexibility that Congress gave the states to serve working poor people,” Super said.
This story contains reporting from The Associated Press.

title: Bruins’ home winning streak halted by Canadiens
text:
BOSTON — Josh Anderson and Jake Evans each had a goal and an assist as the Montreal Canadiens leapfrogged the Boston Bruins in the Atlantic Division standings with a 5-2 win on Thursday night.
Now 9-0-3 in its last 12 games, Montreal came in trailing Boston by one point for the top spot in the division. Kirby Dach, Cole Caufield and Phillip Danault also scored for the Canadiens, who improved to 10-0-2 when leading after two periods. Jacob Fowler made 30 saves.
Boston’s seven-game winning streak on home ice was snapped. Jeremy Swayman was pulled after allowing four goals on 17 shots and was replaced by Michael DiPietro, who made 13 saves.
Casey Mittelstadt scored both of Boston’s goal. The Bruins outshot Montreal, 32-30.
Dach opened the scoring with a wraparound goal 2:34 into the contest. He skated behind Swayman with a long reach and scored his second goal of the season.
Montreal made it 2-0 when Anderson planted himself in front of Swayman and knocked in a rebound for his eighth goal of the season.
The Canadiens extended their cushion when Evans went scored on a breakaway after taking a pass from Anderson. Montreal ended Swayman’s night at 11:46 of the second period when Caufield fired a shot from just outside the left circle into the top corner.
Swayman’s early exit and subsequent replacement by DiPietro marked the first time this season that Boston made an in-game change at goalie.
Mittelstadt got Boston on the scoreboard with a backhand move after Danault scored against DiPietro on a long one-timer from the top of the right circle. Mittelstadt’s second goal came during the opening minute of the third period.
It was the first of four regular-season meetings between the Original Six franchises.
Up next
Canadiens: Host Colorado on Saturday
Bruins: Continue four-game homestand against Minnesota on Saturday
