Catholic Charities Maine opens Lewiston location
text:
Lewiston, ME – Catholic Charities Maine celebrated the opening of its newest location in Lewiston with a blessing of the historic Priory building and open house on November 6 at 27A Bartlett Street.
The new Lewiston location marks an important expansion for Catholic Charities Maine as the organization celebrates 60 years of providing help and creating hope to individuals and families of all faiths across Maine.
“We are very pleased to establish a presence in Lewiston and to deepen Catholic Charities Maine’s service to the greater Lewiston Auburn community,” said Steve Letourneau, CEO of Catholic Charities Maine. As we commemorate 60 years of service throughout Maine, this expansion represents an important investment in our future and in our ability to respond to the evolving needs of individuals and families. The Priory provides an exceptional opportunity to bring together programs, strengthen community partnerships, and extend our mission of service to Maine’s most vulnerable.
Catholic Charities Maine entered into a long-term lease agreement with Prince of Peace Parish to occupy the Priory, a 20,000 square-foot, four-story building adjacent to the Basilica of Saints Peter and Paul. The more than 130-year-old building has undergone renovations and accessibility improvements in preparation for its new use.
The Priory will become home to several Catholic Charities Maine programs, including:
Behavioral Health Network
Education Services for Blind & Visually Impaired Children, for children from birth through age 21 statewide
Independent Support Services, homemaker services program for seniors and adults with a disability that serves statewide
Office of Maine Refugee Services
Parish Social Ministry
SEARCH, a volunteer senior companion program that serves in nine counties
“We are grateful to Prince of Peace Parish for this partnership and for the opportunity to utilize this historic property in furtherance of our shared commitment to serving the community,” Letourneau said.

title: Side Door Coffeehouse to welcome Maine native Jud Caswell
text:
Mainer Jud Caswell will headline Friday’s Side Door Coffeehouse at 8:30 p.m. at the Unitarian Universalist Church of Brunswick, 1 Middle St. Caswell’s performance will be preceded by an open mic starting at 7 p.m. Admission is $12 for adults and free for children 17 and under.
Caswell is an award-winning songwriter and multi-instrumentalist who has been performing in his native state of Maine and beyond for more than 25 years. His record, “Live at the Seagull Shop,” was the No. 1 album on the Folk Alliance International radio charts in March 2020. Caswell is currently releasing a series of albums that he recorded during the early months of the pandemic. Visit judcaswell.com to listen to his music and more.
The Side Door Coffeehouse is a venue for local musicians and others (professional and amateur) to share their talents, and for residents and visitors of the Midcoast community to enjoy great entertainment and conversation in a relaxed setting. Organized by a group of volunteers from the Unitarian Universalist Church of Brunswick, the Side Door Coffeehouse operates on the second Friday of every month except August.

title: Bond denied for man accused of burying his 11-month-old son alive
text:
LEXINGTON, S.C. (WIS/AP) – Bond was denied Thursday for the father accused of burying his 11-month-old son in a dog crate in a clump of scrubby pines.
Michael Comer showed no remorse for attempting to kill his son, Koah, and tried to leave the state, Tyler Douglas, lead investigator for the Lexington County Sheriff’s Department, told Judge Gary W. Reinhart. Reinhart approved a public defender for Comer and set a hearing for Dec. 10.
Comer, 25, is charged with attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary.
Comer has been in custody in Lexington County since Monday, when his son was reported missing.
An attorney for Comer has not yet been appointed.
Koah, who rescuers found after about 24 hours, was released from a hospital Tuesday night, Sheriff Jay Koon said.
Comer’s mother told authorities about previous suicidal statements her son had made and that he had talked about taking Koah to New York, where he claimed to have friends who could help him find work.
John Comer said he’d opened his home to his son and grandson on Monday after Michael Comer said they needed a place to stay. On Wednesday, he showed an Associated Press reporter the small hole on a neighbor’s property where rescuers uncovered the child.
“I cannot imagine how somebody could come to the point that that would be the right thing to do, or the thing to do at all,” John Comer told the AP.
Authorities haven’t revealed anything about Comer’s motive. He was sentenced in October to probation after pleading guilty to domestic violence involving the boy’s mother.
Koah’s parents “have had some situations,” the sheriff said.
“Children,” he said, “sometimes get caught in the middle.”
Dozens of first responders scoured the countryside for the boy with reddish blond hair. After a full day of searching, authorities found freshly disturbed soil and heard cries from below, the sheriff said.
The boy likely survived because of cool temperatures and an air pocket created by a towel that was wrapped around the crate below ground, he said.
“By the grace of God, [it] probably provided enough air for him to survive ur estimation of the last 24 hours under that dirt,” Koon said.
Koah was soon freed and “clinging to life,” the sheriff told reporters.

title: Maine ought not have elected Paul LePage

title: Windham hotel owner is building adjacent apartment complex
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Erik Heyland, owner of the Dormir hotel in Windham, is constructing a three-story apartment building adjacent to the hotel on Route 302.
The building, tentatively named Roosevelt Apartments, is expected to be completed in the spring, with marketing for rentals beginning over the next two months.
Heyland said work on the apartment complex, including permitting and construction, has taken around half a decade. The planning board performed a site walk of the property in late 2022.
The building will consist of 50 units, with a mix of studio apartments and one- and two-bedroom units. Roughly half of the units will have two bedrooms, ranging in size from 1,000 to 1,200 square feet.
The building will have an elevator in the center, uncommon for buildings of its size in Windham. According to Fire Chief Brent Libby, elevators are typically not required for buildings of less than four stories.
The building will be “barrier-free,” said Heyland, with no steps at the entrance, and residents will use access codes to enter.
Another feature touted by Heyland is a “community room” on the first floor, for residents to host activities with friends, such as watching sports matches.
Residents of the apartment building will have access to some of the services in Dormir, such as the fitness center, indoor pool and breakfast, as well as discounts on rooms and renting the hotel’s event center.
Anyone interested in renting one of his apartments can go to Dormir and provide staff with contact information, Heyland said.
The building is just one of multiple housing construction projects ongoing in Windham, including a 172-unit development on Tandberg Trail.

title: Snowmaking commences ahead of November 20 opening day
4 months after ICE shooting in Biddeford, questions linger about state and federal investigations
text:
Elizabeth Emen said she has been waiting to hear from investigators.
On July 13, her brother, David Brouillette, was working for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement when he shot and killed Johan Sebastian Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old father from Colombia.
Emen said she learned about the shooting from a family member days later, and immediately thought back to the last message she had received from her brother: a racist email about her partner at the time, who is Colombian.
“The connection was so strong that I knew I would need to share that,” Emen said in an interview Thursday.
Now, four months after the shooting, Emen said she is struck that the Department of Homeland Security still hasn’t shared information about the shooting. The agency has declined multiple times to identify the agent involved or discuss Brouillette’s employment.
The DHS Office of Inspector General and the Office of the Maine Attorney General launched investigations into the shooting, according to public announcements in July. Both agencies said they couldn’t share any updates on Thursday.
Emen said she is sharing her experiences now in the hope that it will lead to a “full investigation and toward justice for the Durán Guerrero family.”
Brouillette has not responded to requests for comment. The attorney general’s office said in July he was being placed on leave, which DHS has declined to address.
‘WHY WOULD THEY GIVE HIM A GUN’
Both Durán Guerrero’s sister and his partner have met with the Maine attorney general’s office at least twice since the shooting, their attorneys say.
Sean Murphy, one of the lawyers for the family, said Attorney General Aaron Frey’s staff told him that it was Frey’s “goal to not leave this to a successor, indicating that there could be a determination by the attorney general’s office by his last day.”
Frey will finish his final term this year. State lawmakers are scheduled to elect a new attorney general on Dec. 2. There’s nothing in state law that says Frey’s successor can’t make their own decision about the shooting.
Emen’s emails were first reported in a New York Times story that was published Wednesday and covered Brouillette’s history and his rushed hiring.
In a statement, Durán Guerrero’s partner, Martha Karolina Rojas Alvarez, said she was “shocked and appalled” by what the Times reported, including interviews with unnamed federal officials who said that Brouillette hadn’t been fully vetted at the time of the shooting.
“Why would they give him a gun?” Rojas Alvarez said. “That is unforgivable, even in God’s eyes. And I can never forgive that man for taking the love of my life from me and for taking my daughter’s father from her. I hope justice is served.”
Murphy said his clients have heard nothing from federal investigators, and they’ve cast doubt on the nature of the federal government’s investigation following a report from CBS that the FBI is not conducting a review for civil rights violations, citing a Department of Justice official.
ICE wrote to Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, on Tuesday, which her office said was the first time the agency has confirmed it is investigating the shooting. Pingree had sent DHS a letter in July asking detailed questions about the shooting, ICE’s hiring and training practices, and whether DHS would review the operation in Biddeford.
In its response to the congresswoman this week, ICE said it has an ongoing investigation but couldn’t provide any information about it.
The Office of Inspector General is expected to investigate any improper use of force under DHS policy. If the agency determines there has been criminal conduct, it can refer the matter to the DOJ for potential charges. The agency lists online several instances in which its investigations have led to charges.
The agency is also actively auditing ICE for use of force incidents, its hiring practices and body camera usage. Pingree and other Democrats, many of whom were recently elected, say they plan to use their authority next year to also investigate the shooting and claw back funding that DHS has received from Republicans.
“Those who empowered Mr. Brouillette must be held accountable,” said Rep. Bennie Thompson, of Mississippi. The top Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee, he is expected to lead the committee starting in January.
Ashley Brouillette, an ex-wife who confirmed David Brouillette’s identity to multiple media outlets the week of July 13, said she spoke to investigators from the state and DHS on July 28.
She said they asked about David Brouillette’s mental health and medication history, and whether she felt he was fit to work for ICE. She and family members have previously raised concerns with Brouillette’s mental health.
“And I said, ‘Absolutely not,'” Ashley Brouillette said on Wednesday. “I don’t think he’s fit to work any job with any kind of weapon.”
MULTIPLE REPORTS
Brouillette’s sister has kept up with news coverage of her brother, she said, although she has not heard from him since his last email in 2021.
Many news reports since the shooting have delved into a lengthy history of abuse allegations against Brouillette, who has filed and been subject of more than eight protection from abuse filings in Kennebec County court. Both of his ex-wives have alleged physical and verbal abuse.
“The fact that there are multiple reports, including my experience, of my brother having biased beliefs, and violent behavior, I think speaks a lot to the systems that gave him power and authority and a weapon,” Emen said.
She said she last had contact with her brother in January 2021, when she reached out to several family members by email to ask if they would help make a surprise video for her child’s fourth birthday. Brouillette replied.
Emen provided the messages to the Portland Press Herald with her brother’s email address redacted, as well as the names of her child and partner. In his response, Brouillette referenced an earlier conversation in which Emen said he had disparaged her partner with xenophobic remarks. In Brouillette’s last email, which contained typos, he wrote that the man “can takes his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries.”
“He does not emulate what it means to be an American … rather he emulates what it’s like to be entitled and think he has a seat a table that has no room for his (or your ignorance). How bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers. He sure doesn’t have a problem with freeloading off of our country, not claiming to be part of it … and then criticizing it.
“You’re dead to me Liz. Enjoy it.”
Emen said Thursday that the email caught her off guard, but that it fit a pattern of racist remarks she had heard her brother make before. She said as adults, they felt close — keeping up over emails, caring about him and wanting to be there for him, despite growing political disagreements over the years.
Before the emails, Emen said Brouillette had also met her partner and kept in touch with their oldest child.
“There has been positivity and openness to those relationships that he conveyed, and his behavior,” Emen said. “And then there was also this sentiment of hate and judgment and bias. He had conveyed quite a range.”
STATE INVESTIGATION
Attorney General Frey’s office has said it’s reviewing both whether criminal conduct occurred, and whether the agent’s use of deadly force was justified.
Once Frey has made a decision, he can send the findings to the state’s deadly force review panel, which is made up of law enforcement officials, prosecutors, forensic experts and civilians. The group, which does not weigh in on whether criminal charges should be filed, is tasked with determining whether a shooting fits best practices and what law enforcement agencies can learn from the incident.
Members of that panel said they haven’t received any information and have no indication when they might be asked to consider the Biddeford shooting. Stephen Burlock, who chairs the panel and is a former prosecutor, said on Wednesday that the group only receives a heads-up when Frey formally refers the matter to the panel.
Burlock also said the panel considers cases chronologically. Sheriff Joel Merry, another member, said on Wednesday that the group is currently reviewing a shooting that occurred in late 2024, suggesting that even if Frey were to refer the case to the panel soon, it would have other cases to review first.
Attorneys for Durán Guerrero’s family said on Thursday that the state still hasn’t returned the car he was driving when he was shot.
Biddeford Mayor Liam LaFountain said in an email that he checks in regularly with the state attorney general’s office on the status of the investigation. He had no updates Thursday.
“I recognize that investigators may need to withhold certain information until their work is complete to protect the integrity of the investigation,” LaFountain said. “A thorough investigation takes time, but Johan’s family also deserves timely answers and swift justice.”
Staff Writer Morgan Womack contributed to this story.

title: Falmouth high schooler publishes women’s health research in medical journal
text:
Hanna Ajemian knew witnessing a birth up close was a make-or-break moment.
Shadowing the labor and delivery team at Penn Medicine in Philadelphia the summer before her junior year at Falmouth High School, she watched eight women give birth — even holding some patients’ legs as they pushed while their husbands passed out in the background.
“I knew that that was kind of going to be the test of if I could stomach it or not, honestly. I was able to, and I loved it,” said Ajemian. “I was like, ‘This is the coolest thing ever.’”
Now, at 17, she’s the lead author on an article published in a medical journal forwarding the field of women’s health.
Ajemian got involved in obstetric research with Lisa Levine, the chief of maternal-fetal medicine at Penn Medicine. Under Levine’s mentorship and the guidance of Falmouth High School teachers, during her junior year, Ajemian analyzed data previously gathered by the University of Pennsylvania. The dataset examined the link between hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, such as preeclampsia, and women developing chronic hypertension 10 years later.
After a year of analysis and writing and editing over a dozen drafts, Ajemian got her study published in the “American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology Maternal-Fetal Medicine” this fall as the lead author. As the high school senior waits to hear back about early college admissions, she answered some questions about her passion for the field of women’s health and what comes next.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
When did your interest in science and research originate?
I’ve always loved science. That’s always just been a part of myself, and I always have known that that’s something that I wanted to do in the future.
My freshman year, I had an internship with a women’s health startup in Ethiopia, and that’s what kind of sparked my interest specifically in women’s health, and really made me see the importance of the field and where it can go in the future — and how we need more people to be in it.
Now you’re making impacts in that field with a publication. Could you explain the findings of your research?
The two main findings were that the severity of preeclampsia (a serious complication of high blood pressure during pregnancy) was kind of non-relevant to the development of chronic hypertension (defined as long-term high blood pressure, which increases your health risk) later on, which was really interesting because one would think that the worse the preeclampsia, the higher your risk is later in life.
The other one was that recurrence is this huge driving factor … For each pregnancy that was complicated by a hypertensive disorder, a woman’s risk for developing chronic hypertension later in life increased by 35%.
These are really good to know because we have strategies in women’s health for preventing and treating preeclampsia. So if we know that, for example, the severity is kind of (irrelevant), we’re not giving out misinformation to women and saying “Oh, you just had mild preeclampsia, you’re probably fine, don’t worry about it.”
You’re clearly passionate about the topic of women’s health. What’s next for you?
I think that I will absolutely do something in women’s health in the future. And I know that it’s kind of early to be saying that, but I think that I’m justified in saying that because I’ve had such exposure to it already, and know that I love it.
My goal is to be an OB-GYN physician, but this research definitely inspired me to be a physician scientist, which I didn’t know was an option. I kind of thought you had to pick one.
Working in person with people is so, so important. But ultimately, the way that we advance as a medical field comes from research and discovering new things and figuring out … new strategies and ways to treat things. Physicians can’t treat disorders that we don’t know anything about.
Aside from now knowing you can watch someone give birth without fainting, what else have you learned about yourself through this research?
You don’t have to wait till you’re older, or have some kind of degree, or be in some kind of position of authority to contribute meaningfully to something that you care about, and that you can be curious and … really take initiative.
I don’t think that (age or experience) should limit you from trying to go out and do something you care about.

title: Morgan Sherwood Barbour
text:
Morgan S. Barbour passed away peacefully at home with family on Oct. 21, 2026 in Bellevue, Wash.
Morgan was born on Feb. 24, 1933 in Brockton, Mass. His family moved back to Maine and settled on Beneva Farm on Middle Road in Warren. He graduated from Warren High School in 1951 and enlisted in the U.S. Air Force, training as a tower control operator.
When volunteers were needed for pilot training, Morgan volunteered, and that began his lifelong love of flying. He met Sarah Morris during flight training in North Carolina, and they were married in 1954.
Morgan retired from the Air Force and went to work as a flight instructor for Boeing in Seattle, Wash. He spent 30 years flying and training pilots from around the world. He loved entertaining and meeting new people.
Morgan is predeceased by his wife of 64 years, Sarah M. Barbour. He is survived by daughter, Marcy Barbour, of Bellevue, Wash.; daughter, Darcy Page (Brad), of Grand Prairie, Texas; granddaughter, Sarah Faye Curde (Nate), of Carnation, Wash.; grandson, Garrett Page, of Dallas, Texas; great-granddaughter, Morgan Curde, of Carnation, Wash.; as well as many nieces and nephews.
A memorial service to be held at the Tahoma National Cemetery in Kent, Wash. on Dec. 7, 2026 at 11:30 a.m.
Memorial gifts may be made to Hospice at evergreenhealthfoundation.com.

title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who reprimanded him
text:

title: Nvidia CEO resigns after his affair with alleged Chinese spy raises national security concerns
text:
Nvidia CEO resigns after his affair with alleged Chinese spy raises national security concerns
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after his extramarital affair raised national security concerns.
The company named Colette Kress as interim CEO. She is the current executive vice president and chief financial officer.
Huang faced growing calls to resign after his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Late Wednesday, media reports said Huang had another extramarital affair with an Nvidia employee who reports to him.
The board of directors said Thursday it also named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones, an entrepreneur and venture investor.
Shares of Nvidia, one of the largest companies in the world, plunged 10% in premarket trading Thursday.
Nvidia's board had gathered to discuss Huang's future after revelations that he was having an affair with a former Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese government agent. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. The Associated Press could not independently confirm those reports.
In its first statement since the scandal broke, Singapore-headquartered Megaspeed International said Thursday that it takes its obligation to comply with U.S. export control laws "extremely seriously."
Details about Huang's affair with the former Megaspeed executive are unclear.
"Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government," said the statement signed by its chairman and CEO, Tan Yong Pong, who also goes by James Tan.
Nvidia has said it had "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.
The New York Times reported that the woman with whom Huang had an affair was Alice Huang, who also goes by the name Huang Le, and was a top executive at Megaspeed. The company prominently touts a partnership with Nvidia on its website. The two are not related.
Last month, the Times reported that U.S. intelligence agencies discovered Nvidia's Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang — and determined she was feeding information directly to Beijing. On Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that the FBI was investigating.
Megaspeed faced claims last year that it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was "no evidence" of such exports. Singapore has also said it is investigating such allegations.
China has denied that it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, who heads one of the world's most valuable companies. Nvidia has become a leader in making chips that power AI and Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. In January, he won Trump's approval for selling to China its H200 chips.
Megaspeed said Thursday that it has cooperated with the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which handles enforcement of national security restrictions on exports of technology, and was ready to "cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority."
Video above: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang talks to reporter Lana Ferguson about AI in North Texas
It said it has hired a U.S. law firm to handle a "comprehensive census" of its computer chips and to verify its export controls.
"Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws," it said.
Apart from questions over national security, Megaspeed's finances also have drawn attention. Its total assets soared roughly 90-fold from late 2023 to 2024, to almost US$3 billion, according to Singapore corporate records.
Revenue surged to over US$294 million in 2024 from none in 2023.

title: ‘What I actually did was split the Republican vote’: Independent Mississippi Senate candidate shares why he stayed in the race
text:
TUPELO, Miss. (WTVA/Gray News) – Independent Mississippi Senate candidate Ty Pinkins says his goal was to elect Mississippi’s first Black U.S. Senator since Reconstruction.
Pinkins was the third and independent option on the ballot, alongside Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic candidate Scott Colom.
About 20,000 votes went to Pinkins, enough to have swayed the election in either direction. His campaign drew attention as the close Senate race went over a week without a clear winner.
Colom ultimately won the seat, with the results officially announced just over a week after Election Day. He will be Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.
Pinkins told WTVA he knew he had no chance of winning the election but remained in the race.
In an interview on the day after the election, Pinkins said the beautiful thing about a democracy is that voters have freedom of speech to vote for whomever they want.
He said a poll showed that if he ran, 70% of his voters would be disgruntled Republican supporters. Pinkins said he believed he drew votes from Republicans and purposely did not campaign in majority-Black areas.
“Here is what needs to be shared. The portion of the vote that I drew – and people were concerned about splitting the Black vote – what I actually did was split the Republican vote,” Pinkins said. “Most of my votes came from Harrison County, DeSoto County, Rankin County, Jackson County, Hancock County, Madison County, Jones County, Pearl River County, Lamar County. All those counties have 13 percent Black population. Sixteen percent Black population. Ten percent Black population because I did not go to the Mississippi Delta. While Scott Colom was going all over this state.”
Pinkins has made national headlines, even as one of the losing candidates.

title: Irma P. Hall, 'Soul Food' and 'The Ladykillers' actor who found fame at 60, dies at 91
text:
Irma P. Hall, 'Soul Food' and 'The Ladykillers' actor who found fame at 60, dies at 91
Irma P. Hall, the veteran actor who brought warmth and authority to matriarchal roles in “Soul Food” and “The Ladykillers,” and whose acting career took off after decades as a teacher, died Tuesday in Dallas. She was 91.
Her family announced her death Wednesday. No cause was given.
Hall was best known to many viewers as Big Mama, the family’s steadying force in the 1997 film “Soul Food.” The role earned her an NAACP Image Award and led to a return as the character in the television series based on the film.
She received a Cannes Film Festival Jury Prize for her performance as Marva Munson, a Bible-reading landlady opposite Tom Hanks in the Coen brothers’ 2004 comedy “The Ladykillers.” Hall also appeared in “A Family Thing,” “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil,” “Beloved,” “Patch Adams,” “Collateral” and Tyler Perry’s “Meet the Browns.”
Hall was 60 when “A Family Thing” brought her a major film role. She played Aunt T., a blind woman whose counsel helps guide two half brothers, played by James Earl Jones and Robert Duvall. The part drew attention to an actor who had spent years developing her craft onstage and in smaller screen roles.
“I was just concentrating on developing this craft,” Hall said in a 1996 interview with The Associated Press. “I guess you really never know where you are; you probably think you are on a lower rung than you really are.”
Hall had not set out to become an actor. Born Irma Dolores Player on June 3, 1935, in Beaumont, Texas, she was raised in Chicago and later returned to Texas for college. She taught English and foreign languages in Dallas public schools for more than two decades.
Her path to the screen began when actor and director Raymond St. Jacques heard her recite poetry in Dallas and cast her in his 1973 film “Book of Numbers.” Hall continued teaching as she took acting roles, then made performance her full-time work in the 1980s. She also helped establish the Dallas Minority Repertory Theatre and remained involved in developing young artists.
Hall’s career included theater, television and film. Her credits ranged from the 1997 Clint Eastwood drama “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil” to the 1998 films “Beloved” and “Patch Adams.” She also voiced Great Aunt T. in the 2001 “Rugrats” Kwanzaa special.
In 2004, Hall was recovering from serious injuries suffered in a car crash, including open-heart surgery, a broken arm and a crushed ankle, when she traveled from a Chicago convalescent center to attend a private screening of “The Ladykillers.”
“I loved the whole thing,” she told The Associated Press. “You never really know until you see it on the screen.”
Hall said she had heard from Hanks and the Coen brothers while recuperating. They had signed her pillow, she said. “Whenever I miss them, I hug it.”
In Dallas, Hall was also a longtime member and Church Mother at Inspiring Body of Christ Church. Her family remembered her as a woman of faith who read to children at the church’s school and stayed active in its theater ministry.
“She started as a teacher in the classroom but ended up being a teacher to the world,” her daughter, Irma Hall Crayton, said in the family’s announcement.

title: Democratic veterans on call for end to Iran War
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Currently Democratic lawmakers and newly elected veterans on Capitol Hill are calling for an end to the Iran war.
The lawmakers, including some who have not yet been sworn in, said voters sent them to Washington in part to end the war. They say they owe it to voters to follow through.
Rep.-elect Zach Dembo (D-Ky.) sayid the Iran war was a large factor in him winning a previously a district President Donald Trump won by 15 points in 2024.
“When we’re trying to figure out what made the American people make decisions like that, one of the things has to be from the beginning, as a veteran, as a former prosecutor, and as a teacher, I emphasized my public service, and that politics should never be inserted into spaces like the Pentagon,” Dembo said.
The lawmakers say it is time to take action, beginning with impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
“We need to do better by you as citizens. We need to do better by the veterans. We need to do better by our allies. By our service members. And that starts with getting Pete Hegseth out of the Pentagon,” Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pa.) said.
Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said Congress can end the war through a combination of War Powers Acts and cutting off funding from the Trump administration.
“Speaking for me, I’m not interested in continuing to throw a blank check to Pete Hegseth for a war the American people never authorized. For a war that Congress never authorized,” Deluzio said.
He said Congress needs to play a role in ensuring a safe exit for the troops already in the area.
“Nothing would ever stop commanders from protecting their troops, whether it’s in a withdrawal, or the base, or otherwise. And so this requires leadership. Our military officers gotta do their jobs,” Deluzio said.
The new Congress will be sworn in Jan. 3, 2027.

title: History on the fly
text:
The Presque Isle Air Museum looks back at almost 100 years of aviation history
WRITTEN BY ANNE GABBIANELLI
“If these walls could talk” is an old saying, and at the south end of the Presque Isle International Airport the walls are talking — sharing history that was once hidden.
“One of the things about the Air Museum is it conveys a story that surprises people,” said Scott Wardwell, airport director.
The Presque Isle Air Museum may have been dedicated in 1999, but it takes visitors back almost 100 years, documenting how Presque Isle was the forerunner to Loring Air Force Base.
In 1930, construction began on 320 acres of land not far from Presque Isle’s downtown business district. It consisted of two grass strips and a 100-by-80-foot hangar. The airfield first hosted the “Barnstormer,” a scenic plane ride business in 1934.
With WWII looming, the federal government allocated funding to establish the Presque Isle Army Airfield, later renamed Presque Isle Air Force Base (PIAFB). The base went on to play a crucial role during the war. The Army Air Corp, which later evolved into the Air Force, called Presque Isle home because of its location.
“We are actually closer to Europe, which was especially important during WWII,” Wardwell said.
In 1942, Boeing’s B17E Flying Fortress bombers were a common sight in Presque Isle because the base was Air Transport Command’s Division headquarters. The Flying Tigers’ American Volunteer Group (AVG), with its own story, offered a great deal to the area’s aviation history.
Now comes what Wardwell calls “a fabulous story.”
The SNARK missile program was the United States’ first intercontinental cruise missile, developed by Northrop. It was designed to deliver thermonuclear warheads over long distances and was in service from January 1959 to June 1961. According to historical accounts in the museum, the Strategic Air Command activated the 702nd Strategic Missile Wing in 1959 at PIAFB as the nation’s first and only operational SNARK base with 30 missiles.
The SNARK had a range of 5,500 nautical miles and could reach an altitude of 50,000 feet. It was jet-engine propelled with a sustained speed of 650 MPH. The trajectory of the missiles was from Presque Isle to targets in the Soviet Union.
In 1960, four of the missiles were placed on 24-hour alert, yet no missile was ever fired in an act of aggression. Just a year later, the Kennedy Administration determined the SNARK program was obsolete, replacing missiles with rockets.
The base went on to host C47s, DC3s, Northrup’s F-20 Tigershark, North American’s F86 Sabre, Republic P47D, Boeing B17G, and more. It’s all captured in the history lining the walls of the Presque Isle Air Museum.
In 1961, the Air Force relocated from Presque Isle to Loring Air Force Base in nearby Limestone.
“A line of B52s came on and required more real estate and nuclear warehousing,” Wardwell said.
Like with the SNARK missiles, Loring’s nuclear program was never put into military action, yet both locations were chosen because of their geographic position, closest to Europe.
As you peruse throughout the museum, there are QR codes offering a gateway to yet more of Presque Isle’s aviation history. The museum is located in the Presque Isle International Airport at 650 Airport Drive and is open seven days a week.

title: West Bath veterans, Richmond Grange members rally community to send deployed troops letters of support
ICE reports record-high immigration arrests and deportations since Trump's return to White House
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said Thursday that it arrested and deported more people during a recent 12-month period than at any time in its 23-year history.
ICE said it deported 483,200 people in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30, up 9% from its previous high of 442,640 in the same period a year earlier and up 78% from 271,480 in 2024, the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.
ICE arrested 474,850 people in the most recent 12-month period, roughly double the 239,890 arrests a year earlier and more than quadruple the 113,430 arrests in 2024.
ICE had not released such precise counts since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, including for 2025.
Figures in a press release do not provide breakdowns of how many people had criminal histories, as previous administrations have reported.
“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, ICE has been unleashed to target and remove illegal aliens so that we can save American lives,” said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
ICE said it made more than 48,000 arrests in September, ending a two-month run of record highs that reached 50,925 in August.

title: Longtime teacher and coach killed in murder-suicide weeks after filing for divorce

BARDSTOWN, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — A husband and wife died in a murder-suicide Tuesday morning in Kentucky.

Police found a man and a woman dead from gunshot wounds.

title: Sen. King, colleagues push to expand VA benefits for Iran war veterans
text:
WASHINGTON (WABI) - Sen. Angus King is joining other lawmakers in pushing to expand toxic exposure protections for veterans of the war with Iran.
The proposed New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would presume toxic exposure for veterans who served in Iran, including its airspace and territorial waters, making it easier for them to access health care and benefits through the Department of Veterans Affairs.
The proposal builds on the 2022 PACT Act, which expanded benefits for veterans exposed to toxic substances, including Agent Orange and burn pits.
The new bill would also require the VA to review overseas assignments for toxic exposures at least every five years.

title: Oklahoma man executed for high-profile 2001 killing, first of 2 executions today
text:
Two executions bring US closer to 40 this year as death penalty draws renewed scrutiny
Hours after Oklahoma put another man to death, a Texas man who was convicted of fatally stabbing three young children in 2003 in a squalid, windowless apartment has been executed.
Oklahoma has carried out the execution of James Pavatt, who was convicted of his role in a high-profile 2001 murder in Oklahoma City.
Pavatt was sentenced to death for the murder of Rob Andrew in 2001. Pavatt still claimed he did not kill Andrew, but the Oklahoma Pardon and Parole Board recommended against granting him clemency last month.
Related video above: Oklahoma death row inmate James Pavatt executed
He was executed shortly after 10 a.m. Thursday at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester.
In Texas, John Allen Rubio, 46, was pronounced dead at 6:47 p.m. after a lethal injection at the state prison in Huntsville. The killings of the baby girl and two toddlers so rocked the city of Brownsville, on the U.S. border with Mexico, that the apartment building was later demolished and the land turned into a park and community garden.
Thursday’s executions were the 36th and 37th this year, with the U.S. on track to surpass 40 executions for a second consecutive year — a pace driven by Florida.
The death penalty has drawn renewed attention since the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September.
Last week, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office, which experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.
Background on Pavatt's case
Rob Andrew and his estranged wife, Brenda Andrew, were separated and going through a divorce when Brenda Andrew began a romantic relationship with Pavatt, who was a life insurance agent at the time and helped Rob Andrew get an $800,000 policy.
Prosecutors argued that Brenda Andrew and Pavatt conspired to kill Rob Andrew so his estranged wife could benefit from the policy.
>> Video Below: Oklahoma man maintains innocence as execution looms in high-profile 2001 murder case
He was fatally shot in the garage of the Oklahoma City home he'd previously shared with his wife as he picked up their two young children before Thanksgiving.
Brenda Andrew told police after her husband was killed that masked intruders shot her in the arm and fatally shot him.
Before Rob Andrew’s funeral, Brenda Andrew fled to Mexico with Pavatt. The pair was captured by Mexican authorities three months later.
At a clemency hearing last month, Pavatt said he was “not guilty of shooting anyone,”
While Pavatt’s family shared home videos portraying him as a loving family man and veteran, he was convicted for his role in Rob Andrew’s murder.
Prosecutors have said that Pavatt and Brenda Andrew plotted to kill her husband, and that no matter who fired the shots, both were equally guilty.
Both of them eventually were convicted of the murder. Brenda Andrew currently sits on death row.
During the investigation, it was revealed that Rob Andrew’s brake lines had been cut a month before his murder. Rob had reported the incident to authorities.
"My brake lines have been cut for my car. That sounds like attempted murder, don't you think?" Rob Andrew told dispatchers.
Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond released a statement in mid-September urging the Pardon and Parole Board to not recommend clemency.
"Rob Andrew was gunned down in his own garage, feet from the children he loved, by a man he had trusted as a friend and an insurance agent," Drummond said in a news release. "Twenty-five years later, Pavatt still won't tell the truth about what he did. There must be justice for Rob."
3 young children beheaded in Texas
Rubio and his girlfriend, Angela Camacho, were accused of killing 3-year-old Julissa Quesada, 14-month-old John E. Rubio and 2-month-old Mary Jane Rubio in the windowless apartment they shared in Brownsville. Camacho pleaded guilty and is serving a life sentence.
An appeals court overturned Rubio’s first capital murder conviction, ruling that Camacho's statements were improperly admitted as evidence in his trial. At his second trial, Rubio again pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity but was convicted and sentenced to death.
According to court records, Rubio wasn’t the biological father of the two older children but treated them as if they were his own.
At various points, Rubio claimed the children were possessed and that he was the “chosen one” intended to save the world.
Defense experts diagnosed him with paranoid schizophrenia, a finding prosecution experts rejected. The defense experts also testified that Rubio's childhood — marked by violence at home, “toxic” parents, drug use and prostitution — damaged him developmentally.
___
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Nvidia shares plunge at open after CEO Jensen Huang resigns
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday, capping a spectacular downfall for a poster boy of the artificial intelligence boom whose exit following reports of extramarital affairs now thrusts the chipmaker into an uncertain future.
After a dizzying series of headlines about Huang’s infidelity and ties to an alleged Chinese spy, his departure sets off a scramble to find a permanent replacement to lead the multitrillion-dollar colossus that grew from obscurity to a perch between Apple and Microsoft at the top of the S&P index.
The resignation sent shares of Nvidia plummeting 14% at the opening bell, before stabilizing. The stock was down about 4% around midday Thursday as investors pondered the lawsuits, investigations, likely corporate jockeying and the resilience of a market driven by the gains of a few tech giants.
“Huang’s departure introduces uncertainty well beyond the company itself,” said Asa Hiken, senior analyst for research firm eMarketer, reflecting fears of wider implications and the possibility of an AI bubble.
The company named Colette Kress, the executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim chief executive. She became CFO in 2013, overseeing the company’s global finance operations. Before that, she worked for three years at Cisco and spent 13 years at Microsoft.
Nvidia had no succession plan to prepare for the possibility of the departure of Huang, who was synonymous with Nvidia for more than 30 years in much the same way Steve Jobs embodied Apple. Nvidia said its board would consider internal and external candidates to replace him.
In a statement Thursday, Kress said that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” and that she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”
The board of directors said Thursday it had also named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones, an entrepreneur and venture investor.
Drumbeat of scandals grew louder
Huang, 63, is one of the world’s wealthiest people, with a personal fortune that Forbes estimates at more than $150 billion. He is the single largest individual shareholder of Nvidia stock.
A drumbeat of scandals around him had grown louder in recent weeks after The New York Times reported Huang’s relationship with a woman the paper said U.S. officials had concluded was a Chinese spy who was recruited to influence California-based Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China.
The discovery set off alarms as high as the White House.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating but remained complimentary of Huang on Thursday, saying he “has done a fantastic job.” Like many top tech CEOs, Huang is close to Trump, who has hosted him at the White House and on Air Force One, and awarded him a National Medal of Science.
Nvidia’s board announced an investigation into the allegations on Sunday, but said it remained confident in Huang’s leadership. Then pressure compounded late Wednesday after reports surfaced of another alleged affair by Huang, this time with an Nvidia employee who reported to him.
The company has said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or its secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.
Nvidia is due to report earnings Tuesday.
Lawmakers still want to question Huang
After Huang’s exit, U.S. lawmakers were still insisting on questioning him about his interactions with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang and the company’s security protocols against espionage.
“Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk,” Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online.
Rep. Brian Mast, chairman of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, said the committee was in contact with Huang’s team as recently as Wednesday night after putting in an initial request for an interview on Nov. 5. Mast said Huang would receive a subpoena to compel his appearance, if necessary.
Alice Huang, the suspected spy at the center of the scandal, is a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair but did not identify her.
The two are not related.
Megaspeed faced allegations last year that it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports.
Singaporean authorities said Thursday that they questioned Alice Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed. They concluded that there wasn’t enough evidence that she had committed a crime but suspected she provided “inaccurate information” to downplay her role at Megaspeed and barred her from returning to the country.
China denies attempting to ensnare executive
China has denied that it attempted to ensnare Jensen Huang. Nvidia has become a leader in making chips that power AI, and Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. In January, he won Trump’s approval to sell Nvidia’s H200 chips to China.
Megaspeed said Thursday that it has cooperated with the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which handles enforcement of national security restrictions on technology exports, and was ready to “cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority.”
The company said it has hired a U.S. law firm to conduct a “comprehensive census” of its computer chips and to verify its export controls.
“Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws,” it said.
Apart from questions over national security, Megaspeed’s finances also have drawn attention. Its total assets soared roughly 90-fold from late 2023 to 2024, to almost $3 billion, according to Singapore corporate records.
Revenue surged to over $294 million in 2024 from none in 2023.
What comes next for Jensen Huang is unclear, though another tech mogul, Elon Musk, said on X that it “would be an honor” to hire him.
At a time of growing alarm about AI’s potential risks, Huang has been a voice of optimism on the technology’s potential. His climb to the top of the corporate world started with an idea born in an unglamorous setting.
Huang and two other engineers gathered in 1993 at a Denny’s in San Jose, California, where they discussed building a computer chip that would make graphics for video games faster and more realistic.
That conversation led to the founding of Nvidia.
___
Associated Press writers Barbara Ortutay in San Francisco, Mae Anderson in New York, Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong and Kevin Freking and Will Weissert in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Advocacy groups sue AI giants to freeze new models, warning of 'catastrophic' risks
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups on Thursday sued five of the world’s leading artificial intelligence companies to halt further development, alleging the tech giants can’t prevent their own creations from causing “catastrophic” harm.
The lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court follows a midterm election that could bring a moment of reckoning for the fast-moving AI industry, as Democrats who won back control of Congress stress the need to regulate the technology.
The filing, first reported on by The Associated Press, asks a judge to stop Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI from developing or deploying new AI models, pointing to documented examples of cyberattacks and other harmful actions by AI systems and the companies’ own alarming acknowledgments that their technology has the potential to someday destroy humanity.
“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products — much less ones that could kill us all — as inevitable,” reads the complaint from the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI. “Plaintiffs bring this suit to stop Defendants from continuing their unlawful path to disaster.”
The AI industry has generated excitement and stock market gains, but also deep fears that the technology could go rogue and escape human control. Recent incidents of AI agents hacking government websites and companies — including when OpenAI’s ChatGPT hacked into another AI company on its own in July — have accelerated those concerns.
President Donald Trump, a proponent of rapid AI development to keep the U.S. ahead of foreign competitors like China, has so far encouraged the companies to police themselves on matters of safety, though he has expressed openness to more guardrails. Congress also has stopped short of regulating the technology, but that may change with its Democratic takeover.
Some CEOs of major AI companies, meanwhile, have voiced support for slowing development of the technology to give safety measures a chance to catch up. They also haven’t held back in recognizing the risks. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, for example, last year said he thinks there’s a 1 in 4 chance AI’s future goes “really, really badly,” compared with a 3 in 4 chance it goes well. Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, told Fox News in 2023 that AI could lead to “civilization destruction.”
The plaintiffs, all nonprofits, allege that the companies named in the lawsuit have violated a California unfair competition law by endangering public health and interfering with the use of property such as computer systems. They claim they’ve had to divert resources away from other planned work to address the acute harms threatened by each of the companies’ advancing AI models.
They also warn that the companies’ goals of creating AI systems that are broadly as smart as humans and can increasingly manage tasks and learn things autonomously could result in a permanent loss of control of the technology and heighten existential risks to humanity.
The companies named in Thursday’s lawsuit didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: Maine writer pens book on oyster industry renaissance
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Long ago, Ralph Waldo Emerson noted that life is a journey, not a destination. How extraordinary when that journey awakens every sense — arriving in a small, rugged shell, steeped in brine, and nurtured by the sea.
I remember where I was, who I was with and what I was experiencing for the first time.
A fresh, raw oyster.
Coaxed into trying it, I acquiesced. Buried in cocktail sauce I squeamishly choked it down, then smiled at the accomplishment. I remember thinking — it would be a good long time before I did that again. Today, fresh oysters are the first item I scan for on a restaurant’s menu.
In “Oyster Society” by Virginia Shaffer the focus on this saltwater bivalve mollusk runs deep. Shaffer’s storytelling may focus on the culinary treat that awaits tucked between hard shells, but the brilliance of her story is that of the people this tiny mollusk impacts, the places its presence sustains and the sheer joy brought to many by a fresh oyster.
Shaffer lives in Bath with her husband. She is a food writer, certified oyster sommelier, and is the founder of Maine’s first oyster culinary tour company — Lady Oyster Tours & Tastings. Shaffer has written about shellfish for over ten years and has been featured on NPR and Boston Chronicle. Her writing has been published in numerous publications. This is her first book.
Leaving a successful corporate life in Boston, Shaffer follows her passion with an ingrained sense of purpose. She spends a decade learning and writing about oysters on her blog. This pursuit takes her many places, harbors many dialogues with people entrenched in the industry, notably revealing the profound impact of oysters on the ecosystem.
It is this purpose that travels many miles, many conversations, in prose that is genuine and comfortable. Her encounters take the reader “along for a ride” to an oyster renaissance happening right now. Sprinkled in amongst the oyster shells are recipes, places to check out for fellow oyster travelers, reference materials and a glossary of the oyster industry businesses and people Shaffer had the pleasure of meeting.
From that first mudflat in Wellfleet, Massachusetts, Shaffer strengthens a passion she knew was real and discovers a journey that had been waiting a long time. “Oysters are a time machine. When you hold one in your hands, you’re seeing and feeling our planet’s 250-million-year-history.”
Her travels after that “muddy encounter” are memorable in the people she meets and the stories they have to share in devotion to all things oysters. From island shacks, town and city bars, seafood expositions, oyster shucking contests and oyster farms, Shaffer is at home expressing it all.
“I was falling in love with the people I was meeting. They were bold, quirky, inviting, and so sure of their vocation. The industry was nothing like the stuffy books I read of burly fishermen charting the high seas—it was a much more diverse representation of North American voices. They had funny names like “Oyster Ninja,” “Dr. Oyster,” “Holy City Oyster Maven,” and “Shucker Paddy.” They wielded knives, fought for the environment, and flipped cages full of oysters.”
In the end Shaffer comes full circle in her journey with this reflection: “Cooking, laughing, and sharing a passion for oysters had to be the richest life of all. The younger me, hiding in a tree or climbing over sharp oyster beds, would have wanted this. I had learned from oysters, found kinship, and in the end, created an experience that provoked the same curiosity in others. For the first time, I felt whole.”
A culinary memoir for sure, but one that isn’t about reaching a final destination; it is a deep dive into the brackish, unforgettable waters of a life shaped by the sea and will satisfy the appetite and appeal to the “wannabe” connoisseur searching for another challenge or the uninitiated wanting to learn all there is to know while trying something new.
And if you are apt to think — “no way” am I trying that, this book still remains worthy of your time because it is a way to get close to knowing a marvelous group of people, special places and a small salt-water bivalve mollusk that in its own grand way impacts it all.
“Oyster Society: Adventures with the Shellfishly Motivated,” by Virginia Shaffer, is published by Islandport Press, 2026, hardcover $26.95.

title: Medomak Lead Testing Results Show Improvement
text:
Recent water testing has shown a “significant decrease” in lead levels compared to testing earlier in October at Medomak Valley High School, according to RSU 40 Superintendent Dan Welch.
The high school remains under a “do not drink” order, first issued on Oct. 13, as many water fixtures still show lead levels above federal limits, Welch said in an email on Oct. 28. The cause of the increased levels is still unknown.
“The results also show that lead levels continue to decrease as water runs through the fixtures,” Welch said. “This is encouraging, as it suggests the issue may be with individual faucets and fixtures rather than the school’s main water supply.”

title: Freeport extends town manager’s contract, reelects council chair
text:
Freeport town councilors extended Town Manager Sophie Wilson’s contract through 2030 and elected council leadership during two meetings Tuesday evening.
Joanna Benoit, who was reelected on Election Day to her at-large post, will serve another term as council chair. District 1 Councilor Daniel Piltch won the vice chair post at Tuesday’s meeting, replacing outgoing District 2 Councilor Eric Smith in the role.
The council also approved a 3 ½-year contract for Wilson, who has served as town manager since 2023. Before moving to Freeport, Wilson worked as Orono’s town manager for more than a decade.
Wilson’s new contract sets her salary at about $169,000.
Benoit, District 3 Councilor Matthew Pillsbury and District 2 Councilor James DeGrandpre were all sworn in to the council Tuesday after winning their elections earlier this month. Benoit and Pillsbury both ran unopposed to regain their posts. Newcomer DeGrandpre won the only contested seat on the council, receiving 875 votes to Steven Doran’s 319.

title: Linda LeMont (1942-2026)
Maine Democrats eye emergency heating aid to begin session
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA — Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree and incoming legislative leaders are in early talks about an emergency bill to help low-income Mainers pay their home heating bills.
The North Haven Democrat said in an interview Tuesday that she’s had “a good conversation” with leaders from both parties about moving a bill soon after lawmakers convene in January if Congress does not increase funding for the Low Income Heating Assistance Program before the end of the year.
About 40,000 Maine households rely on LIHEAP.
“Right off the bat, I am very worried about the price of heating oil and just sort of basic safety for Maine people,” Pingree said.
About half of the homes in Maine rely on home-heating oil, the price of which has skyrocketed since the U.S. launched its military campaign in Iran in February. As of Nov. 2, prices were up over 80% since last year and hit a record high of $6.04 a gallon in October.
Fast-tracking an emergency heating and energy package to kick off a session would not be unprecedented. After the 2022 midterm election cycle, lawmakers quickly approved a bill that provided $450 checks to most taxpayers, plus $40 million for LIHEAP and $10 million to help people who didn’t qualify for the program.
It’s unclear whether direct checks would be included in the package that is currently being discussed.
But House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, D-Biddeford, said in an interview Tuesday that speed and ease of administration would be a priority.
Fecteau said he would be relying on the Maine Community Action Partnership, which administers LIHEAP and other energy assistance programs, for information about how much additional funding may be needed.
“The key piece here is making sure people get the help they need as fast as they can,” Fecteau said.
Earlier this week, Gov. Janet Mills joined other New England governors in calling on Congress to provide an additional $3 billion in LIHEAP funding.
“No one should be cold in their homes because Trump decided to wage an unnecessary, unwanted war with Iran,” Mills said in a written statement.
The governors noted in a letter to congressional appropriators, including Republican Sen. Susan Collins, that the National Energy Assistance Director’s Association projected a 50% increase in heating oil prices this winter, which could cost low-income households in the Northeast an additional $1.1 billion.
Democrats expanded their majorities in the state House and Senate last week. While they hold a supermajority in the Senate, Democrats will need Republican support in the House to pass an emergency measure, which requires a two-thirds vote.
Incoming House Republican Minority Leader Rep. Ken Fredette of Newport said in an interview Wednesday that he will discuss a possible emergency bill with his caucus once the overall cost and funding source is identified.
The state’s so-called rainy day fund is flush with cash, which would be tapped. But lawmakers must confront a projected $1.3 billion budget gap in 2028-29, which may put spending cuts on the table.
“I don’t think as Republicans, we want anybody necessarily going cold this winter because of the high cost of heating oil,” Fredette said. “I think that’s something we need to really look at and figure out what’s the right number and also where does the money come from.”
Senate President Mattie Daughtry, D-Brunswick, said she hopes both parties will be able to come together on heating aid, if needed.
“We’re all hurting — it doesn’t matter whether you’re in Wallagrass or Brunswick,” Daughtry said. “So I would hope that folks would be willing to work on that.”

title: Rapper Yella Beezy convicted of hiring gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 on busy interstate
text:
DALLAS (AP) - Rapper Yella Beezy was found guilty on Wednesday of hiring the gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 in a brazen daylight attack on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020.
Yella Beezy, 35, whose real name is Markies Conway, was unanimously convicted of capital murder by a Dallas County jury in the death of MO3, whose real name was Melvin Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
In September, a jury found Kewon White guilty of capital murder for fatally shooting Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Prosecutors said the killing was the result of an yearslong escalating feud between Conway and Noble. Both men lived in Dallas.
“We don’t know what turned it for the jurors. … We appreciate the verdict,” lead prosecutor Tommy Adams told reporters. “We think they got it right today.”
“It’s been one of the most challenging cases over the last six years,” he added.
Prosecutors said Conway paid White $40,000 for the shooting.
Noble, 28, was driving on Interstate 35 in south Dallas around noon on Nov. 11, 2020, when White pulled alongside him, authorities said. White stepped out of his vehicle holding a gun. Noble got out of his own vehicle and began running on the freeway as White shot at him, authorities said.
Prosecutor Tommy Adams said White wore a mask and fired over 40 rounds from an AK-47-style pistol while chasing Noble.
White shot Noble and a bystander who was inside a car, police said. The bystander survived, but Noble died at a hospital.
During closing arguments, prosecutors showed jurors a video clip of Conway talking about revenge in an interview, saying he would “get his lick back.” Prosecutor Krystal Biggins drew a comparison between Noble’s killing and a roadway shooting that injured Conway in 2018.
In October 2018, Conway survived being shot while driving on a tollway in the Dallas suburb of Lewisville when someone pulled up next to him and opened fire, hitting him three times.
“This was for the world to see,” Biggins said. “Over a rap beef, we are here for capital murder.”
The defense argued that prosecutors did not prove their case. “This is capital murder, and the state has brought you a lot of speculation,” defense attorney John Gussio said.
Noble had more than 800,000 Instagram followers and was best known for a 2019 remix of “Errybody,” with Baton Rouge, Louisiana, rapper Boosie Badazz.
Conway is best known for his 2017 single, “That’s On Me,” and the 2019 song “Bacc At It Again” with Quavo and Gucci Mane.

title: Black Friday scams to watch for and how to avoid them
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Some Black Friday deals can cost shoppers more than they save, and Kyle James, a writer for ConsumerAffairs, identified the biggest red flags this year.
The first is what are known as “ghost websites.” These are fake sites promoted through phony social media ads with offers that seem too good to be true.
“The ads are really convincing. Sometimes they’ll use celebrities in their ads. They’ll use some really good marketing tools. You’ll see brands that you recognize. And a lot of people will click on it and go to these ghost websites, and those websites are designed to either place your order, and you never see the product. Or they’re going to steal your credit card information and you’re never going to hear from them again,” James said.
Before clicking, shoppers can type the company’s name into a browser and search it with the word “scam.”
Another trick involves social media ads claiming a “store closing” or “final close-out.” The ads send shoppers to a fake website that collects their personal information.
Another scam involves fake customer service numbers.
“A lot of times these scammers will buy sponsored Google listings for like ‘BestBuy’ customer service, and in many cases, it will be up above the actual BestBuy phone number. And they want you to call it and they’re going to get you and try to get your credit card information or try to do something nefarious,” James said.
Shoppers should use a store’s app or official website to find the real customer service number.
The final scam involves text messages about a “delayed delivery” or a “problem with your order.”
James said a legitimate company will not text customers to verify a tracking number or an address. Shoppers should not click links in those texts or give any information.
