title: Maine is short family doctors. A new Farmington residency program could help.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new family medicine residency program in Farmington could breathe new life into a workforce hampered by turnover and growing challenges to deliver rural healthcare.
MaineHealth Franklin Hospital, a critical access hospital in Farmington with four family medicine practices, is navigating a number of challenges. The hospital lost primary care physicians this year. Recruitment is slow. And Franklin is one of the only options for care in the area, so it must respond to a broad range of medical needs, said Dr. Libby Abbas, a family medicine physician.
She said a residency program can play a key role in improving access to care.
“People have really gotten used to this turnover, and it’s led to fragmentation of care, and, I think, worse health outcomes,” said Abbas, who will lead the residency program. “And so my goal is to hopefully create more physicians that want to not only train here, but maybe stay here when they’re done and allow us to have that longevity that I think leads to better outcomes.”
MaineHealth, one of the state’s largest health systems, won a $750,000 grant from the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) to develop the family medicine residency program. Two residents will start the three-year program each year, with the first class kicking off in July. Abbas is interviewing candidates out of the hundreds who applied.
Residents will train in behavioral health, addiction medicine, geriatrics, pediatrics, general surgery and emergency medicine. MaineHealth will fully fund the program after the HRSA grant ends in 2027, said Dr. Kalli Varaklis, who oversees grants for the health system.
Leaders say residency programs can draw providers to rural areas and give them a reason to stay.
Kacie Staples, 28, is two years into a rural internal medicine residency program at MaineHealth Stephens Hospital, a critical access hospital in Norway. Raised in a tiny town in Minnesota before attending medical school in Missouri, Staples knew she wanted to practice rural medicine.
More than a year before she graduates from the residency, she knows she wants to do it in Maine.
“My dream is to stay in western Maine, up in Norway, and do oncology for the patients up there,” Staples said. “I think it’d be really hard to leave that community.”
Residency is a period of intensive clinical training for medical school graduates on the path to becoming physicians. Programs are usually multiple years and focus on one or more specialties. Varaklis said MaineHealth has more than 400 residents and fellows across nearly two dozen programs.
Maine has four other residency programs for family medicine, located at practices in Bangor, Lewiston, Augusta and Portland. Between 2011 and 2017, those programs produced 211 family medicine physicians; 47% stayed in-state, according to a report by the Robert Graham Center, a national think tank.
More recent national data shows upward of 60% of family doctors are practicing in the state they trained in. That trend is important for Maine, which will be short 120 primary care doctors by 2030, mostly due to increased utilization by an aging population, according to a Robert Graham projection.
When Maine’s facilities lose providers to retirement, career changes or other styles of care, many replace them with temporary doctors, or “locum tenens,” until they can hire a full-time provider. No matter how proactive the hospital, Abbas said, it takes “a very long time and a lot of money” to recruit a physician. Franklin Hospital has used locums in family medicine for years.
Abbas said once the hospital finally fills a spot, “we lose another person.”
But six of the seven graduates from Stephens’ rural internal medicine residency program now work in rural Maine. “They’ve almost replaced the existing internal medicine practitioners, all who are aging in Norway,” Varaklis said.
She said another MaineHealth program, a month-long rural elective rotation, has drawn nearly 150 residents from across the country to train in dozens of specialties, like obstetrics in Norway or psychiatry in Farmington. The health system has recruited more than 20 of them.
And no matter the specialty, leaders say participants in the residency programs in rural Maine will learn to think on their feet. They’ll have to. Franklin Hospital offers the major specialties, like obstetrics and orthopedic surgery, but it does not have pulmonology, sleep medicine and other subspecialties. Stephens does not have gastroenterology.
Those specialists are in Portland, more than an hour’s drive from both hospitals.
“You can’t just call someone,” Staples said, “or you can’t have those providers come take a peek at the patient. So you really have to be more creative: OK, what are the other tests we can do to prove this is what we think we’re dealing with? What other resources do we have to find out what’s going on?”
She’s found it thrilling. No day is the same. But after a year in Norway, she says the reliability, steadiness and trust of her patients are what make her excited to learn and grow as a provider.
One patient often tells Staples she listens better than any doctor she has seen. She doesn’t want to lose her.
Staples responds, truthfully: I don’t want to leave.
“It takes special people that are going to come here and stay here,” Abbas said.

title: Please Stop Taking Your Shoes Off in the Movie Theater
text:
Please, For the Love of God, Keep Your Shoes on in the Movie Theater
The Alamo Drafthouse in Downtown Brooklyn was busy on Monday night. Stylishly dressed patrons filtered out of an event in the theater’s bar, while guests milled about in the lobby, happily debating You Can See Everything and Wicker.
At the center of the hubbub, surrounded by standees for Godzilla Minus Zero and I Play Rocky, was an unusual sign, placed on a stand about six feet in front of the employee responsible for checking tickets. In all caps and zero punctuation, it read:
“SHOES MUST BE WORN AT ALL TIMES INSIDE THEATERS”
That is not a good sign. No one posts a reminder to customers like that proactively. You only take that kind of drastic action after you have had multiple problems with people waving their naked toesies around in your movie theater. This wasn’t the only “NO SHOES NO SERVICE” sign at the Alamo, either. All but one of the seven auditoriums on the Brooklyn Alamo’s top floor had an identical sign hung by the door.
READ MORE: Movie Theaters Are Not Just for Blockbusters
Equally amused and nauseated, I took a picture of the sign in the lobby and posted it to my Instagram account. I have never gotten more DMs about anything I have ever posted in 15+ years on Instagram, not even the photo of Timothée Chalamet pancakes slathered in purple goo.
Some of the response were simple vomit or gritted-teeth emojis. Others shared horror stories. One friend told me that on a recent trip to a theater, the person seated next to them not only took off their shoes, but their socks as well. A colleague revealed that they just had dealt with a foot nudist at a screening of You Can See Everything. And a longtime film industry veteran told me that when they worked at an art house theater several years ago people removing their shoes was a “constant issue.”
What’s worse, they said, was that one time they “caught someone clipping their toenails in theater too.”
(Should I have put a trigger warning on this post? That was an oversight on my part, sorry.)
As gross as these stories were, they were also kind of reassuring — because in the last few years I’ve watched in horror as people all around me have started de-shoeing with increasing regularity. A few months ago at a screening of The Invite — at this same Alamo Drafthouse in Brooklyn, come to think of it — I sat next to a woman who casually tossed her shoes to the ground once the lights dimmed in the auditorium. Thankfully, her dogs were not barking, aromatically speaking. But she did start picking at her toes at one point and that was a wee bit distracting/disgusting.
Until these sign popped up in the Alamo, I assumed I was the only one who found this behavior extremely off-putting. It just seemed like the social contract had shifted at some point, and going barefoot in the movies had somehow been shifted onto the list of acceptable movie-theater activities. Barefoot in the park or a Gene Saks romantic comedy? That’s one thing. But in a movie theater? Where you are in close proximity to many strangers four hours at a time, and where seating is now often assigned in advance so you can’t simply get up and move to another empty seat if the dude next to you decides now would be a good time for a DIY pedicure?
It didn’t sit well with me. But I appeared to be alone on a well-shod island on the matter, because the more I went to the theater the more frequently I observed this behavior. Frankly, I have had far more issues over the past few years with footwear (or the lack thereof) in theaters than with loud patrons or cell phone usage.
As to the matter of why this has become more prevalent, I have to assume it has something to do with more and more people returning to theaters after a prolonged period of watching movies almost exclusively at home. During the pandemic, theaters across the world shut down and cinephiles were forced to fend for themselves.
Every movie lover sets their own rules in their personal home theater. Now, with attendance on a upswing, multiplexes are luring bringing back customers who got a little too comfortable screening films at home. Or maybe this is a symptom of the broader incivility that has infected so many aspects of public life over the last decade.
(Could the rise of Crocs also play a contributing factor? Those things are far too easy to take on and off. They’re like slippers that society has deemed socially acceptable for out-of-home use. In my personal experience, I would estimate that one out of every four shoeless theater patrons is wearing Crocs.)
Whatever the reason, I am glad that someone decided to, uh, put their foot down. Follow the signs. Keep your shoes on. It’s a movie theater, not a damn Quentin Tarantino movie.

title: InvestigateTV+: Printers carry hacker risks
text:
(InvestigateTV) — An outdated setting on an office printer can give hackers easy access to sensitive information, and InvestigateTV+ uncovers how it could put doctors, schools, even police at risk.
Then, we go inside one company’s bid to pause death to buy time for science, and why some see it as a bold step.
Plus, we decode the colors of the underground utility system and explain the free step that can help homeowners avoid disaster.
Network Nightmares
InvestigateTV found possible printer problems across the country after receiving a confidential audit of several agencies’ machines.
Humming in the corner of offices across America, many modern office printers and multifunction devices do more than scan and copy documents. Depending on the model and settings, they may store documents, scan histories, address books, network settings or other sensitive information. Modern office printers can also have hard drives, firmware and default passwords that may never get changed.
Cryonics and the questions that remain
People frozen for years then thawed out and awake in a different time. It’s a common scene in popular science fiction movies.
But this isn’t the script of a blockbuster, a nonprofit in Arizona is attempting to make it a reality. Since the 1970s, Alcor has specialized in cryonics, defined as the practice of preserving life by pausing the dying process using subfreezing temperatures.
Alcor is betting on future science to do what today’s cannot.
Call before you dig
As the weather warms up, many homeowners are getting ready for landscaping and other yard projects. But before you dig, experts say one phone call could prevent disaster.
“You can’t assume you know what’s underground. You have to assume that you don’t,” said Sarah Magruder Lyle, president and CEO of Common Ground Alliance.
A jam band for mental health
A group of veterans has turned their shared experiences into a mission, using country music to address mental health stigma in the military community.
Vet Jams, a band that performs at bars around the New Orleans metro area, combines live music with open conversations about therapy and mental health support for veterans.

title: Waldoboro Rejects $50,000 Legal Fees for Cellphone Tower Lawsuit
text:
With a vote of 1,330-1,208, Waldoboro residents rejected the use of $50,000 in legal fees to combat a federal lawsuit from a wireless infrastructure developer at the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
The fees would be used to pay for litigation in the ongoing lawsuit originally filed on Sept. 11 by Blue Sky Towers LLC, which is alleging a violation of federal law with the stalling of a cellphone tower proposal at 2734 Friendship Road. The company maintains that it is authorized by law to place a cell tower in the proposed location due to a lack of coverage in the surrounding area.

title: Father of boy who survived being buried alive is charged with attempted murder in South Carolina
text:
LEXINGTON, S.C. (AP) — A South Carolina man accused of burying his 11-month-old son in a dog crate in a clump of scrubby pines was scheduled for a bond hearing Thursday.
Michael Comer, 25, has been charged with attempted murder, burglary and unlawfully placing a child at risk in connection with the disappearance and rescue of his son, Koah, who survived and is expected to make a full recovery. Comer has been in custody in Lexington County since Monday, when his son was reported missing.
Koah, who was found by rescuers after about 24 hours, was released from a hospital Tuesday night, Sheriff Jay Koon said.
John Comer said he’d opened his home to his son and grandson on Monday after Michael Comer said they needed a place to stay. On Wednesday, he showed an Associated Press reporter the small hole on a neighbor’s property where rescuers uncovered the child.
“I cannot imagine how somebody could come to the point that that would be the right thing to do, or the thing to do at all,” John Comer told the AP.
Authorities haven’t revealed anything about Comer’s motive. He was sentenced in October to probation after pleading guilty to domestic violence involving the boy’s mother.
Koah’s parents “have had some situations,” the sheriff said.
“Children,” he said, “sometimes get caught in the middle.”
Dozens of first responders scoured the countryside for the boy with reddish blond hair. After a full day of searching, authorities found freshly disturbed soil and heard cries from below, the sheriff said.
The boy likely survived because of cool temperatures and an air pocket created by a towel that was wrapped around the crate below ground, he said.
Koah was soon freed and “clinging to life,” the sheriff told reporters.
___
Breed reported from Wake Forest, North Carolina, and McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Associated Press writers Ed White in Detroit, Michael R. Sisak in New York and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

title: Blue Hill renews liquor license for restaurant it has taken to court
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Apart from regular business and updates, the Blue Hill Select Board’s major focus at its meeting on Monday, October 26, was to consider the renewal of two liquor licenses for restaurants in town. The first, for Marlintini’s Grill, was predictably non-controversial and was passed unanimously by the board with only one comment, in favor, from a member of the public.
The second liquor license renewal, for Pub Ciao LLC, doing business as Blaze Blue Hill, might have been expected to be more controversial given past and ongoing disputes, now stretching over a five-year period, between the restaurant and town government regarding permits, noise complaints, code violations and a land-use disagreement that is the subject of a lawsuit.
Prior to considering the liquor license renewal, the select board opened the floor to public comments. Blaze’s owner, Matt Haskell, reiterated his position. “We did have permits from the town and from the Department of Environmental Protection. We went through the process,” Haskell said.
“There was an issue with the stage,” Haskell said, “and the stage is gone. But that other stuff that everybody talked about was all permitted five and a half years ago.”
Speaking in support of Blaze, Blue Hill native Darlene Hatch asked, “Why are we harassing Blaze? We want these restaurants in town and
Hatch recalled that when the space occupied by Blaze had been vacant in the past, it became, “the local hangout for kids, loud and obnoxious, tires spinning, screaming, partying in the parking lot.” Blaze and its employees, Hatch said, also were good for the local economy. “We service all of their vehicles [Hatch manages the Blue Hill Garage] and they spend money at a lot of other businesses in town.”
Haskell then spoke, recalling his efforts to work with the town, the legal fees he has incurred, the investment he has made in Blaze, and the disparity between what he says transpired in terms of permitting and interactions with the town’s code enforcement officer and the select board’s interpretation.
Select Board member Scott Miller then talked about whether or not the ongoing legal dispute over possible land-use violations should be considered when voting to extend Blaze’s liquor license.
Blue Hill resident — and neighbor of Blaze — Rich Boulet then addressed the board. “I want to say that Blaze has done a great job complying with your [the town’s] conditions that were set last October for the special amusement permit, and I’ve appreciated that. I haven’t noticed more than two events per week and they have all ended promptly at 9:30 p.m.”
Miller then proposed a motion to renew Blaze’s liquor license and special amusement permit for one year with the same conditions that are presently in place. The motion was seconded and approved unanimously by the board.

title: Gardens Aglow opens Saturday at Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens in Boothbay
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BOOTHBAY, Maine (WABI) - Gardens Aglow opens Saturday at Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens in Boothbay and runs through Jan. 2.
A mile-long path glows with more than 750,000 LED lights. Strung end to end, the lights would stretch about 65 miles, the distance from South Portland to Boothbay.
This year’s theme is “Gathered in Maine.” Organizers told WABI the theme has a double meaning.
Gretchen Ostherr, president and CEO of Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens, explained the meaning.
“It is both about the gathering and harvesting that Mainers and the natural world are doing during the winter and this time of year. And then it’s also about how we all gather together this time of year,” Ostherr said.
“Many people will say, yeah, we come from Massachusetts, we came from New Hampshire. We came from up in Aroostook County and we’re spending the night. I mean, a lot of people make it a big event as part of their holiday season,” she said.
Ticket information
Ticket prices start at $20 for adults and are on sale now. Tickets should be purchased online or over the phone, 633-8000.
The gardens is competing again for a USA Today Readers’ Choice award in the best botanical garden holiday lights category. It is currently ranked No. 2.
People can vote once a day through Nov. 30 at 10best.usatoday.com.
Park and Ride to Gardens Aglow
The Boothbay Harbor Region Chamber of Commerce provides shuttles from downtown Boothbay Harbor to the gardens on weekend nights during Gardens Aglow.
Shuttles run continuously from 3:45 to 9 p.m. from the Boothbay Harbor Town Office to the entrance of Gardens Aglow.

title: These 25 Maine areas could see more investment under federal program
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than two dozen communities across the state are readying for what could be a tidal wave of investment over the next decade. It could also just be a trickle. Or it might not come at all.
State and federal officials this week announced the 25 “tracts” that have been selected as the next federal Qualified Opportunity Zones, a designation designed to help draw private, long-term investment to low-income areas.
Maine’s current 32 Opportunity Zones have been in place since 2018 and are set to expire.
Gov. Janet Mills announced Tuesday that she selected the 25 areas from a list of 78 options.
Eight of the 25 tracts — including parts of Westbrook, Brunswick, Augusta and East Millinocket — were also designated in the previous round.
But areas that missed out a decade ago, like Sanford, Biddeford, Houlton, Machias, Skowhegan and Dover-Foxcroft, will get their shot at attracting some needed investment.
A lack of reporting requirements makes it impossible to tell how successful the program is. There’s no way to know whether a project used Opportunity Zone funds unless a developer volunteers the information.
The program appears to have been used successfully in at least a handful of times in Maine, including for projects in South Portland, Brunswick, Waterville and Augusta.
Data from elsewhere in the country, however, suggests mixed results.
OPPORTUNITY KNOCKS
The Opportunity Zone incentive program was established in 2017 by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act to encourage long-term investments in low-income urban and rural communities nationwide. It was made permanent last year and reintroduced as the Opportunity Zone 2.0 program, which offers additional incentives for selections in rural areas, has tighter qualifying criteria and new reporting requirements.
Eligible communities are determined based on income and poverty thresholds.
It has been hard for municipalities to track the success of the program because there has not been a requirement to report whether a project is using the incentive. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, however, Opportunity Zones attracted more than $100 billion in the last 10 years. Another $100 billion is expected in the next decade.
The program allows investors to create or invest in so-called “opportunity funds” through which they can reinvest capital gains — profits from the sale of investments — into designated areas tax-free for at least five years, then get a 10% tax break on the initial investment. That increases to 30% in designated rural areas. Any profits they make annually through the investment after 10 years are tax-free.
Governors nominated eligible communities for the designation, which were then certified by the U.S. Department of the Treasury.
Maine’s 32 current zones were selected by former Gov. Paul LePage and will expire at the end of 2028. The new zones will take effect Jan. 1, 2027, so there will be a roughly two-year overlap.
‘TRANSFORMATIVE IMPACT’
Mike Duguay, commissioner of the Maine Department of Economic and Community Development, said state officials spent the last year consulting with developers, local leaders and financial professionals to determine where investment “can have the most transformative impact.”
“We did not approach these designations lightly,” he said in a statement. “This was a bottom-up effort to ensure that these federal tools are working hard for Maine’s specific needs.”
Tony Armstrong, a commercial real estate broker and adviser, was thrilled to see Dover-Foxcroft make the cut this time around.
He has been working to redevelop Browns Mill, the former Maine Leathers Tannery, in the Piscataquis County town.
The project has the potential to see the same kind of transformation as mill projects in Lewiston and Biddeford, if on a smaller scale, Armstrong said, but hasn’t had the necessary “oomph” to draw the kind of attention needed.
At the same time, the Piscataquis County Economic Development Council has been trying for years to recruit a developer to build an 80-room hotel.
That, too, hasn’t quite made it over the finish line.
“This kind of program … is going to make the difference,” Armstrong said.
WASTED OPPORTUNITY?
But other parts of the state that could desperately use an infusion of investment, like large swaths of northern and western Maine, were passed over, despite being some of the most rural parts of the state.
According to Brady Meixell, a senior research associate at the Urban Institute who is studying opportunity zones and their impact, that may not be a bad call.
The Urban Institute found that in Ohio, more than two-thirds of the state’s opportunity zones did not receive a single dollar of investment from 2020-24. The vast majority of money flowed into metropolitan centers like Cleveland and Columbus.
Ohio is the only state with Opportunity Zone data because of reporting requirements to get a matching state-level credit, so the Urban Institute views the Midwestern state as a sort of case-study of the program’s efficacy.
Governors in other states, Meixell said, took a lesson from those results: “There are going to be some very disinvested tracts that are eligible that it would feel good to select because you want to drive capital into them, but Opportunity Zones just are not the program that’s going to do that,” he said. “To some of degree, some of those might be wasted picks.”
Only 39% of tracts selected for the Opportunity Zone 2.0 program were in rural areas, despite the added incentives.
There are “Goldilocks tracts” he said, in areas that could be poised for greater development but need an extra push to get there.
But in many cases, governors overcorrected and prioritized areas that already had a large number of jobs and a higher percentage of multifamily housing (which is the most common use for Opportunity Zones).
“A meaningful number of zones were already ascending rapidly before designation,” Meixell said.
Based on the data from Ohio, those are the zones most likely to see significant investment —those that were already experiencing greater income and home value growth in the years before the program launched.
Essentially, the zones receiving the most money from investors were the ones that didn’t need an incentive to court development in the first place.
A BOON FOR BAYSIDE
According to the Urban Institute, Bayside is one of those communities.
The neighborhood already has hundreds of units in the pipeline and hundreds more in pre-development.
Portland officials initially tried to decline Bayside’s potential designation.
In a March meeting, members of the Housing Economic Development Committee feared the city could face another Urban Renewal by welcoming in a developer without any control over what is built in the neighborhood while investors line their pockets at the expense of longtime residents.
But Duguay sent a letter to Mayor Mark Dion, outlining how the program works.
“Being designated as an Opportunity Zone does not take away local control over land use, zoning, or project approvals. It is merely a federal tax incentive program, not a land-use or permitting regime,” he wrote. “In a nutshell, the program changes who might provide capital, not who makes the decision on whether a project gets approved.”
Chris Marshall, co-founder of GreenMars Real Estate in Portland, has plans for a more than 300-unit housing development in Bayside. The Opportunity Zone will be crucial in bringing in the investors that project needs, he said.
While Marshall is primarily focused on Bayside, he was excited to see the city’s other tract, which includes Riverside Street and the Riverton neighborhood.
The area has more commercial and industrial space than the kind of high-density multifamily housing that often draws opportunity zone investors, but it’s a prime location near the highway with access to highly skilled workers, making it ripe for economic development, he said.
“You need economic activity to boost wages,” he said. “If we can get more supply in one zone (in Bayside) and increased wages in another zone, that’s a win/win and work both sides of the equation on housing affordability,” he said.

title: Investigators determine cause of fire that destroyed Ashland home
text:
Maine investigators determine cause of fire that destroyed Ashland home
77-year-old man taken to hospital for smoke inhalation, a cat died in the fire and a dog that ran away remains lost
Maine investigators determine cause of fire that destroyed Ashland home
77-year-old man taken to hospital for smoke inhalation, a cat died in the fire and a dog that ran away remains lost
The Maine State Fire Marshal's Office has revealed the cause of a fire in Ashland that started in a garage and ultimately destroyed a home.
The Ashland Fire Department responded to the fire at 27 Despres St., which is in the town's Sheridan neighborhood, shortly before 3:10 p.m. Monday.
When firefighters arrived at the scene, they saw heavy flames coming from the garage that were spreading into an adjoining home.
Both the garage and the home are considered a total loss. Two people have been displaced as a result of the fire.
A 77-year-old man who had been working in the garage before the fire started was transported to Northern Light A.R. Gould Hospital in Presque Isle to be treated for smoke inhalation.
No injuries to firefighters were reported. One cat died in the fire, while a dog that ran away from the property during the incident remains lost.
Investigators from the State Fire Marshal's Office determined the fire started in the garage while a lawn tractor was being repaired. According to investigators, gasoline spilled onto the garage floor during the repair and a space heater ignited the resulting gasoline vapors.
The fire has been ruled accidental.
The Ashland Fire Department received mutual aid from the Portage, Mapleton and Masardis fire departments, as well as the Maine Forest Service and Ashland Ambulance.

title: ‘Help us’: Kids rescued after holding handwritten note against home’s window
text:
KISSIMMEE, Fla. (Gray News) - Police in Florida are praising the bravery of a child who held a handwritten note that read “Help us” against a window while hiding during a domestic disturbance.
Kissimmee Police say they responded Oct. 26 to a domestic disturbance involving 33-year-old Andre Janard Smithson at the Florida Ridge Condos. A woman inside the home told her sister that Smithson was “beating” her, WTSP reports, citing an arrest affidavit.
Family members told police that children were in the home, and they feared for their safety.
Using a drone, police found three kids hiding in a guest room. Meanwhile, Smithson and the victim were in the master bedroom with their 5-month-old daughter, according to WTSP.
One of the kids held a handwritten note against the window that read “Help us.” Police later praised the child’s bravery in a Facebook post about the incident.
WTSP reports that Smithson spoke to officers by phone and refused repeated requests to let the victim and kids leave the home. Police say the kids were able to safely escape while Smithson was distracted.
With help from a SWAT team and crisis negotiators, police say Smithson eventually surrendered peacefully. He was arrested on charges of false imprisonment and an outstanding active warrant.
Smithson reportedly told investigators he wanted to spend time with his infant daughter before going to jail, according to WTSP.

title: Storm Shifting South, Bulk of Moisture Remains Offshore
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Clouds will continue to increase this evening as the storm that we have been watching all week inches closer.
The biggest change to the forecast has been a the storm trending farther to our south. This means that the bulk of the precipitation will shift offshore and a few spots along the coast could see a few light rain showers into early Friday.
Friday: Looking Dry & Cloudy
At this point in time, it looks like all the precipitation besides a few light showers will remain off the coast. This means a dry but clouds day along the coast Friday. Those farther inland will remain dry with breaks in the clouds possible. Highs will be in the 30s and 40s. Winds will also be weaker out of the NNE with gusts to 25 mph possible.
Saturday: Scattered Rain/Snow Showers
The low will lift to our northeast on Saturday. Expect plenty of clouds with highs again in the 30s and low 40s. There will be a chance of scattered rain and snow showers. For those from the Foothills towards the coast should expect isolated rain showers. The mountains and north will see the best chance of scattered snow showers. Accumulations will be possible but is looking like a coating that will remain to grassy surfaces. NNW winds will gust to 20 mph.
The second half of the weekend will be drier with partly to mostly cloudy skies. Highs on Sunday will be a few degrees warmer maxing out in the 40s.
Next Week: Drier & Warming-Up
An upper-level ridge will build into the northeast next week promoting drier and warmer conditions. Highs for many will jump back into the 50s by Wednesday and thereafter. A few inland areas could make a run at close to 60°.

title: Eddington woman out on bail in infant overdose case booked into jail again
text:
EDDINGTON, Maine (WABI) - An Eddington woman who was out on bail in connection with an infant’s reported overdose has been booked into jail again, following a search.
The Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office says Wood turned herself in on Wednesday.
Authorities said they seized suspected illegal drugs during a traffic stop Sunday and stopped Wood from destroying potential evidence.
Wood, 36, faces charges of unlawful possession of scheduled drugs, falsifying physical evidence and violating conditions of release.
Wood was previously released on bail in connection with an incident in May involving an infant who reportedly overdosed on drugs.
She is expected to appear in court Thursday afternoon.
Status on the school board
Wood is a member of the RSU 63 School Board, representing Eddington.
Town Manager Shawna Hinkley said earlier this year that there is no recall process for RSU 63 school board members. Under an absenteeism policy, a member who misses three consecutive meetings is removed from the board.
Wood missed two consecutive meetings after the July warrant. She was released on bail in time to attend the third and kept her seat.
WABI reached out to RSU 63 School Board Chair Rachel Downs for comment. Downs confirmed Wood is still an elected member of the board.
“The district will continue to follow applicable district policies and Maine law, including 20-A M.R.S. § 1474 which outlines the circumstances under which a vacancy on a regional school unit board may be declared,” Downs said. “Since this is a matter involving an elected official and pending law enforcement matters, the School Board does not have further comments at this time.”
The town of Eddington has been contacted for more information.
Earlier case
The Sheriff’s Office was searching for Wood in July on separate charges connected to an infant overdose. Wood was taken into custody several days later while leaving a home in Eddington.
Her attorney said in court that Wood had been on vacation and did not know about the warrant until she saw news reports online. The defense also said Wood was on her way to turn herself in when she was arrested.
Officials said Wood’s 9-month-old child overdosed in May, and Wood and the baby tested positive for cocaine and fentanyl. A grand jury indicted Wood in October on charges related to the incident.

title: Our healthcare system is failing us. There are alternatives.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Ben Hagopian is a direct primary care physician in South Portland.
Open enrollment season is here again. And like clockwork, it arrives with another double-digit premium hike and another round of shrinking benefits.
Next year, if you carry conventional health insurance and get sick, you will face up to $12,000 in out-of-pocket costs — $24,000 for a family — on top of your monthly premiums.
I’ve worked in health care for 20 years, and every year the system grows more absurd, more painful, and less affordable.
A growing number of Americans want major reform — Medicare for All chief among them. But that’s probably not politically realistic or fiscally feasible, at least not soon. Fortunately, necessity has bred alternatives, and they’re already delivering better access, better quality, and real cost control.
For hospital-based care, more employers and individuals are contracting directly with independent physicians and hospitals for cash-pay care, at discounts of 80% to 90% off insurance list prices for services like elective surgery and specialty procedures. For the right candidates — and it’s worth doing your homework on any company or plan — health sharing has also become a cost-effective way to cover emergency or high-cost needs at a fraction of traditional insurance premiums.
For everyday care, most people get most of their care in a clinic, and here the case is already made: direct primary care (DPC) can beat insurance-based primary care on cost, quality, and access. DPC physicians charge a flat monthly fee — often around $100 — for essentially unlimited visits and direct digital access. Compare that to a conventional practice, where physicians juggle thousands of patients and squeeze them into rushed 10- to-15-minute visits that can frustrate both doctors and patients.
Drug costs are another major driver of the crisis, and innovation is showing up here too — from GoodRx, a free app that finds discounted prices, to Cost Plus Drugs, which ships low-cost generics (and now some specialty medications) straight to your door.
For those not ready to leave insurance behind. Startups like Firefly Health are building leaner, smarter health plan products meant to disrupt the market and actually bend the cost curve. And next year, Community Health Options is rolling out a plan built around free DPC and low-cost mental health care at its core.
The future of health care isn’t the all-purpose plastic card we’ve all grown up carrying. The status quo is more frustrating — and less sustainable — by the year. Businesses, towns, school districts, unions, and families are watching their budgets buckle under health costs, and more of them are realizing that real health care isn’t a card in your wallet. It’s timely, high-quality, affordable access to care.
The insurance and pharmaceutical industries are powerful, and policymakers aren’t coming to save us anytime soon. So ask yourself: when will you have had enough? When does the pain of doing nothing finally outweigh the cost of change?

title: Linda LeMont (1942-2026)
Black voters view Scott Colom's historic US Senate win through lens of Mississippi's racial legacy
text:
It’s been nearly 150 years since a Black man has represented Deep South and deep red Mississippi in the U.S. Senate.
That changed Wednesday evening as Democrat Scott Colom was declared the winner over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, who had been endorsed by President Donald Trump. For many in the state and for Black Americans across the nation, Colom’s victory reflects the ambitions that were thwarted by generations of systemic oppression and violence.
Janice Johnson, who lives in Greenville in the Mississippi Delta, says having a Black senator has been a long time coming. “In the last few years we have seen great strides,” she said.
Out of all the southern states, Mississippi has a special place in the struggle over Black Americans’ exclusion from the nation’s promises of freedom and justice. There’s Ida B. Wells-Barnett, the Mississippi-born journalist who investigated 19th century lynching across the South, and Emmett Till, the 14-year-old whose 1955 kidnapping and murder by white men in Mississippi reinvigorated the Civil Rights Movement.
There’s Medgar Evers, the NAACP’s first Mississippi field secretary who organized Black voter registration until his 1963 assassination, and Fannie Lou Hamer, the civil rights leader who challenged Mississippi’s all-white delegation at the 1964 Democratic National Convention.
Rep. Bennie Thompson, who represents Mississippi’s 2nd District, was a student organizer for Hamer while studying at Tougaloo College, where Colom’s victory celebration was held Wednesday night. And now, Thompson is watching his mentee, Sen.-elect Colom, fill a more than 145-year gap of Black leadership in statewide office.
“From my perspective, I now have a partner in Washington,” Thompson said before introducing Colom.
“I can’t help but think about Medgar Evers on Veterans Day,” Colom said during a victory speech. “A moment like this, where he served his country and came home to Mississippi, when they wouldn’t let him vote. But he had the faith that Mississippi could make progress. … He had faith that a day like this was possible.”
He added, “All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this.”
Johnson, who watched part of Colom’s victory speech from home, says she understands that Black voters, alone, aren’t responsible for Colom’s win. White voters, too, had to be fed up with the state’s economy, school systems and crumbling health care infrastructure for the poor — Black and white — under Republican rule.
“The most important part is we’ve got to have faith that Mississippi is ready to do the right thing,” an elated Johnson told The Associated Press on Thursday. “We as a people — and Mississippi as whole — are ready to show the nation. We have to work together, and that was his message. He wants to help pull us together.”
Jerome Dunn, a barber in Jackson, echoed Johnson’s sentiment.
“It takes everybody to vote, not one single race,” said Dunn, 59, who is Black and also voted for Colom. “I think people are looking for him to work for everybody. People are tired of Republicans and what they believe.”
Two came before Colom
Blanche K. Bruce, a Republican, was the second Black man in the Senate from Mississippi after that state’s legislature elected him to a six-year term. He served from 1875 to 1881. Hiram Revels, another Republican, was the first after the Senate voted to seat him in 1870 to fill a vacancy left empty since the start of the Civil War. Revels’ term expired about a year later.
Bruce and Revels were among 16 Black men from southern states who served in Congress during the period of Reconstruction, which aimed to address the inequities experienced by Black people during enslavement, while preparing reentry for the 11 Southern states that seceded from the union at the start of the U.S. Civil War.
Once Reconstruction ended and federal troops were withdrawn, freed slaves in the South lost many of the freedoms gained following the war as Southern states enforced racial segregation through Jim Crow-era laws.
White conservatives have dominated Mississippi’s Statehouse and congressional delegation ever since. Nearly all were white Democrats as laws restricted where Black people could live, work and go to school. That weight carried on through the Civil Rights era, but during the late 1960s white elected leaders in Mississippi switched political parties and became Republicans.
Colom’s win represents “a pretty significant change in Mississippi politics,” said Brian Shoup, head of political science and public administration at Mississippi State University.
“We haven’t seen a Democrat win the Senate since the 1980s and even then that was a traditional kind of more southern conservative Democrat,” the professor said. “We haven’t had an African American senator since the era of Reconstruction, so this is obviously a very significant and important election in Mississippi history.”
Mississippi has been burdened by its racial legacy
Black voters in Mississippi and across the South were faced with the reality of redistricting efforts designed to reduce Black representation in elected positions, set off in late April by a Supreme Court decision that gutted the landmark Voting Rights Act of 1965. The ruling helped fuel increased voter turnout.
But it’s difficult for many to ignore Mississippi’s troubling past involving race relations, from the lynching of Black people by the Ku Klux Klan and other mobs to the killings of Evers and Till.
In his 1963 “I Have a Dream” speech, civil rights icon the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. referred to Mississippi as a state “sweltering with the heat of injustice, sweltering with the heat of oppression.”
Colom’s election is historic and means things are changing in parts of the South, said Elnora Fisher, 68, of Greenville, who was born and raised in Mississippi where she remembers that simply living often didn’t seem fair to Black people.
“As I understood, my grandparents always tried to save up to vote,” Fisher said. “They had to pay a tax to vote.”
As a child during the 1960s, Fisher said her mother took her to an NAACP meeting. “While we were there the white police stopped the meeting and made us leave,” she said.
Black people in Mississippi should be ecstatic with Colom as a U.S. senator, Fisher added.
“Here in Mississippi, so much has been taken from the poor people and given to the rich people,” she said. “I hope Colom will give back to the people who helped get him where he is.”
Good may come of it all with so many eyes on the results of the contest between Colom and Hyde-Smith, said Shoup, the professor. Mississippians, along with the rest of the nation, may be ready to begin healing from the past.
“This race, the fact that it has been so close, and it has activated so much turnout, might portend the prospects of maybe being able to talk about these things in a more civil and open fashion,” he said.
_____
Sophie Bates in Jackson, Miss., and Aaron Morrison in New York contributed. Williams is a member of AP’s Race & Ethnicity team. He reports from Detroit.

title: Aroostook County artists recall winter of the past
text:
WRITTEN BY JEN LYNDS
For many Mainers, winter darkness is an interminable shroud. It camouflages the reds and golds of fall and constricts summer abundance.
In the hands of two Aroostook County artists, however, the season sings. Photographer Christopher Mills and Frank Sullivan, a fine artist and teacher, capture beauty in the winter barrenness. Using paint, brushes, pencils, and snapshots, they transform hills and plains of white into snowbound landscapes that showcase the magic of The County.
With a range of skills and talents, both men have captured Aroostook County winters throughout their careers.
Sullivan is a Littleton resident and the author of two books about his work. His latest, “Drawing Is Everything,” was released in June. The artist, who is also a musician, noted in the publication that music often influences his work. He expanded on that during a recent interview, saying he often treats seasons as musical “keys.”
“Winter and fall are like the minor keys,” he explained, describing the deeper, sadder, more melancholic sounds on an instrument. “Spring and summer are the major keys. They are happier and more joyful. I’m drawn to the melancholy and the nostalgia, and winter means that to me. So when I look at the winter, I am reminded of what used to be there. I want to put that on the canvas.”
Sullivan has painted many Aroostook County winter scenes in his 21 years in the region. One oil on canvas painting, “When The Spell Is Broken,” was completed in 2023. Sullivan said he was snowshoeing in Littleton when he saw “a cool, mysterious, dark kind of space.”
He returned home, completed a drawing from memory, and then transferred it to canvas. Thick, textured brushwork adds shadow and coats the snow against the moody black background. Shades of blue and gray, cooler hues that fit well into the painting, produce the mass of trees and branches.
Sullivan created another 2023 pastel on Arches watercolor paper, titled “The Way Home.” It was created while he was recovering from COVID. After convalescing, he went for a walk, saw a scene he loved, and returned home to recreate it from memory.
“It really spoke to me,” he recalled.
Christopher Mills owns Christopher A. Mills Photography. The Houlton resident and self-taught photographer has taken breathtaking pictures of Aroostook county’s seasons, especially in winter. Magazines in Maine and across the country have featured his work, and he has produced calendars from his photographs.
“We are kind of spoiled up here with the winter,” Mills said. “There are so many trees and so many opportunities for beautiful shots. After every snowstorm, the snow sticks to the trees. You get amazing light. Even without the light, you get excellent opportunities for black-and-white shots. It is hard not to come away with a great picture.”
In winter, Mills rises early, packs his gear, and throws his snowshoes or skis into his vehicle. He often traverses snow-packed logging trails and dense woods. He said he relies on lens warmers to keep his lens from fogging up in below-zero temperatures.
“I learned that the hard way,” he said, laughing.
In a favorite winter snapshot from 2024, the emerald and magenta Northern Lights shot high above the snow-draped evergreens. The Big Dipper shone above the tree line. Another favorite is a photo of a barn just outside of Houlton, taken in February 2023. It showcased a solitary barn set back against a tangerine-and-crimson sky, with a barren, windswept field of snow below.
“It was stunning,” he said.

Tree fest and 6 other fun family events in the Brunswick area
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OK, time for some real talk.
In these columns I always try to be as community minded and broadly minded as I can, making sure that I give you a chamber perspective, and keep you informed of insights from the business community, but I try not to be too self serving. However, the Merrymeeting Tree Fest is a week and a half away, and it’s the chamber’s biggest event of the year and about 50-60 organizations get trees, wreaths, or sponsor, and there are gifts that represent another 80-100 businesses. It’s my favorite thing we do, and I have a bunch of updates about that, as you may have read in the last column, or the one before.
I have pushed the most recent updates to the bottom of this column, but please do take a look at it, as there are still literally almost a dozen ways you can be a part of it whether you are a business, an organization, or a citizen. Also, with the new name and new location, there are literally positive changes happening daily, and in some case, hourly.
Here are six other holiday fun activities to mark your calendar for:
GARDENS AGLOW
Nov. 14-Jan. 2 in Boothbay Harbor.
We are days away from “Gathered in Maine” the 2026 theme for Gardens Aglow at the Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens. If you have never been to Gardens Aglow, it is worth the trip and tickets as it is a truly unique experience in coastal Maine. Sure, the social media pictures everyone shares are great, but you can’t imagine the stillness and holiday spirit that fills you when you walk around the gardens amid the display. For more information, check out MaineGardens.org/Gardens-Aglow, but trust me, it’s beautiful.
CHAMBER AFTER HOURS
Nov. 19 at the Brunswick Landing Y, 5-7 p.m.
All right, this one is a bit self serving, but it’s also a great night for businesses to connect with each other under the holly-glow of our Merrymeeting Tree Fest. The tree sponsors and wreath sponsors are all invited to meet the chamber members and holiday minglers for a preview night of what will be an incredible festival. Non-members are invited to join us, as admission to any Chamber After Hours is just a business card. My thought has always been, what better way can I show you the value of the chamber than by putting you in a room with dozens and dozens of supporters? You can RSVP on the chamber website at MidcoastMaine.com.
BURPEES FOR TURKEYS
Nov. 21 in Brunswick, 2 p.m.
WILCOX Wellness & Fitness Brunswick is gearing up for its annual Burpees for Turkeys fundraiser on Saturday, Nov. 21.
For every $5 donated, WILCOX community members and trainers will complete one burpee, raising funds for three local organizations addressing food insecurity: Mid Coast Hunger Prevention Program, The Teen Center at People Plus, and Big Brothers Big Sisters of Greater Brunswick. While Big Brothers Big Sisters doesn’t directly provide food assistance, its mentoring programs support children and families in other meaningful ways, helping ease pressures so families can focus on essential needs like food.
Last year, WILCOX Brunswick raised over $10,000, and they’re hoping to make an even bigger impact this year! Also, you may recognize the emcee in a turkey suit (spoiler: it’s me — I swap out the Cory the Elf costume for a couple of hours to be a turkey).
SANTA’S ARRIVAL AND JINGLE BELL WALK
Nov. 28 in Bath, 3:45-5:30 p.m.
Both Bath and Brunswick welcome Santa to their downtowns on Saturday, Nov. 28.
In Bath, the event is through Main Street Bath and features a gathering at Library Park at 3:45 p.m. where you pick up a silver jingle bell in preparation to celebrate the arrival of Santa and Mrs. Claus at 4 p.m. Then, join the Jingle Bell Walk, through downtown to the Custom House lawn. There you will enjoy cookies, cocoa, the Amethyst Choir singing, ponies from Shetland Yard Stables, and photos with Santa by soggy dog designs.
DOWNTOWN TREE LIGHTING
Nov. 28 in Brunswick, 3-6 p.m.
This Brunswick Downtown Association event features cocoa, coffee, cookies, family photos with the Clauses, horse-drawn carriage rides, holiday carols performed by Una Voce Chamber Choir and the Brunswick High School choirs, with the tree lighting at 5:45 p.m. It is one of the biggest-attended events in Brunswick annually bringing hundreds to downtown.
SILVER BELLS AND BRIGHT NIGHT BATH
Dec. 1-25 and Dec. 11 in Bath.
Main Street Bath is celebrating its silver anniversary — 25 years — and so Silver Bells is the theme of its monthlong celebration known as “Old Fashioned Christmas.” Traditions like the trolley caroling, magic letter boxes, and the Paul Revere bell ringing on Dec. 31 are back, as is the very popular Bright Night Bath on Dec. 11. New this year is a different take on its squirrel scavenger hunt, and a daily advent calendar-style “opening” featuring a different downtown business each day from Dec. 1 to Dec. 25. For more information, VisitBath.com.
MERRYMEETING TREE FEST
Nov. 20-22 and Nov. 27-29 at the Brunswick Landing Y.
For more information and registration (volunteers, trees, donations, otherwise) visit MidcoastMaine.com or MidcoastMaine.com/Merrymeeting-Tree-Fest.
For daily updates follow the Merrymeeting Tree Fest Facebook page.
Here are seven things to know as we are less than 10 days out:
• More volunteers needed: Great fun, easy, and it will get you in the holiday spirit.
• Paid volunteerism: Earn $30 per shift for your favorite nonprofit.

title: 6-day search for missing teen ends with emotional reunion
text:
(Gray Media) - A 17-year-old who was missing for six days in the Australian wilderness was reunited with his mother after rescue crews found him.
“Amazingly, William is in good spirits and, for the most part, in good health,” police said.
William’s mom dropped him off with a friend on Nov. 6 to go camping. He went to pick up camping equipment nearby and didn’t return.
His friend searched the area but couldn’t find William.
Authorities conducted an extensive search of the area and then brought William to safety.
Crews were doing an aerial search when they saw a tackle box in bushland and found William lying by a creek nearby.
Victoria police shared a video showing the team spotting the teen from above.
You can hear his mother crying as she reaches out to her son for a long hug.

title: Paul LePage’s victory confirmed after ranked-choice count, state says
Why the 'blue wave' didn’t hit Bangor’s City Council race
text:
Terry Dinkins learned how Bangor voted in Maine’s statewide races on election night before he learned the outcome of the City Council race in which he was competing.
After hearing that the “blue wave” hitting much of the nation had swayed Bangor voters toward Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson, Dinkins was prepared to learn that those voters had also chosen more liberal candidates for council.
Twenty minutes later, Bangor’s results showed that Dinkins and two other candidates on the conservative end of the 12-person pool had won.
“I was kind of amazed,” Dinkins said. “We must have got a lot of Democrat votes.”
Last week’s results marked a shift from recent years in which progressive groups seemed to dominate in the city’s local elections. The disconnect between how Bangor voters approached the local election compared with statewide races shows a desire for more balance on the council and the impact of growing organizing on the right. Outsized spending on this year’s council race could also set a new precedent for Bangor’s elections.
Many voters saw the three winning candidates — Anthony Cote, Terry Dinkins and Joseph Pratt — as people who would disrupt the status quo on the council, according to Cote. He named public safety, needle litter and homelessness as issues that motivated his supporters, including some Democrats.
Voters have been unhappy with the council’s work this year.
“Last week, six days ago, you were given an edict and a direction,” resident Stephen Brough said at Monday’s council meeting after the new members were sworn in. “In nine months, when campaign season starts, we’d better see some positive results. No more needles on the streets.”
Lewiston voters seemed to move in a similar direction, approving limits on the number of needles that syringe service programs can hand out and sending the mayoral race to a runoff.
While the three winners in Bangor mostly campaigned on more conservative ideas, they focused on local issues, which could’ve helped draw voters across the political spectrum.
State Sen. Joseph Baldacci, D-Bangor, was one of those voters who wanted to see a shift in the makeup of the City Council. The state legislator and former council chair ran for Congress this year as a Democrat, but he also voted for Cote and Pratt, he said.
Baldacci said he doesn’t believe all Bangor voters marked their local ballots through a partisan lens, instead focusing on local issues and candidates who “would inject some new energy into the City Council.”
“Voters in Bangor, myself included to an extent, were tired of the bickering and the petty grievances and the insults and really wanted a City Council that focuses on the issues that they care about,” he added.
Rick Fournier, another former council chair, felt the election results were “all about balance.” Fournier said he saw both the blue wave that tipped the scales toward Democrats in the House and Senate and the council election outcome as a rejection of extremism and a desire for more balance across all levels of government.
“But it is so incredibly unique that everyone went blue except Bangor, and Bangor is an incredibly blue town,” he added. “This blue wave that occurred, to a large degree, I think that’s primarily about [President Donald] Trump.”
Fifty-eight percent of Bangor voters chose Jackson in the U.S. Senate race. In Bangor’s 12-person local race, the winning slate of conservative candidates, all of whom were endorsed by a new political action committee called Concerned Citizens of Bangor, were followed by the three progressive candidates endorsed by the labor-aligned nonprofit Food and Medicine.
There were also 7,169 blanks on the local ballot, which means the election was likely decided by some combination of liberal-leaning voters who either chose conservative candidates at the local level or left their City Council ballots blank.
Everything in the council race seemed to be bigger this year, from yard signs to fundraising totals.
“We had really good candidates that ran good campaigns,” said Philip Henry, the local real estate investor who spearheaded the Concerned Citizens of Bangor PAC that spent more than $15,000 on the race. Henry pointed to the winning slate’s many years in Bangor and their level of community involvement.
Dinkins started campaigning in the spring and encountered many residents who already knew of him because of his work running a warming shelter in his church during the winter. He thinks that background could’ve drawn more Democrats to his campaign, he said.
Dinkins raised by far the most money of any candidate, hitting nearly $15,000 as of the most recent campaign finance reporting deadline. That’s far above what anyone else has raised for a Bangor City Council campaign in the last few years.
“If I was going to run for council, I wanted to win,” Dinkins said.
It’s hard to say exactly how much of a role the PAC played in getting its preferred candidates elected, but all three incoming councilors agreed it had some kind of effect.
Cote said that while he doesn’t believe advertising swung many voters who would’ve otherwise chosen the progressive slate, he thinks the Concerned Citizens group helped consolidate a set of candidates to vote for amid a large pool.
All three of Food and Medicine’s endorsed candidates won last year, when it was the only local group that meaningfully organized around a slate of contenders, and that past success was eye-opening, Cote said, for other groups that wanted to be more competitive in the council race.
“You had to get your name out there,” he said.
Pratt said he thinks that overall, the PAC’s endorsement helped the three candidates win and aided turnout, but it also discouraged some people. He himself had mixed feelings about the PAC’s social media ads and noted that one couple who supported his petition to get on the ballot took Pratt’s sign off their lawn after his Concerned Citizens endorsement was released.
The new councilor saw that reflected in the differential among the top three candidates. At third place, Pratt was nearly 700 votes behind Cote, the first-place candidate. Pratt said he would’ve expected the results to be tighter if everyone relied just on the PAC endorsements alone.
Most of the PAC’s spending went to Facebook and Instagram ads designed by Harris Media, a conservative political marketing agency, that reached upwards of 100,000 people, according to the Meta Ad Library.
“Effective advertising does affect people,” Jack McKay, Food and Medicine’s executive director, said. “A lot of people get their news through social media.”
One of those ads called on residents to vote out “socialist Leonard,” referring to the incumbent candidate Joe Leonard who failed to win another term. Leonard declined to comment for this story.
McKay noted that his group didn’t attack any of the opposing candidates. “I think it’s good to have differences of opinion, but to do it in a respectful way,” he said.
His group spent about $300 on promoting its municipal slate this year. That total was smaller than the previous year, and the group released its endorsements on Oct. 15, a week later than last year.
McKay noted that winning the U.S. Senate race was the focus within Food and Medicine, where Jackson used to work. That prioritization meant that Democrats and progressive groups were relatively disorganized in Bangor’s council election.
“Everybody forgets about local and municipality races,” Adam Baker, the runner-up, said. “I think from the Democratic Party downwards, they have a very top-down approach.”
Andrei Yermakov, another of Food and Medicine’s endorsed candidates, said he was frustrated to see that little attention was given to municipal races among progressive organizations. Maine People’s Alliance, another progressive group, hasn’t donated to Bangor City Council candidates since 2023, according to a BDN review of past candidates’ campaign finance reports.
Yermakov added that he was shocked by the number of blanks on the City Council ballot, which told him that many voters were uninformed about the race.
One thing many Bangor residents seemed to agree on was a distaste for the attempt by Jonathan Bush, the Cape Elizabeth resident and wealthy tech entrepreneur, to influence the race with an expensive social media campaign that criticized the current council but didn’t name particular candidates.
In Fournier’s view, Bush’s ads and any spending by people other than the candidates themselves made the race more partisan.
“It shouldn’t be political. It shouldn’t be about parties. It’s about what’s best for Bangor,” he said. “If someone’s running for office locally, they should be raising their own money. There shouldn’t be outside influences coming in, spending money.”

title: Community center in Biddeford launches community fridge
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Reach community center in Biddeford launches community fridge
A new resource for free food is up and running in Biddeford in the form of a community fridge.
Just outside The Reach community center on Alfred Street, a fridge, freezer and non-perishable pantry that includes hygiene items have been set up.
The Reach director Kate Frank said the community fridge is open to everyone and the motto is simple: take what you need, and share what you can.
"We're starting this up and getting it running, but the intention and the hope is that the community actually takes ownership of this," Frank said. "Like, they want to stock it and they want to be like, 'Hey, guys, this is in the fridge, who can bring whatever?' So the beauty of this is that you never know what's going to be in there."
The community fridge at 118 Alfred St. will be available 24/7 year-round.
More information about what items can and cannot be donated, how things need to be labeled, how to volunteer and ways people can help support the fridge is available on The Reach website. The community fridge also has an Amazon wish list, as well as a Facebook page.

title: ‘I have a problem’: Pastor admits to sexually assaulting child, sentenced to life in prison
text:
PONCE DE LEON, Fla. (WJHG/Gray News) - A Florida pastor has been sentenced to life in prison for sexually battering a teenage boy who was under his custodial authority.
State Attorney Larry Basford announced that Circuit Judge Russell Roberts sentenced Randon Lee Carroll, 41, on Tuesday.
Prosecutors said the reported abuse happened earlier this year.
Carroll had been scheduled to stand trial in October but entered an open plea to sexual battery of a victim over 12 but under 18 while under his custodial authority. He also pleaded to sexual performance by a child for videotaping some of the acts, prosecutors said.
An open plea leaves the sentence to the judge.
According to the State Attorney’s Office, Holmes County Chief Prosecutor Jake Cook had not offered Carroll a plea deal other than life in prison.
Prosecutors said Carroll confessed to the sexual acts, saying, “I have a problem. I shouldn’t have done it.”
The details the defendant gave during his interview matched the details given by the victim.
During Tuesday’s sentencing hearing, Cook presented the state’s case, cross-examined defense witnesses and asked Roberts to impose the maximum sentence.
“I think this is the worst possible act that can be committed against a child. Your honor and the state request that he die in prison,” Cook told the judge.
In a written impact statement, the victim’s mother described the family’s strong religious beliefs and questioned how a pastor could deliver sermons while sexually battering a child.
“It takes a wicked person to do that,” she wrote. “There’s no way this is of God. This is pure evil.”
Cook said he hoped the sentence would provide justice for the victim and his family.
Basford thanked the Holmes County Sheriff’s Office for investigating the case.

title: Video shows Mount Washington weather observer hacking away at ice
text:
Video shows Mount Washington weather observer hacking away at ice on wind instruments
The Mount Washington Observatory has shared a video that shows one of its weather observers working hard to de-ice instruments at the summit of the highest peak in the Northeast.
The observatory said the summit of Mount Washington has been largely locked in freezing fog over the past several days, which has caused rime ice and glaze ice to accumulate on its wind instruments.
Weather observers have been going up to the instrument tower at least once every hour to de-ice the instruments, according to the observatory.
A video shared by the observatory shows a weather observer named Bailey de-icing the wind instruments early Wednesday morning in hurricane-force wind gusts. Bailey can be seen using a large rubber mallet to chip away at the ice that formed on the instruments. You can watch that video in the player at the top of this page.

title: ‘School mom’ to ‘school grandma’: Secretary has served students for 52 years
text:
ELGIN, Neb. (KOLN/Gray News) -Brenda Kuhlman opens the door to greet students each morning at Pope John XXIII Central Catholic School, where she has worked for more than 50 years.
“And they’re so happy to be here. And yes, the morning hugs are wonderful,” Kuhlman said.
Kuhlman has been the school’s administrative assistant and office manager since she was 17.
“So my electives, I did the shorthand, the bookkeeping, the typing, and all of that,” Kuhlman said. “And it was probably about December of my senior year, the administrator asked me if I would be interested because the secretary that was here was moving on.”
Kuhlman said the Catholic school opened in 1967, eight years before she started this job. She grew up southwest of Clearwater, Nebraska, and attended a country school before high school in Elgin.
“It was a big adjustment going from maybe four in my class to 56 in high school,” she said.
Kuhlman met her husband at the school and raised six children south of Raeville. Now her grandchildren attend Pope John Central Catholic.
“It’s been my life for that many years,” Kuhlman said.
The school serves eight parishes in surrounding communities. Kuhlman said students come to Elgin from communities including Raeville, Petersburg, Neligh, Clearwater and Ewing.
“I just remember coming here as a 7th grader. And Brenda just became that like school mom for us,” said Lauren Borer, who returned to her alma mater as a teacher. “And now that my kids go here, like they kind of see her as like the school grandma.”
Today, the school has about 130 students from prekindergarten through 12th grade. Kuhlman keeps the school running smoothly for all of them.
“It’s kind of cute when you see students, the younger students, like if you’re shopping or in church and they’re going, what are you doing here? I thought you lived at school,” Kuhlman said.
Deb Warren says she’s known Kuhlman “forever.” Warren attended class with Kuhlman and graduated in 1972. Then she served as the development director while Kuhlman worked in the office.
“Oh, she’s driven. She is a detailed kind of person. So depending on what job you’re working or if you’re doing fundraising or something, Brenda knows all the details,” Warren said. “She keeps the school running like a well-oiled machine for sure.”
Kuhlman’s office duties range from managing funds to returning lost backpacks.
“Brenda gets invited to everyone’s graduation, everyone’s wedding, baby announcements. She’s just well thought of by both the parents, but also their kids,” Warren said.
Kuhlman continues to add to scrapbooks that preserve school history.
“So she knows the stories and the history, but most importantly, she knows the people. And so if we ever have a question about what happened, way back when, she knows everything,” Borer said.
The scrapbooks include photographs of graduates that she also displays in her office.
“And it seems like you get attached to the classes, more attached as I get older for some reason, and it’s hard to see some of them leave,” Kuhlman said. “And just stop in to visit. That’s great to see them do that.”
Leaving her desk and duties at the school someday would be even harder for Kuhlman.
“I guess as long as my health holds out and stuff, I’ll keep working, or until they kick me out, one of the two,” Kuhlman joked.
After 52 years, Kuhlman is in no hurry to retire, not while she’s watching generations grow up in Elgin.

Democrat Scott Colom wins Senate seat in Mississippi
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since 1881.
The race was called more than a week after the midterm elections, after local election officials processed thousands of absentee and provisional ballots.
The Associated Press called the race Wednesday. With 99% of ballots counted, Colom led by fewer than 5,000 votes.
“There were times when I was tired and I felt like I couldn’t keep going, but I kept the faith,” Colom said to supporters at his victory party at Tougaloo College in Jackson, Mississippi, Wednesday night.
Colom will also be the first Democrat to represent Mississippi in the Senate in nearly 40 years. John C. Stennis, a segregationist, retired in 1989.
His win adds to the Democratic majority in the Senate, as well, which now stands at 55-44 with eight seats flipped. The Senate race in Alaska remains uncalled.
“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters,” said Colom.
Sen. Hyde-Smith, an ally of President Donald Trump, was running for her second full term. She was initially appointed to fill a vacancy and then won a special election in 2018.
Hyde-Smith released a video Wednesday night conceding the race.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well, as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state,” Hyde-Smith said.
Only 14 Black senators have ever been elected or appointed in the U.S.
When the 120th Congress is sworn in Jan. 3, seven Black senators will be serving.

title: Sisters give birth minutes apart, outdoing their other sisters who gave birth days apart
text:
CENTER POINT, Iowa (KCRG/Gray News) - Two Iowa sisters pregnant at the same time had due dates weeks apart, but they ended up having their babies within minutes of each other.
Linn County Supervisor Brandy Meisheid was due to have her baby on Nov. 13, while her sister, Allison Sweeney, was due on Halloween. But the two ended up having their sons on the same day, just 29 minutes apart.
Doctors had to induce Meisheid early, and Sweeney’s baby also arrived early. Cousins Myles and Kohen now share the same birthday: Oct. 22.
“Having a family with four girls, it’s always a lifelong dream to be pregnant together, but it was never anything we put pressure on ourselves to do,” Meisheid said. “It was just a ‘Could you imagine if this ever happened and how great that would be?’ And God had plans to let it happen.”
4 babies in 4 months
Myles and Kohen aren’t the only new additions to the family.
Meisheid and Sweeney’s other two sisters – Taylor Campbell and Rachel Mantermach – both had their babies, Charles and Merritt, about four months ago, just three days apart. The four cousins now go by the Quad Squad.
Meisheid says Myles and Kohen were born in hospital rooms next to each other, and Myles and Merritt were born in the exact same room.
“So, everybody shares something in this story. There’s just too much coincidence for it not to be a greater purpose or something,” she said.
All four sisters and babies are happy and healthy.
