title: Microsoft confirms Outlook outage affecting users worldwide
text:
Microsoft Outlook still down for users; company continues to look for fix
NOTE: As of 8:15 p.m. ET, Microsoft Outlook remains down for most users.
You don't got mail.
Thousands of users reported issues using Microsoft Outlook Thursday afternoon.
Microsoft confirmed the outage on social media.
"We're investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods," the company wrote on X. "While we're working to mitigate impact, we've confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region."
According to Downdetector, at its peak at 1:15 p.m. ET, over 130,000 users reported problems accessing Microsoft's email platform.
There are also reports of less widespread issues with Microsoft Copilot, Teams, OneDrive and Store.
Microsoft provided an update later Thursday, explaining that it was exploring all options to fix the problem.
"We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact. We've paused all deployments, we're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure, and we're restarting affected servers to return them to service," the company said.
At around 9 p.m. ET, the platform remained down for many users, but Microsoft said it was seeing progress in its attempts to get it back online.
"We’re seeing positive results with our efforts to restart affected infrastructure and recover server availability in an isolated manner," the company wrote. "We’re actively monitoring the performance of these portions of infrastructure to verify stability, which we suspect will support improved availability as these actions are subsequently expanded more broadly."
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

title: Three UMaine football storylines to follow against Albany
Mainers can’t afford childcare. How did we get here?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Trust for Local News wanted to get a sense of how people feel about living and working in Maine. So, we commissioned a survey to find out. Over the next few weeks, we’ll be exploring the results and hearing from dozens of people who participated. You can read all about it here.
Katie Hawkins was laser focused on having a healthy pregnancy.
It wasn’t until she was eight months in that she realized she also should have been worrying about daycare.
Hawkins, 44, put her name on about 10 waitlists, casting a much wider net than she would have liked from her home in South Portland. But she still hadn’t secured a spot when, 12 weeks after giving birth to her son in January, she returned to work as an attorney.
“It did start to become really, really nervewracking,” she said.
For Hugh Carroll’s family, daycare was never even in consideration. When the 32-year-old from North Yarmouth and his wife had their first son, they balked at the cost and decided that one of them staying home would be the only option. His wife left her full-time job, and now takes care of their two sons, ages 3 and 5.
Earlier this year, more than 800 residents responded to a survey conducted by the Maine Trust for Local News, in partnership with the Siena Research Institute, about life in Maine.
More than half, 54%, said a person in their community is unlikely to have access to affordable childcare. The cost of raising children was one of the most negatively rated aspects of life in the state — and Mainers felt much more pessimistic about it than Americans in general did.
The impacts of Maine’s unaffordable childcare are wide-reaching: Parents leave the already strapped workforce. Fewer people have children, contributing to declining birthrates, which have ripple effects for hospitals, K-12 school enrollment, the sustainability of Maine’s colleges and universities, and eventually the labor force and economy.
The average cost of childcare in Maine is actually lower than, or comparable to, many other states. But it’s compounded here by scarcity, said Mattie Daughtry, the president of the State Senate who has made childcare a focus of her legislative agenda.
“It isn’t even just a matter of affordability, it’s a matter of whether they can access that care,” Daughtry said. “The economics just do not work: they don’t work for families, and they don’t work for providers.”
Carroll, who works in construction, described his family as middle or even upper-middle class, but when he saw friends paying $2,000 a month for daycare, he knew it simply wasn’t an option. Despite their frustrations about the sky-high cost, he and his wife are glad their kids are getting quality time with their mom.
“I don’t have any regrets about how we did it,” he said. “We’re just lucky I’m able to afford to support her staying home with them.”
Hawkins was able to find a home daycare center near her, but it took about two months after she had gone back to the office. Her mother stepped in and watched her son in that time, but only temporarily.
“Ultimately, we found childcare through word of mouth, which was just a bit of luck,” Hawkins said. “Probably the best luck I’ve ever had.”
HOW DID CHILDCARE GET SO EXPENSIVE?
Childcare providers operate on razor-thin margins, due to the high costs of labor and of insurance on both their buildings and for their employees, Daughtry said. Because daycare centers often have just a few employees, it’s hard to get an affordable insurance rate. Many of those workers have children themselves, driving up costs further.
But owners are also reluctant to raise their tuition too much and pass those costs on to families.
“My friends who have kids in childcare are paying as much as their mortgage,” Daughtry said.
The median annual cost of infant childcare in Maine is between $10,000 and $15,000, depending on the county, according to 2024 data from the National Database of Childcare Prices. That represents between 11% and 17% of the median family income, with families in Penobscot and Washington counties getting hit the hardest.
The state also has significant childcare deserts, Daughtry said, and few to no options for people who work nontraditional hours, like doctors, nurses or Bath Iron Works employees.
When affordable childcare isn’t available, parents may drop out of the workforce, or grandparents may retire early to watch their grandchildren.
WHAT ARE THE IMPACTS?
In 2023, the Greater Portland Chamber of Commerce, along with the nonprofit United Way of Southern Maine, got together to survey 1,200 employees at local businesses about their childcare challenges. Quincy Hentzel, director of the chamber, said she was hearing constantly that the lack of providers was exacerbating workforce issues.
One question they asked: Do all of the adults in your family work full time? There were 269 people who responded no.
“The follow-up question to that was: If you answered no, would access to affordable childcare enable all adults in your household to work full time? And 84% of them said yes,” Hentzel said. “So that, to us, was a sign that there are a lot of people who want to be in the workforce who can’t because we don’t have enough childcare.”
Maine not only has to attract people from outside the state and country to come and work here, she said, but also make the workforce easier to access for those who already live here.
Childcare costs can also come with another significant economic downside: discouraging people from having kids altogether.
That’s according to a recent study that linked rising childcare costs in the U.S. to declining birthrates. Abigail Dow, now a post-doctoral fellow, conducted the research for her economics PhD at Boston University.
Dow found that in the 2010s, in communities where regulatory changes to childcare drove up costs, fertility rates did in fact drop: A 10% increase in prices decreased birth rates by about 5.7%, she found, or a reduction of about four births per 1000 women.
She also found that more women are delaying motherhood because of costs, and putting more time between births to avoid having two children in childcare at the same time.
There are caveats, Dow said. Countries outside the U.S. where childcare and maternity leave are much more affordable and accessible are also experiencing dropping birth rates. But the prevailing understanding among researchers is that affordability — along with changes in reproductive rights and evolving attitudes about parenting — is a big piece of the puzzle.
WHAT HAS BEEN DONE?
Lawmakers, companies and nonprofits have been working for years to offset the price and scarcity challenges.
Daughtry has introduced bills, including one during the last session to allocate an additional $15 million to clear the waitlist for the state’s childcare affordability program, which helps pay the costs for families making 125% or less of the state’s median income. (Some of that money, $10 million, was eventually integrated into the supplemental budget.)
She’s eyeing bills for the upcoming session to address the high building insurance costs for providers, childcare deserts and ongoing funding for the affordability program, which again has a waitlist.
In the years after the pandemic, the state began offering stipends to childcare workers to help the industry stabilize amid a period of high staff turnover. The funding faced potential cuts in 2025, but was restored after employees and owners rallied in opposition, saying the supplemental funding was critical.
Following their survey, United Way opened two new childcare centers through public-private partnerships, designed to provide care for working families.
A facility in South Portland opened in early summer, and another site in Freeport came online a few weeks later. The South Portland location currently serves between 60 and 70 kids, while the other has 50 to 60.
For now, both facilities keep regular hours, but Josh Waxman, a senior vice president with United Way, said they’re hoping to be open 24/7 within a few years to serve late-shift workers. It all depends on the availability of staff, Waxman said, which remains the biggest challenge.
“We need to treat early childhood care like the meaningful career it is,” he said.
Hawkins, the new mom from South Portland, said it never crossed her mind to leave the workforce. She’s a lawyer, and saw many other women at her company model working parenthood. But when her son, Lincoln, was a month old, she took him to a playgroup. The other parents all chatted about their childcare woes.
“I was both reassured and a bit scared by the number of parents in that circle who said things like, ‘I’m going back to work next week and we don’t know what we’re doing for childcare,’” she said.
Daughtry isn’t a parent yet herself, but she wants to be, and she wants other families to have the opportunity too.
“I grew up in Maine, and it’s the best damn place to be a kid,” she said.

Paul LePage wins Maine's 2nd Congressional District race after ranked-choice voting tabulation
The Republican former governor has been in Washington for new member orientation as his Democratic opponent, State Auditor Matt Dunlap, conceded the race last week
Former Gov. Paul LePage has won the election for Maine's 2nd Congressional District seat in the U.S. House of Representatives following a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
The Maine Secretary of State's Office ran the tabulation of 341,526 ballots on Thursday and announced the results live on YouTube.
When the blanks ballots were eliminated during the first round, LePage had 50.63% of the vote. The Republican candidate then went up to 50.81% when the second-choice votes were allocated, while State Auditor Matt Dunlap, the Democratic candidate, finished with 49.18%.
LePage has been in Washington throughout the week for new member orientation because Dunlap conceded the race last week. Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said that even though Dunlap conceded, the ranked-choice tabulation still had to be completed in order to have a certified election under state law.
The tabulation, which took three days to complete, was conducted at the Maine Department of Public Safety Headquarters, which is located at 45 Commerce Drive in Augusta. The process was open to the public and livestreamed on the Secretary of State's YouTube page on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday. The Secretary of State's Office staff took Wednesday off in observance of Veterans Day.
In ranked-choice voting races, like the race for CD2, a candidate must receive more than 50% of first-choice votes as counted on Election Day in order to win the race outright. On Nov. 5, two days after Election Day, the Secretary of State's Office announced that LePage had 49.894% of the vote while Dunlap had 48.307%. The lone declared write-in candidate in the race, independent Gregory Ward, received 0.036% of the vote while there were 6,017 blank ballots (1.763%). Since no candidate received more than 50% of the total ballots case, the Secretary of State's Office determined the race would proceed to a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
The Secretary of State's Office said the results are unofficial until the official tabulation of the votes cast is communicated to Gov. Janet Mills.
How the tabulation works
The first step in the ranked-choice tabulation process is to verify the vote totals from every municipality to ensure accuracy. Then, the votes are tabulated in rounds, with the lowest-ranked candidate eliminated in each round until there are only two candidates remaining. The candidate determined to have received the majority of the votes — more than 50% — in the final round is declared the winner.
More info about CD2
At more than 27,000 square miles, Maine's 2nd Congressional District is the largest congressional district by area east of the Mississippi River. CD2 includes all of Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Somerset, Waldo and Washington counties, as well as the Kennebec County communities of Augusta, Belgrade, Chelsea, Farmingdale, Fayette, Gardiner, Hallowell, Manchester, Monmouth, Mount Vernon, Oakland, Randolph, Readfield, Rome, Sidney, Vienna, Wayne and Winthrop.

title: Jackson shares update from Washington during new member orientation
text:
Sen.-elect Troy Jackson shares update from Washington during new member orientation
Sen.-elect Troy Jackson spoke with Maine's Total Coverage in his first local television interview since defeating five-term incumbent Sen. Susan Collins in the midterm election.
Jackson is in Washington this week for new member orientation, as the Democrat from Allagash prepares to be sworn into the U.S. Senate on Jan. 3, 2027.
In his interview with Maine's Total Coverage, Jackson said he supports calls to provide an additional $3 billion in federal heating aid through the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP).
Jackson also reiterated his call for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to be abolished. He also said he still does not plan to vote for Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York to serve as Senate majority leader.
In addition, Jackson said he has requested to serve on several committees, including the Senate Appropriations Committee, which is chaired by Collins. Jackson said that he had not met with Collins as of Wednesday morning.
"I don't know about a meeting," Jackson said. "I mean, I'm certainly happy to, but I expect at least a call over the phone. I expect our staff members to have a good conversation. I know that's what she immediately expressed."
Jackson also said he would co-sponsor "Medicare for All" legislation if it gets introduced early next year.
The full interview with Jackson will air on Total Maine at 10 a.m. Sunday.

title: Aging Untold: The rules of texting and social media keep changing
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, changing norms around texting and social media are blurring boundaries for older adults.
Then, hackers took over one woman’s Facebook to dupe her friends. We share ways to stay connected safely.
Plus, hear from world-renowned dementia expert, Teepa Snow, on bringing peace back to daily care.
Texts, group chats and social media might not be the types of communication that you are most comfortable with.
However, they are not going anywhere if you want to stay connected with loved ones across generations.
Teepa Snow is a nationally recognized dementia care educator, occupational therapist and founder of Positive Approach to Care, and she joined Aging Untold to share her philosophy and some tips for families.
Instead of using language that focuses on decline, Snow uses the term “brain change.” The reason is that while people with dementia lose some abilities, they change others, she said.
“People think all the time of brain failure and brain loss, and I talk about brain change because the reality is neuroplasticity exists whether you have dementia or you don’t,” Snow said. “So let’s use what we have and let’s use what they have.”
Snow is sharing tips family members can use when a loved one with dementia refuses to shower, take medication or get dressed.
Then, Snow shares the one thing she wants families to know.
A woman in Arizona said hackers hijacked her Facebook account and scammed her friends out of thousands of dollars.
She said they posed as her and said she needed to sell her father’s possessions to put him in assisted living. She learned about it when her father sent her a text.
Read the full article here to see what happened and how you can protect yourself.
Dennis Bussey was looking for someone to go hiking with, and his efforts have created a community of thousands of people who are not only hiking but also preserving Virginia history.
Bussey founded James River Hikers, which describes itself as “hiking with history.”
One of the hikers’ volunteer projects is cleaning gravestones at Shockoe Hill Cemetery, the final resting place for some of Virginia’s historic figures.

title: Sisters give birth minutes apart, outdoing their other sisters who gave birth days apart
text:
CENTER POINT, Iowa (KCRG/Gray News) - Two Iowa sisters pregnant at the same time had due dates weeks apart, but they ended up having their babies within minutes of each other.
Linn County Supervisor Brandy Meisheid was due to have her baby on Nov. 13, while her sister, Allison Sweeney, was due on Halloween. But the two ended up having their sons on the same day, just 29 minutes apart.
Doctors had to induce Meisheid early, and Sweeney’s baby also arrived early. Cousins Myles and Kohen now share the same birthday: Oct. 22.
“Having a family with four girls, it’s always a lifelong dream to be pregnant together, but it was never anything we put pressure on ourselves to do,” Meisheid said. “It was just a ‘Could you imagine if this ever happened and how great that would be?’ And God had plans to let it happen.”
4 babies in 4 months
Myles and Kohen aren’t the only new additions to the family.
Meisheid and Sweeney’s other two sisters – Taylor Campbell and Rachel Mantermach – both had their babies, Charles and Merritt, about four months ago, just three days apart. The four cousins now go by the Quad Squad.
Meisheid says Myles and Kohen were born in hospital rooms next to each other, and Myles and Merritt were born in the exact same room.
“So, everybody shares something in this story. There’s just too much coincidence for it not to be a greater purpose or something,” she said.
All four sisters and babies are happy and healthy.

title: Maine veterans share message for younger generations
text:
Maine veterans share message for younger generations
Maine is home to more than 100,000 veterans, with many agreeing on one common message: freedom is not free.
Maine veterans share message for younger generations
Maine is home to more than 100,000 veterans, with many agreeing on one common message: freedom is not free.
Dozens of veterans and their families gathered for a spaghetti dinner on Wednesday night in Sabattus. Hosted by the local 4-H club, veterans and their families got to sit for a free meal in a small show of thanks for their service. Veterans enjoying the pasta ranged from Vietnam-era service members to those who fought in the War in Iraq.
"I was thinking college and right after that I was thinking that I was at the right age and that they were going to need people, so I made that choice," said Ryan Cunningham, who served in the United States Army.
Cunningham made the choice to join right after the September 11th attacks. Like many of his fellow brothers and sisters in uniform, he did so out of love for his country.
"It was the honor of my life to be able to defend this great nation," said Cunningham.
"I have a button that says "women are veterans too" because I think it is important to know that women are a vital part of the service," said Tracey Rancourt, a United States Coast Guard veteran.
Rancourt joined the Coast Guard in 1983, inspired by her father and stepfather who served before her. At the time, there were not many women on board the ships, but serving meant the world to her.
"Women can do the same work men do in the military," Rancourt said.
Both Rancourt and Cunningham have the same message to the younger generation: that freedom is not free.
"The young kids need to know that men and women sacrificed a lot to make this country great, and we need to hold onto that," said Rancourt.
She also emphasized the importance of thanking military spouses, families, and veterans from all generations.
"I hold a lot of respect for World War II veterans, Korean, and especially Vietnam veterans because of what they came home to," said Rancourt.

title: ‘Malcolm in the Middle’ star, race car driver Frankie Muniz hospitalized after Daytona crash
text:
DAYTONA BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Actor and race car driver Frankie Muniz has been released from a hospital following a practice-lap crash at Daytona International Speedway.
The 40-year-old star of “Malcolm in the Middle” was practicing for a Proud to Honor Veterans Day Classic event, a benefit race set for Wednesday night at Daytona’s road course.
“I am disappointed I won’t be able to take part in Ford’s Proud to Honor event tonight,” Muniz said in a statement. “I was looking forward to honoring the service of our veterans and racing against these other amazing drivers.”
Muniz said he was a “little sore,” but the Mustang he was driving did its job to protect him.
“I want to thank everyone at Ford Racing, Daytona International Speedway and the staff here at the hospital,” Muniz said. “I especially want to thank everyone who has reached out and for all the prayers.”
Muniz and NASCAR driver Austin Cindric were set to represent Team Air Force in an exhibition race that benefits six nonprofits that support military and veteran communities through the Proud to Honor Fund, according to a NASCAR release.
A dozen Ford Racing drivers were split into six teams to race head-to-head in Mustang Dark Horse cars in honor of a branch of the U.S. military.
Musical performances by the Zac Brown Band, Russell Dickerson, Jo Dee Messina, Brittney Spencer, and Warren Zeiders were also part of the event.
Muniz was nominated for an Emmy and two Golden Glove Awards for his work in “Malcolm in the Middle” and was one of the best known child actors of his time. He has also appeared in films such as “Big Fat Liar,” “Deuces Wild,” “Agent Cody Banks” and “Racing Stripes.”
According to his website, Muniz took a hiatus from the entertainment world in 2006 to pursue professional racecar driving.
He began competing in the Formula BMW USA Championship and later went on to race in the Champ Car Atlantic Championship from 2007-09. Muniz was fourth in the 2009 championship standings with two races to go before a season-ending injury resulted in multiple surgeries, the website said.
In 2024, Muniz ran 38 races each on the NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts and trucks series.
He’s participated in 117 trucks series races over the last three years, with one top-10 finish at Daytona in 2025.

title: Paul LePage officially deemed the victor of Congressional District 2 race
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Former Governor Paul LePage is officially going to be Maine’s next congressman.
Ranked choice tabulations in Augusta ended just after 1 p.m. on Thursday. LePage, a republican, won with 50.81% of the vote. Democratic challenger Matt Dunlap received 49.18%.
LePage fills the seat currently held by Rep. Jared Golden (D) who opted to not run for re-election. Golden, a democrat, has held that seat since 2019.
Unofficial first-round results showed Paul LePage leading Matt Dunlap. LePage received 49.894% of the vote in the initial results—just short of a majority. Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said the state was legally obligated to begin ranked-choice tabulation, despite Dunlap appearing to concede.
“It’s not surprising, given that he had 49.89% of the vote going into the process,” Bellows said. “But, it does, under ranked-choice voting, give him a majority plus one. And that is always the goal in ranked-choice voting, is that the winner has the backing of a majority of the voters.“
Tabulation began Monday morning. Bellows said since it seemed unlikely that the ranked choice tabulation would change the final outcome, her office thought it was wise to reduce costs by not requiring staff to work overtime and conduct the process during working hours.
LePage declared victory the day after the election, saying the gap was too much for Dunlap to overcome.
In a concession statement shared with the press on Nov. 5, Dunlap said “This isn’t the result we were hoping for, and I’m disappointed that we came short. Congratulations to Paul LePage, I wish him the best. I want to thank every volunteer who knocked doors, made calls, and made their voices heard. Your support inspired me, and I’m honored to have worked side by side with you over the past year.”
Congressman-elect LePage has already started orientation in Washington. “
The Maine Ranked Choice Voting process only confirmed what we already knew, Paul LePage is the Congressman-Elect for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District,” said Senior LePage adviser Brent Littlefield. “Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people. As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”
Local Recounts
Bellows also announced today recounts were requested in four races by the November 10th deadline:
- Senate District 18 in Oxford County
- House District 96 in Lewiston
- House District 106 in Windham
- Kennebec County Commissioner, District 2
Bellows said they will start those recounts Monday.

title: Death toll rises to 6 in Brooklyn building collapse as rescuers dig through rubble
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Firefighters early Thursday removed the bodies of four more people who died after a three-story building in Brooklyn collapsed at the edge of a construction site, bringing the death toll to six, and they kept digging through the rubble to find others who may be trapped beneath the wreckage.
At least 17 people were hospitalized with injuries, including four in critical condition after the building came down Wednesday afternoon. The New York City Fire Department confirmed the additional deaths, and the other two deaths were announced Wednesday.
Scores of firefighters and police officers wielding pickaxes and power saws clambered over the rubble pile overnight, punching holes through the ruins to pull dust-covered people from beneath piles of twisted wood and brick.
Rescuers used dogs to sniff for survivors. Firefighters used orange buckets as they removed debris from the rubble piles trying to reach people who may be trapped.
“This has been an incredibly challenging and fast-moving situation, with precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a news conference Wednesday. “This type of rescue is exactly what the FDNY trains for.”
Heavy rain was forecast for the city on Thursday afternoon. It wasn’t immediately known how that would affect search efforts.
The cause of the collapse was under investigation, but New York City’s buildings commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, noted that when the building fell, construction workers were excavating an empty lot next door for a new building.
Much of the rubble from the collapsed building — a mixed-use structure with apartments sitting atop ground-floor commercial space — wound up in a huge pile inside the construction pit. Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.
About 250 firefighters were working the scene, Mamdani said.
On Wednesday night, firefighters pulled a woman — still alive and moving — out of a hole they had dug into the rubble pile, hoisting her up on a stretcher and rushing to a waiting ambulance. Additional people were pulled from beneath the pile as the night went on.
Seven of the casualties were children, authorities said, without specifying whether any were among the dead.
FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the rescue teams were performing “dangerous and perilous” work. “Every move is choreographed,” she said.
One firefighter sustained minor injuries, fire officials said.
Phone and email messages seeking comment were left Wednesday with the architect, property owner and general contractor listed in city records as being associated with the construction project.
One resident of the collapsed building, Anderson Velez, told the New York Post he was at work when his wife called and said she and their two kids, ages 7 and 2, were trapped in the wreckage.
“She called me when the building collapsed while she was inside with rubble on top of her. She was screaming for someone to help get my son out and then the call cut off,” he said.
Velez said he later learned that his family had been pulled from the rubble alive.
___
Associated Press writers Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed to this story.

title: Video shows Hegseth and staff reprimanded by guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
text:
Video shows Hegseth and staff reprimanded by guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
WASHINGTON — A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery.
See video of the incident in the player above.
Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh could be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that “all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s top spokesman, said that “while commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.”
Hegseth on Thursday awarded the soldier who reprimanded them a Joint Service Commendation Medal.
“We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist,” Hegseth said in a post on social media. “Carry on Patriots.”
A Pentagon official confirmed that Hegseth welcomed the 3rd Infantry Regiment, known as The Old Guard, to the Pentagon “where he proudly awarded Specialist Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026.
The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from World War I, World War II and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the Army’s 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as “The Old Guard," since 1948.
Hegseth and his staff were at the tomb as part of a larger ceremony commemorating Veterans Day that also was attended by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.
The incident comes a day after Hegseth narrowly survived an effort to impeach him by lawmakers in Congress.
The effort was led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and backed by Democrats. However, while Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed efforts to impeach the defense secretary. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.
Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal.
A core part of his argument included the assertion that criticisms of him and his handling of the U.S. military were tantamount to an indictment against the nation’s service members and their successes.
“On the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime,” Hegseth said Tuesday.
“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth argued. “This is sabotage.”
Following the reprimand at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, the reaction from Democrats was swift.
Rep. Gwen Moore, D-Wis., said Hegseth demonstrated “his utter lack of fitness for his office.”
“One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier,” she wrote in a social media post.
It was not the first time members of Trump's team have caused controversy at Arlington National Cemetery.
During his campaign for a second term, Trump attended a ceremony in 2024 to honor U.S. forces killed in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. A campaign staffer reportedly shoved a cemetery employee trying to prevent two people from filming and photographing the event.
Trump, who had been invited by troops’ families, later shared a video on TikTok showing him at the cemetery with a voiceover blaming the Biden administration for the “disaster” of the Afghanistan withdrawal.
U.S. law prohibits campaign or election-related activities within national military cemeteries.

title: Beloved doctor dies after falling down stairs while getting up to use bathroom in his sleep
text:
STANFORD, Ky. (WKYT/Gray News) - A beloved doctor in Kentucky is being remembered after he tragically lost his life following an accident at home.
Dr. James Turpin, 53, an emergency room doctor at Ephraim McDowell Fort Logan Hospital in Stanford, died Wednesday, days after falling on Sunday morning.
According to Dr. Eric Guerrant, a friend and colleague of Turpin, the emergency room doctor fell down a flight of basement stairs after getting up in the middle of the night to use the bathroom.
Turpin suffered serious injuries and was taken to UK Hospital for treatment before succumbing to his injuries on Wednesday.
Turpin also oversaw medical services with emergency medical services in Lincoln and Casey counties.
In 2017, he was named the EMS medical director of the year for the eastern district of Kentucky.
Turpin was said to have an incredible work ethic, working his way up through medical practice from a licensed practical nurse to a registered nurse and then through medical school.
Friends noted Turpin had a way of making hard times much better.
“He made these little bracelets that said, ‘Here to help.’ That was James, and we all wore the bracelets, and that changed the whole demeanor of the practice during a tough time,” Guerrant said. “He had that attitude. He was here to help.”

Father of baby found buried alive in South Carolina denied bond
text:
Father of baby found buried alive in South Carolina denied bond
Officials in South Carolina are providing new details about a baby found buried alive in a dog crate as his father was denied bond in court on Thursday.
Michael Comer is charged with attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary. He was denied bond Thursday morning, and a judge set his next hearing for Dec. 10.
Comer accused of taking baby on Monday
The Lexington County Sheriff's Office said Koah Sharpe was taken by his father, Michael Comer, Monday afternoon, according to investigators.
“Koah was in the care of Comer’s mother. She left Koah with Comer to run an errand while another caregiver was coming over,” Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said. “When the caregiver got there, Comer was gone and Koah was with him.”
Deputies were called around lunchtime Monday and responded to Comer’s father’s house on Parthenon Road in Batesburg-Leesville, Koon said. Both doors were open, the house was empty and baby items were found in the house.
Security footage was found from later Monday of Comer in Batesburg-Leesville, but Koah was not with him, according to investigators.
Investigators said they know that Comer traveled to multiple locations within Lexington County on Monday; however, Comer did not have access to a vehicle.
Comer found
Comer was found and arrested Monday night hiding in an outbuilding in Batesburg-Leesville, resulting in the initial burglary charge, according to investigators. Koah was not with him.
Search for Koah
More than 100 law enforcement and public safety officers came together to search for Koah, Koon said.
Koah found buried alive
According to Koon, a search party found freshly disturbed ground not far from Comer’s father’s house.
As they started searching that area, they could hear Koah crying.
“As you can imagine, the race was on. Everyone was trying to get him out,” Koon said.
“He immediately was placed in the care of EMS and transported to the hospital as soon as they got him out.”
Update on Koah
Koah was released from the hospital Tuesday night, according to Koon. He is with family members and, according to information provided to investigators by his medical team, he is expected to make a full recovery.

title: Woman said hackers hijacked her social media and defrauded her friends
text:
PHOENIX (Aging Untold) — An Arizona woman says her Facebook account was hijacked. Now, the hackers are scamming her friends out of thousands of dollars and even sending the victims to her home.
Melissa Stombaugh is fed up with Facebook after hackers reportedly took over her account.
Posing as her, they posted messages claiming she had to put her father in assisted living, and she was forced to sell his stuff.
“My dad sent me a text, trying to be funny,” she said.
“Like, ‘Hey, you’re not going to wait till I’m dead to start selling all my things?’ And I’m like, what are you talking about?”
That’s when Stombaugh checked her Facebook account and saw a post with a list of items for sale, all very cheap.
“Everything from a truck, (to) a Peloton. Pretty big-ticket items,” she said.
Stombaugh’s friends started sending money, thinking they were helping, but all the funds ended up in the hacker’s Venmo account.
When Stombaugh’s social media friends started arriving to pick up their new belongings, they were surprised to learn that the items didn’t exist, and it wasn’t Melissa they had been communicating with.
“She showed up and I was like, hello? She’s like, ‘Oh, my husband’s out here looking at the truck.’ And I said, the truck? ‘Yeah, the one that we put the deposit on that you have for sale.’ I had no idea,” Stombaugh said.
The hackers changed the email address and devices on Stombaugh’s account, so she was completely locked out of her own Facebook account.
She even tried reaching out to the scammers directly.
“I set up a fake account attempting to access them,” she said. “I went on and chatted with them like I was a fake person in an attempt to see if I could get them to try to sell me something.”
Stombaugh and her friends reported the issue to Facebook, telling them it was a scam. She said that didn’t help.
“Facebook’s response to me was, we don’t see anything wrong with this post,” she said. “It didn’t go against any standards. So we’re going to leave it up.”
That’s when Stombaugh decided to contact our investigators.
Multiple attempts were made to reach Facebook regarding Stombaugh’s issue. Facebook did not respond to the inquiries.
How to prevent this from happening to your account
“Someone said, ‘well, did you have the two-factor authentication turned on?’ And I said, no, what’s that?” Stombaugh said.
Two-factor authentication links your devices to your Facebook account so scammers can’t take over even if they have your password.
To set this up:
- Go to “Settings” on Facebook
- Then select “Passwords and Security”
- From there, it’ll walk you through the process of setting up two-factor authentication
Stombaugh said she has it set up on her other accounts now and wishes she had known about it earlier.
“Because at this point, if I could delete all of my Facebook, I would delete it myself and just be done with Facebook,” she said.
“Which is sad because I really did enjoy sharing our family’s, you know, memories and stuff with people, but not at this cost,” Stombaugh said.

title: 5 people are shot in the trendy Logan Circle neighborhood of the nation’s capital, police say
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Five people were shot early Thursday in a trendy Washington, D.C., neighborhood within walking distance of the White House, said police, who were responding to multiple locations.
The shooter had not been caught, and the locations of the shootings were unclear, police department spokesperson Nicole Deaner said.
The shootings were reported in Logan Circle, about 1 mile north of the White House. No other details are immediately available, police Officer Nathan Clarke said.
Police urged people to avoid the area of the 1500 block of 15th Street, which includes a VIDA fitness center, St. Luke’s Episcopal Church and residences and is around the corner from a Whole Foods supermarket. Much of the block was cordoned off. Schools near the scene were placed on lockdown.
Streets around the area also were blocked off during a massive police response. The federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives said it sent agents to the scene to help. And the FBI said its Washington field office was helping local police with the investigation.
Witness Ryan Dubicki was in his nearby apartment around 8 a.m. when, he said, he “heard about five bangs.”
“They were really spread out so I thought it was construction,” he said. It was only a short time later that he looked out “and there were cops everywhere.”
His apartment building managers sent a notice that there was a possible active shooter.
The neighborhood has seen violence before. In early August 2025, a onetime member of President Donald Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency was assaulted early on a Sunday morning in the Logan Circle neighborhood by a group of teenagers attempting to carjack him and a woman, authorities said.
Days later, Trump fulfilled his threat to bypass local authority and imposed direct federal control over the city, sending in hundreds of National Guard members to reduce crime. That deployment continues today.

title: The rules of texting and social media keep changing — what older adults should know
text:
(Aging Untold) — If you are more used to phone calls and handwritten notes than texts and group chats, you might feel a bit like you are out of the loop.
There are unwritten rules about what to share, when to reply and who to trust, and the Aging Untold experts are walking you through them.
The rules are hard to find, and they keep changing
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said she recently ran into the new rules herself.
“I got a text from my godson and he shamed me for the length of the text that I sent him,” O’Rourke said. “OK, so there’s rules out there, and I don’t know what they are.”
She pointed to Emily Post and Miss Manners as places to find up-to-date information on the rules.
The rules have never stood still, gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.
“The reality is the rules have always been changing. They’re fluid,” Cradduck said. “They’re different from the 20s to the 30s to the 40s to the 50s.”
Handshakes meant something. Scammers are counting on that.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said older adults need to know what has changed.
“They’re used to that handshake really meaning something,” Rogers said. “And now you have the scams or the fast relationships that are growing because of the new technology.”
Rogers said older adults are looking for connection, which is why they need to be careful.
“They’re looking for that interaction and the trust,” Rogers said.
Some things don’t change, Rogers said, including “consistency, transparency.”
Relationships that once took years to build now often start on social media, Cradduck said.
“The walls are gone,” she said. “So now you’re telling intimate details about your life to a virtual stranger. And that’s not just our kids doing it or our older people. Everyone has fallen into that.”
Check with a buddy before you reply
To guard against fraud, O’Rourke suggested having a person to check in with.
“I want to have people to have a buddy, have somebody that you check in with to say, ‘I’m about to respond to this text, I’m about to jump on this Facebook,’ and check it out with somebody before you jump in,” O’Rourke said.
“We’re all learning together, so just have a comfort level with that,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
Don’t let caution keep you offline
Ambrose said scams should not push older adults away from technology.
“You should, because it’s going to keep you sharper, and it’s going to keep you in relationship with the younger people in your life and with your friends,” Ambrose said. “This is how we communicate today.”
Learning to text well helps people stay in touch with children who are busy working and raising kids, Cradduck said.
“I understand that that may not be the most comfortable way to communicate, and it might not have fit your norm,” she said. “But it is the norm of society.”
Key takeaways
- Meet your family where they are. Adapting to new technology keeps you connected.
- Don’t take changing norms personally. A text may feel short, but the rules are different now.
- Stay cautious online. Don’t let digital speed replace common sense boundaries.

title: Six Waldo County Fire Departments Makes Important Updates After Mill Fire
text:
Officials Suspend Fines And Support Waldo County Fire & Rescue Departments To Fix Citations Issued After Robbins Mills Fire
More efficient processes and safety procedures are being implemented in several Fire Departments across Maine following the conclusion of the investigation into the Robbins Lumber mill fire and explosion that took place in Waldo County this past May.
Read More: Bangor Firefighters Contain Early Morning Center Street Blaze
The Maine Department of Labor and the Maine Occupational Safety and Health program looked into the Fire and Rescue Departments in Appleton, Belmont, Lincolnville, Montville, Morrill, and Searsmont and issued citations for the areas in which those departments needed improvements to meet state or federal standards.
"MEOSH issued citations related to the lack of an effective accountability system for tracking the location of firefighters on scene on May 15 to all six fire departments. As a result of the lessons learned that day, all of the fire departments have augmented their accountability systems. MEOSH also issued citations to five departments related to the use of personal protective equipment (PPE), including firefighting gear and breathing apparatus, to keep personnel safe from the hazards of a fire scene. "
Each department mentioned has already started to make changes and update their protocol, policies, or equipment to move towards compliance with the expected standards.
All five departments resolved the immediate deficiencies and have committed to attending Respiratory Protection Program training delivered by SafetyWorks! in Waldo County in January.
The Maine Fire Chiefs' Association and Maine Fire Service Institutes will help the departments in their efforts to improve by holding special training sessions in the area over the winter.
Read More: Two Fires Strike Belfast Area Over One October Weekend
To support the departments' efforts to improve internal operations as well as coordination and incident command of major mutual aid emergencies, the Bureau is coordinating with the Maine Fire Chiefs' Association and Maine Fire Service Institute to provide training for these departments' chiefs and officers in Belmont in February.
Bureau Director Kate Burkhart says there were civil penalties attached to the citations that added up to $108,000, but the bureau suspended almost all of the fines so that the small-town departments could put their efforts and money into the much-needed improvements instead.

title: Maddie Fitzpatrick off to great start for UMaine women’s basketball in new prominent role
text:
University of Maine basketball forward Maddie Fitzpatrick found herself in an unfamiliar role the past two seasons.
After a tremendous career at Cheverus High School in Portland, which included being named the two-time Maine Gatorade Player of the Year and then being selected Miss Maine Basketball, Fitzpatrick blew out her knee during summer workouts in 2024 and missed her entire freshman season.
Then, last year, she found herself in a reserve role, averaging only nine minutes per game for a veteran Black Bear team.
Two games into this season, Fitzpatrick is certainly making up for lost time.
She had 14 points, 17 rebounds and three assists in the season-opening 70-68 victory over Siena and then poured in 19 points, grabbed nine rebounds and added four assists and two steals in an 87-62 win over Merrimack.
Both games were part of the America East-Metro Challenge series.
Fitzpatrick was named the America East Player of the Week, which she called a very nice honor. When asked if she has surprised herself, she said she hadn’t thought about it.
“I’m doing what my team needs and what my coaches have asked me to do,” Fitzpatrick said.
“Being injured changed my perspective on that and on last year, too. I’m just taking whatever comes my way. I’m not taking [anything] for granted. I’m really grateful to be healthy and to be able to play and help my team win.”
Even though Fitzpatrick was coming off knee surgery last season, she insisted she was 100% healthy. But the Black Bears had three quality veterans in America East Player of the Year Adrianna Smith, All-America East third team guard Asta Blauenfeldt, and third-leading scorer and rebounder Sarah Talon.
“We had a bunch of good players playing my position so it was like a learning year for me,” said the 5-foot-11 Fitzpatrick, who averaged 1.5 points and 1.4 rebounds per game.
“It’s always hard not to play but if I had looked at it with a negative perspective, I wouldn’t have learned as much as I did. My teammates helped me a lot with that. I hadn’t played in over a year so I had to learn how to be in that routine and schedule and how to play again. It sounds silly but that’s the reality of it.”
Prior to this season, she had a lot of meetings with her coaches to understand her upcoming role. She also worked out constantly, including spending a lot of time with sports performance coach/director of basketball operations Matt Peyton.
“I am definitely a list-maker and I try to plan everything out. I asked them what I needed to work on in order to be the player they wanted me to be for our program,” Fitzpatrick said. “Coach [Amy Vachon] said my defense needs a lot of work.
“Our coaches are very honest. It’s something I appreciate a lot. It’s a reason I committed here,” said Fitzpatrick. “I just put my head down and did what they asked. That’s all you can do at the end of the day.
“I’ll do whatever the team needs whether it be shooting and scoring, rebounding, playing defense or making the right pass. I’ve really tried to be a leader for the team, on and off the court. Someone who will be there for her teammates.”
Vachon said she is “really proud” of Fitzpatrick.
“She worked so hard in the offseason to get in the best shape of her life,” Vachon said. “She is quicker and her defense has improved a ton. She is playing on both sides of the ball at a high level. She is rebounding and being aggressive, offensively, which is what we need her to do.”
Going through rehabilitation after undergoing knee surgery was “one of the hardest things” Fitzpatrick — a three-time former Bangor Daily News All-Maine Schoolgirl first team selection — said she’s endured.
But she wasn’t alone. Smith also suffered a season-ending knee injury and underwent surgery.
“It was definitely easier because I had [Adrianna Smith] with me,” Fitzpatrick said. “We were kind of on the same timeline. I was very grateful to be able to develop a relationship with her during our recovery. We spent so much time together, we both helped each other in different ways. She is someone I look up to.”
Fitzpatrick understands that there are questions about how good the team can be after losing its top three scorers in Smith, Blauenfeldt and Talon.
“They had a really big impact, but they also taught us a lot of stuff while they were here that we can use. We are a different team, but we are taking what we learned from the past upperclassmen and using it while also finding our own way as well,” Fitzpatrick said.
The Black Bears will be tested on Friday night at 7 p.m. when Oregon, which went 23-13 and won an NCAA Tournament game last season, invades the Skip Chappelle Court in the Memorial Gym. The Ducks come to Maine to finish a two-game New England road trip, having beaten Vermont on Wednesday night, 81-56.
Oregon returns two of its top three scorers in leading point-producer Katie Fiso (15.5 points per game) and third-leading scorer and leading rebounder Ehis Etjute (12.5 ppg, 9 rpg).
“Those Big Ten teams are really good competition. It’s going to be exciting, it’s going to be fun. It will be a good test,” Fitzpatrick said.

title: Hermon QBs embrace unique snap split with state title in sight
text:
Hermon’s Ethan Curtis has played quarterback for nearly his entire life.
“Since he was in diapers,” Hermon head coach Kyle Gallant joked. “Since he was just a kid.”
“I’ve been playing quarterback since the third grade,” the senior Curtis said. “All the way up through the youth leagues.”
Quarterback is the position Curtis has always known. So, three weeks ago, when Gallant asked Curtis if he’d be willing to split snaps with junior Griffin Dunton heading into the Class C playoffs, one might expect a hesitant response from the senior.
But that’s just not who Curtis is.
“Whatever I’ve got to do to help the team out and go get us a win, I’m always willing to do it,” Curtis said. “Our main goal is to get a Gold Ball. I’m happy to do anything in my power to make that happen.”
“Ethan Curtis is probably the most humble, wholesome human being that I have ever coached in my life,” Gallant said. “When I approached him and told him what I was thinking, his immediate response was, ‘Coach, I’ll do whatever you need me to do to win us a Gold Ball.”
Curtis, a 1,000-yard passer and all-conference QB in 2026, has played great this season, Gallant reiterated. But after back-to-back close losses to Class C powers Greely and Leavitt late in the year, Gallant wanted to try something new to take pressure off his senior’s shoulders.
The idea? Let Curtis split snaps with Dunton, who Gallant called an “incredible” athlete.
“Ethan’s an incredible quarterback; that decision had nothing to do with him. He’s played great football for us this year,” Gallant said. “Ethan is just more of a pocket passer, and teams had started keying in on our RB Sam Hopkins.
“We can throw Griffin in there on some plays, and he has the speed with his legs that keeps teams honest and makes them decide to either commit to [pursuing] Sam or Griffin. It makes it harder on defenses having to make that decision.”
Dunton is a speedy, 6-foot wide receiver who can make defenders miss with the ball in his hands. Gallant wanted to see him get more touches each game. Splitting time with Curtis — a talented pocket passer — and Dunton out of the wildcat formation has proved a successful formula for Hermon the past two weeks.
When Curtis is in at quarterback, Dunton lines up at wide receiver. When Dunton is playing quarterback, Curtis does the same. Both players are skilled at each position.
“We can both play QB, and we can both catch,” Dunton said. “It’s something that’s hard to plan against.”
“The cool thing about it is that I started my freshman season here playing a little bit of wide receiver when we had a more experienced starting QB,” Curtis said. “So it’s something I’m familiar with and something I can bring to the table.”
On Oct. 30, in the Hawks’ regular-season finale against York, Curtis made the most of his fewer snaps, completing seven of nine passes for 105 yards and two touchdowns. The following week, in the Class C state quarterfinal win over Nokomis, Dunton shouldered the load. He rushed nine times from under center for nearly 150 yards and a score.
Dunton realized how well Hermon’s new split-snap game plan was working quickly in last Friday’s matchup against Nokomis.
“Well, [Nokomis] had to call a timeout pretty early in the first quarter because of how we were moving the ball,” Dunton said. “I kind of realized at that point, ‘OK, they may not know what to do with both of us.”
Curtis and Dunton will take the new split-snap QB system into this Friday’s Class C semifinal matchup at Greely. The Hawks fell 28-14 to the defending state champions on Oct. 16, but there’s a sense of rejuvenation about the team heading into the matchup.
“It’s all about the will and the want with this team,” Dunton said. “I think all 40 guys are willing to put in the work and have the belief that we can win a Gold Ball. Everybody has a role, and they’re all bought into whatever role will help us achieve that goal.”
Hermon will take on Greely in the Class C state semifinals Friday at Greely High School in Cumberland Center. Kickoff is slated for 7 p.m.

title: Teen who spent years building lawn business has nearly $20,000 worth of equipment stolen
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRAIRIE VILLAGE, Kan. (KCTV/Gray News) - A Kansas teen who spent years building a lawn care business says he had about $20,000 worth of equipment stolen the night before Halloween.
Sonny Gallardo is the owner of Sunnyside Jobs LLC. He started as a sixth grader knocking on doors and raking leaves with his grandfather.
Those small jobs grew into mowing lawns.
Four years later, the business was big enough for a five-person crew.
“I just like doing it; it gives people joy and gives me joy. I love making people happy,” Gallardo said.
Ring doorbell video appeared to show someone stealing Gallardo’s trailer.
The stolen items included five mowers, two weed eaters and two blowers that were on the trailer.
Gallardo’s family said the work vehicle was also emptied.
“It was $20,000 worth of equipment. It took me three years to get that equipment, and it’s a bummer,” Gallardo said.
The equipment was stolen before Gallardo had a chance to get the business insured.
Gallardo’s mother started a GoFundMe to help him rebuild that has already raised thousands of dollars.
“I really was speechless. I didn’t believe it. I still can’t believe it right now. I’m just thankful to God for all these people who are donating money,” Gallardo said.
According to Prairie Village police, an investigation remains ongoing despite not having any immediate leads in the case.
Police are asking people to watch for large amounts of lawn equipment in yards or being sold online.
“Nothing is going to put me down. I mean, you can try your best, but I’m never going to go down. I love this stuff too much. It’s been my dream since I was little,” Gallardo said.
Gallardo said he remains working and available for lawn care work.

title: High mortgage rates put a damper on Maine’s housing market
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s housing market is showing promising signs of leveling out. Inventory has been steadily climbing. Prices have, for the most part, stayed around $400,000. Homes are sitting on the market longer.
That should have prospective buyers, many of whom have been boxed out of the market for years, racing to open houses to put in offers.
But that’s not happening, according to preliminary data released Thursday by the Maine Association of Realtors and Maine Listings.
Instead, they’re staying on the sidelines as high mortgage rates stand in their way.
Here are three takeaways from Maine’s October market.
1. Mortgage rates kept sales low
Last month, 1,556 houses changed hands, according to data from Maine Listings.
That’s a roughly 6% decrease from October 2025, but a tiny 2% increase from September.
It ends, if only just, a three-month sales slide.
Judy Oberg, president of the Maine Association Realtors, said in a news release that buyer demand has softened heading into the fourth quarter of the year.
The year-over-year sales decrease comes amid rising inventory. Last month there were 6,528 homes on the market, the most since December 2019, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.
But high mortgage rates are keeping many would-be-buyers at bay.
Lawrence Yun, chief economist for the National Association of Realtors, said mortgage rates last month climbed to their highest level since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023.
According to mortgage buyer Freddie Mac, the average mortgage rate last month was about 7.34%.
That has fallen somewhat, but remains higher than the mid-6% rates that have been typical in the last year.
As of Nov. 5, the most recent data available, the average rate on a 30-year-mortgage was about 7.18%
2. Prices may be leveling
Sale prices also fell last month, likely also a result of the increased inventory.
The median home sale price across Maine fell to $400,000 in October, a roughly 3.6% decrease from September and a 6% drop from October of last year.
“Statewide, buyers have more homes to choose from than last year and more room to negotiate,” said Oberg, who is also an associate broker at Oberg Insurance and Real Estate Agency in Bridgton. “Sellers are facing more competition from other listings and that’s reflected in the median sold prices.”
The dip comes just one month after several counties saw record-breaking prices. In September, six of Maine’s 16 counties had median sale prices over $500,000.
Last month, just Cumberland and York counties broke the half-a-million mark, with medians of $582,000 and $554,500, respectively.
Aroostook County held its spot as the only county with prices below $200,000, with a median sale price of $160,000.
Statewide, median prices have largely stayed between $400,000 and $425,000 for much of the year, peaking at $436,000 in June.
The increased inventory is also giving buyers more room to negotiate. Homes stayed on the market for an average of 23 days last month, according to Maine Listings. That’s the longest that listings have lingered since March.
Appropriately priced homes in desirable areas are still selling quickly. Houses in Cumberland County sold, on average, within 11 days. Houses in Washington County, however, sat on the market for an average of 65 days.
3. Maine followed national trends
Maine’s housing market faced similar headwinds as the rest of the country.
Nationally, single-family home sales dropped almost 6% from September, and more than 8% from October 2025, according to the National Association of Realtors.
Meanwhile, prices inched up to a median of $421,900, a negligible year-over-year increase of about 0.4%.
Regionally, sales in the Northeast were level month over month and fell about 4% from the same month last year.
The median price rose about 3% year over year to $519,600.
According to Yun at the national association, home sales last month reached their lowest level since August 2010.
But despite a tepid month, homeowners across the country have seen sizable housing wealth accumulation over the last few years, Yun said, and the number of distressed property sales (foreclosures and short sales) remains historically low.
“Based on the current underwhelming home sales pace at a time of consistent job growth, there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline,” he said.

title: ‘General Hospital’ actor Randall England dies at 75
text:
(Gray News) - Actor Randall England, known for his role as Jack Slater on the popular soap opera “General Hospital,” has died. He was 75.
England died on Sept. 25 surrounded by loved ones, according to an obituary shared by his family. He died following a battle with esophageal cancer, according to Deadline.
“An actor, model, writer, producer and musician, Randall lived a life full of interesting people and stories. Of all his roles, being a father and ‘Pappaw’ to his grandchildren meant the most to him,” the obituary read.
England appeared on “General Hospital” from November 1984 through June 1985 as the villainous jewel thief Jack Slater, according to the Hollywood Reporter.
His other television appearances include “The Young and the Restless,” “Dallas” and “Baywatch.”
England also starred in the films “Beverly Hills Chihuahuas” and “Cat City,” as well as Maroon 5’s music video, “Sugar.”
“Charming, loving, and generous with his time and energy, Randall was someone people could count on. Friends, family, and former students have remembered his authenticity and the steady presence he offered in their lives. He offered encouragement and advice freely. His legacy lives on in the people he loved, taught, and supported,” his obituary read.
England is survived by his daughter Micaela Reed and his son-in-law Sam Reed, as well as his sister Linda Baker, grandchildren Katherine and Julian, and his mother Catherine Burgess.
The family asked for donations to be made to the Esophageal Cancer Action Network in lieu of flowers.

title: A new study provides a ‘beacon of hope’ for people living with long COVID
text:
Scientists may finally have some good news for people with long COVID
Scientists may finally have some good news for people with long COVID
A bout of COVID-19 can make you feel lousy — and in some cases, can trigger serious complications — but for some folks, the story isn’t over even after they recover from the initial illness. That’s because they develop long COVID, a chronic condition that can affect nearly every organ of the body.
Some people with long COVID struggle with debilitating fatigue or joint and muscle pain, while others deal with changes to their sense of taste and smell. One of the most frustrating parts of the condition is that there’s still so much unknown about it, including how long all those symptoms can persist.
But research may finally provide some answers: A new study suggests that long COVID doesn’t last forever for most patients — and even presents a possible timeline for recovery. Here’s what doctors want you to know about the findings.
Related video above: Maryland experts urge flu shots ahead of flu season start
Prevention spoke with Dr. Amesh A. Adalja, an infectious disease expert and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security; Dr. Jennifer Abeles, long COVID researcher and clinical assistant professor of medicine at University at Buffalo’s Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences; Harrison T. Reeder, lead study author, an instructor in investigation at MGH Biostatistics, and an instructor in medicine at Harvard Medical School; Dr. Eve Bowers, an assistant professor of clinical medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center.
What did the study find regarding long COVID recovery?
The study, which was published in Annals of Internal Medicine, analyzed data from 1,019 people in the RECOVER-Adult cohort, a nationwide, observational study that tracks people with long COVID. The study followed patients and their symptoms over time, starting 12 months after their initial COVID-19 diagnosis.
After analyzing the data, the researchers discovered that 36% of patients had an improvement in symptoms by 24 months after their COVID-19 infection. By three years, 50% of participants had sustained symptom improvement and 56% showed a substantial drop in symptoms, along with a better quality of life. What’s more, at that three-year mark, nearly 27% reached complete remission — meaning, they recovered from long COVID.
But the timeline for recovery wasn’t the same across the board; the type of symptoms mattered. “People whose main problem was lost smell or taste did far better than those with symptoms across multiple body systems, fewer than one in five of whom improved,” said Adalja, the infectious disease expert.
“These findings underscore both the potential for natural recovery and the urgent need for placebo-controlled therapeutic intervention trials,” the researchers wrote in the study.
Overall, “the findings are very encouraging and provide a much-needed beacon of hope for patients living with long COVID,” said Bowers. “They reinforce that recovery is possible, even when symptoms have persisted for a prolonged period,” she adds.
Still, she notes that people should be cautious when interpreting the findings. “We need to be careful not to equate improvement with full recovery,” she said. “Many patients continue to experience significant symptoms and functional limitations years after their initial infection.”
Bowers said she’s seen patients even five years later who struggle with debilitating fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, exercise intolerance, and autonomic conditions like postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), a chronic autonomic nervous system disorder marked by a rapid increase in heart rate when someone moves from lying down or sitting to a standing position. “These symptoms can interfere with their ability to work, care for their families, or carry out everyday activities,” says Bowers.
In general, though, the study’s findings echo what doctors see with patients. “In my experience, we do see gradual improvement of symptoms as time goes on,” said Jennifer Abeles, the long COVID researcher.
How is long COVID treated right now, and can anything speed up recovery?
There is a range of options for patients with long COVID, but no overall protocol to address everything all at once. Adalja said that doctors will often “target the most disruptive symptoms” in an attempt to help patients feel better.
Depending on the type of long COVID they have, that may include having a patient pace their activity, undergo smell training, and focus on getting good sleep. It’s also important for patients to be evaluated for conditions like POTS, per Adalja.
Nothing has been proven to speed up recovery once someone has long COVID, he said. “The best-tested candidate failed: In a large trial, 15 or 25 days of Paxlovid [an antiviral approved to treat COVID-19 infection] did no better than placebo,” he points out.
Some doctors will prescribe low doses of naltrexone, an opioid receptor antagonist, off-label for long COVID. “Small studies without placebo groups suggest it may help fatigue, sleep, and brain fog, but the evidence is weak,” Adalja said. Still, he adds that it’s “reasonable” to talk to your doctor about this possibility to treat your symptoms.
Many people can benefit from physical therapy and occupational therapy, according to Abeles. In many cases, gentle movement and gradual progression is the name of the game. “The treatments for long COVID aren’t the same as therapy provided for other illnesses,” she said. “It’s important to provide therapy that is paced in accordance with what the patient can tolerate. To push a patient with long COVID is likely to make their symptoms and disease much worse and set them back.”
And if you come across something that promises a quick fix, approach with caution. “Be wary of expensive supplement ‘protocols,’” Adalja said. “Many people improve on their own, which makes useless treatments look effective.” That’s one reason we need more placebo-controlled trials, to tease out which treatment protocols actually hasten recovery—as opposed to patients simply getting better on their own with time, he said.
Can you get long COVID twice?
That’s unclear. “There is ongoing work looking at the impact of reinfections on long COVID risk,” said Harrison T. Reeder, lead study author, an instructor in investigation at MGH Biostatistics, and an instructor in medicine at Harvard Medical School. “It is a major concern that reinfections might exacerbate long COVID or that cumulative reinfections may increase [the] risk of developing long COVID.” Still, Reeder notes that scientists just don’t know the answer yet.
Adalja agrees that we don’t currently have the data to suggest that people who already have long COVID are especially prone to it after another infection. However, he adds that it’s “plausible” that some people are more susceptible to the complication than others.
Abeles said she’s seen patients who have a “recurrence” of long COVID symptoms after they get reinfected, “sometimes at the same level and sometimes much worse,” she said.
Is there anything you can do to cut your chances of long COVID in the first place?
Some people are at a higher risk of developing long COVID, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Those include:
- Women
- Hispanic and Latino people
- People who have experienced more severe COVID-19 illness, especially those who were hospitalized or needed intensive care
- People with underlying health conditions
- People who did not get a COVID-19 vaccine
And if you’ve already had long COVID, getting vaccinated might be even more important.
“People with long COVID should minimize the severity of future episodes of COVID-19, and staying up to date on vaccination is a way to lower that risk,” said Adalja.
Bowers agrees. “Prevention remains particularly important for individuals already dealing with the consequences of a previous infection,” she said.
If you get sick with COVID-19 again (and have risk factors that put you at higher risk of serious illness), taking Paxlovid may help lower your chances of getting long COVID, per new research. Just keep your expectations in check. “The long COVID data are observational and the benefit is modest, so it’s not a guarantee,” said Adalja.
Metformin — a drug commonly used to treat type 2 diabetes — is another option if you get the virus again. Research suggests that taking a two-week course of the medication can lower the risk of developing long COVID. Scientists haven’t yet investigated whether this works similarly on people with existing long COVID, but Adalja said it’s “sensible” to consider this option as well.
Reeder stresses that there’s a need for more research into treatments to speed up recovery for long COVID patients. “While many people do see symptoms improve over time, there are also many people whose long COVID symptoms persist for years,” he said.

title: Rapper Yella Beezy convicted of hiring gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 on busy interstate
text:
DALLAS (AP) - Rapper Yella Beezy was found guilty on Wednesday of hiring the gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 in a brazen daylight attack on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020.
Yella Beezy, 35, whose real name is Markies Conway, was unanimously convicted of capital murder by a Dallas County jury in the death of MO3, whose real name was Melvin Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
In September, a jury found Kewon White guilty of capital murder for fatally shooting Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Prosecutors said the killing was the result of an yearslong escalating feud between Conway and Noble. Both men lived in Dallas.
“We don’t know what turned it for the jurors. … We appreciate the verdict,” lead prosecutor Tommy Adams told reporters. “We think they got it right today.”
“It’s been one of the most challenging cases over the last six years,” he added.
Prosecutors said Conway paid White $40,000 for the shooting.
Noble, 28, was driving on Interstate 35 in south Dallas around noon on Nov. 11, 2020, when White pulled alongside him, authorities said. White stepped out of his vehicle holding a gun. Noble got out of his own vehicle and began running on the freeway as White shot at him, authorities said.
Prosecutor Tommy Adams said White wore a mask and fired over 40 rounds from an AK-47-style pistol while chasing Noble.
White shot Noble and a bystander who was inside a car, police said. The bystander survived, but Noble died at a hospital.
During closing arguments, prosecutors showed jurors a video clip of Conway talking about revenge in an interview, saying he would “get his lick back.” Prosecutor Krystal Biggins drew a comparison between Noble’s killing and a roadway shooting that injured Conway in 2018.
In October 2018, Conway survived being shot while driving on a tollway in the Dallas suburb of Lewisville when someone pulled up next to him and opened fire, hitting him three times.
“This was for the world to see,” Biggins said. “Over a rap beef, we are here for capital murder.”
The defense argued that prosecutors did not prove their case. “This is capital murder, and the state has brought you a lot of speculation,” defense attorney John Gussio said.
Noble had more than 800,000 Instagram followers and was best known for a 2019 remix of “Errybody,” with Baton Rouge, Louisiana, rapper Boosie Badazz.
Conway is best known for his 2017 single, “That’s On Me,” and the 2019 song “Bacc At It Again” with Quavo and Gucci Mane.
