title: Farmington schools target academic gains after declines in test scores
‘School mom’ to ‘school grandma’: Secretary has served students for 52 years
text:
ELGIN, Neb. (KOLN/Gray News) -Brenda Kuhlman opens the door to greet students each morning at Pope John XXIII Central Catholic School, where she has worked for more than 50 years.
“And they’re so happy to be here. And yes, the morning hugs are wonderful,” Kuhlman said.
Kuhlman has been the school’s administrative assistant and office manager since she was 17.
“So my electives, I did the shorthand, the bookkeeping, the typing, and all of that,” Kuhlman said. “And it was probably about December of my senior year, the administrator asked me if I would be interested because the secretary that was here was moving on.”
Kuhlman said the Catholic school opened in 1967, eight years before she started this job. She grew up southwest of Clearwater, Nebraska, and attended a country school before high school in Elgin.
“It was a big adjustment going from maybe four in my class to 56 in high school,” she said.
Kuhlman met her husband at the school and raised six children south of Raeville. Now her grandchildren attend Pope John Central Catholic.
“It’s been my life for that many years,” Kuhlman said.
The school serves eight parishes in surrounding communities. Kuhlman said students come to Elgin from communities including Raeville, Petersburg, Neligh, Clearwater and Ewing.
“I just remember coming here as a 7th grader. And Brenda just became that like school mom for us,” said Lauren Borer, who returned to her alma mater as a teacher. “And now that my kids go here, like they kind of see her as like the school grandma.”
Today, the school has about 130 students from prekindergarten through 12th grade. Kuhlman keeps the school running smoothly for all of them.
“It’s kind of cute when you see students, the younger students, like if you’re shopping or in church and they’re going, what are you doing here? I thought you lived at school,” Kuhlman said.
Deb Warren says she’s known Kuhlman “forever.” Warren attended class with Kuhlman and graduated in 1972. Then she served as the development director while Kuhlman worked in the office.
“Oh, she’s driven. She is a detailed kind of person. So depending on what job you’re working or if you’re doing fundraising or something, Brenda knows all the details,” Warren said. “She keeps the school running like a well-oiled machine for sure.”
Kuhlman’s office duties range from managing funds to returning lost backpacks.
“Brenda gets invited to everyone’s graduation, everyone’s wedding, baby announcements. She’s just well thought of by both the parents, but also their kids,” Warren said.
Kuhlman continues to add to scrapbooks that preserve school history.
“So she knows the stories and the history, but most importantly, she knows the people. And so if we ever have a question about what happened, way back when, she knows everything,” Borer said.
The scrapbooks include photographs of graduates that she also displays in her office.
“And it seems like you get attached to the classes, more attached as I get older for some reason, and it’s hard to see some of them leave,” Kuhlman said. “And just stop in to visit. That’s great to see them do that.”
Leaving her desk and duties at the school someday would be even harder for Kuhlman.
“I guess as long as my health holds out and stuff, I’ll keep working, or until they kick me out, one of the two,” Kuhlman joked.
After 52 years, Kuhlman is in no hurry to retire, not while she’s watching generations grow up in Elgin.

title: Eddington school board member is back in jail
text:
An Eddington school board member has been arrested again. This time on drug charges.
Brittany Wood, 36, was charged with possessing drugs, falsifying physical evidence and violating her conditions of release, according to the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office.
Those charges stem from a Sunday traffic stop, when deputies seized drugs and stopped Wood from allegedly “destroying potential evidence.”
Over the next couple days, deputies unsuccessfully tried to get Wood — who sits on the Regional School Unit 63 school board, which comprises Clifton, Eddington and Holden — to surrender willingly. The sheriff’s office then asked Tuesday night for the public’s help in finding Wood.
She was booked at the Penobscot County Jail in Bangor on Wednesday afternoon. The circumstances of her arrest weren’t immediately available Thursday morning.
Wood was out on bail for domestic violence aggravated assault and endangering the welfare of a child, charges stemming from the May 31 overdose at a Clewleyville Road home in Eddington that sent a 9-month-old infant into cardiac arrest. The infant was revived after CPR and two doses of naloxone, an opioid-overdose-reversing antidote.
In July, the sheriff’s office asked for the public’s help in locating Wood when she didn’t turn herself in on a previous arrest warrant.
While she had an active arrest warrant out in the overdose case, Wood allegedly was spending time in Boston and at Times Square.
Eventually, Wood returned to Maine, and she was arrested about 7 p.m. on July 14 as she left a Brewer home as a passenger in a white pickup truck.
On Thursday morning, Wood was still listed as a member of the RSU 63 school board. Her term expires in June.

title: Woman said hackers hijacked her social media and defrauded her friends
text:
PHOENIX (Aging Untold) — An Arizona woman says her Facebook account was hijacked. Now, the hackers are scamming her friends out of thousands of dollars and even sending the victims to her home.
Melissa Stombaugh is fed up with Facebook after hackers reportedly took over her account.
Posing as her, they posted messages claiming she had to put her father in assisted living, and she was forced to sell his stuff.
“My dad sent me a text, trying to be funny,” she said.
“Like, ‘Hey, you’re not going to wait till I’m dead to start selling all my things?’ And I’m like, what are you talking about?”
That’s when Stombaugh checked her Facebook account and saw a post with a list of items for sale, all very cheap.
“Everything from a truck, (to) a Peloton. Pretty big-ticket items,” she said.
Stombaugh’s friends started sending money, thinking they were helping, but all the funds ended up in the hacker’s Venmo account.
When Stombaugh’s social media friends started arriving to pick up their new belongings, they were surprised to learn that the items didn’t exist, and it wasn’t Melissa they had been communicating with.
“She showed up and I was like, hello? She’s like, ‘Oh, my husband’s out here looking at the truck.’ And I said, the truck? ‘Yeah, the one that we put the deposit on that you have for sale.’ I had no idea,” Stombaugh said.
The hackers changed the email address and devices on Stombaugh’s account, so she was completely locked out of her own Facebook account.
She even tried reaching out to the scammers directly.
“I set up a fake account attempting to access them,” she said. “I went on and chatted with them like I was a fake person in an attempt to see if I could get them to try to sell me something.”
Stombaugh and her friends reported the issue to Facebook, telling them it was a scam. She said that didn’t help.
“Facebook’s response to me was, we don’t see anything wrong with this post,” she said. “It didn’t go against any standards. So we’re going to leave it up.”
That’s when Stombaugh decided to contact our investigators.
Multiple attempts were made to reach Facebook regarding Stombaugh’s issue. Facebook did not respond to the inquiries.
How to prevent this from happening to your account
“Someone said, ‘well, did you have the two-factor authentication turned on?’ And I said, no, what’s that?” Stombaugh said.
Two-factor authentication links your devices to your Facebook account so scammers can’t take over even if they have your password.
To set this up:
- Go to “Settings” on Facebook
- Then select “Passwords and Security”
- From there, it’ll walk you through the process of setting up two-factor authentication
Stombaugh said she has it set up on her other accounts now and wishes she had known about it earlier.
“Because at this point, if I could delete all of my Facebook, I would delete it myself and just be done with Facebook,” she said.
“Which is sad because I really did enjoy sharing our family’s, you know, memories and stuff with people, but not at this cost,” Stombaugh said.

title: Trump administration plans to make it harder to get grocery assistance
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trump administration plans to make it harder to get grocery assistance
President Donald Trump's administration is planning to make it harder to get food aid through the federal government's big grocery assistance program that serves about 1 in 10 Americans.
The administration says the proposed rule would close a loophole by no longer allowing some people who receive benefits under the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program to automatically qualify for the separate Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program too.
About 6.3 million people could lose eligibility for SNAP by the 2029 fiscal year if the proposed change takes effect, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which administers the program. That is on top of 5.5 million people who already have lost SNAP benefits over the past year.
The plan is laid out in a proposed rule published Tuesday on how to run SNAP, and the government is seeking public comment until next month. If it is accepted, the rule would not take full effect for about two years.
The proposal addresses the link between 2 federal programs
At issue are two separate federal programs. The TANF program provides federal grants to states, which set their own eligibility rules for distributing cash and other benefits to low-income families with children. The incomes of recipients vary by program and state.
Federal guidelines generally limit SNAP food benefits to those earning less than 130% of the poverty level, a little over $1,700 monthly for an individual or nearly $3,600 for a family of four. To reduce duplicative paperwork, the federal government allows people who already receive TANF benefits to automatically qualify for SNAP — though they still have to apply.
Some states have used that automatic eligibility to expand SNAP benefits to people who might not otherwise qualify. In 2009, President Barack Obama's administration encouraged states to provide people a minimal TANF-funded benefit, such as an informational pamphlet or telephone hotline, as a way of qualifying them for the food program.
Forty-one states and the District of Columbia have some form of broad-based categorical eligibility for SNAP, according to a USDA report from last year.
Trump's team put forth a similar plan 7 years ago
The first Trump administration proposed to clamp down on such tactics in 2019. But that proposal was withdrawn by President Joe Biden's administration in 2021.
"Simply put, we did not want to remove millions of people from the program, particularly working poor or children," said Stacy Dean, a former USDA official under Biden who now is executive director of the Global Food Institute at George Washington University.
The latest proposal is more sweeping and could prevent states from basing SNAP eligibility on TANF-funded benefits such as job-related counseling or one-time vouchers for vehicle repairs so that people can get to work, said David Super, a law professor at Georgetown University who has studied the food aid program.
"The administration here is basically proposing to eliminate the flexibility that Congress gave the states to serve working poor people," Super said.
SNAP is also connected to other programs for low-income people
Being in a household that receives SNAP benefits also makes school children eligible for free meals. The Agriculture Department says that nearly 1.8 million children would lose eligibility with their family losing SNAP — but that 97% of them would still qualify for free or reduced price school meals through another process.
But the government says some of the children would not get the lunches, even if they are eligible, if their families don't apply.
The proposal comes at a time when the number of people receiving the aid has fallen sharply — and on the heels of sweeping election gains for Democrats across the country.
"The public indicated they want their elected officials to focus on making life affordable," the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning policy research institute, said in an analysis of the proposal. "Yet the Trump Administration is doubling down on making it harder for people to feed their families."
It has been a period of flux for the food aid program
As of July, the Department of Agriculture, which runs SNAP, said 36 million people were receiving the aid. That was down by 13% from a year earlier. Over that time, another federal requirement expanded a work requirement to more enrollees, including those ages 55 to 64 and to parents whose youngest children are at least 14.
Trump's big 2025 tax and policy law that broadened the work requirement also requires states to start shouldering about three-fourths of the cost of running it, up from half. And they will also have to pay some of the costs of the benefits if their error rates exceed certain thresholds. Congressional Democrats are pushing for a delay in implementation of that change.
The newly proposed rule from the Trump administration "is just one of many things right now that states are grappling with that would reduce access to SNAP," said Carolyn Vega, director of policy analysis for the advocacy group Share Our Strength.
The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities is concerned that the eligibility change may result in higher error rates for states — making them have to pay for more of the cost of benefits.
Patricia Anderson, an economics professor at Dartmouth College, said that out of the various administration efforts to reduce SNAP, "this one seems the most reasonable" because some people with higher incomes qualify through categorical eligibility.
But she said there is a different conversation that can be had about whether the SNAP eligibility guidelines are too strict.

title: Portland Jazz Orchestra concert to benefit 2 Midcoast organizations
text:
UUCB Concerts for a Cause will host the Portland Jazz Orchestra at 7:30 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 21, at the Unitarian Universalist Church of Brunswick. All proceeds from the concert will benefit Midcoast New Mainers Group and Tedford Housing.
The Portland Jazz Orchestra is Maine’s premier concert jazz ensemble. Under the direction of Dr. Chris Oberholtzer, this 18-piece jazz ensemble performs a variety of instrumental and vocal big band literature. PJO enjoys playing works written by members and local musicians and often performs music from the libraries of Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Stan Kenton, Bill Holman, Patrick Williams, Woody Herman and Maria Schneider, to name a few.
PJO is made up of professional musicians, many of whom are both performers and educators in New England. Collectively, PJO members have recorded, toured and shared stages with artists such as Natalie Cole, Tony Bennett, Wayne Bergeron, The New York Voices, Barry Manilow, Roberta Flack, The Temptations, the Artie Shaw Orchestra, the Smithsonian Jazz Masterworks Orchestra and the Glenn Miller Orchestra.
Tickets are $25 for adults and $10 for students/children, and will be available at the church office, Gulf of Maine Books or online at ticketstripe.com/pjojazz.
To learn more about UUCB Concerts for a Cause, visit uubrunswick.org/concerts.

title: Maine volunteers build shelters for stray cats ahead of winter
text:
Maine volunteers build shelters for stray cats ahead of winter
More than 40 shelters are being spread across Oxford County.
Maine volunteers build shelters for stray cats ahead of winter
More than 40 shelters are being spread across Oxford County.
Cats may have nine lives, but surviving a Maine winter shouldn't cost them one.
In Oxford County, a group of animal lovers is turning ordinary plastic storage tubs into potentially lifesaving shelters for stray and feral cats. With winter approaching and animal shelters already facing overcrowding, the effort is aimed at protecting cats that have nowhere else to go.
Across the United States, an estimated 30 million to 40 million community cats live outdoors. In Maine, the number is believed to be in the thousands, leaving many vulnerable to freezing temperatures, snow and harsh winter conditions.
A core group of about 10 volunteers has been working alongside Oxford County Animal Control Officer Brandon Holmes for months to address the growing population of community cats through a program known as trap-neuter-return, or TNR.
"On top of the shelters being crowded, there's also a lot of community cats. They are unowned some of them are unfriendly enough to go to a shelter even if they could take them," Holmes said.
TNR involves humanely trapping outdoor cats, having them spayed or neutered, allowing them to recover and then returning them to their outdoor environment. The approach helps prevent unwanted litters while providing an alternative for feral cats that may be too unsocialized to be adopted into traditional homes.
But with colder weather arriving, the group recognized another urgent need: keeping those cats safe and warm.
More than 20 additional volunteers joined a recent shelter-building effort in Oxford County, helping construct more than 40 insulated outdoor cat shelters using materials donated by the community.
The shelters are designed to be simple, affordable and easy enough for families to make at home. Depending on the materials purchased or already available, the project can cost $100 or less.
Each shelter uses two plastic storage tubs, with a smaller tub placed inside a larger one. Styrofoam insulation helps reduce heat loss, while straw provides a dry, insulating space for cats to curl up inside. A small entrance allows the animals to get in and out while limiting their exposure to wind and cold.
While blankets and towels might seem like an obvious way to keep animals warm, volunteers warn that they can actually be dangerous when used as bedding in outdoor winter shelters.
"Because Hay and blankets and really most things we would think of to keep warm absorb moisture and freeze in sub-freezing temps and give the cat hypothermia," said volunteer Shelby Stevens, who previously worked at an animal shelter for more than three years.
Stevens emphasized that natural straw, not hay, should be used inside the shelters.
Unlike blankets and hay, straw helps resist moisture and provides insulation, reducing the risk of cats becoming wet and dangerously cold.
The advice is simple: Straw is for strays, hay is for horses.
For many involved in the project, the effort is about much more than providing a warm place to sleep.
Holmes and the volunteers have spent months working to address the challenges facing community cats, including overcrowded shelters, unwanted litters and the difficulty of finding homes for animals that have spent much of their lives outdoors.
Not every volunteer needs to trap cats or build shelters to make a difference.
Leigh Dunning, who joined the group about four weeks ago, said getting involved was as simple as responding to a social media post.
"I found this on Facebook just a are you interested in helping cats? I clicked it I filled it out, it was easy," Dunning said.
Dunning now helps care for cats following their spay and neuter surgeries, giving them time to recover before they are returned outdoors.
Others can contribute by doing laundry, donating supplies or helping with other tasks that support the group's ongoing rescue efforts.
The volunteers hope that flexibility encourages more people to get involved, even if they have limited time or resources.
While stray and feral cats may be more noticeable during warmer weather, Holmes says their absence from view during the winter can create a misleading impression.
"I actually get a lot less calls about the cats in the winter because people are out there so they’re not seeing it as much but that doesn’t mean that the suffering isn’t happening," Holmes said.
He explained that preparing the shelters before the coldest weather arrives is especially important.
"It’s just we’re not seeing it so providing this getting it done before the real cold snaps here so we can get these out in the yard so that they’re ready for when the cats need them is super important," Holmes said.
The shelters provide cats with a place to escape bitter winds, snow and freezing temperatures, particularly when other shelter options may not be available.
For volunteer Mariel Geiger, the work can be emotional, but moments of affection from the animals make the effort worthwhile.
"These kitties thank us in many different ways, even this one," Geiger said as her foster kitten nibbles on her thumb.
Still, she knows the challenges facing animal rescuers extend well beyond winter.
"On the frontline of rescue, we do see some heartbreaking stuff," Geiger said. "I think if we keep working together, we can make this world a much better place for these kitties overall."
The Oxford County project is something families and individuals can recreate at home using supplies commonly found at hardware and home improvement stores.
To build a basic insulated shelter, you'll need:
One large plastic storage tub, approximately 30 gallons, and one smaller tub, approximately 20 gallons.
Styrofoam insulation to fit between the tubs.
Natural straw for bedding.
A small flowerpot or similar material to create a protected entrance.
A permanent marker and cutting tools to create the opening.
Begin by cutting an entrance through the plastic tubs, making sure the openings align. Place the smaller tub inside the larger one, adding Styrofoam insulation between them. Fill the inner tub with loose straw, then secure the lids to help keep rain and snow out.
Position the completed shelter in a protected location away from heavy foot traffic and prevailing winds. Keeping the entrance clear of accumulating snow and replacing damp or dirty straw as needed can help maintain a safer space for outdoor cats.
Avoid using blankets, towels or hay as bedding, since they can retain moisture and increase the risk of hypothermia.

title: The fish of 10,000 casts: Chasing muskie in Aroostook County
text:
WRITTEN BY DYLAN SAVAGEAU
A foot-long lure is a curious thing to throw at a fish, particularly when you might spend an entire day doing it without getting so much as a follow. But that’s muskie fishing on the St. John River, where anglers in Aroostook County pursue one of Maine’s most unusual game fish. Muskellunge, better known as muskie, have earned the nickname the “fish of 10,000 casts” for good reason. They can follow a lure right to the boat and disappear without striking, leaving an angler to wonder how close he came to hooking the fish of a lifetime.
Some of the lures used to catch them are roughly the length of an average brook trout. The tackle is heavy, the casts are relentless, and there are no guarantees. That’s part of the appeal. A muskie might be watching your lure without you ever knowing it, and the next cast could be the one that finally draws a strike.
Muskies are powerful predators, built for ambush and armed with rows of sharp teeth. Maine’s Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife reports that muskies commonly measure 30 to 36 inches and weigh between five and 10 pounds, although larger fish are possible. The state’s largest recorded specimen weighed 22 pounds, 12 ounces.
Muskies are not native to Maine. Their presence in the St. John River system traces back to introductions in Quebec during the 1970s. From there, the fish spread downstream and established populations in suitable waters throughout the drainage.
The St. John drainage was once known more for its native brook trout and salmon fisheries, and the introduction of muskellunge has raised concerns about the effects of an introduced predator on those populations. Maine fisheries researchers have documented concerns about the effects of introduced predatory fish on native species. Muskie fishing offers a distinctive opportunity for anglers, but its history also serves as a reminder that introducing a fish can have lasting consequences for the waters it inhabits.
The St. John Valley offers several places to pursue muskies. The river runs past Fort Kent, Frenchville, Madawaska, and Van Buren, with connected waters offering additional opportunities to pursue these fish.
Anyone planning to fish for muskies should leave the ultralight rod at home. Muskie tackle needs enough backbone to cast heavy lures throughout the day and handle a large fish at close quarters. A stout rod, a dependable reel, braided line, and a bite-resistant leader are standard equipment. Bucktail spinners, oversized crankbaits, and swimbaits are common choices, to work around weed edges, submerged timber, and breaks in the current. The idea is to put a substantial meal in front of a fish holding near cover or waiting for prey to pass within striking distance. Trolling swimbaits and diving plugs are another option, particularly when exploring unfamiliar water.
Fort Kent has helped put this unusual fishery on the map. Each summer, the town hosts the International Muskie Derby, bringing anglers to the St. John River and its tributaries in pursuit of a qualifying fish. Established in 2003, the event has become part of the region’s fishing culture, drawing visitors who are willing to spend long hours casting for a fish that may never show itself. For those who do connect, the catch is often the beginning of a story that gets told long after the tackle has been put away.
Before heading out, anglers should check current Maine fishing regulations and access conditions, particularly near the international boundary with New Brunswick. There are no length or bag limit restrictions to conserve existing muskie fisheries, however only Beau and Glacier lakes are open to muskie fishing during the ice fishing seasons, according to the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife.
Muskie fishing doesn’t promise steady action. Most casts won’t produce a fish, and plenty won’t even produce a follow. But somewhere in the St. John, a 40-inch muskie could be holding in a weed bed, waiting for an easy meal. Somebody’s going to put a lure in front of it. Might as well be you.

title: 2 beloved street vendors identified as victims of the Los Angeles metro station crash
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Authorities have identified two of the three women killed when the driver of a minivan crashed outside a Los Angeles metro station this week.
The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner identified the women as Teodora Villalobos, 57, and Maria Peck, 73. Both were killed on the sidewalk Tuesday by blunt force injuries, the medical examiner’s office said.
Authorities did not immediately release the identity of the third victim, pending the notification of family, the medical examiner’s office said in an email on Thursday.
Peck and Villalobos were food vendors in Los Angeles’ North Hollywood neighborhood who were killed when the minivan plowed into a busy intersection during the height of the evening commute. Friends and family members built a memorial to the women, who were widely known for selling hot dogs and other street food, by leaving flower bouquets, notes, photos and candles on the sidewalk where they were struck.
Police arrested the driver, 61-year-old Ihor Demianenko, for investigation of driving under the influence and three counts of murder. His bail was set at $6 million. It was not immediately known when he would appear in court.
Melissa Villalobos told KABC-TV that her mother worked hard and tried to help those in her community.
“When she sold here, if people didn’t have money to pay for the food, she would still give food to those who didn’t have anything,” she said.
Peck worked as a vendor for more than a decade six days a week, even on holidays, according to a GoFundMe page set up to support her family. The page said Peck found joy in being part of the community and didn’t want to scale back her hours even as she aged.

title: Leaps of faith and hard work: Women build businesses in Aroostook
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WRITTEN BY JEN LYNDS
For Kaitie Gilmour, the path to entrepreneurship began after she left Massachusetts and made a home in Houlton. For Mackenzie Corriveau, it started while she was still in high school. Their journeys took different turns, but both women found opportunities in Aroostook County and embraced the challenges of building businesses from the ground up.
Gilmour owns Mrs. Kaitie’s Laugh and Learn Academy, a child care center that opened in 2023 at 18 High St. in Houlton. A Massachusetts native, she moved to Aroostook County after graduating from high school. Her parents had arrived a few months earlier.
The academy was not Gilmour’s first child care experience. She started a home-based day care in 2019, then opened the larger facility when someone approached her about it. She also decided to keep the home-based business. Both facilities are fully licensed by the Maine Department of Health for 61 children across two locations.
At the academy, children receive two meals and snacks and engage in a learning curriculum to keep them educated and entertained.
“We base our days off of the Maine Learning Standards and the Infant and Toddler Learning Standards. We keep the children busy all day,” Gilmour said.
Gilmour gained firsthand experience with the cost of childcare, which led her to enter the field.
“I was originally in the healthcare field,” she explained. “But I had three children at the time, and my husband had just graduated college. He got a really great job, and with that job, we could no longer qualify for subsidy. That meant we couldn’t afford childcare.”
She stressed the importance of having reliable, affordable childcare in the area.
“Families cannot work without it,” she said. “Childcare is the workforce behind the workforce. People are physically willing and able to work, but without reliable, affordable childcare, they cannot be in the workforce.”
Mackenzie Corriveau of Wallagrass started her business, Kenzie’s Paradise 4 Paws, at age 16. Her business includes grooming, boarding, and daycare. She said she had always loved animals and had always wanted to open a business. She had been around dogs her whole life, so it felt like a good fit.
“As a first step, I shadowed a local groomer,” she explained. “I thought that I could really do it. I started taking classes online, and another local groomer mentored me. That is how I got started.”
Corriveau said the community gave her a great deal of support, and her client list grew during that first year. She ran the business through high school and while taking college classes. She hired three employees and graduated from the University of Maine at Fort Kent while continuing to learn entrepreneurship. She said each year, though filled with ups and downs, taught her maturity and responsibility.
“There have been times my friends have wanted me to go out, and I have to work,” she said. “Some of the days that I thought were going to be eight-hour days became 12-hour days. Occasionally an employee calls out, and I have to stay late. I have to be responsible and think of the business.”
She doesn’t expect to expand or open a second business in the future.
“I like keeping it small, with a small client list,” she said. “This is the best little venture here.”
Corriveau said that if she could go back in time and tell her 16-year-old self anything, it would be that “everything is going to be okay.”
“In the beginning, I put a lot of pressure on myself,” she recalled. “I would tell myself to relax and enjoy the ride. You don’t have to be perfect.”

title: Obituary: Ruth Ida Seigars-Herrick
Preserve remains of World War II water tower
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
An important part of World War II history is about to vanish from Bangor’s landscape. The decaying 1941 checkerboard steel water tower on Venture Way, near the city’s airport, along with a 60-year-old tower on outer Hammond Street, have been replaced by a 3.3 million-gallon tank near the older tower.
Sitting on a hill overlooking the original Dow Army Air Field, the old tank was a welcoming landmark visible to returning B-17, B-24 and other flight crews from Europe grateful to be back home. After the war, it was painted its familiar red-and-white design, and a topping light swept the sky and surrounding neighborhoods.
As historians, we urge the Bangor Water District to preserve parts of the dismantled tank for public viewing. Perhaps they could be displayed next to the tower light in the Maine Air Museum, and in other museums, or outside the Thomas Hill Standpipe. Chuck Harrison, general manager of the water district, and the water district board of trustees, have already expressed interest in exploring a preservation plan.
Few tangible reminders of Bangor’s crucial wartime effort remain, so we believe saving sections of the old water tower is vital. The time is now. Please seize this opportunity for history’s sake.
Richard R. Shaw
Bangor
Brian N. Swartz
Hampden
David H. Bergquist
Chichester, N.H.

title: We wanted a new life – and we found it at Cary Medical Center in Aroostook County
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
COURTESY OF CHAD JOHNSON, RN, INPATIENT NURSE MANAGER AT CARY MEDICAL CENTER
After working as an ICU nurse in New Mexico, my wife and I felt it was time for a change. We were both born and raised in the desert, and we dreamed of a place with trees and lakes, a place where we could experience all four seasons, as well as a different pace of life for our kids. That dream led us to move across the country to Aroostook County.
Moving to a place we’d never visited was intimidating, but the moment I connected with staff at Cary Medical Center, I knew we were making the right decision. I had seen an advertisement that the hospital was one of the Best Places to Work in Maine, so I applied for a job as an ICU nurse.
The hospital felt like family from the start. During my interview process, I met with the department manager over Zoom, received photos from Human Resources of the snowy Maine winters to share with our kids, and even got a personal call from the CEO, Kris Doody.
I had to ask her probably three or four times who she was because a CEO calling a staff nurse usually isn’t a thing. Once all that happened I was like, you know what? I think this is the place.
There were plenty of unknowns traveling to a corner of the country we had never visited, let alone lived in.
The culture is extremely different, so that’s something we had to adjust to. We had never visited Maine in our whole life, or ever even been in New England before, so just to move up here and do something completely different and meet all kinds of new people was the hardest part.
That was nearly three years ago. Now, we’re fully settled in. Our kids are thriving in school. My wife, who was a stay-at-home mom during our transition, has taken on a part-time job she enjoys. We spend evenings by the fire and weekends in our backyard surrounded by trees — something we never could have done in the heat of the Southwest.
Sure, the move came as a culture shock, but the people here are incredibly welcoming, and the support we’ve received both at Cary and in the community has made all the difference. Cary Medical Center truly is one of the best places to work, and Northern Maine is one of the best places to live. We love exploring and finding hidden gems throughout the region.
We came for a fresh start. We stayed because it feels like home.

title: New cafe opens inside the Eartha building in Yarmouth
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new cafe has opened in Yarmouth inside the Garmin building on Route 1. Sitting next to Eartha, a Route 1 landmark and the world’s largest rotating and revolving globe, the business is aptly called Eartha Cafe.
The cafe, which opened shortly after Labor Day, is operated by the owners of Clayton’s Cafe, which is also in Yarmouth and has served sandwiches, baked goods and coffee since 1994.
The new cafe also houses the food preparation space for both Eartha Cafe and Clayton’s. Its menu offers breakfast items and sandwiches similar to Clayton’s, as well as protein smoothies and salads, rice bowls and weekly specials.
“With this location in particular, our team can have a lot of creative freedom. They really want to showcase their culinary talents,” said Justin Chadwick, the director of operations for Clayton’s and Eartha Cafe.
The space previously housed Magno Terra Cafe, which was forced to abruptly leave the location this summer when Global Village LLC, the real estate holding company founded by the DeLorme family that owns the property, decided to end the lease, according to Magno Terra’s owner. Global Village LLC could not be reached for comment.
The owners of the building approached Clayton’s about filling the vacant space, Chadwick said.
Eartha Cafe is already seeing a wide range of customers, he said.
“Whether you’re a local stopping in for lunch or a visitor coming to see Eartha, there’s something to be said about a place that you can feel welcomed, get good food, stop in, and just enjoy your surroundings — and that’s really kind of what we’re all about,” Chadwick said.

title: Trump administration wants to sell public lands and shrink the federal estate
text:
Trump administration wants to sell public lands and shrink the federal estate
President Donald Trump's administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate," according to a new plan presented by the Interior Department.
Related video above: Post-midterms, President Trump focuses on DC beautification projects
Agency officials said the sale of federal property would allow the government to focus resources on “nationally significant" lands, which were not defined. They offered no details on what parcels could be sold, nor the scope or location of potential sales.
The proposal drew quick pushback from some lawmakers, including Trump's former Interior secretary, Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke, showing it faces strong headwinds in Congress even before Democrats assume the majority in January.
The Interior Department's five-year strategic plan also calls for land transfers and exchanges to support greater energy production, a centerpiece of the administration's pro-fossil fuel policies. It reflects the Trump administration’s view of most public lands as assets to be used, rather than to be set aside for preservation.
The Interior Department oversees more than 750,000 square miles of land — an area greater than Texas and California combined — along with vast underground mineral reserves. That puts the agency at the center of a contentious, decades-long debate over whether the government controls too much land.
The Associated Press sent emails to Interior officials Wednesday requesting comment and further details.
Most public lands are in Western states. In some, the government controls the vast majority of land, protecting it from potential exploitation but also hindering growth. Nevada, for example, is almost 80% under federal control.
Interior officials said a portion of any land sale proceeds would be returned to the buyer for conservation purposes elsewhere.
Yet it’s uncertain if Interior Secretary Doug Burgum can achieve the administration’s goals without cooperation from Congress.
Federal law puts significant constraints on public land sales, said Mark Squillace, a professor of natural resources law at University of Colorado Law School.
Land cannot be sold if it’s under protected status. And before a sale can occur, it must be deemed appropriate under certain criteria. Those include cases of land that is uneconomic to manage or where a sale would “serve important public objectives, including but not limited to, expansion of communities and economic development.”
Zinke’s office said in a statement that he “remains firmly opposed to the sale or transfer of public lands." It said Zinke would vote against any legislation on the issue if it happens before the lawmaker leaves Congress after this term.
The ranking Democrats on the House and Senate natural resources committee — buoyed by their party's success in last week's midterm elections — pledged to fight any land sales.
Democratic New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich said federal lands “belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in.”
California Democratic Rep. Jared Huffman said Democrats would resist the move.
“Americans love their public lands and sent a clear message last week: the Trump administration’s schemes to auction off our treasured resources and silence opposition must stop now. Democrats in Congress are going to deliver," Huffman said.
Some Western lawmakers last year sought to sell vast tracts of land in Utah and Nevada, saying that could generate revenue and ease growth pressures in booming cities. Among the proposals, Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee suggested selling more than 2 million acres to states or other entities.
Those efforts failed amid bipartisan opposition.
The plan sets out a road map for the Interior Department's priorities and actions between 2026 and 2030. Future administrations would not be bound by it.
The department regulates mining, drilling, grazing, recreation and other activities that many state and local officials want greater control over. Interior includes the Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, Fish and Wildlife Service and Bureau of Indian Affairs.
The agency's strategic plan was last updated four years ago under former Democratic President Joe Biden.
Burgum and Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner last year proposed using “underutilized” federal land for affordable housing. Turner said some 7 million homes were needed. Officials under Biden also sought to use public lands for affordable housing, although on a smaller scale.

title: Rape suspect killed in officer-involved shooting, authorities say
text:
CARTHAGE, New York (WWNY/Gray News) - State police said a rape suspect was killed in an officer-involved shooting Wednesday in New York.
Troopers in New York said the situation started when they pulled over a vehicle to apprehend a man wanted on a bench warrant on a first-degree rape charge.
According to troopers, the man pointed a handgun at a state police investigator and was not complying with verbal commands to disarm before a member of the state police fired their gun, striking the man.
Medical aid was provided at the scene, and the man was taken to Carthage Area Hospital in critical condition, where he later died.
Police did not release the name of the suspect or the law enforcement officer who shot him.
Dispatch report
Multiple police agencies were called to the scene. Jefferson County dispatchers said they received a report of someone suffering a gunshot wound in the vicinity of West Street and South Washington Street.
Dispatchers said the person was reportedly conscious and able to speak.
At the scene
Yellow police tape was seen at either end of West Street between South Washington and Thorpe streets.
Residents described the neighborhood as a calm place to live.
“To see this in my front yard is kind of nerve-racking because I’ve lived here for about a year and a half and it’s been a really safe neighborhood,” Samantha Ortiz, who lives nearby, said.
AG’s Office investigating
Troopers said the state Attorney General’s Office is investigating the shooting, as it does with any officer-involved shooting.

title: Judge allows Trump defamation case against BBC to proceed but tosses 1 claim
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation case against the BBC remains on track, for the moment.
A federal judge in Florida ruled late Tuesday that Trump’s defamation claim could go forward, though he did not rule on the merits. The publicly funded British broadcaster had sought to dismiss the case.
Judge Jeffrey Kuntz did dismiss part of the lawsuit, tossing out a Trump claim that the BBC’s actions violated a Florida law concerning unfair business practices.
Trump filed his lawsuit against the BBC in December. The Republican president accused the BBC of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, “Trump: A Second Chance?” The 33-page lawsuit accused the BBC of broadcasting a “false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump,” calling it “a brazen attempt to interfere in and influence” the 2024 U.S. presidential election.
The BBC apologized about the editing of Trump footage
The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers had spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021, before the storming of the U.S. Capitol, to make it seem that Trump was directly urging violence.
The broadcaster apologized over the editing, and that was something the judge made note of in his ruling Wednesday allowing the case to go forward. The head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But the broadcaster denies Trump’s claims that it defamed him.
In October, a different judge in Florida ordered Trump to sit for a deposition in the case by Dec. 11. Lawyers for the BBC had complained that Trump was delaying his appearance in his own lawsuit. Charles Tobin, an attorney for the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”
The BBC said in a statement after Tuesday’s ruling that it was “surprised by this decision but respect the court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage.”
“We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process,” the broadcaster said.
Trump called Kuntz’s latest ruling a major victory.
“A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth, just handed down by highly respected District Court Judge, Jeffrey T. Kuntz, of the Southern District of Florida,” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.
“We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” Trump wrote Tuesday evening.
Judge said that BBC editing was ‘creating something different’
In his ruling, Kuntz described the editing done in the documentary, splicing together two parts of the speech, as more egregious than mere routine editing.
“Editing is often required,” the judge wrote. “However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement. This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech. BBC also had the entire speech available to them for nearly three years by the time of the documentary.”
The judge also wrote that Trump might have a plausible argument to demonstrate malice — whether or not he can ultimately prove this at trial — given past BBC reporting about him.
“Trump paints a picture that demonstrates the BBC has a record of allowing the publication of false statements in their portrayal of Trump,” the ruling said. “BBC asks the Court to put on blinders and treat the Panorama team as if they were blocked off from the rest of the organization, ignorant of everything else going on at BBC.”
The lawsuit is one of several skirmishes between Trump and the news media during his second term. Through administrative and executive action and sometimes through lawsuits, he has chosen to take a more aggressive approach toward the press and toward coverage he dislikes.

title: 14-year-old volleyball player loses part of her leg after collapsing during practice
text:
CASA GRANDE, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - A 14-year-old volleyball player needed the lower half of her leg amputated after she collapsed during practice because of a heart condition she didn’t know she had. She is now determined to walk and play volleyball again with a prosthetic.
Delilah Mendez, a 14-year-old student-athlete at Casa Grande Union High School, loves playing volleyball. She had big dreams of getting a college scholarship, but two months ago, everything changed when she had a health crisis during practice and collapsed on the court.
“I couldn’t catch my breath, and then, I felt dizzy at the same time,” Delilah said.
Her mother, Rosie Mendez, received a call that her daughter had passed out.
“I thought maybe she was just dehydrated or something small, so I didn’t think anything serious until they told me she didn’t have a pulse,” Mendez said.
‘She is a fighter’
Delilah was rushed to a local hospital then flown to Phoenix Children’s Hospital, where she was placed on a heart and lung machine to keep her alive. Doctors determined she had an underlying heart condition and needed surgery right away.
But complications led to blood clots and circulation issues, and doctors had to amputate the lower half of Delilah’s left leg.
“She is a fighter. She went through a lot. She even surprised me with how strong she was with everything, especially her leg. That was really hard for me to tell her about that,” Mendez said.
Mendez says Delilah is trying to stay positive.
“She’s a very independent person. She always likes to do everything on her own. That’s the part where I think she might be struggling a little bit,” Mendez said.
Goal to return to volleyball
After two months in the hospital, Delilah is home, playing video games and spending time with her younger brothers. She knows the road to recovery will be long, but she is determined to walk and play volleyball again with a prosthetic.
“It’s gonna be pretty hard, but I think I can get through it,” Delilah said. “I want to get through this and learn how to walk again with a prosthetic and do all the things I used to do.”
Mendez believes her daughter will one day return to the court.
“I believe she is strong, and she’s shown us she is strong. I believe she’s gonna be back out there, and I will be very proud of her,” she said.
Delilah is currently walking with crutches and getting stronger every day. She says support from friends, family and teammates has made a difference.
“My volleyball team has sent cards, and they’ve been really supportive. My best friend has been visiting me. She’s on the volleyball team, too,” she said.
Classmates have made signs and T-shirts to raise money for Delilah and her family as they deal with rising medical bills. A GoFundMe has also been set up to help the family.

title: Disabled American Veterans volunteers raise money to help disabled veterans heat their homes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - Volunteers with Disabled American Veterans (DAV) Chapter 10 are raising money to help disabled veterans in Aroostook County pay to heat their homes in the winter.
Disabled veterans in Maine often lack help with heating costs, according to DAV volunteers. Members of the group say many veterans do not qualify for other help because of their disability benefits.
Gap in heating help
Tayleigh Lopez, a disabled veteran and DAV volunteer, said other programs often leave disabled veterans out.
“A lot of organizations out there that try, they say they help, but a lot of veterans that are disabled, they don’t qualify because of their disability income,” Lopez said.
Raffles fund the program
For five months of the year, Lopez, DAV Chapter 10 Commander Andy Drost and other DAV volunteers put together raffles to raise money to fill the gap.
“What money we raise stays here in the county. So we help veterans that can help with what money we got,” Drost said.
Other help for veterans
Each veteran can get help once a year. Volunteers said they have helped veterans in other ways.
“A lot of us volunteer to help some veterans with basic winterization, like covering their windows, fixing door sweeps on their doors,” Lopez said.
“We do what we can with what we got,” Drost said.
This year, the group raised close to $30,000. It has started helping veterans in Aroostook County stay warm.
How to start

title: This country band is breaking the mental health stigma among veterans
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - A group of veterans has turned their shared experiences into a mission, using country music to address mental health stigma in the military community.
“I literally get on the microphone and say it’s okay to go to therapy. And people will turn around from the bar. It’s weird. Right? And it’s not a normal thing. But that’s kind of the idea,” said Jason Davey, the band’s leader and a Marine veteran who served in Iraq in 2003.
Personal tragedy sparked military service
Davey said his decision to enlist began with family tragedy.
“My brother actually signed up before me. He was a few years older, and unfortunately, he passed away. So, we had the full 21-gun salute. And after his funeral, I just kind of got it in my head that I wanted to finish his enlistment. So, I signed up so I could finish what he started,” Davey said.
After serving overseas, Davey married, started a family and settled in New Orleans. Years later, he faced another loss.
“I lost my wife about four years ago now, and I started my therapy journey before she passed away. And it just kind of made me realize how important it is. And there’s just a lot of people in the military that don’t seek that avenue. It’s this kind of social stigma that really exists in the military,” Davey said.
Veterans find connection through shared experience
Davey said therapy helped save him, along with connections with other veterans who understood his experiences.
“I’ve never told my wife anything about being in Iraq, but you will tell a complete stranger sitting at the bar stool next to you everything about it. There’s just certain rapport and trust that you have with somebody else that’s been through the same thing,” Davey said.
Three years ago, Davey partnered with Army veteran Chet Pierson to form Vet Jams.
“Me and Jason Davey, we were sitting right here, talking about mental health. He’s like, I play guitar. I play harmonica. He’s like, I got a great idea. Let’s form a band and start talking about mental health for veterans,” Pierson said.
Mission targets veteran suicide rates
Pierson, who served in Desert Storm and was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 1992, said the band’s mission is to meet veterans where they are.
“The 22 a day, 6000 a year for 20 years. And more veterans kill themselves than we have in combat. You know, that’s a staggering number,” Pierson said.
More than 20 musicians have played with Vet Jams in a rotating lineup of veterans using music as support.
“Togetherness can save lives. Music saves lives. Camaraderie saves lives,” Pierson said.
The band performs for free and hopes to take the stage at Jazz Fest one day. More information is available at vetjams.org.

title: Rape suspect killed in officer-involved shooting, authorities say
text:
CARTHAGE, New York (WWNY/Gray News) - State police said a rape suspect was killed in an officer-involved shooting Wednesday in New York.
Troopers in New York said the situation started when they pulled over a vehicle to apprehend a man wanted on a bench warrant on a first-degree rape charge.
According to troopers, the man pointed a handgun at a state police investigator and was not complying with verbal commands to disarm before a member of the state police fired their gun, striking the man.
Medical aid was provided at the scene, and the man was taken to Carthage Area Hospital in critical condition, where he later died.
Police did not release the name of the suspect or the law enforcement officer who shot him.
Dispatch report
Multiple police agencies were called to the scene. Jefferson County dispatchers said they received a report of someone suffering a gunshot wound in the vicinity of West Street and South Washington Street.
Dispatchers said the person was reportedly conscious and able to speak.
At the scene
Yellow police tape was seen at either end of West Street between South Washington and Thorpe streets.
Residents described the neighborhood as a calm place to live.
“To see this in my front yard is kind of nerve-racking because I’ve lived here for about a year and a half and it’s been a really safe neighborhood,” Samantha Ortiz, who lives nearby, said.
AG’s Office investigating
Troopers said the state Attorney General’s Office is investigating the shooting, as it does with any officer-involved shooting.

title: ‘Malcolm in the Middle’ star, race car driver Frankie Muniz hospitalized after Daytona crash
text:
DAYTONA BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Actor and race car driver Frankie Muniz has been released from a hospital following a practice-lap crash at Daytona International Speedway.
The 40-year-old star of “Malcolm in the Middle” was practicing for a Proud to Honor Veterans Day Classic event, a benefit race set for Wednesday night at Daytona’s road course.
“I am disappointed I won’t be able to take part in Ford’s Proud to Honor event tonight,” Muniz said in a statement. “I was looking forward to honoring the service of our veterans and racing against these other amazing drivers.”
Muniz said he was a “little sore,” but the Mustang he was driving did its job to protect him.
“I want to thank everyone at Ford Racing, Daytona International Speedway and the staff here at the hospital,” Muniz said. “I especially want to thank everyone who has reached out and for all the prayers.”
Muniz and NASCAR driver Austin Cindric were set to represent Team Air Force in an exhibition race that benefits six nonprofits that support military and veteran communities through the Proud to Honor Fund, according to a NASCAR release.
A dozen Ford Racing drivers were split into six teams to race head-to-head in Mustang Dark Horse cars in honor of a branch of the U.S. military.
Musical performances by the Zac Brown Band, Russell Dickerson, Jo Dee Messina, Brittney Spencer, and Warren Zeiders were also part of the event.
Muniz was nominated for an Emmy and two Golden Glove Awards for his work in “Malcolm in the Middle” and was one of the best known child actors of his time. He has also appeared in films such as “Big Fat Liar,” “Deuces Wild,” “Agent Cody Banks” and “Racing Stripes.”
According to his website, Muniz took a hiatus from the entertainment world in 2006 to pursue professional racecar driving.
He began competing in the Formula BMW USA Championship and later went on to race in the Champ Car Atlantic Championship from 2007-09. Muniz was fourth in the 2009 championship standings with two races to go before a season-ending injury resulted in multiple surgeries, the website said.
In 2024, Muniz ran 38 races each on the NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts and trucks series.
He’s participated in 117 trucks series races over the last three years, with one top-10 finish at Daytona in 2025.

title: ‘I have a problem’: Pastor admits to sexually assaulting child, sentenced to life in prison
text:
PONCE DE LEON, Fla. (WJHG/Gray News) - A Florida pastor has been sentenced to life in prison for sexually battering a teenage boy who was under his custodial authority.
State Attorney Larry Basford announced that Circuit Judge Russell Roberts sentenced Randon Lee Carroll, 41, on Tuesday.
Prosecutors said the reported abuse happened earlier this year.
Carroll had been scheduled to stand trial in October but entered an open plea to sexual battery of a victim over 12 but under 18 while under his custodial authority. He also pleaded to sexual performance by a child for videotaping some of the acts, prosecutors said.
An open plea leaves the sentence to the judge.
According to the State Attorney’s Office, Holmes County Chief Prosecutor Jake Cook had not offered Carroll a plea deal other than life in prison.
Prosecutors said Carroll confessed to the sexual acts, saying, “I have a problem. I shouldn’t have done it.”
The details the defendant gave during his interview matched the details given by the victim.
During Tuesday’s sentencing hearing, Cook presented the state’s case, cross-examined defense witnesses and asked Roberts to impose the maximum sentence.
“I think this is the worst possible act that can be committed against a child. Your honor and the state request that he die in prison,” Cook told the judge.
In a written impact statement, the victim’s mother described the family’s strong religious beliefs and questioned how a pastor could deliver sermons while sexually battering a child.
“It takes a wicked person to do that,” she wrote. “There’s no way this is of God. This is pure evil.”
Cook said he hoped the sentence would provide justice for the victim and his family.
Basford thanked the Holmes County Sheriff’s Office for investigating the case.

Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including a doctor and a child, Health Ministry says
text:
Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including a doctor and a child, Health Ministry says
An Israeli airstrike hit one of the main hospitals still operating in the Gaza Strip on Thursday, killing six people, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy, Gaza’s Health Ministry said.
Related video above: Israeli President Isaac Herzog officially hands Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form the next government
The Israeli military said the strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants, without providing evidence. The commander it identified was not among the dead.
The strike hit the hospital's surgical wing, the ministry and witnesses said. Footage showed several wards and operating rooms heavily damaged or destroyed, with debris scattered across hospital beds and equipment and rebar dangling from holes in the ceiling. At least 28 people were wounded.
Among the dead were Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira, a general surgeon, and at least two patients, one of them the 13-year-old, according to the ministry.
Gaza's healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by a yearslong war. The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals across the territory, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters. Israel has also destroyed medical equipment and supplies and killed or detained hundreds of healthcare workers.
Work is halted in several areas of the hospital after the strike
British surgeon Goher Rahbour, who is volunteering at Nasser Hospital, said that the strike occurred just after midnight and shook the whole building.
“It was extremely smoky,” said Rahbour, who was on the fourth floor of the surgical department at the time. The recovery area on the same floor was reduced to rubble, he said.
He said he had been operating alongside Abu Shaira just hours before the strike. “Lovely guy, happy and smiling,” Rahbour said.
Ahmed al-Farra, a doctor and the general director of the hospital, said no warning came before the attack. He said surgeries had been suspended, as had work in the radiology department and the laboratory, because of damage to the building where medical personnel were already struggling to provide care due to supply shortages and “miserable” conditions.
He said other nearby medical facilities were not equipped to do the type of “specialized surgeries” that Nasser Hospital had been providing, leaving patients in need of them to “face an unknown fate.”
He said an attack on a hospital should be met with a forceful response from the international community. “Imagine if this event happened in another country in the world. Would the world fall silent about it? No, by God, no.”
“No one’s safe here,” he added, switching from Arabic to English.
Israel has targeted Nasser before
A report from the United Nations, World Bank and European Union said in April that more than 1,800 medical facilities in Gaza have been partially or completely destroyed since the conflict began.
Israeli forces have previously attacked Nasser Hospital. In 2025, the military killed 22 people when it struck a gathering point for local reporters at the complex. Among the dead were five journalists, including Mariam Dagga, who worked for The Associated Press.
In armed conflict, hospitals and their staff are protected under international humanitarian law. A hospital can lose its protected status, however, if it is used for military purposes.
Hamas security men have been seen in hospitals during the war, controlling access to certain areas. In a statement on Thursday, the military said Hamas had “established a presence within the hospital complex” and that the commander had turned it “into a headquarters.”
The war in Gaza started on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage. Since then, Israel’s retaliatory offensive has killed more than 74,600 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records, and its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.
Israel has continued to strike Gaza despite a U.S.-backed ceasefire and controls at least 60% of the enclave. Since the truce went into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes and gunfire have killed 1,622 people, health authorities say. Five Israeli soldiers have also been killed during that period.

title: Richard Posner, prolific legal scholar and outspoken appeals court judge, dies at 87
text:
Richard Posner, a prodigious legal scholar and outspoken former federal appeals court judge who pioneered the use of economic theory to resolve legal questions, has died. He was 87.
Posner’s opinions have been cited extensively in textbooks that have educated generations of lawyers.
The University of Chicago Law School, where he served as a senior lecturer and one of his sons, Eric Posner, is a professor, said Posner died Tuesday.
Over a nearly 40-year career on the Chicago-based 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, Posner developed a reputation as an acerbic and witty writer and tough questioner.
In a 2014 opinion striking down same-sex marriage bans in Wisconsin and Indiana, he blasted the states’ appeals to tradition, noting historically “bad traditions” such as “cannibalism, foot-binding, and suttee.” He also took aim at their argument that opposite-sex couples need inducements to marry for the sake of their children.
“Heterosexuals get drunk and pregnant, producing unwanted children; their reward is to be allowed to marry. Homosexual couples do not produce unwanted children; their reward is to be denied the right to marry,” he wrote. “Go figure.”
Posner was appointed to the court in 1981 by Republican President Ronald Reagan, but his legal opinions ran from conservative to liberal, and Posner described his approach to judging as pragmatic. Posner was a leading figure in the use of economic theory to analyze legal rules and institutions. His 1973 textbook, Economic Analysis of Law, was foundational and remains in print today.
As a judge, he wrote thousands of legal opinions, including in a seminal 2017 ruling that found the 1964 Civil Rights Act also barred discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender workers.
“I don’t see why firing a lesbian because she is in the subset of women who are lesbian should be thought any less a form of sex discrimination than firing a woman because she’s a woman,” Posner wrote.
Outside the court, he authored hundreds of academic articles and dozens of books, and did not withhold his opinions about American institutions. In 2016, he called the Supreme Court “highly politicized,” saying that “probably only” a couple of the justices were qualified, and even they were “not great.”
As a legal scholar, Posner was uniquely “prolific, influential, and endlessly curious,” University of Chicago Law School Dean Adam Chilton said.
“He was a giant whose influence on our legal system, the field of law and economics, and on our law school cannot be overstated,” Chilton said in a statement.

title: Presque Isle fire chief considering safety changes after blaze rekindles and destroys building
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Presque Isle fire officials may change how soon they allow people back inside once a fire is out.
An Oct. 31 blaze destroyed 572 Main St., which housed a business space on the ground floor and several apartments. No tenants were injured.
Firefighters cleared the scene and residents returned to their homes, but a second wave of fire erupted and destroyed the building. Amid questions as to why people were allowed back inside the first time, the Presque Isle Fire Department is considering procedural changes to keep residents away longer in case a fire restarts.
Michelle Gattuso lived in the third-floor apartment and lost everything, including her two cats.
“I believe the fire department should have done something different,” Gattuso said. “I believe that they should never have let anybody go back in that building for at least 24 hours. That’s what I would like to establish as a new protocol.”
The first fire started a little after 2 a.m., she said. There was no smoke in her apartment, but crews evacuated everyone and had them move their vehicles out of the parking lot. A firefighter told residents that it was safe to go back inside, she said.
About two hours later, she heard banging on her door and her apartment was full of smoke, she said. Everyone was evacuated again as the fire increased and ultimately took down the building, which she said had a history of safety problems.
“They didn’t warn us to be prepared in case it rekindled,” she said. “When you hear it from the firefighters, you believe you’re safe.”
The Maine fire marshal’s office determined a smoldering ash bucket in an attached shed caused the fire. Investigators found the original fire was still burning, undetected, through “multiple layers of wall and roof materials,” which eventually burst into flames, Maine Department of Public Safety spokesperson Aaron Turcotte said Nov. 2.
Presque Isle firefighters were confident the first fire was completely out, Chief Darrell White said.
“We checked all the parts with thermal imaging cameras twice and felt pretty confident we got the fire out, and we allowed people back into the building,” he said. “The reason we let them back in [was] the fire was on the exterior part of the main building and we were confident that we had extinguished it all and there was no extension.”
The attached lean-to which stored firewood and ashes was attached to the outside wall of the main building, as was the chimney, he said. Local and state investigators believe that sparks or an ember flew from the original fire, got in behind the chimney and started burning, White said.
The department is rehashing its procedures.
“We definitely would change the way we do things and keep people out for a longer time,” he said. “We would recommend they be allowed back in, but remain on a fire watch and not go to sleep.”
The building is a total loss, the fire department reported.
Developer Chad Graham bought the property from Eugene Knight in 2021. City officials found periodic code violations, according to records obtained by the Bangor Daily News.
Code enforcement officials notified Knight in 2012 about mold, a broken bathroom exhaust fan, a refrigerator leaking water and lifting carpet behind a refrigerator. A 2021 letter told Knight to replace steps and handrails, add a thermostat cover, replace a broken window, install window screens, replace front door framing and ceiling tiles and address mold.
A 2023 letter to Graham noted such things as holes in a wall and kitchen flooring and a broken windowpane, and told Graham to add ground fault circuit interrupters, carbon monoxide and smoke detectors, and to update fire extinguishers. The deficiencies were resolved at that time, according to Graham and code enforcement.
The fire’s cause wasn’t related to code violations, Graham said. The building had nine apartments and one commercial space.
“We were able to place a few of the tenants and we had a couple of other landlords who were accommodating with a handful more,” he said.
He plans to rebuild in the spring after demolition and site cleanup.
Gattuso is grateful for her employers at Pat’s Pizza, who offered her immediate support and a place to live, she said.
“I have a job that I love. I’m in a town that I love. I’m OK,” Gattuso said.
But she worries for people who might experience a similar situation. She’d like to start a foundation to help people and pets displaced by fires.
She hopes the fire department changes its procedures and will keep people out of a building for at least 24 hours to make certain flames don’t restart.
“That’s something I want to change out of all of this,” she said. “If good comes from this, then that will be a success story.”

title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Senate seat in Mississippi
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since 1881.
The race was called more than a week after the midterm elections, after local election officials processed thousands of absentee and provisional ballots.
The Associated Press called the race Wednesday. With 99% of ballots counted, Colom led by fewer than 5,000 votes.
“There were times when I was tired and I felt like I couldn’t keep going, but I kept the faith,” Colom said to supporters at his victory party at Tougaloo College in Jackson, Mississippi, Wednesday night.
Colom will also be the first Democrat to represent Mississippi in the Senate in nearly 40 years. John C. Stennis, a segregationist, retired in 1989.
His win adds to the Democratic majority in the Senate, as well, which now stands at 55-44 with eight seats flipped. The Senate race in Alaska remains uncalled.
“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters,” said Colom.
Sen. Hyde-Smith, an ally of President Donald Trump, was running for her second full term. She was initially appointed to fill a vacancy and then won a special election in 2018.
Hyde-Smith released a video Wednesday night conceding the race.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well, as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state,” Hyde-Smith said.
Only 14 Black senators have ever been elected or appointed in the U.S.
When the 120th Congress is sworn in Jan. 3, seven Black senators will be serving.

title: From tagging to bite archives: How researchers track sharks on Florida's Gulf Coast
text:
From tagging to bite archives: How researchers track sharks on Florida's Gulf Coast
Researchers with Friends of Rookery Bay are tagging and tracking sharks on Florida's Gulf Coast to better understand their behavior and movements.
Their first catch was a bull shark. "That’s the umbilical scar right there. So this is the young of the year. It’s healed up, but it’s not completely missing. This is a male," researchers said while examining the shark.
The team later caught a lemon shark, which underwent a more advanced tagging process. Researchers performed "shark surgery," placing an acoustic transmitter inside the shark to track its movements more precisely.
"These are the acoustic tags. I'll make an incision in the belly of the shark, just wide enough to stick this tag in fully," researchers explained.
The acoustic tags allow scientists to monitor sharks as they swim near receivers placed throughout the bays. "If this tagged shark swims within range of those receivers and the receivers hear the right signal coming off of it, it’ll record the time of day and what tag you heard," researchers said.
While researchers track a lot, they don't monitor shark attacks.
Leah Lendel, an 11-year-old shark attack survivor, shared her experience with sister station WBBH from June of last year when a shark nearly ripped off her hand off the coast of Boca Grande.
"I feel something like bite on my hand. I start screaming, my mom starts screaming, and then I just swung my hand out, and then it’s all in blood," Lendel said.
After making a full recovery, Lendel still wonders why the shark attacked. "I’m like, am I even going to have a hand anymore? Are they going to amputate it?" she said.
Gavin Naylor, director of the Florida Program for Shark Research at the University of Florida, manages the shark attack files, an archive of shark bite incidents. "It’s an archive of all of the shark bites that have been recorded that we know about, that have been in the news or that people contact us about. We talk to the victims and to witnesses, and we find out as much as we can," Naylor said.
The shark attack files, which began 60 years ago with the Navy, now contain about 7,000 incidents. "We can start to see trends that we wouldn’t be able to before," Naylor said.
Despite the research, shark attacks remain rare, and local governments do not track them. "In general, the counties, the state government, and the federal government don’t investigate it. It does have an economic impact, but only from time to time. But in terms of injuries to people, it’s a very minor problem," Naylor said.
The research aims to better understand shark behavior. "We are curiosity-driven. We want to understand what makes these animals tick. And one of the things that they do is they’re occasionally implicated in biting people," Naylor said.
As for Lendel, her experience has inspired her to study sharks. "I want to be a marine biologist and, like, go out with people and scuba dive with sharks," she said.
Her goal is to find answers to the questions she and many others have about shark behavior. "Then you can see why they bite and how to prevent it," Lendel said.
