title: How everyday Americans reclaimed their communities from Big Tech
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Matthew McDonald is a novelist, playwright, and screenwriter whose work explores working-class life, community, and economic change. He lives in Down East Maine.
For years, Americans have been told that the digital future is inevitable and that local communities must simply adapt to its demands. Increasingly, those demands have arrived in the form of massive data centers: sprawling industrial facilities that consume enormous amounts of electricity and water while reshaping rural landscapes and residential communities.
Supporters call them engines of innovation. Critics see something different. To many residents, they represent a new model of development in which the priorities of billion-dollar technology companies outweigh the concerns of the people who actually live nearby.
This election cycle, voters pushed back.
What were expected to be contests over familiar political issues became, in many places, debates about local control and community consent. Across the country, residents challenged proposed data centers through ballot initiatives, zoning measures, moratoriums, and local elections. The details varied from place to place, but the message was remarkably consistent: communities want a greater voice in decisions that will shape their future.
From New England towns to Midwestern townships and rapidly growing communities in the South, voters questioned whether the economic benefits promised by developers justified the costs. Residents raised concerns about electricity consumption, water usage, environmental impacts, noise, traffic, and the long-term transformation of agricultural or residential land into industrial infrastructure.
Here in Maine, voters in communities such as Wells have shown that residents are no longer willing to be spectators while decisions that could reshape their towns are made on their behalf. In Ohio, local voters pursued charter amendments and zoning restrictions aimed at limiting large-scale development. Similar debates unfolded elsewhere as residents sought a stronger role in determining what kinds of projects belong in their neighborhoods.
At the heart of these disputes is a simple question: Who gets to decide the future of a community?
Technology companies argue that data centers are essential to the growth of cloud computing and artificial intelligence. That may be true. But many residents are asking why their communities should bear the costs without meaningful local input. They are questioning whether higher demands on infrastructure, natural resources, and public services are justified when many modern facilities create relatively few permanent jobs after construction is complete.
These concerns are not anti-technology. They are pro-community.
The debate is not about whether technological progress should occur. It is about whether progress should be imposed on communities or developed with their consent. Residents are increasingly rejecting the idea that decisions affecting their quality of life should be made primarily in corporate boardrooms or negotiated behind closed doors.
For decades, elected officials in both parties have welcomed large-scale development projects with the promise of economic growth, often accompanied by tax incentives and public subsidies. Voters are now asking tougher questions about what communities receive in return and who ultimately benefits.
The growing resistance to data-center development is a reminder that local democracy still matters. When citizens organize, attend meetings, gather signatures, and cast ballots, they can shape the future of their communities. Whatever one’s position on data centers, that principle is worth celebrating.
This election cycle demonstrated that many Americans want a greater say in the decisions affecting their towns, neighborhoods, and natural resources. In the end, the message was straightforward: communities are not just sites for development. They are places where people live, work, raise families, and build their futures. And increasingly, they expect to have a voice in what happens next.

title: Rapper Yella Beezy convicted of hiring gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 on busy Dallas interstate
text:
Rapper Yella Beezy convicted of hiring gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 on busy Dallas interstate
Rapper Yella Beezy was found guilty on Wednesday of hiring the gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 in a brazen daylight attack on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020.
Yella Beezy, 35, whose real name is Markies Conway, was unanimously convicted of capital murder by a Dallas County jury in the death of MO3, whose real name was Melvin Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
In September, a jury found Kewon White guilty of capital murder for fatally shooting Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Related video above: Prosecutor Tommy Adams says Yella Beezy trial 'was a lot of sleepless nights'
Prosecutors said the killing was the result of a yearslong escalating feud between Conway and Noble. Both men lived in Dallas.
“We don’t know what turned it for the jurors. … We appreciate the verdict,” lead prosecutor Tommy Adams told reporters. “We think they got it right today.”
“It’s been one of the most challenging cases over the last six years,” he added.
Prosecutors said Conway paid White $40,000 for the shooting.
Noble, 28, was driving on Interstate 35 in south Dallas around noon on Nov. 11, 2020, when White pulled alongside him, authorities said. White stepped out of his vehicle holding a gun. Noble got out of his own vehicle and began running on the freeway as White shot at him, authorities said.
Prosecutor Tommy Adams said White wore a mask and fired over 40 rounds from an AK-47-style pistol while chasing Noble.
White shot Noble and a bystander who was inside a car, police said. The bystander survived, but Noble died at a hospital.
During closing arguments, prosecutors showed jurors a video clip of Conway talking about revenge in an interview, saying he would “get his lick back.” Prosecutor Krystal Biggins drew a comparison between Noble’s killing and a roadway shooting that injured Conway in 2018.
In October 2018, Conway survived being shot while driving on a tollway in the Dallas suburb of Lewisville when someone pulled up next to him and opened fire, hitting him three times.
“This was for the world to see,” Biggins said. “Over a rap beef, we are here for capital murder.”
The defense argued that prosecutors did not prove their case. “This is capital murder, and the state has brought you a lot of speculation,” defense attorney John Gussio said.
Noble had more than 800,000 Instagram followers and was best known for a 2019 remix of “Errybody” with Baton Rouge, Louisiana, rapper Boosie Badazz.
Conway is best known for his 2017 single, “That’s On Me,” and the 2019 song “Bacc At It Again” with Quavo and Gucci Mane.

title: This Maine cranberry entrepreneur brought albino berries from wild bogs to home gardens
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
John Harker has always liked fruit and always liked farmers.
That brought him to Maine in 1980, and unexpectedly brought him to cranberries — the development and tending of which would shape his career.
The Mt. Vernon man led the introduction of cranberry growing to home gardeners across the country. He was a key player in developing Maine’s small commercial industry and created the first commercially available white cranberry plant from a cutting found on a wild bog on the island of Vinalhaven.
His work opened a new agricultural venture to the state for farmers to diversify, brought a new opportunity for home food production across the country and revealed the diversity of one of Maine’s native fruits — even as the state’s commercial market peaked and then declined.
“It’s been a really neat little crop to grow,” he said. “It’s been fun growing it, and we’ve had a lot of fun with it.”
A 3-by-5-foot plot will yield about three pounds, the equivalent of five fresh bags from the supermarket. It may not save much money to grow cranberries at home, but they provide bragging rights at Thanksgiving and add a little more self-reliance, Harker said.
Cranberries grow in the wild in wet, sandy areas from Canada to Tennessee and into the northern Midwest.
Long before Harker brought them to backyards and commercial bogs here, they were first cultivated in English estate gardens in the 1700s from a sample sent back across the Atlantic Ocean from a trip gathering botanical samples, according to his research.
But the knowledge didn’t transfer back to the Americas, where commercial production was underway by 1816. A Cape Cod farmer had observed that his cranberry plants became more productive when covered with sand from the dunes and turned that into a farming technique. Massachusetts’ “cranberry fever” quickly scaled up into large commercial bogs, selling berries to sailors to help prevent scurvy among other uses.
Commercial growing also spread up to Maine, popular among dairy farmers with low-lying fields. Harker has found remnants of them from Alfred to Calais.
But the state had no commercial production by the start of the 1990s, when cranberries came across his radar as he worked for the state to help develop new crop opportunities.
A grower from Massachusetts wanted help setting up a bog here amid a boom time in the cranberry industry, which blossomed into a “major development” in Maine, Harker said.
Technology to dry cranberries had just hit the market, juice was popular and research about their health benefits helped fuel “exploding” demand.
And Maine was well-suited for it, especially its wild blueberry fields in Hancock and Washington counties, where two of the major processors expanded for a time into juice production.
Commercial bogs mimic wild conditions with peat moss and sandy soil and are built so they can be flooded and drained — once so water will freeze over the plants to protect them in winter, sometimes in the spring for insect control, and during the fall harvest if the berries are being picked for juice. Berries sold fresh are raked dry with mechanical harvesters, similar to wild blueberries.
By around 1998, cranberry production peaked at about 200 acres statewide, a tenth of what Harker and his state coworkers had hoped to achieve.
But other states had gotten in on the boom too, and bog construction was expensive. By the end of the decade, the market collapsed. Some small growers stuck with their bogs, and today most grow for the fresh market.
Twenty-five Maine farms were growing cranberries in 2022, according to the latest agricultural census, eight more than in 2017. But production dropped in the last 15 years from an estimated 20,000 to 30,000 100-pound barrels to around 5,000 in 2024, according to reports to the University of Maine Cooperative Extension. The state’s largest grower stopped producing a decade ago, the university noted.
All along, Harker and his wife, Deb, were experimenting in their own three-quarter-acre bog at home. His training had taught him that to teach someone how to grow something, he should know what he was talking about.
Harker started thinking about home growers, too, and developed potted cranberries for garden transplanting in the late 1990s that he sent out with informational packets.
At the time, only one or two other growers in the country were selling cranberries to gardeners — more like ‘twigs’ than his larger plants that were ready to produce fruit in the first year.
His business took off among adventurous gardeners, and he later took on a friend’s account selling cranberries to Maine-based seed company Fedco.
“Nobody had any information out there at all,” Harker said. “…It was really us who started the whole concept of trying to do it in the home garden.”
He had also crisscrossed the state exploring its many wild bogs in search of varieties that might be better adapted to production in Maine.
He collected more than 500 types to plant and experiment with in his home research bog: pear-shaped, dark purple, bright red, and in one case, off a friend’s tip, a rare white berry from a wild bog on Vinalhaven.
“There’s so much variability out there, so much variety,” he said. “It’s fascinating.”
That white fruit, likely caused by a genetic mutation, seemed to have potential for the home garden market, where white strawberries had recently been introduced. So Harker started working on breeding it and building up stock and, several years ago, the Blushing Moon white berry hit the market.
It’s white with a red tinge, with more meat and slightly less acidity than a typical berry.
A chance use of a potted plant for a Thanksgiving centerpiece led to another line of business supplying cranberry floral arrangements all over the country and a florist market in Boston with decorative cranberries, where the albino choice proved especially popular for arrangements between fall and winter.
The Harkers have been slowly winding down their business, Cranberry Creations, into retirement. While the future of the florist supply venture is sorted out, he’s hoping to find someone to take on the part of the business that supplies Fedco.
Looking back on his career — and his decades in cranberries — Harker would like to think of himself as an “idea guy” and an advocate for farmers who helped them stay in the business, he said, and added that education is critical to do so.

title: Bucksport appoints new deputy fire chief
text:
Bucksport has a new deputy fire chief, completing a full turnover of leadership in its emergency services departments.
The Town Council promoted Capt. Joseph Wardwell to the role Thursday. He will be sworn in and begin at the start of 2027, when longtime deputy chief Michael Denning retires.
“I’m very excited to be able to recommend this promotion,” Town Manager Jacob Gran said before the council’s unanimous approval. “I’m very proud of our leadership staff and proud of the town of Bucksport and the fact that we have very qualified individuals … with the knowledge and expertise, willing to step into these leadership roles.”
Bucksport’s three public safety leaders are its deputy fire chief, deputy police chief and public safety director, who oversees the town’s police and fire departments. All three new leaders were appointed this year.
Public Safety Director David Winchester, previously Bucksport’s deputy police chief, was appointed in September to replace Sean Geagan, who retired in July after 37 years to become coordinator of student behavior and school safety at the local school district, RSU 25. Daniel Harlan was promoted last month to Winchester’s former role.
“We’ve seen a lot of these internal promotions and I think that’s really a testament to our team,” Gran said Thursday, also referencing Public Works Director Matt Pierce, who replaced Jay Lanpher after his May departure.

title: North Country Associates announces transition to new operator, sale of assets to new ownership
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Tide Group and Vantage Point Capital will take over much of North Country’s network of nursing homes and residential care facilities pending state approval
LEWISTON — North Country Associates, one of Maine’s most trusted providers of post-acute, long-term and residential care services, announced the sale of 15 facilities that it owns or co-owns with Sandy River Company. Under an agreement, Tide Group, a multi-state nursing home management company, will become the new operator of the facilities, and Vantage Point Capital, LLC, an investment firm with extensive experience in the healthcare sector and specifically senior living, will become the new owner.
The sale is expected to be completed in early 2027, once final agreements and the required state and federal approvals are in place. Throughout the process, North Country will continue to operate its network of post-acute, long-term care and assisted living facilities. The new operator will take over employment of North Country staff and intends to maintain continuity of facility operations following the transaction.
“North Country is in a healthy, stable position today, and that is exactly why now is the right time to plan for its future,” John Orestis, North Country’s president and owner since its founding in 1982, said. “Our goal from the start of this process was to find new stewards who would carry this company’s legacy forward and preserve its capacity to care for older adults in Maine. We found that in Tide Group.”
Orestis, an attorney and former mayor of Lewiston, is 83 and said the timing of the sale reflects North Country’s healthy position as a company as well as his own desire to spend more time with family.
Under the agreement, North Country and its affiliated facility owners will sell a portfolio of 15 skilled nursing, long-term care, residential care, memory care and independent living facilities located around Maine. Altogether, the locations employ nearly 1,400 staff and have a census of about 1,000 patients and residents.
The transaction includes the following facilities: Borderview Rehab & Living Center (Van Buren); Breakwater Commons (Rockland); Edgewood Rehab & Living Center (Farmington); Fallbrook Commons (Portland); Fallbrook Woods (Portland); Farmington Congregate at Orchard Park (Farmington); Maplecrest Rehab & Living Center (Madison); Market Square Health Care Center (South Paris); Orchard Park Rehab & Living Center (Farmington); Russell Park Rehab & Living Center (Lewiston); Sanfield Rehab & Living Center (Hartland); Schooner Estates Senior Living Community (Auburn); Schooner Memory Care (Auburn); Southridge Rehab & Living Center (Biddeford); and Summer Commons (Sanford).
Six of the facilities operate as MaineSail Care Communities and are either solely owned by John Orestis or jointly owned by North Country and Sandy River Company of Portland.
North Country will retain operation of five facilities, which it will continue to manage for the foreseeable future. These include the Sarah Frye Home, a nonprofit residential facility in Auburn, and three Intermediate Care Facilities for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities (ICF/IID): Harris House in Livermore Falls, Klearview Manor in Fairfield, and Northland Living Center in Jackman. A new memory care assisted living facility currently under construction in Damariscotta – Clippership Landing – is also not part of the sale and will open in 2027 and be managed by North Country.
Tide Group, a growing healthcare organization operating 36 facilities across multiple states, including skilled nursing, long-term care, assisted living and memory care communities, will become the operator of the facilities included in the sale. The Maine communities will join Tide Health New England, where Tide currently operates 15 facilities in Massachusetts, supported by an experienced local leadership team.
“As Tide expands into Maine, its goal is to build upon North Country’s strong foundation and continue its longstanding legacy of care,” Tide Group Founder and CEO Brian Ramo said
The transaction remains subject to regulatory review and approval under Maine’s Certificate of Need law and applicable federal requirements. North Country is informing staff, patients, residents and families of the sale and will host meetings to discuss the process. Until the sale is complete, all facilities will continue to operate as usual. Additional updates on the sale process will be provided to stakeholders.
“Our people are the reason North Country has earned the trust of patients, residents and their families for more than 40 years, and that will not change through this process,” North Country CEO Mary Jane McDade said. “We are grateful to work with Tide Group and Vantage Point and look forward to welcoming them into our locations.”

title: York County Food Hub receives grant that will help centralize resources
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
York County Food Hub in Biddeford receives grant that will help centralize resources
Community leaders came together on Thursday to celebrate a grant that will support the newly established York County Food Hub.
The York County Food Hub recently began operating at a warehouse in Biddeford with the goal of expanding the capacity of local food pantries, promoting food rescue and encouraging regional food sharing.
The grant will help the Food Hub centralize resources and logistics support from the Biddeford location.
"We're building what we call the county's first food security hub," said Alex Gramling, president of the York County Food Hub. "This is not another pantry. This is the infrastructure and scale that our pantries and food programs need to feed York County."
Gramling said the York County Food Hub studied other successful food hubs across the nation, including Wayside Food Programs in Portland.
More information about the York County Food Hub, including how people can help the organization meet its goals, is available online.
Maine House Speaker Ryan Fecteau and Farms for Food Equity founder Penny Jordan were among those who visited the York County Food Hub on Thursday.

title: A recipe for miracles: Hanukkah Mexicana returns to the Chocolate Church Arts Center
text:
There is a power to food. My grandfather, David Levy, aka Poppy, was the son of extremely poor Lithuanian immigrants. He grew up during the Depression, scraping by with whatever his family had. Later, he became a tire salesman in Worcester, Massachusetts. If I ever left food on my plate, it pained him to his soul. He taught me to waste not, want not. That “enough” is already more than enough. He taught me to love life’s simple pleasures: a Saturday afternoon nap, a Werther’s Original butterscotch candy and a good laugh.
Every Hanukkah, I make Poppy’s potato latkes, following his mother’s recipe. Three ingredients. One goal: crispiness.
On Friday, Dec. 4, at 6 p.m., the Chocolate Church Arts Center proudly presents our third annual Hanukkah Mexicana. It’s one of my favorite events, and it’s a little bonkers. Maine has among the smallest Mexican and Jewish populations in the country. People ask, “Why this event? Who is it for?” My answer ranges from “Who isn’t it for?” to “I don’t know … but I love it.”
Here’s what happens. First, there’s food. Thanks to Brunswick’s culinary wizards at Vessel & Vine, we’ll serve a delicious selection of Mexican-Jewish dishes, including potato latkes with molé sauce. We’ll have Mexican-Jewish–inspired cocktails and mocktails, too. (Both are for purchase.) The first hour is devoted to eating, drinking, and roving mariachi and klezmer musicians.
Then the festivities begin. The Casco Bay Tummlers take the stage with some of the finest klezmer music north of Lynn, Massachusetts. Expect singing, dancing and holding hands, just as my ancestors did in the old world. Next comes the extraordinary, award-winning Veronica Robles Mariachis, whose energy and joy are irresistible. The evening culminates when both bands take to the stage in a klezmer-mariachi mash-up I call Kleziachi. There’s poetry in Spanish, English, Hebrew and Ladino, and a grand finale featuring a giant dreidel piñata descending onto the stage. Children of all ages take a swing, Mexican candy rains down and mayhem ensues.
I love the theatrics, the humor, the unbridled joy. But at the heart of it all is the humble latke, a poor man’s potato fritter. Greasy, salty, crispy and delicious. The oil in which it’s fried reminds us of Hanukkah’s miracle: When there wasn’t enough oil, what little remained lasted far longer than anyone imagined.
Hanukkah Mexicana celebrates miracles. That it happens in Maine. That the Chocolate Church Arts Center exists. That we find ourselves together in this world, in this life. Perhaps the greatest miracle is that we have enough. Enough to share, to laugh, to dance, to celebrate with gusto, imagination and fellowship. And if you’re skeptical, come watch the kids dance and swing at the piñata. I bet you’ll come around to the miraculous.
Matthew Glassman is executive and artistic director of the Chocolate Church Arts Center in Bath.

title: Medomak Middle School Closed After Bedbugs Found in Classroom
text:
The Medomak Middle School building will be closed until Thursday, Nov. 12 after bedbugs were found in a classroom, RSU 40 Superintendent Dan Welch announced in an email on Wednesday, Nov. 4.
Two bedbugs were discovered on Nov. 4 by a teacher. No further specimens have been found in a school building or vehicle, Welch said in an interview.
Classes at the middle school went remote Thursday, Nov. 5 through Tuesday, Nov. 10. There was no school on Wednesday, Nov. 11 in observation of Veterans Day followed by no school for Veterans Day on Wednesday, Nov. 11, Welch said.

title: Scott Colom makes history in Mississippi. Two other Black men did the same 150 years before him
text:
When Scott Colom takes the oath of office for the U.S. Senate in January, he will not be the first Black senator from Mississippi to make history. But he will be the first in nearly 150 years and the first chosen by voters rather than state lawmakers.
Colom, a Democrat, was declared the winner Wednesday over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Here are some things to know about the two previous Black senators from Mississippi, Hiram Rhodes Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce.
The first Black member of the U.S. Congress
Revels became the first African American to serve in either chamber of Congress when he took his Senate seat on Feb. 25, 1870.
Born to free parents in North Carolina in September 1827, he traveled throughout the country as an adult doing religious work and educating other Black people, according to biographies on National Park Service and U.S. Senate websites. After the Civil War, he settled in Natchez, Mississippi, where he served as presiding elder of the African Methodist Episcopal Church.
Revels was elected as a Natchez alderman in 1868 and was one of 35 Black men elected to the state legislature the next year. Mississippi’s U.S. Senate seats had been vacant since the state seceded from the Union in January 1861. Revels was selected by his fellow state legislators to fill one of the seats, and a white man was chosen for the other.
“An opportunity of electing a Republican to the United States Senate, to fill an unexpired term occurred, and the colored members, after consulting together on the subject, agreed to give their influence and votes for one of their own race for that position, as it would in their judgement be a weakening blow against color line prejudice,” Revels later recalled, according to a U.S. Senate website.
Revels was seated two days after Mississippi was readmitted to the Union and served just over a year, until March 3, 1871, when his term ended.
The last Black Senator from Mississippi
The Mississippi legislature chose Bruce to be the first African American to serve a full term in the U.S. Senate. He was seated in 1875 and became the first Black man to preside over the Senate in 1879. Born into slavery in 1841 — his father was a white man who owned his mother — Bruce was the only formerly enslaved person to serve in the U.S. Senate, according to the Senate and National Park Service websites.
Bruce was born in Virginia and his father moved his plantation operation to Mississippi, where Bruce began picking cotton at age 8. He escaped to Kansas early in the Civil War, established a school for Black children in Missouri in 1864 and attended Oberlin College in Ohio for two years before a lack of funds caused him to withdraw.
He returned to Mississippi, where he became a wealthy businessman and landowner and held several positions in local government before he was elected to the U.S. Senate by state lawmakers. He served in the Senate from 1875 to 1881.
Unlike Colom, Mississippi’s previous Black senators were Republicans
Reconstruction, the 12-year period after the Civil War from 1865 to 1877, was when the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments were adopted, abolishing slavery, establishing birthright citizenship and prohibiting denial of the right to vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.”
The Republican Party was the party of President Abraham Lincoln during the Civil War. He issued the Emancipation Proclamation on Jan. 1, 1863, declaring all enslaved people in rebellious states “are, and henceforward shall be free.”
A total of 17 Black men served in the U.S. Congress during Reconstruction, 15 in the House of Representatives and Revels and Bruce in the Senate. The Senate wouldn’t have another Black member until 1967, when Sen. Edward Brooke of Massachusetts took office as the first Black person to be popularly elected to that body.

title: Obituary: Mildred “Charlene” (Parker) Mushero
Democratic veterans on call for end to Iran War
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Currently Democratic lawmakers and newly elected veterans on Capitol Hill are calling for an end to the Iran war.
The lawmakers, including some who have not yet been sworn in, said voters sent them to Washington in part to end the war. They say they owe it to voters to follow through.
Rep.-elect Zach Dembo (D-Ky.) sayid the Iran war was a large factor in him winning a previously a district President Donald Trump won by 15 points in 2024.
“When we’re trying to figure out what made the American people make decisions like that, one of the things has to be from the beginning, as a veteran, as a former prosecutor, and as a teacher, I emphasized my public service, and that politics should never be inserted into spaces like the Pentagon,” Dembo said.
The lawmakers say it is time to take action, beginning with impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
“We need to do better by you as citizens. We need to do better by the veterans. We need to do better by our allies. By our service members. And that starts with getting Pete Hegseth out of the Pentagon,” Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pa.) said.
Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said Congress can end the war through a combination of War Powers Acts and cutting off funding from the Trump administration.
“Speaking for me, I’m not interested in continuing to throw a blank check to Pete Hegseth for a war the American people never authorized. For a war that Congress never authorized,” Deluzio said.
He said Congress needs to play a role in ensuring a safe exit for the troops already in the area.
“Nothing would ever stop commanders from protecting their troops, whether it’s in a withdrawal, or the base, or otherwise. And so this requires leadership. Our military officers gotta do their jobs,” Deluzio said.
The new Congress will be sworn in Jan. 3, 2027.

title: Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust to hold 2 events at Salt Bay Farm
text:
Guided hike
Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust invites community members of all ages to celebrate National Take a Hike Day with a free guided walk at Salt Bay Farm Preserve in Damariscotta from 2-4 p.m. Tuesday.
Led by naturalist Sarah Gladu, the two-hour excursion will guide participants through rolling fields and along the scenic shores of Great Salt Bay to visit ancient shell mounds. Highlights of the hike include watching for late migratory birds heading south and exploring the salt marsh for signs of mink and other local wildlife.
One of few intact saltwater farms in the Midcoast and a regional birding destination, this 146-acre preserve encompasses diverse habitats. Features include salt and restored freshwater wetlands with an observation platform, a popular sledding hill, and trails through forest and meadow along Great Salt Bay, Maine’s first Marine Shellfish Preserve. It is also the home of Twin Villages Foodbank Farm.
Due to the number of visiting school groups and other programs that take place at Salt Bay Farm, it is one of a handful of Coastal Rivers preserves where hunting is not permitted.
This program is free of charge, thanks to member support. Registration is required at coastalrivers.org/events.
Thanksgiving races
Twin Villages Foodbank Farm invites community members of all ages to celebrate Thanksgiving morning with the annual Foodbank Farm 5K and 1-Mile Walk or Fun Run. The volunteer-organized event takes place on Thursday, Nov. 26, at Coastal Rivers’ Salt Bay Farm, located at 110 Belvedere Road in Damariscotta.
Both the 5K trail run and 1-mile walk start at 9 a.m. The 5K course features two loops across broad, mown trails along the Great Salt Bay, taking runners through scenic fields with rolling hills. The race is not officially timed, but there will be someone at the finish line to let participants know their finish time. Vegetable prizes will be awarded to the top male and female finishers as well as those with the best costumes.
Participation in the event is completely free, though monetary donations of any amount to Twin Villages Foodbank Farm are encouraged. All proceeds directly support the farm’s mission to grow and donate fresh, nutritious produce to neighbors in need throughout Lincoln County.
Participants can register in advance online at at twinvillagesfarm.org/foodbank-farm-5k/, with online registration closing at noon on Nov. 25.
For additional details about the event, registration or making a donation, contact Sarah Cawthon at [email protected] or call Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust at 207-563-1393.
TVFF’s mission is to grow and distribute healthy food for those who need it most in Lincoln County. TVFF serves pantries in Newcastle, Jefferson, Boothbay, Wiscasset, Waldoboro, Whitefield and New Harbor, and share tables and youth food programs like FARMS at the YMCA.
Growing 50,000 pounds of food each season on 3 acres since 2015, the Foodbank Farm provides fresh food for free, thanks to community support. The Foodbank Farm also operates Community Food Storage Hub, where as much as 30,000 pounds of food is collected each year from grocery stores, farms and local growers, and stored until it can be used by a community partner.
The farm operates in close partnership with Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust, which donates use of its prime farmland at Salt Bay Farm and provides administrative support. Coastal Rivers is a nonprofit, nationally accredited land trust with active programs in land conservation, water quality, trails and public access, and nature education in the Damariscotta-Pemaquid region.

title: Presque Isle community gathers for Veterans Day ceremony
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Community members gathered in Presque Isle on Veterans Day for a ceremony to honor those who served and to teach the next generation why their service matters.
The city joined members of the Civil Air Patrol and Disabled American Veterans to recognize those who have served.
City recognizes veterans
Kim Smith of the City of Presque Isle said the ceremony was held to celebrate veterans and make sure they are remembered.
“We are here today to celebrate our veterans and make sure that they are remembered. They’ve given so much for our country,” Smith said. “I think it’s especially important this year being that it’s America’s 250th anniversary which was fought by citizen soldiers to guarantee our freedom.”
Veteran recalls Desert Storm service
Veteran Tayley Lopez served during Desert Shield and Desert Storm. Lopez said talking about those experiences still brings strong emotions.
“Oh boy. I choke up every time I talk about it. So I’m going to try not to cry. I was in Desert Storm. I was in (Desert) Shield into (Desert) Storm. And I remember going back, not being remembered. We went when we were told we supported freedoms of other people as well. And I did what I had to do to help make sure somebody was not oppressed,” Lopez said.
Civil Air Patrol holds vigil
Members of the Civil Air Patrol also took part in a Veterans Day vigil. Ian Lister of the Civil Air Patrol helped prepare participants for their ceremonial duties.
“We’re here for the Veterans Day vigil to honor those fallen soldiers that fought. So my position here, I’m the primary lead for the vigil, the walking back and forth. I’m the one who’s teaching everybody the gun movements,” Lister said.
Lydia Masters, 15, is among the participants. Masters of the Civil Air Patrol joined the program nearly two years ago. She said it teaches leadership, integrity and volunteer service.
“Just respect the veterans. They’ve done a lot and they’re willing to serve the country and they’re risking their lives for your freedom. So always respect them no matter what. And you never know what they may have gone through during service. So just make sure that you respect them,” Masters said.

title: Obituary: Carol Ducey Heineman
text:
HINGHAM, Mass. – Carol Ducey Heineman, 88, of Hingham, Mass., passed away peacefully on Nov. 6, 2026, surrounded by her loving children and sister.
Born on Dec. 27, 1937, in Brooklyn Heights, N.Y., Carol grew up in Manhasset, N.Y. She graduated from St. Mary’s Catholic High School and went on to earn a degree in Education from Immaculata University in Pennsylvania. Carol began her career as a nursery school teacher before devoting herself to her family.
In 1960, Carol married Frederick Ducey, also of Manhasset. Carol embraced her role as a mother, creating loving homes in Port Washington, N.Y.; Northbrook, Ill.; Westport, Conn.; and Glens Falls, N.Y. Fred passed away in 1991 following a battle with cancer.
In 1992, Carol found love again and married Herbert “Herb” Heineman of Glens Falls, N.Y., who was also widowed. Together, Carol and Herb shared 32 wonderful years of companionship and family life until Herb’s passing in March 2025 at the age of 93.
Carol’s Christian faith was a guiding force throughout her life. She led numerous Bible study groups and remained actively involved in church communities. She found particular joy in volunteering. Most recently, Carol generously dedicated her time and resources to The Root Cellar in Portland. Carol will be remembered for her devotion to her family, her steadfast faith, and her generous spirit.
Carol is survived by her four children: Karen Bailey, Kathleen Calderini, Joanne Avantaggio, and Frederick Ducey, Jr.; three stepdaughters: Kim Cole, Kerry Mendez, and Jane Carlson; thirteen grandchildren; nine great-grandchildren; and her cherished sister, Fran Nottleson.
A private family burial service will lay Carol to rest alongside her beloved husband, Herb, at Riverside Cemetery in Yarmouth.
Please visit http://www.lindquistfuneralhome.com to view Carol’s tribute page and to sign her online guestbook.
In lieu of flowers, memorial contributions may be made in Carol’s honor to The Root Cellar, a faith-based organization serving local residents in need. http://www.therootcellar.org

title: Longtime NBC Sports broadcaster Dan Hicks dies at 64, his family says
text:
(AP) - Sportscaster Dan Hicks, who was the voice of golf, Olympic swimming and Notre Dame football during a 35-year career at NBC Sports, has died, his family and NBC announced Thursday. He was 64.
Hicks died late Wednesday in Connecticut. He died of an acute illness, according to his wife, Hannah Storm. He had been scheduled to call Notre Dame’s game Saturday.
“Our family is heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected passing of Dan,” Storm said in a statement. “He was a devoted husband of over 30 years, loving father to our three daughters, and cherished friend to so many. His loss is immeasurable.
“Dan was truly one of a kind and, quite simply, the person everyone wanted to be around. When he walked into a room, he brought the energy, the laughter and the people together. He was endlessly kind, thoughtful and funny, and he made everyone feel like they mattered.”
Hicks was best known as the lead announcer for golf, as well as swimming and skiing at the Olympics and Notre Dame football. He joined NBC in 1992 following three years at CNN.
“I’m incredibly lucky to stay at one place this long. It takes a lot of things going your way as far as NBC continuing to have the properties that I’ve been a part of through the years,” he said during an Associated Press interview in September. “So lots of variables, lots of things that can happen in your career. But I think I appreciate it more and more the longer it’s been.”
Hicks’ favorite sport was golf
Hicks was on the call for 27 tournament victories by Tiger Woods, including three at the U.S. Open. His most famous was 2008, when Woods, playing with shredded ligaments in his left knee and a double stress fracture in his leg, faced a 12-foot birdie putt on the 18th hole at Torrey Pines to force a playoff.
“He asked what it was like on the 18th,” Roger Maltbie, who was on the ground for NBC at Torrey Pines, said Thursday. “I said Tiger expected to make it. Everyone expected him to make it. He had that invincible aura at the time.”
The putt curled in the right side and Hicks said, “Expect anything different?”
Hicks was a tower announcer from 1995-99 before taking over as the main voice in 2000.
“He was a great quarterback, a point guard. If you listen to his broadcast, to me he was terrific at passing the ball around,” Maltbie said. ”He always had a question. He always got you engaged. That’s a big part of the job.”
Hicks called 27 U.S. Opens and 23 U.S. Women’s Opens. USGA CEO Mike Whan said in a statement that Hicks “was a true friend to the game and to the USGA, but more importantly, a wonderful person whose warmth, generosity, and friendship touched everyone fortunate enough to know him.”
Hicks also called the Ryder Cup, British Open and PGA Tour events, including The Players Championship.
“Dan’s voice filled our living rooms with his steady narration of countless golf broadcasts, calling some of the game’s biggest moments,” the PGA Tour said in a statement. “The sound of his voice is woven into our memories of the game, and the warmth he brought to the broadcast was matched only by the kindness he showed those around him.”
One of NBC’s most versatile Olympic announcers
Hicks worked a total of 16 Olympics — nine Summer, seven Winter — with his first being the 1992 Barcelona Games as a host for the Olympic triplecast.
“Dan Hicks was an extraordinary colleague, friend and person,” NBC Sports’ Rick Cordella, Sam Flood and Molly Solomon said in a statement. “He was an exceptional storyteller and caller of games and events who elevated some of the biggest moments in sports history.”
Hicks called swimming at the Olympics eight times with Rowdy Gaines. The duo chronicled Michael Phelps’ eight gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Games and Katie Ledecky’s 14 medals across four Olympics (2012-24).
“My heart is broken. Danny wasn’t just my partner in the booth for eight Olympics. He was one of my closest friends, someone I trusted with everything, both in and out of that arena. He was the glue that held us all together at all of those Games,” Gaines posted on social media. “He made me laugh like no other person ever has. We shared thousands of races and a friendship that went way beyond the pool deck. I’ll miss his voice, his steadiness, and just having him next to me.”
Hicks was on the call for alpine skiing for the last four Winter Games as well as speed skating in 2002, ’06 and ’10.
Two-time Olympic champion Ted Ligety, who was NBC’s alpine skiing analyst the last two Olympics, said Hicks excelled at calling races but also telling athletes’ stories.
“I was always in awe of his ability to know so much about so many sports so fluidly. And his curiosity, he didn’t come in ever with this idea that he knew what was up — he asked a million questions and was really curious. He was able to instantly bring that into the broadcast,” Ligety said. “It’s fun to sit there next to somebody and watch them at their craft at such a high level. Beyond that, just fun to sit next to him and be with him and after a call, share a beer. Just a genuinely fun and awesome dude. The amazing part is his on-air personality and likeableness was only greater in real life.”
Two stints calling Notre Dame football
This was Hicks’ seventh season calling games for Notre Dame, from which his wife graduated in 1983. He did it from 2013-16 before returning in 2024.
Fighting Irish athletic director and former NBC Sports president Pete Bevacqua said Hicks “was a fixture here on campus and in the broadcast booth as one of the great voices for Notre Dame Football. ... More importantly, a dear friend over the course of the last quarter century.”
Hicks also called regional NFL games on NBC from 1992-97, five French Opens and some NBA coverage from 1992-2000.
Hicks is survived by Storm — his wife of 32 years — and their three daughters Hannah, Ellery and Riley.
___
AP Sports Writer Pat Graham in Denver and AP Golf Writer Doug Ferguson in Jacksonville, Florida, contributed to this report.

title: House approves bill to boost compensation for many veterans, with some floor drama
text:
House approves bill to boost compensation for many veterans, with some floor drama
The House passed a major package of veterans bills Wednesday on Veterans Day — but not without confusion and controversy.
The centerpiece of the package is an effort to boost compensation for an estimated 58,000 veterans who are medically retired because of combat-related injuries. That objective has broad, bipartisan support in Congress, but lawmakers and veterans groups aren't on the same page about how to get there.
The dilemma lawmakers are trying to resolve is this: Under current law, combat-injured retirees with less than 20 years of service give up a portion of their military retirement pay when they also receive Department of Veterans Affairs disability compensation. Lawmakers from both parties are trying to change that so that those retirees get all of their injury compensation and military retirement pay.
Related video above: Trump's Veterans Day event
The change would lead to an average compensation boost of about $1,450 more per month, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
Republicans brought to the floor a bill that would help pay for the income boost for those retirees by changing how the department rates tinnitus or sleep apnea. Those changes would lower disability compensation for some future veterans, though they would not affect current veterans receiving compensation for those conditions. Democrats overwhelmingly opposed that trade-off and denounced the measure as the bill was debated.
“It does not take care of veterans. It takes from them,” Rep. Raul Ruiz, D-Calif., said of the Republican bill.
Republicans had to pull the bill from consideration earlier this year because they didn’t have the votes to pass it. This time, Democratic leaders again encouraged their members to oppose the measure because they said cutting benefits for one group of veterans to fund new benefits for another is not the answer.
The House chamber was packed and noisy as lawmakers talked among themselves following an earlier vote. As is the normal course of business, the House clerk read the title of the veterans bill and then the presiding officer, Rep. Addison McDowell, R-N.C., said the question for the House was on passage of the bill and that those in favor should say aye and those opposed should say no.
“The ayes have it,” McDowell said. “The bill is passed.”
Normally, Democrats would interject and ask for a roll call vote. But none came. And Republicans simply put the onus on Democrats, with Rep. Mike Bost, chairman of the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs, calling Democrats “asleep at the wheel.”
“If nobody calls for the vote, it's passed, which is a good thing," said House Majority Leader Steve Scalise.
“If a few of them want to go voice their objections, they can go and make it clear on the House floor why they are against our veterans on Veterans Day. But I was proud to support it,” Scalise said. “I'm glad it passed.”
Rep. Mark Takano, the ranking Democratic member of the Veterans’ Affairs Committee, said there was no opportunity for the minority to ask for a recorded vote.
“The intention was to sneak this through,” Takano said. “Well, all I can say is, I think it's a shallow, a hollow victory because it will go nowhere in the Senate.”
Cory Geisler, the national commander-in-chief at the Veterans of Foreign Wars, blasted the voice vote in a statement.
“If congressional leaders believed this proposal was worthy of passage, they should have had the courage to let every member’s position be recorded for the country to see,” Geisler said. “Playing political games with veterans’ benefits while avoiding public accountability is cowardly and dishonorable.”
Democrats have their own bill dealing with the issue that is expected to be voted on Thursday. Supporters used a discharge petition to get around Republican leadership and force a vote on the floor. But the Democratic measure does not include offsets.
Takano said that while some Republicans have voiced concerns about the price tag of his bill they also have no problem sending soldiers to war and approving the Pentagon budgets that come with it, or in passing tax breaks that primarily benefit the wealthy.
“Why then do they insist on balancing the budget on the backs of our veterans?” Takano said.
If the Democratic-led bill passes, the Senate could pick the one it favors, or neither, leaving it for a Democratic-controlled Congress to take the issue on next year.

title: Maine data center developers amend permit application
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY, Maine (WMTW) - The Androscoggin Mill was once the largest paper mill in Maine, and soon it will be a data center.
Earlier this week, the developers at the mill amended its permit application.
The notice updating the use of the mill to be for computer equipment, not paper machines and the parking lot that is set to be redeveloped for HVAC. There is also a change to the air license application that will cover the mill’s backup generators in the event of a power outage.
“[Get] people back in the area, the stores will get busier, things will get better. There’ll be reasons for people to stay in the area,” Lucian Richard said.
He’s worked at the mill for 35 years and remembers a time there were 1800 employees. He said it will benefit the community to get people working in the mill again.
Town leaders in Jay said the location of this project makes all the difference.
“It’s a site that had industrial uses still has all of the industrial, infrastructure to support it,” Jay Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere said.
That infrastructure includes the electrical grid. Tony McDonald is the developer of the mill and said he took over a Central Maine Power contract from the former owners.
“It’s been around since 2009, and we’re just using the power that’s provided for in that contract. There’s no new power here. It’s just utilizing that existing contract and that existing equipment,” McDonald said.
This project was the subject of a large debate during the last legislative session. The legislature passed a first-in-the-nation bill that would have put a temporary moratorium on data centers and would have required the state to create a council to ensure Maine is ready for them.
Gov. Janet Mills advocated for that measure to include an exemption for Jay, which was already in the works at the time.
The legislature failed to pass that amendment, leading to the governor to use her veto pen.
“I want to give Janet Mills credit. Janet Mills took time. She grew up here. She knows about this mill. And she took a lot of guts for her to do something by vetoing that bill,” Tom Saviello, former environmental manager at the Androscoggin Mill, said.
During our Commitment 2026 Democratic gubernatorial primary debate, Governor-elect Hannah Pingree said she would have signed that bill. Just this week, she was asked about this project specifically and reiterated the call for a moratorium.
“I certainly look forward to learning more from the town and the developer,” Pingree said. “That being said, I heard pretty loudly and clearly from Maine people that the development of data centers in Maine without very strong regulations in place is not something that people are interested in.”
The developers are holding an open house on Dec. 10 to answer any questions community members might have.

title: Midcoast housing project aims to serve demand for ‘missing middle’
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Developers have partnered with the Lesher Foundation and a philanthropist couple who lives in Knox County to bring 24 new apartment units to 7 Cross St. in Rockport, creating a neighborhood to serve the “missing middle.”
“Our teachers and our nurses make too much money on paper to qualify for these subsidies,” said Mary Jane Young of the Lesher Family Foundation. “And they are people we need here. People should be able to live where they work.”
Developers Caleb Lincoln and Ed Libby of Lake City Holdings have broken ground on the $8 million project comprising two 12-unit multifamily residential buildings to serve that very sector.
The buildings will be located next to the former Anchor Church at the corner with Route 90. The church itself will soon be home to the Children’s House Montessori School. The site is very close to Camden Rockport Elementary School.
The developers expect the project to take about a year for construction and to have new tenants moving in by October 2027.
Lincoln got his start working on downtown revitalization projects in Rockland and learned how funding for housing projects works. When it comes to applying for funding through Maine Housing, having outside private funding can be very helpful in competing for points to become a priority project.
The developers partnered with the Lesher Foundation and Hope residents Ann and Rick Bresnahan previously on an 18-unit family apartment complex at 7 Madelyn Lane in Rockport and the Leshers have also supported Habitat for Humanity’s Compass Point project. In recent years the foundation has helped bring 52 units of housing to Rockport.
Those involved explain that the housing crisis in the area calls for an “all hands on deck” approach.
“It’s not just going to be government subsidies, although that’s an important piece of the puzzle,” Lincoln said.
The Bresnahans also contributed to the Cross Street project.
In addition, this has become a partnership of young local professionals. Lincoln, Libby, Young, Landscape Designer Asa Peats and Lajoie Brothers Construction Project Manager Nick Kava are all Camden Hills graduates.
Young and Lincoln noted in an interview that they love this local community where they are from, and that was part of what made this project exciting.
The construction was approved by the Planning Board in June.
“I work in many communities across Maine, and Rockport stands out as one that ‘walks the walk’ on tackling the housing crisis head on with updated zoning to accommodate more housing in the right places,” Libby said. “Rockport’s staff and volunteer boards have a ‘can do’ attitude which is critical to having these complex projects come to fruition.”
The apartments for the most part will be one- and two-bedroom units. There will be two three-story buildings with pitched roofs and architectural structures designed to match the surrounding area, including exposed timbers to mirror the church building. The colors are likely to be darker blues and greens to blend into the tree line.
The neighborhood may soon be more walkable with plans in place for a multi-use pedestrian/bicycle path along Route 90.
“Children’s House Montessori is thrilled to be a partner in this emerging neighborhood,” said Rachel Nixon of the school. “The development will create additional spots for affordable, high-quality childcare in the midcoast, increase the affordable housing stock for young families who can walk their children to the Montessori School, and offer nature and gardening ‘out the back door.’ This is a win-win-win for our area!”
She said Children’s House will close on the 3 Cross St. property in January 2027, and the renovation is scheduled to begin in early February.
“Lajoie Brothers will be leading the project, which notably will add one more infant/toddler classroom,” Nixon said. “Asa Peats, a Montessori alum, is our landscape designer, working alongside teachers to envision and create a nature-playscape; each classroom has a door directly to the outside. We plan to welcome students and families to the school for the 2027-2028 school year.”
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Harpswell Select Board members oppose expansion
text:
All three members of the Harpswell Select Board recently expressed opposition to expanding the board to five members, addressing recent calls for the change.
David Chipman, the member who brought up the issue at a meeting on Nov. 5, argued that a three-member board promotes transparency. Two members constitute a quorum, which requires a public meeting. On a larger board, he said, two members could discuss town business in private, without a public record.
“It’s worked very well,” Chipman said about the three-member board. “It’s very secure, it’s very open, and I see no reason to change that.”
“I don’t agree with you all that often, David, but you’re right on the money,” Select Board Chair Kevin Johnson said.
The board’s third member, Matt Gilley, echoed Johnson’s agreement and said there may not be enough candidates to fill a five-member board. Gilley ran unopposed in 2025, although Chipman and Johnson had opponents in 2024 and 2026, respectively.
Three residents have called for an expansion from three to five members in recent letters to the editor published in the Harpswell Anchor.
Orr’s Island resident Liz Taylor said five members would make the board more representative and reduce the chance of a deadlock when one member must recuse himself or herself from a vote.
North Harpswell resident Steve M. Musica said he managed towns with three- and five-member boards, and five was “almost a no-brainer.” He suggested one seat for each of three districts, along with two at-large seats.
Great Island resident Kathy Hirst called on the town to place the question before voters in March 2027.
At the Nov. 5 meeting, Chipman said he and the late Select Board member Elinor Multer explored forms of governance on a town committee in the late 1990s. At the time, some residents were interested in an alternative to the three-member Select Board system that Harpswell has used since its incorporation in 1758.
But at Town Meeting in 2000, Harpswell voters rejected two measures that would have expanded the board to five members, each by a margin of more than 2-to-1.
Sam Lemonick is a staff reporter at the Harpswell Anchor. He can be reached at [email protected].

title: Beloved doctor dies after falling down stairs while getting up to use bathroom in his sleep
text:
STANFORD, Ky. (WKYT/Gray News) - A beloved doctor in Kentucky is being remembered after he tragically lost his life following an accident at home.
Dr. James Turpin, 53, an emergency room doctor at Ephraim McDowell Fort Logan Hospital in Stanford, died Wednesday, days after falling on Sunday morning.
According to Dr. Eric Guerrant, a friend and colleague of Turpin, the emergency room doctor fell down a flight of basement stairs after getting up in the middle of the night to use the bathroom.
Turpin suffered serious injuries and was taken to UK Hospital for treatment before succumbing to his injuries on Wednesday.
Turpin also oversaw medical services with emergency medical services in Lincoln and Casey counties.
In 2017, he was named the EMS medical director of the year for the eastern district of Kentucky.
Turpin was said to have an incredible work ethic, working his way up through medical practice from a licensed practical nurse to a registered nurse and then through medical school.
Friends noted Turpin had a way of making hard times much better.
“He made these little bracelets that said, ‘Here to help.’ That was James, and we all wore the bracelets, and that changed the whole demeanor of the practice during a tough time,” Guerrant said. “He had that attitude. He was here to help.”

title: Nvidia shares plunge at open after CEO Jensen Huang resigns
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday, capping a spectacular downfall for a poster boy of the artificial intelligence boom whose exit following reports of extramarital affairs now thrusts the chipmaker into an uncertain future.
After a dizzying series of headlines about Huang’s infidelity and ties to an alleged Chinese spy, his departure sets off a scramble to find a permanent replacement to lead the multitrillion-dollar colossus that grew from obscurity to a perch between Apple and Microsoft at the top of the S&P index.
The resignation sent shares of Nvidia plummeting 14% at the opening bell, before stabilizing. The stock was down about 4% around midday Thursday as investors pondered the lawsuits, investigations, likely corporate jockeying and the resilience of a market driven by the gains of a few tech giants.
“Huang’s departure introduces uncertainty well beyond the company itself,” said Asa Hiken, senior analyst for research firm eMarketer, reflecting fears of wider implications and the possibility of an AI bubble.
The company named Colette Kress, the executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim chief executive. She became CFO in 2013, overseeing the company’s global finance operations. Before that, she worked for three years at Cisco and spent 13 years at Microsoft.
Nvidia had no succession plan to prepare for the possibility of the departure of Huang, who was synonymous with Nvidia for more than 30 years in much the same way Steve Jobs embodied Apple. Nvidia said its board would consider internal and external candidates to replace him.
In a statement Thursday, Kress said that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” and that she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”
The board of directors said Thursday it had also named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones, an entrepreneur and venture investor.
Drumbeat of scandals grew louder
Huang, 63, is one of the world’s wealthiest people, with a personal fortune that Forbes estimates at more than $150 billion. He is the single largest individual shareholder of Nvidia stock.
A drumbeat of scandals around him had grown louder in recent weeks after The New York Times reported Huang’s relationship with a woman the paper said U.S. officials had concluded was a Chinese spy who was recruited to influence California-based Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China.
The discovery set off alarms as high as the White House.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating but remained complimentary of Huang on Thursday, saying he “has done a fantastic job.” Like many top tech CEOs, Huang is close to Trump, who has hosted him at the White House and on Air Force One, and awarded him a National Medal of Science.
Nvidia’s board announced an investigation into the allegations on Sunday, but said it remained confident in Huang’s leadership. Then pressure compounded late Wednesday after reports surfaced of another alleged affair by Huang, this time with an Nvidia employee who reported to him.
The company has said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or its secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.
Nvidia is due to report earnings Tuesday.
Lawmakers still want to question Huang
After Huang’s exit, U.S. lawmakers were still insisting on questioning him about his interactions with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang and the company’s security protocols against espionage.
“Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk,” Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online.
Rep. Brian Mast, chairman of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, said the committee was in contact with Huang’s team as recently as Wednesday night after putting in an initial request for an interview on Nov. 5. Mast said Huang would receive a subpoena to compel his appearance, if necessary.
Alice Huang, the suspected spy at the center of the scandal, is a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair but did not identify her.
The two are not related.
Megaspeed faced allegations last year that it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports.
Singaporean authorities said Thursday that they questioned Alice Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed. They concluded that there wasn’t enough evidence that she had committed a crime but suspected she provided “inaccurate information” to downplay her role at Megaspeed and barred her from returning to the country.
China denies attempting to ensnare executive
China has denied that it attempted to ensnare Jensen Huang. Nvidia has become a leader in making chips that power AI, and Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. In January, he won Trump’s approval to sell Nvidia’s H200 chips to China.
Megaspeed said Thursday that it has cooperated with the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which handles enforcement of national security restrictions on technology exports, and was ready to “cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority.”
The company said it has hired a U.S. law firm to conduct a “comprehensive census” of its computer chips and to verify its export controls.
“Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws,” it said.
Apart from questions over national security, Megaspeed’s finances also have drawn attention. Its total assets soared roughly 90-fold from late 2023 to 2024, to almost $3 billion, according to Singapore corporate records.
Revenue surged to over $294 million in 2024 from none in 2023.
What comes next for Jensen Huang is unclear, though another tech mogul, Elon Musk, said on X that it “would be an honor” to hire him.
At a time of growing alarm about AI’s potential risks, Huang has been a voice of optimism on the technology’s potential. His climb to the top of the corporate world started with an idea born in an unglamorous setting.
Huang and two other engineers gathered in 1993 at a Denny’s in San Jose, California, where they discussed building a computer chip that would make graphics for video games faster and more realistic.
That conversation led to the founding of Nvidia.
___
Associated Press writers Barbara Ortutay in San Francisco, Mae Anderson in New York, Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong and Kevin Freking and Will Weissert in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Cause of Sheridan Fire Released
text:
SHERIDAN, Maine (WAGM) - The cause of the fire in Sheridan that injured one worker and displaced two residents has been released.
According to the Maine State Police, on Monday, November 9 at approximately 3:09 p.m. the Ashland Fire Department responded to a reported structure fire at 27 Despres Street in Sheridan. Upon arrival, firefighters encountered heavy fire conditions in the garage, with flames spreading to the adjoining residence. Three fire trucks were used to shuttle water to the scene and approximately 20 firefighters spent five hours extinguishing the fire, leaving the scene around 8 p.m. Ashland Fire Chief Donald Bouley says the home was on a dead-end street, so no roads were closed during the incident. The fire ultimately resulted in the total loss of both the garage and home. The fire displaced the home’s two occupants. One cat perished in the fire, and one dog escaped from the property. As of that afternoon, the dog had not been located.
The fire has been classified as accidental. Investigators from the Maine Office of State Fire Marshal determined the fire started in the garage while a lawn tractor was being repaired. Officials say during the repair, gasoline spilled onto the garage floor, and a nearby space heater ignited the resulting gasoline vapors. The 77-year-old man who had been working in the garage before the fire was transported to Northern Light A.R. Gould Hospital in Presque Isle for treatment of smoke inhalation. The Ashland Fire Department received mutual aid from the Portage, Mapleton, and Masardis Fire Departments, the Maine Forest Service, and Ashland Ambulance during the response.

title: Family of man electrocuted at Bangor job site files wrongful death lawsuit
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The family of a Brewer man electrocuted at a Bangor job site more than two years ago has filed a wrongful death lawsuit.
In a six-page lawsuit filed on Nov. 6 in Penobscot County Superior Court, the family of 19-year-old Brady Adam Andrews allege that Newport-based Bowman Constructors was negligent and failed to maintain a safe job site.
On June 24, 2024, Andrews was working as an electrician’s helper for CC Electric, which Bowman hired to assist with electrical work at the job site on the seventh and eighth floors of an Exchange Street office building, according to the lawsuit.
As he climbed a ladder to test a wire above a suspended ceiling, Andrews came in contact with an unguarded live wire and was electrocuted, the lawsuit says.
His co-workers called 911, and Andrews died in the ambulance on his way to Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center.
It was his first day on the job.
Brady was a graduate of Brewer High School and United Technologies Center, according to his obituary. He was working to gain experience before going back to school to become an apprentice.
The lawsuit alleges that Bowman didn’t provide Andrews and other workers with necessary personal protective equipment and that a master electrician was not on-site when Andrews was electrocuted.
The lawsuit seeks damages and other costs.
The family is represented by the law firm Berman & Simmons.

title: Paul LePage wins Maine’s 2nd District after ranked-choice count
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine — Former Gov. Paul LePage, a Republican, won Maine’s 2nd Congressional District on Thursday, beating Democrat Matt Dunlap after a ranked-choice tabulation, according to unofficial results from the secretary of state’s office.
LePage, who declared victory last week, beat Dunlap, the state auditor, by nearly 5,500 votes, finishing with 50.8% of votes to 49.2%. Blank and write-in ballots had left LePage just short of a majority on Maine’s first ballot, requiring the ranked-choice count in Augusta.
His win flips the seat U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, a centrist Democrat, has held since 2019, in a district President Donald Trump carried three times. LePage will be the only Republican in Maine’s congressional delegation after a midterm in which Democrats ousted U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, kept the governor’s office and expanded their legislative majorities.
The count was never likely to change the outcome. Dunlap conceded a week ago, when LePage led by about 5,400 first-choice votes. LePage had a majority in the first round of the count, once ballots that ranked no one were set aside.
The only ballots left to move were the 1,243 cast for write-in candidates. Of those, 254 ranked Dunlap as their next choice and 180 ranked LePage. Most of the rest ranked no one else. Even if all of them had gone to Dunlap, he still would have lost by more than 4,200 votes.
LePage still ended up with a slightly bigger margin than he had on election night. The state’s count gave him a bigger first-round lead than the towns had reported, more than making up for Dunlap’s gain from the write-ins. The final margin is outside the threshold for a state-funded recount.
LePage has already started the job. He joined incoming members of Congress for orientation in Washington on Monday, where he pitched himself as a dealmaker after his party’s losses.
The count confirmed a result that was never in doubt, Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a Thursday statement. He said LePage has been meeting with national leaders and “making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people.”

title: Mavericks trounced by Timberwolves
text:
MINNEAPOLIS — LaMelo Ball made six 3-pointers and finished with 22 points and a season-high nine assists, and the Minnesota Timberwolves beat the Dallas Mavericks 133-94 on Thursday night for their most lopsided victory of the season.
Bones Hyland scored 24 points off the bench to lead the Timberwolves, who won their fifth straight game. Ayo Dosunmu added 18 points, Jaden McDaniels scored 16, and Jonathan Kuminga had 14 points and eight rebounds.
Minnesota shot 61% in the first half to build a 15-point advantage, then blew it open by outscoring Dallas 36-17 in the third quarter.
Zaccharie Risacher scored 22 points off the bench for the Mavericks, who had their three-game winning streak snapped. Cooper Flagg, who scored 43 against Indiana in his last game, was held to 12 points and Kyrie Irving had just 10.
The Wolves beat the Mavs for the seventh straight time and did it easily. Their previous largest margin of victory in a game this season was 25 points, and their 44-point lead in the fourth quarter was their biggest at any point this season.
Ball scored 16 points in the first half and Hyland came off the bench to make all three 3-pointers as Minnesota took a 67-52 lead to the break. A 17-4 surge out of the locker room extended it to 84-56 when Ball threw an alley-oop pass to Rudy Gobert.
Naji Marshall scored 13 points for Dallas, which shot 37%.
Up next
Mavericks: Visit Cleveland on Saturday
Timberwolves: Host Chicago on Saturday

title: Maine Man Who Picks Up Litter While Running Finds Wallet Full of Cash
text:
Maine Man Who Picks Up Litter While Running Finds Wallet Full of Cash
We often drive down our local roads and notice the trash, but one young Portland man is doing something to try to make it disappear. His name is Ben, and his Instagram, ploggarun, is all about picking up one piece of trash at a time.
Why? To make the world more beautiful.
Ben practices something called “plogging,” which comes from a swedish word and is a combo of running, jogging and picking up litter. Instead of passing trash on his runs, he now stops to collect it and dispose of it properly.
And believe it or not, this whole thing started with a conversation with his wife.
Ben pitched her an idea: What if he started grabbing the bottles he saw along his running route? He decided to give it a try, and on his first run, he counted 63 bottles. At five cents each, that was $3.15.
The next time, he brought bags and started collecting them.
Since then, Ben has turned those bottle deposits into more than $550, this is all while making his city a little cleaner. He is a South Portland native, and he invests in his community with this.
He's been doing this since January 2025, and what started as a simple idea has turned into something much bigger.
Ben describes the feeling as a mix of frustration and appreciation. He doesn't want to see all the trash, but he also realizes that if nobody else is going to pick it up, he'll do it.
And apparently, a whole lot of people are here for it. Ben now has more than 130,000 followers supporting his “trashfluencing” journey.
But Ben's impact goes far beyond picking up litter.
During one of his plogging runs, he came across a wallet filled with cash. And I'm talking a thick stack of cash sitting inside a zip-up wallet.
Rather than walking away or keeping what he found, Ben immediately turned it over to a nearby police officer.
It's a small moment, but one that says an awful lot about the kind of person he is.
In a world where it's easy to focus on everything going wrong, stories like this are a refreshing reminder that good people are still out there.
Babes, the next time you're driving, walking or plogging around Portland and spot someone in a bright yellow shirt jogging with a bag of collected trash, give Ben a wave or even a thank-you.
He’s cleaning up our community, inspiring others to do a little better, and proving that sometimes the biggest difference starts with simply stopping to pick something up.
