Oklahoma man executed for killing of girlfriend’s husband, with a Texas lethal injection to follow
text:
McALESTER, Okla. (AP) — An Oklahoma man was put to death Thursday for the fatal shooting of his girlfriend’s estranged husband as he arrived to pick up his two young children before Thanksgiving. It was the first in a pair of executions in the U.S. scheduled for Thursday.
James Pavatt, 73, received a lethal injection at the state penitentiary in McAlester. His breathing did not appear labored during the execution, and he was declared unconscious about six minutes before being pronounced dead at 10:12 a.m. CST.
In Texas, John Allen Rubio was set to be put to death Thursday evening. The 46-year-old was convicted of fatally stabbing and beheading three young children in 2003 in Brownsville, a border city with Mexico.
Although the death penalty is getting renewed attention after the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee in September, the U.S. is on track to surpass 40 executions for a second consecutive year — a pace driven by Florida.
Last week, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office, which experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.
On Thursday, former Oklahoma death row inmate Richard Glossip pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of being an accessory in a 1997 murder and awaits sentencing in December. Glossip, who had been on the brink of execution three times, was released on bond in May after spending nearly 30 years in prison. The U.S. Supreme Court had overturned his conviction and he was awaiting a retrial.
Oklahoma advertising executive killed in garage
When Pavatt was asked if he had any last words, he shook his head no. As a chaplain read to him from a Bible, he appeared to be mouthing some words, but they could not be heard.
Pavatt was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder in the 2001 death of Rob Andrew, a 39-year-old advertising executive. Pavatt attended the same church as the Andrew family and had been having an affair with Rob Andrew’s wife, Brenda Andrew. She was convicted at a separate trial and is currently the only woman on death row in Oklahoma.
Weeks before the shooting, Rob Andrew told police someone was trying to kill him after the brake lines on his car were cut. Brenda Andrew told police after her husband was killed that masked intruders shot her in the arm and fatally shot him.
Pavatt and Brenda Andrew went to Mexico with her two children after the shooting and were arrested three months later while reentering the U.S.
At a clemency hearing last month, Pavatt said he was “not guilty of shooting anyone,” and that he’d fallen in love with Brenda Andrew and believed “everything she told me.”
“It was not until my trial that I began to see the extent to which I had been manipulated by Brenda,” Pavatt told the board. “I can see why the jury believed that we were both involved in Rob’s murder.”
Prosecutors have said that Pavatt and Brenda Andrew plotted to kill her husband, and that no matter who fired the shots, both were equally guilty.
No family members of Rob Andrew or Pavatt witnessed the execution, although his daughter and her husband visited him the night before, a prison spokesperson said.
3 young children beheaded in Texas
Rubio and his girlfriend, Angela Camacho, were accused in the killings of 3-year-old Julissa Quesada, 14-month-old John E. Rubio and 2-month-old Mary Jane Rubio in the squalid, windowless apartment they shared in Brownsville, located on Texas’ border with Mexico.
Camacho pleaded guilty and is serving a life sentence.
Rubio’s first capital murder conviction in the killings was overturned by an appeals court, which ruled that statements by Camacho were wrongly allowed as evidence in his trial. Rubio again pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity for his second trial but he was once again convicted and sentenced to death.
Rubio, according to court records, wasn’t the biological father of the two older children but treated them as if they were his own.
At various points, Rubio claimed the children were possessed and that he was the “chosen one” intended to save the world. Defense experts diagnosed Rubio as suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, a determination rejected by prosecution experts.
Defense experts testified his childhood — filled with violence at home, “toxic” parents, drug use and prostitution — damaged him developmentally.
The apartment building where the children were killed was later demolished and the land was turned into a park and a community garden.
Rubio was set to be executed Thursday evening at the state prison in Huntsville.
____
Graczyk reported from Huntsville, Texas.

title: Bangor’s bus system to add transit director, CDL training center
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Changes are coming to Bangor’s bus system, from its storage garage to City Hall.
The Community Connector, which has served Bangor and surrounding communities since the 1970s, recently received more than $9.8 million from the Federal Transit Administration, MaineDOT and the City of Bangor and its stakeholders.
Community Connector administrator Laurie Linscott said the grants are to renovate the bus barn and prepare infrastructure for battery-electric buses.
“The building hasn’t been touched since 1960 when it was built. We needed to update the building,” Linscott explained. “We really can’t buy any [battery-electric buses] until we have the infrastructure to charge them. So that’s how the grant came to be, is just getting ready for battery electric buses.”
The 18-month construction project is expected to begin in late winter or early spring of 2027.
Along with upgrades to the bus barn, it will include a new CDL training center. Linscott said the center addresses a nationwide need.
“We’re very short. We need CDL drivers. We need them to have their P endorsement. And the training center will allow us to continuously train and hopefully have retention,” Linscott said.
The bus system is currently run by the city manager’s office. The Bangor City Council on Monday approved a director of transit position to oversee the Community Connector’s finances and operations.
Bangor City Manager Carollynn Lear said the position is expected to pay $150,000 a year. She said it should not create a large tax burden because the bus system is funded through several sources, including surrounding towns.
“We’ll be looking for someone who has experience and expertise, specifically with transit administration,” Lear said. “They’ll run the bus system, they’ll be responsible for overseeing all of the employees, crafting the budget, applying for grants and federal funding to fund the bus system, to keep the taxpayer impact of the system pretty low, and then sort of creating a strategic vision for the bus system for the future.”
Lear said finding the right person will be a challenge.
“We are really the only public transit system in our area, so it’s not as though we can poach from nearby cities and towns. We’ll have to probably recruit at least from Southern Maine, if not from other states for the role in order to find someone who has transit experience,” Lear said.
Linscott said rides should not be interrupted by the construction, just where buses are stored when they are not on the road.
“We’re going to stay in the building as long as we can. We are looking and preparing to move out in early 2027, probably indefinitely until we can move back in,” Linscott clarified. “We are looking at staying in the old CNG lot right across from Public Works.”

title: The rules of texting and social media keep changing — what older adults should know
text:
(Aging Untold) — If you are more used to phone calls and handwritten notes than texts and group chats, you might feel a bit like you are out of the loop.
There are unwritten rules about what to share, when to reply and who to trust, and the Aging Untold experts are walking you through them.
The rules are hard to find, and they keep changing
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said she recently ran into the new rules herself.
“I got a text from my godson and he shamed me for the length of the text that I sent him,” O’Rourke said. “OK, so there’s rules out there, and I don’t know what they are.”
She pointed to Emily Post and Miss Manners as places to find up-to-date information on the rules.
The rules have never stood still, gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.
“The reality is the rules have always been changing. They’re fluid,” Cradduck said. “They’re different from the 20s to the 30s to the 40s to the 50s.”
Handshakes meant something. Scammers are counting on that.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said older adults need to know what has changed.
“They’re used to that handshake really meaning something,” Rogers said. “And now you have the scams or the fast relationships that are growing because of the new technology.”
Rogers said older adults are looking for connection, which is why they need to be careful.
“They’re looking for that interaction and the trust,” Rogers said.
Some things don’t change, Rogers said, including “consistency, transparency.”
Relationships that once took years to build now often start on social media, Cradduck said.
“The walls are gone,” she said. “So now you’re telling intimate details about your life to a virtual stranger. And that’s not just our kids doing it or our older people. Everyone has fallen into that.”
Check with a buddy before you reply
To guard against fraud, O’Rourke suggested having a person to check in with.
“I want to have people to have a buddy, have somebody that you check in with to say, ‘I’m about to respond to this text, I’m about to jump on this Facebook,’ and check it out with somebody before you jump in,” O’Rourke said.
“We’re all learning together, so just have a comfort level with that,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
Don’t let caution keep you offline
Ambrose said scams should not push older adults away from technology.
“You should, because it’s going to keep you sharper, and it’s going to keep you in relationship with the younger people in your life and with your friends,” Ambrose said. “This is how we communicate today.”
Learning to text well helps people stay in touch with children who are busy working and raising kids, Cradduck said.
“I understand that that may not be the most comfortable way to communicate, and it might not have fit your norm,” she said. “But it is the norm of society.”
Key takeaways
- Meet your family where they are. Adapting to new technology keeps you connected.
- Don’t take changing norms personally. A text may feel short, but the rules are different now.
- Stay cautious online. Don’t let digital speed replace common sense boundaries.

title: Caribou ceremony honors veterans and teaches children
text:
CARIBOU, Maine (WAGM) - Veterans and civilians of all ages stood side by side at the veteran cemetery in Caribou on Veterans Day to honor those who serve.
Veterans there said the ceremony was just as important to them as seeing the children who attended.
Chase Cochran, a Boy Scout, was one of many children at the ceremony. As the ceremony ended, the Boys Scouts ran towards an area where veterans had conducted the 21-rifle salute just moments ago.
“So, when they shot the guns, shells came out, and some of the kids wanted to get some,” Cochran said.
Before his friends ran to get shell casings, they stood in the cold and listened as local veterans were honored.
“The younger ones come out, and they get to see, and they look at it as kind of like a role model for the future,” said Paul Watson, District 1 commander of the VFW.
The ceremony was also about teaching the younger generation about what it takes to be a veteran, said Roger Felix, commander of the VFW in Caribou.
“They took the oath, and they continued to march forward because they knew they weren’t doing it for them. They were doing it for the people back home, and if the fire, that drive, dissipates over years, then what do we have?” Felix said.

title: Meet the Maine cranberry farmers keeping tradition alive with 1930s equipment
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
COLUMBIA, Maine (WABI) - For Christine Alexander, a 1930s cranberry separator is more than a piece of equipment. It is a connection to her family’s past and a way to keep an old farming tradition alive.
“We like doing things the way that they used to be done. My family was in cranberries back in the 30s in Wareham, Massachusetts. I just enjoy doing the history part and keeping things authentic,” said Alexander.
Alexander met her husband, a cranberry farmer, while she was in high school. The couple later came to Maine to develop cranberry bogs for a blueberry company. When a farm became available, they took the opportunity to begin farming for themselves.
At Sugar Hill Cranberry Company, the Alexanders use both dry and water harvesting. For the fresh-fruit crop, workers gather berries with scoops or a mechanical harvester before feeding them into the vintage separator.
The machine blows out leaves and vines, then sends the berries over rocking boards. Good cranberries bounce onto a conveyor belt, where workers sort them by hand before packaging.
This year, Alexander said, the harvest has been especially difficult. Drought and hot weather the previous year affected the vines and reduced yields, she said. Repeated rain and the need to irrigate for frost protection also kept the bogs wet during the dry-harvest window.
“This is the first time in 47 years that we’ve finished our water harvest before we were able to dry harvest,” she said.
Christine said that Cranberries remain a small but important Maine crop, She estimated there are fewer than 10 growers and fewer than 100 acres of cranberry bogs in the state today.
As for the next harvest, Alexander said it is too early to know what the yield will be. The farm plans to prune its vines and watch next year’s buds develop.

A $50 million investment is funding upgrades and improvements at state parks across Maine.
State officials celebrated the investment Thursday at Sebago Lake State Park in Casco, where they cut the ribbon on a new day-use entrance station.
The funding comes from Gov. Janet Mills' Maine Jobs and Recovery Plan, which uses federal money allocated through the American Rescue Plan Act.
Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Commissioner Amanda Beal said the funding has allowed staff to take on multiple projects at parks across the state.
"Being able to access such a sizeable amount of resources really allowed our staff to focus on doing multiple projects in parks across the state," Beal said.

title: Does heating your home with wood cost less than heating oil?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Yes.
Heating with wood generally costs less than heating with oil in Maine, according to Efficiency Maine’s home heating comparison.
The quasi-state agency’s estimates put wood stoves among the least expensive options to operate. Pellet stoves, natural gas furnaces and ductless heat pumps also cost less to run than oil boilers. Heat pumps also can provide air conditioning in summer.
The Maine Department of Energy Resources compares fuels by the cost of usable heat, accounting for typical heating system efficiencies. Its firewood prices include local delivery, but actual costs vary by seller and region.
Maine’s average heating oil price rose about 77% between November 2025 and early November 2026, according to state surveys.
Total heating costs also depend on insulation, stove or furnace efficiency, and how much fuel is used. The comparisons exclude equipment and installation expenses. Wood heating also requires storage, regular cleaning and time spent handling fuel.

title: Aging Untold: The rules of texting and social media keep changing
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, changing norms around texting and social media are blurring boundaries for older adults.
Then, hackers took over one woman’s Facebook to dupe her friends. We share ways to stay connected safely.
Plus, hear from world-renowned dementia expert, Teepa Snow, on bringing peace back to daily care.
Texts, group chats and social media might not be the types of communication that you are most comfortable with.
However, they are not going anywhere if you want to stay connected with loved ones across generations.
There are unwritten rules about what to share, when to reply and who to trust, and the Aging Untold experts are walking you through them.
Teepa Snow is a nationally recognized dementia care educator, occupational therapist and founder of Positive Approach to Care, and she joined Aging Untold to share her philosophy and some tips for families.
Instead of using language that focuses on decline, Snow uses the term “brain change.” The reason is that while people with dementia lose some abilities, they change others, she said.
“People think all the time of brain failure and brain loss, and I talk about brain change because the reality is neuroplasticity exists whether you have dementia or you don’t,” Snow said. “So let’s use what we have and let’s use what they have.”
Snow is sharing tips family members can use when a loved one with dementia refuses to shower, take medication or get dressed.
Then, Snow shares the one thing she wants families to know.
A woman in Arizona said hackers hijacked her Facebook account and scammed her friends out of thousands of dollars.
She said they posed as her and said she needed to sell her father’s possessions to put him in assisted living. She learned about it when her father sent her a text.
Read the full article here to see what happened and how you can protect yourself.
Dennis Bussey was looking for someone to go hiking with, and his efforts have created a community of thousands of people who are not only hiking but also preserving Virginia history.
Bussey founded James River Hikers, which describes itself as “hiking with history.”
One of the hikers’ volunteer projects is cleaning gravestones at Shockoe Hill Cemetery, the final resting place for some of Virginia’s historic figures.

title: Longtime teacher and coach killed in murder-suicide weeks after filing for divorce
text:
BARDSTOWN, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — A husband and wife died in a murder-suicide Tuesday morning in Kentucky.
According to the Nelson County Sheriff’s Office, officers responded to a home following a reported shooting.
Police found a man and a woman dead from gunshot wounds.
The Nelson County Coroner’s Office identified the couple as 54-year-old Brian Harman and 52-year-old Keyata Harman.
A neighbor said Keyata Harman taught at Bardstown Middle School and served as head volleyball coach at Nelson County High School.
“Our hearts are heavy as we mourn the loss of one of our own,” the school posted on social media Tuesday night. “Keyata was a true servant leader whose passion for the sport and dedication to her athletes extended far beyond the court.”
According to court documents, Keyata Harman filed for divorce on Oct. 15, and the couple has been separated since Sept. 1, 2025.
A neighbor said she heard multiple gunshots that night. But she brushed it off as someone deer hunting before seeing police and two coroner vans on the Harman’s lawn.
“We never had any issues with them at all,” neighbor Nancy Ulrich said. “They were the perfect neighbors. They would help you. It’s just a great loss. They are going to be missed.”
Ulrich said Keyata Harman was outgoing and friendly, and Brian Harman was a little more reserved but nice.
Court documents stated the couple had four kids together.

title: Teen who has autism found alive after missing for nearly a week in the Australian woodlands
text:
Teen who has autism found alive after missing for nearly a week in the Australian woodlands
A 17-year-old boy with autism was found alive Thursday after six days lost in eastern Australian woodlands.
The boy, whom police identified only as William, had begun camping with a teenage friend when he disappeared last Friday near Walhalla, a former gold-mining town 115 miles east of Melbourne, police said.
A police helicopter crew found him surrounded by wilderness, lying asleep on a flat rock beside a creek, and he was later reunited with his mother. William was in good spirits and mostly in good health, the police statement said.
Video shot from the rescue helicopter showed he was shirtless and sunburned. He was wearing shorts and boots and was using towels as blankets.
"I'm just over the moon that he's alive," his mother, Elizabeth, told reporters. The AP has decided not to provide her family name to avoid identifying her son.
"And he's never leaving the house again. He's grounded for life. He's not going anywhere ever again," she joked.
William was later taken to a hospital for his health to be monitored, police said.
William's family have said he has Level 2 autism. That requires "substantial support," according to the Australian advocacy group Autism360.
Such a person may have marked deficits in verbal and non-verbal social communication and rely heavily on routines and predictable activities. Disruption can cause significant distress.
The Southern Hemisphere spring weather had been mild for the past week in the alpine region where William was lost, and there had been little rain.
Elizabeth had dropped off her son and his friend last Friday for a weekend of camping. William walked a short distance from the campsite to the drop-off location to collect more camping equipment but never returned to his friend, police said.
After becoming lost, William trekked for days up and down "some very steep terrain," Acting Police Inspector Jason Benbow said.
He spent the last two days where he was found at the creek, trapped by the steepness of his surroundings 1.2 miles from his campsite, Benbow said.
"He woke up to the sound of the helicopter, gave them a thumbs up, and they winched him to safety," Benbow told reporters.
The extensive police search for him involved more than 100 emergency services personnel and volunteers.

title: UMF and Maine DOE bring Maine educators together to support the learning of every student with Inclusive Education Initiative
text:
FARMINGTON — The Maine Dept. of Education Office of Special Services and Inclusive Education and the University of Maine at Farmington recently hosted more than 150 dedicated school leaders and educators, from Millinocket to Sanford, at their annual Inclusive Education Leadership Symposium on the UMF campus.
An inclusive education happens when all students experience belonging and are presumed capable of learning and worthy of a high-quality, challenging and equitable education.
In its fourth year, the symposium brought together a network of Maine school and district leaders to learn, collaborate, solve problems and share experiences and effective practices to support the learning of every student in general education classrooms and the broader school community.
The Maine DOE and UMF initiative is led by Kate MacLeod, associate professor of special education, and Jessica Apgar, assistant professor of special education, to help educational leaders throughout Maine make meaningful connections with national and state experts and other Maine school leaders engaged in the work of inclusive change.
“The Symposium is one of my favorite days of the year,” MacLeod said. “It is a wonderful opportunity to gather a group of school leaders from across the great state of Maine, celebrate their vision, honor their work and support them to build more inclusive schools.”
The symposium featured distinguished speakers including a keynote workshop by Jennifer Greer, Lindsey Hayes, Cat Merkle, members of the Collaboration for Effective Educator Development, Accountability and Reform Center, a national technical assistance center funded by the U.S. Department of Education’s Office of Special Education Programs.
Leadership sessions were also led by MacLeod, Apgar, CEEDAR facilitators and Tracy Whitlock of the office of special services & inclusive education with the Maine Department of Education, as participants worked on action-planning for the future.
Whitlock from Maine DOE says, “School leaders are busy and the Inclusive Education Leadership Symposium provides time and space for them to come together as teams to learn, collaborate and plan for meaningful inclusion for all of their students. It is an energizing and empowering day.”
Participants found the sessions a valuable professional development resource and noted, “I’m leaving the symposium with tools and strategies to continue to move the work forward in our district.”
The Symposium is in conjunction with the Maine Inclusive Education Project a 5-year initiative (2025-30), run by the Maine DOE in partnership with UMF, focused on helping public elementary schools in Maine move away from segregated special education silos and increase the time students with disabilities spend in general education classrooms.
The goal of inclusive education is to prepare all students to learn and grow together in ways that lead to meaningful and inclusive post-secondary lives.
“What a dream to do this work,” Apgar said. “I am grateful for our collaboration with the Maine DOE and CEEDAR partners who make the magic happen and care deeply about supporting leaders and educators to create schools where all students learn and belong.”
This multi-year project is currently partnering with three Maine public schools that are working to develop inclusive school culture, systems, schedules, structures and practices. These model schools include Leeds Central School, Downeast School and Turner Elementary School that will serve as learning sites for the State.
The model schools are open to scheduled leadership and educator visits, host UMF student teachers, share best practices with the field at conferences and events, and participate in ongoing research to inspire equitable, statewide systems change.
The Maine Inclusive Education Project is supported through federal grant funding and a partnership with the University of Maine.

title: City of Portland racing to hire staff to work at winter warming shelter
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
City of Portland racing to hire staff to work at winter warming shelter
The city is hoping to open the shelter on Dec. 15, but that depends on being able to hire and train enough staff
City of Portland racing to hire staff to work at winter warming shelter
The city is hoping to open the shelter on Dec. 15, but that depends on being able to hire and train enough staff
Last week, the Portland City Council voted to use $735,000 in opioid settlement funds to help operate a low-barrier winter warming shelter at 166 Riverside Industrial Parkway this winter. That is where the city's shelter was located last winter. The funding allocation was reduced from an initial proposal of $900,000.
The shelter will also get funding from MaineHousing, but the opening of the shelter is dependent upon hiring and training enough staff.
An open hiring event is scheduled from 9 a.m. until 3 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at Portland City Hall. The city says it is looking to hire 21 people to work at the shelter. Positions include:
- Senior Human Services Counselors
- Human Services Specialists/Shuttle Drivers
- Shelter Attendants
- Custodians
City officials say they are hoping to open the shelter on Dec. 15.
During the hiring event, people can meet hiring staff, apply on-site, learn about employee benefits, and explore career opportunities with the City of Portland. Retention bonuses of up to $1,500 are available for warming shelter staff.
Applicants are encouraged to bring a resume if available, though staff will be able to help anyone who wants to apply on the spot.
Visit portlandmaine.gov/Jobs to read complete job descriptions.
The shelter will include free shuttle service to and from the shelter each night, and guests will receive an evening meal.
Shelter plans have changed in recent weeks and a vote on the funding was postponed by a week. The city said Seeds of Hope is no longer willing to operate a shelter at Elena's Way because of community resistance and regulatory challenges. Preble Street also declined to operate a shelter at that location, according to a city update last month.
Shelter Criteria
In May, the city added new criteria that will trigger the opening of the emergency warming shelter on Riverside Drive.
The shelter did not open during a blizzard warning in early 2026. Ask 8 Investigates looked into the criteria after many people reached out and voiced concerns about the fact that the shelter did not open. In fact, Portland did officially meet blizzard criteria during the storm.
The shelter did open the next night, when temperatures dropped. A city spokesperson told 8 Investigates at the time that they would continue to look at changes to when they open the shelter.
At the time, the criteria stated that the shelter would only open when the daily low temperature drops to 15 degrees or below, or if more than 10 inches of snow accumulates.
Now, the city has updated the criteria, showing that it will open the shelter if the National Weather Service issues a blizzard warning or ice storm warning.
The stated procedures also now say that if the forecast changes with less than 48 hours' notice to more severe conditions that meet the threshold, "the Emergency Management Coordinator will immediately convene the HHS Director, Social Services Director, and Assistant City Manager to consider warming shelter activation. The decision to activate the warming shelter with less than 48 hours' notice will be determined by the availability of staff needed to safely operate the facility."

title: Holden first responders deliver food, gift cards as part of 25 Days of Kindness
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) -A knock at the door brought food, gift cards and a reminder of community support to residents at Holden Square Apartments.
Members of the Holden Police Department, Fire Department and Highway Department joined Husson University criminal justice students to deliver boxes of food and $50 Hannaford gift cards to about 20 residents. The effort was part of the police department’s 25 Days of Kindness initiative.
Chief Eddie Benjamin said many of the residents are older adults living on fixed incomes. He hopes the gifts will help them through the winter.
A lesson in community service
For the Husson students, the delivery was a chance to see community service in action. Benjamin hopes they’ll carry that experience into their future careers.
“They’ll be the leaders of tomorrow so its good to show them how it’s done and they can maybe like replicate this initiative wherever they go,” Benjamin said.
Husson senior Sophia Lamy said the Holden officers set an example of how police can connect with their community beyond difficult moments.
“We should be caring about the community not when they’re at their worst but even when they’re at their best and celebrating them through their milestones in life,” Lamy said.
A legacy of kindness
Former Holden Police Chief Chris Greeley started 25 Days of Kindness in 2017. Benjamin said the initiative has grown each year, and he hopes the department’s efforts would make Greeley proud.
“Oh he is looking down on me happy and he is like see how much work it is and you know it’s worth it, it’s definitely worth it and I’m sure he’s happy right now,” Benjamin said.
Though the initiative bears the name 25 Days of Kindness, its message reaches beyond the holidays: supporting neighbors is something the community can do all year long.

Region 10 Tech awarded $1M grant to cultivate Maine’s future workforce
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Region 10 Technical High School in Brunswick was recently awarded a $1,080,000 grant from the MELMAC Education Foundation in Augusta.
On Oct. 27, community members, business partners, students and staff gathered to celebrate the receipt of the grant. Wendy Ault, executive director of MELMAC Education Foundation, along with Janelle MacDermott, board member and treasurer for MELMAC, presented an oversized check to Shawn M. Chabot, superintendent/director at Region 10; Doug Dumont, Region 10 program director; and Gretchen McCloy, the ASPIRE ELO (extended learning opportunity) coordinator. The check represents an overall investment of $1,080,000 from MELMAC, which will be used at Region 10 over five years to “Cultivate Maine’s Future Workforce Together.”
The “Together” is a key component of the ASPIRE program. Instructors and administrators at Region 10 will be working closely with business and community partners to create opportunities for students to engage with meaningful work related experiences in the real world. Students will be provided opportunities to learn and practice their soft skills in addition to the technical skills they are learning in the classrooms and workshops at Region 10. These experiences could range from a one-hour informational interview with a local employer, to working with a mentor from the community on a short-term project as part of an ELO, to the semester- or yearlong opportunities through CO-OP and pre-apprenticeships.
Jason Darling, COOP and pre-apprenticeship instructor at Region 10, has a longstanding tradition of getting students out for school-to-work experiences while they are enrolled at Region 10. He is excited about the future of the ASPIRE grant to invite more students at Region 10 to be able to access these career exploration opportunities.
“Offering ELOs to our students will allow us to expose them to more career options and give them a head start on the career pathway planning that we focus on in our school,” Darling said in a prepared release. “It’s an awesome opportunity for them to be able to get a real world look at a potential career and how the skills they are learning translate to the workplace.”
Local employers are encouraged to reach out to McCloy to discuss partnerships and workforce pipelines. McCloy can be reached at [email protected] or 207-729-6622. McCloy is also curating a “job board” for current Region 10 students and for recent graduates who are looking for employment, and welcomes job postings from local employers.
The ASPIRE Region 10 Tech program also will allow for greater outreach to pre-K through grade 8 learners in Regional School Unit 5, Maine School Administrative District 75 and Brunswick communities. Region 10 staff will be working closely with the sending schools to find ways to introduce younger students to technical education. Region 10 instructors are currently working with McCloy to create hands-on activities that could be shared with younger learners.
“This grant allows us to step fully into our identity as a modern career and technical education school — reinforcing a culture grounded in innovation, professionalism and real opportunity for every student who walks through our doors,” said Region 10 Assistant Director Doug Dumont. “At Region 10, we see a real responsibility — and a huge opportunity — to step up. We’re here to bridge that ‘opportunity gap’ for our students and our community. We are deeply committed to supporting our students right here in Brunswick, as well as across the communities of MSAD 75 and RSU 5. We want to make sure they’re connected with real-world professional networks, great mentors, and clear pathways to high-paying careers right here in Maine.”

title: Two people arrested, nearly two pounds of drugs seized in Bridgton bust
text:
Two people arrested, nearly two pounds of drugs seized in Bridgton, Maine, bust
Police say they went to a home to do a bail compliance check and ended up finding a drug operation.
Two people arrested, nearly two pounds of drugs seized in Bridgton, Maine, bust
Police say they went to a home to do a bail compliance check and ended up finding a drug operation.
Two people are facing charges after police say officers seized nearly two pounds of drugs in Bridgton.
Officers went to a home on Forest Avenue at about 8:15 p.m. on Tuesday for a bail compliance check, but say they ended up finding drugs and evidence of drug trafficking inside the home.
Police seized 1.6 pounds of suspected cocaine, 120 grams of suspected methamphetamine, including fake Adderall pills, and 23 grams of suspected fentanyl, mostly in fake Xanax pills. Police also seized $10,000 in cash and material used to package and distribute drugs.
Benjamin Lane-Robichaud, 24, was charged with two counts of aggravated trafficking in scheduled drugs and one count of unlawful possession of scheduled drugs.
Kayli Goodwin-Blundell, 19, was charged with two counts of violation of condition of release.
"The Bridgton Police Department remains committed to addressing illegal drug trafficking while recognizing the devastating impact substance use disorders have on individuals, families, and our community. If you or someone you know is struggling with substance use, we encourage you to seek help. Recovery is possible, and resources are available. Individuals seeking assistance can contact a trusted healthcare provider, local recovery organization, or dial 211 to connect with available services throughout Maine," police wrote in a release.

title: Iran war raises government shutdown risk — some lawmakers say the risk is worth taking
text:
Iran war raises government shutdown risk — some lawmakers say the risk is worth taking
With a Dec. 11 deadline approaching, lawmakers are divided over funding for President Trump’s war in Iran, raising concerns about a possible government shutdown.
Iran war raises government shutdown risk — some lawmakers say the risk is worth taking
With a Dec. 11 deadline approaching, lawmakers are divided over funding for President Trump’s war in Iran, raising concerns about a possible government shutdown.
Congress is facing the possibility of another government shutdown as lawmakers weigh competing demands over President Donald Trump's war in Iran.
Some Democrats want to use the Dec. 11 funding deadline to force restrictions on the war. But at least one Republican says limiting the president's military authority could be more dangerous than a shutdown.
Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Alabama, said he would not want to restrict the president's authority if nuclear weapons were involved, even at the risk of a government shutdown.
"If they get nuclear weapons, you won't be worrying about a shutdown," Aderholt told Hearst Television on Thursday.
He stressed that he was not advocating for a shutdown.
Democrats consider tying government funding to the Iran war
Some Democrats want the next government spending bill to include restrictions preventing federal money from being used to continue military operations against Iran.
On Thursday, Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland joined independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont in demanding those restrictions as part of any short-term funding agreement.
Their joint statement opposed providing billions of dollars in additional war funding and called for language restricting the administration's use of appropriated funds to continue fighting.
Rep. Ro Khanna, D-California, has called for a December spending bill prohibiting federal money from being used for U.S. combat operations in Iran. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Virginia, has advocated similar restrictions.
But Democratic leadership has not committed to making those demands a condition of keeping the government open.
Asked Thursday whether Democrats should be willing to risk a shutdown to end the war, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries pointed to ongoing negotiations led by Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee.
"There are four corners negotiations that are ongoing, led by Rosa DeLauro," Jeffries said, explaining that she was working through Democratic priorities ahead of the Dec. 11 deadline.
"I don't want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro," he added.
Jeffries nevertheless emphasized his party's opposition to additional war funding.
"House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump's war machine, to Pete Hegseth's war machine over in the Middle East," Jeffries said.
Incoming Democrats weigh the risks
Representative-elect Dan Koh, D-Massachusetts, told Hearst Television he wants the war to end and the government to remain open.
But when White House Correspondent Christopher Salas asked whether it was worth risking a shutdown to use every piece of leverage Democrats have to end the war, Koh had a one-word answer: "Absolutely."
Koh will take office in January, after the Dec. 11 funding deadline.
Rep.-elect Jacqui Irwin, D-California, echoed his call for a tougher approach.
"We should use every bit of leverage we have to stop this war, this war of choice," Irwin said when asked whether Democrats should take that approach even at the risk of a shutdown.
What another shutdown could mean for Americans
The funding dispute presents a strategic dilemma for Democrats. Refusing additional war funding alone would not necessarily end military operations financed with money Congress has already appropriated.
The debate comes roughly a year after a 43-day government shutdown disrupted air travel, delayed federal paychecks and caused disruptions to food assistance and some government services.
Another funding lapse could again force some federal workers to stay home while requiring others to continue working without immediate pay. Air travel and federal services could face disruptions depending on the length and scope of a shutdown.

title: Users report email app Microsoft Outlook is down
text:
(Gray News) - Microsoft products, particularly Microsoft Outlook, appear to be down, according to user reports.
Downdetector received more than 130,000 reports from users experiencing problems with the email app. A spike in reports began at about 1:10 p.m. ET.
Outages were reported worldwide.
Users also reported problems with other Microsoft products, including Microsoft 365. There were more than 48,000 user reports involving Microsoft 365, according to Downdetector.
Microsoft 365 reported they were looking into users “experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods.” As of 1:48 p.m., the company reported it is “redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load.”

title: Is Outlook down? Widespread outage hits Microsoft apps
text:
A widespread outage hit Microsoft platforms including Outlook on Thursday, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant’s suite of apps.
Nearly 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook just after 1 p.m. ET. New reports have since fallen from that peak, but many said they couldn’t send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether.
Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft’s workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services.
Microsoft said that it was investigating disruptions, notably related to its email and Teams applications.
In updates posted on social media, Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft said it was aware of users “experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas.”
Microsoft later explained that a portion of its infrastructure was “experiencing elevated load” — which it said was “likely contributing to the connectivity errors.” The company determined a number of servers were “unexpectedly unavailable” due to a problem that caused them to fail during automated checks.
Microsoft did not immediately provide more information around what might be causing that failure, but added that it was testing a fix.
“We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact,” the Microsoft 365 Status account wrote on X.
Earlier in the day, the company said it had “successfully restored” problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

title: Penobscot County deputy dropped off homeless man in Bangor days before alleged crime spree
text:
A Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office deputy drove a homeless man from Glenburn to downtown Bangor last month, where the man is accused of then going on a crime spree.
The deputy dropped Ryan Sawyer, 38, off on Oct. 5 on Franklin Street despite knowing he was homeless and that he was barred from entering the city’s homeless shelter. Over the next two days, he allegedly committed six different crimes in Bangor and has been held in the Penobscot County Jail since.
Sawyer’s case is an example of how officers with the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office and other municipal police departments transport homeless people from nearby towns to Bangor, even if they have no plan for where to go when they get here. But it’s a difficult trend to quantify, as no departments track how often this happens.
While such moves can strain Bangor’s limited resources, one expert said it is still the most compassionate option available.
The sheriff’s office was first called to check on Sawyer while he was walking with his pants down on Pushaw Road in Glenburn around 10 p.m., according to a police report obtained by the Bangor Daily News through a Freedom of Access Act request.
Penobscot County Deputy Garrett Carlson requested EMS evaluate Sawyer because he was not able to form sentences, according to the report. Medics found Sawyer was able to answer questions and was cognizant.
Sawyer, who was from Glenburn, didn’t have a place to live and was dressed inappropriately for the cold weather, the report said.
Another deputy, who drove Sawyer to Bangor, said they didn’t feel comfortable leaving the man on the side of the road. The deputy didn’t sign the report with their full name.
Sawyer is barred from the Bangor Area Homeless Shelter due to a no trespassing order from the Bangor Police Department, so he could not be brought there, the report said. The police report later says he is banned from “the area shelters.”
Sawyer told the deputy he wanted to be taken to Brewer, but the deputy drove him to the sheriff’s office on Franklin Street and pointed him in the direction of the Joshua Chamberlain Bridge, the report said.
Penobscot County Sheriff Troy Morton and Chief Deputy John Knappe did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Bangor Police Chief Mark Hathaway declined an interview. Sgt. Jeremy Brock, the department’s spokesperson, said it faces significant challenges from the large number of homeless people in the city.
“Our teams continue to manage the current population as effectively as possible while preparing for the demands anticipated with the arrival of an incoming population,” Brock said.
With so few options available to police in such situations, it may have been the best that could be done at the time, said Katie Spencer White, the co-chair of the Maine Statewide Homeless Council and CEO of the Mid-Maine Homeless shelter.
“It sounds like this was a compassionate response,” she said.
Sawyer couldn’t be taken into protective custody for mental health, the report said. Maine law has strict requirements for such a step, including that the person needs to pose a “likelihood of serious harm.”
There are more support resources in service center cities, Spencer White said. But those communities are struggling with the growing homeless population.
People come to Bangor for services including the sober houses, methadone clinics, emergency rooms and psychiatric hospitals, Hathaway said during an Oct. 5 Bangor City Council Government Operations Committee meeting. Surrounding cities and towns don’t have any of those resources.
“I think everybody understands that we’re caring for a large chunk of the state’s most vulnerable people, some of the most sick,” Hathaway said.
Many in Bangor point to substance use as the biggest problem facing homeless people here, but their mental health is a greater struggle, he said.
Homeless people being driven into Bangor is a regular occurrence because neighboring towns don’t have shelters or services, Bangor Area Homeless Shelter Director Boyd Kronholm said. Some of the people who have been dropped off at the shelter didn’t even know it existed, he added.
The sheriff’s office usually checks to see if the shelter has any beds open before driving someone there, Kronholm said. Beds are rarely available.
Banning someone from the shelter for an extended period of time is a last resort, Kronholm said. He couldn’t speak to Sawyer’s case, but said a long-term ban usually happens if someone puts others in danger.
There are two overnight warming centers opening Nov. 15 at Brick Church and Mansion Church, Kronholm said. The city also runs a street outreach team that offers some services.
Two days after Sawyer was dropped off in Bangor, he was arrested and charged with aggravated criminal mischief, disorderly conduct, terrorizing and violating his conditions of release.
He allegedly broke windows at a Hammond Street business, threw apples at passing cars and walked down a street screaming, police said.
“The idea that your police officers are not addressing these issues — we’re just overwhelmed,” Hathaway said at the Oct. 5 meeting. “If every community took care of the most vulnerable, we might not be having this conversation right now.”

title: Maine nonprofit association joins national awareness campaign
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Association of Nonprofits is encouraging residents to recognize and support the more than 3,000 charitable nonprofits across the state as part of a national awareness campaign during Nonprofit Appreciation Month.
“If you live, work or spend time in Maine, there’s a good chance a nonprofit is part of your story,” said Jennifer Hutchins, the group’s executive director.
“From everyday moments to times of urgency, local nonprofits are neighbors helping neighbors,” she added. ” It’s our civic responsibility to uplift, value and support them.”
The group highlights the important role nonprofits play in Maine communities through essential services, education, arts and culture, environmental protection and community support. Residents are encouraged to share nonprofit stories, attend events, volunteer, and make donations.
According to the association, Maine’s nonprofit sector employs one in six workers, contributes approximately $16 billion to the state’s economy, and mobilizes about 400,000 volunteers annually.
Mainers can learn more and find ways to participate in the national Nonprofits Get It Done campaign at NonprofitMaine.org/NonprofitsGetItDone.

title: Cat dies in Aroostook house fire
text:
An accidental fire took place at an Ashland home Monday, killing one cat.
The fire was caused by a gasoline spill, according to the Maine Department of Public Safety. While a lawn tractor was being repaired in the garage, gasoline spilled onto the floor and its vapors were ignited by a space heater.
The home and garage were a total loss.
Two occupants were displaced by the fire, including a 77-year-old man who was taken to a hospital for treatment of smoke inhalation.
One cat died. A dog escaped from the property and has not been found.

title: 2 students, teacher stabbed at middle school, police say
text:
WARRENTON, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - Two students and a teacher were stabbed at a middle school in Missouri, according to authorities.
Warrenton police said a male student stabbed two students and a teacher with a 4- to 5-inch blade inside a classroom at Black Hawk Middle School around 7:55 a.m.
One student was flown to a children’s hospital, and the teacher was also taken to a hospital. The other student suffered “superficial wounds,” police said.
The suspect is in custody, and there is no threat to the public.
Police said all classrooms had been cleared as of 10:41 a.m.
The Warren County R-III School District said all schools in the district will dismiss at 12:41 p.m., and all Black Hawk Middle School sports have been canceled.

title: Lewiston Leaf Collection is November 16
text:
LEWISTON, ME – Lewiston Public Works (LPW) will start its Leaf Collection service at 7 AM on Mon., Nov. 16. Residents must place their leaves in closed, compostable paper bags at curbside by that time.
For the first time, the City will take collected leaves to a recycling service, which requires the use of compostable paper bags.
To participate in curbside leaf collection on Mon., Nov. 16:
Do not use plastic bags.
Use compostable paper bags only.
Close each bag securely so leaves do not spill out when crews load the bags into the truck.
Place compostable bags curbside by 7 AM on Mon., Nov. 16.
You may put out as many bags as you need.
LPW crews will make one pass through each neighborhood starting on Mon., Nov. 16.
Once crews have collected leaves on your street, they will not return.
If you miss Leaf Collection on Mon., Nov. 16 or want to get rid of leaves now, you have two options:
Option 1: Use your regular trash collection day.
If you use your regular trash collection day, place leaves in a plastic or compostable bag and close it securely. Put the bag inside your trash cart. Make sure the trash cart lid is completely closed.
Option 2: Bring leaves to the Solid Waste Facility.
The facility is at 420 River Road and is open weekdays from 7:15 AM to 2:45 PM and Saturdays from 8 AM to 11:50 AM.
If you bring leaves to the Solid Waste Facility, you may use compostable paper bags or plastic bags. If you use plastic bags, staff will direct you to empty the leaves into a leaf collection bin.
There is no charge to bring your leaves to Solid Waste Facility as long as your leaves are in a compostable paper bag.

text:
NEWPORT, Maine (WABI) - The Nokomis Warriors are Class B state field hockey champions after their 1-0 victory over Freeport on Saturday.
MaKenzie Watson’s goal propelled Nokomis to the state title, capping off a 17-1 season.
“Our passing this year has been incredible, especially compared to our years in the past. Just connecting and letting the ball do the work is definitely a big part of our game and won us that game. title: US envoys arrive in Moscow for meeting with Putin following talks in Abu Dhabi
text:
US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then head for Dublin to see Zelenskyy
U.S. envoys met Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin before heading to Ireland for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as Washington sought new momentum for its peace efforts.
Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump's son-in-law, brokered talks this week between delegations from Moscow and Kyiv. The session in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, brought the first direct discussions between Ukrainian and Russian representatives in nine months as the push for a settlement stalled.
The talks produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced. Plans for another round of talks were announced as well, with Witkoff and Zelenskyy saying Europe will join, though they gave no details about which countries or how many.
Kushner and Witkoff met with Putin for about two hours before going to Dublin, where they met with Zelenskyy for more than an hour as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.
Europe seeks a place at the negotiating table
Kushner said one goal of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader’s blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent’s broader security arrangements.
In Abu Dhabi, several European security advisers were involved on the sidelines but not in the main three-way talk.
Speaking to reporters before boarding a plane to leave Moscow, Witkoff said the next round of talks has been agreed upon. Russian state TV showed Witkoff saying that “the Europeans will join at the next meeting,” but he did not elaborate.
Zelenskyy in Dublin indicated the Europeans would not be on the sidelines. “Next meeting, Europe will be during negotiations, will be a negotiation team – not some way, not separately. They will have a voice,” he said.
The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.
Russia, meanwhile, doesn’t want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine’s military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent.
But Washington and European capitals have sometimes seemed at odds in their diplomatic efforts. Trump has repeatedly sided with Putin, last month waiving sanctions and striking a deal to import Russian diesel, in moves that dismayed Ukraine and European leaders.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov argued that for Europe to join peace talks, it first must name a representative.
“The Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar. If someone takes the initiative to establish contact with the Russian side, such people are facing ostracism.”
Many in Europe also see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO’s eastward expansion as a main security threat and has demanded the alliance’s troops be pulled back from Russia’s borders.
Putin's aide calls the talks ‘constructive’
Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine — a possibility that alarms European leaders.
Thursday’s talks were “substantive, constructive, frank and useful,” Putin’s aide Yuri Ushakov said.
He added that the Kremlin leader reminded Witkoff and Kushner about Moscow’s proposals from 2021 -- before it sent troops into Ukraine -- demanding that NATO roll back the alliance’s military deployments in Central and Eastern Europe. Russia will update those with “fresh considerations,” Ushakov said.
Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire — an idea long floated by Europe to prevent a new attack by Moscow — would be “absolutely unacceptable” and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate target. “In other words, the war would resume immediately,” the Russian president said.
He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled.
Fighting continues as another bitter winter approaches
Zelenskyy is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are “very much aligned” on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January. “But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire,” Rutte said.
Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line.
Russia’s bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow’s drone and missile strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a “weaponization of winter.”
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-manufacturing plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said.
Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said.
U.S. Starlink problems return, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine is experiencing another slowdown in the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that the country needs to defend itself against Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said Thursday on social media.
Military units have recorded “significant disruptions,” including speed restrictions limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph), Zelenskyy said, adding that a military investigation established that the restrictions weren't random errors.
Ukraine uses Starlink and Starshield for intercepting Russian drones and launching its own strikes.
Last month, limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations and alarmed Kyiv officials who fear U.S. support could drop off.
Elon Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn’t be used for offensive strikes against Russia.
Zelenskyy said the speed limits cover operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and that Kyiv is trying to find out from U.S. officials what is going on.
Russian colonel reportedly killed by a car bomb
A Russian serviceman was killed in St. Petersburg early Thursday when his vehicle exploded, according to the Investigative Committee, the country’s main criminal investigation agency. It didn’t identify the victim or say who was behind the bombing.
The Fontanka news outlet said the victim was a colonel and that a bomb in his car exploded as he drove off.
Several senior Russian military officers have died in bombings and other attacks that Moscow blames on Ukraine. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some attacks on Russian soil.

title: GOP control in Knox County reduced to 2 officials in probate office
text:
Probate Judge Carol Emery and Register of Probate Julie Allen are the sole Republicans who hold seats in Knox County that are elected in a partisan election.
Emery was uncontested for the seat that she has held since 1990. With this election, she became Maine’s senior Probate Judge, and is serving in that capacity longer than any of the other 15 judges across Maine.
Republican Julie Allen of Union serves as Knox County register of probate. Allen has worked for the county for 36 years and was elected register of probate in November 2024 following the retirement of Elaine Hallett. Registers of Probate are elected for four-year terms.
Probate Judges are elected from each of Maine’s 16 counties and also serve four-year terms.
Emery said politics does not come into the judge or register jobs.
“This is really not a political office. We follow state law and state Supreme Court rulings,” she said.
The office oversees matters such as estates, guardianships, and name changes.
She is married to former Congressman David Emery. David Emery served as a Republican state legislator for Rockland, being elected in 1970 and reelected in 1972. He then launched a what seemed to be quixotic race against incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Peter Kyros in 1974.
Emery won a close race (a few hundred votes out of nearly 200,000 cast) and served for 8 years before attempting to win a U.S. Senate seat held by Democrat George Mitchell who had been appointed to the position when Edmund Muskie resigned to be Secretary of State for President Jimmy Carter. Mitchell won that race.
When David Emery entered politics, Knox County was solidly Republican. That changed beginning with the 1970s Watergate scandal, when a young Gary Fowlie of Rockland was elected to the Maine House after David Emery won election to Congress. Attorney Jean Chalmers of Rockland was elected to the state Senate in 1984, being the first Democrat to hold that office since the 1930s.
County commissioner seats were traditionally held by Republicans. Upon Richard Parent’s retirement in 2024, all three seats became held by Democrats.
Today, there are no Republicans other than Carol Emery and Allen who are registered Republicans who hold an office where candidates run under a party label. Republican state Rep. Abden Simmons of Waldoboro did not seek re-election this year and his seat was won by former Democrat and now independent Clinton Collamore.
Judge Emery is a past Secretary and President of the Maine Probate Judges Assembly (MPJA) whose membership includes the probate judges from each of Maine’s 16 counties. She has served as the Maine Probate Judges’ representative on the Committee on Judicial Ethics, appointed by the Maine Supreme Judicial Court. That Committee is charged with reviewing and taking appropriate action regarding complaints of incompetency or misconduct within Maine’s judicial system.
She has also served on the Maine Probate Rules and Forms Committee, also appointed by the Supreme Judicial Court, which oversees the Probate Court’s e-filing system. She currently serves as a member of the Civil Legal Services Fund Committee, which reviews the allocation of funding to organizations that provide legal assistance to the poor and elderly.
She and her husband are residents of Tenants Harbor. They have one adult son, Dr. Albert Emery, now practicing medicine in Ann Arbor, Michigan.

title: Portland Trails urges caution following coyote sightings in Evergreen Woods
text:
Those walking in or near Evergreen Woods in Portland are being urged to beware of coyotes.
Portland Trails, which maintains the wooded trail network abutting Evergreen Cemetery, said Thursday afternoon that coyotes have been spotted recently on Ludlow Street. That’s on the southwest side of the woods.
“If you encounter a coyote while you’re on a trail or just walking down the street, make loud noises, wave your arms to make yourself bigger, and protect small children and dogs,” Portland Trails advised in a social media post Tuesday.
The organization also encouraged trail users to always give any wild animals ample space.
Those with concerns about an animal’s behavior are directed to contact Portland animal control at 207-874-8575.

title: Police: Suspect in child exploitation operation arrived to meeting with 2-year-old
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A Louisiana police department said it made 10 arrests in an undercover Internet Crimes Against Children operation, which began Oct. 23.
The Kenner Police Department said the undercover operation targeted adults who used social media and online apps to solicit minors for sexual purposes.
This is the department’s fourth operation this year, officials said.
How the arrests were made
Detectives said they made 10 arrests during this latest operation. Six of those suspects engaged in explicit sexual conversations with people they believed were underage girls, police said. When the suspects arrived at the arranged meeting place, they were met by Kenner police and arrested.
Four others were arrested on warrants.
Suspect arrived with 2-year-old child
One suspect, Jasmine Gatlin, 40, of New Orleans, arranged to meet someone he believed was a 15-year-old girl, officials said. Undercover detectives told the suspect not to bring the 2-year-old with him, but he arrived with the child anyway, officials said.
Gatlin was arrested and the child was released into the care of the suspect’s grandmother, according to Kenner police. In addition to indecent behavior with a juvenile and computer-aided solicitation of a minor, Gatlin was charged with improper supervision of a minor by parent or legal custodian.
Those arrested
The 10 arrested in the operation were identified as:
- Douglas Glen Brown, 40, New Orleans
- Terrance Williams, 45, Des Allemands
- Dwayne Crisp, 43, New Orleans
- Troy Verrett Jr., 35, Marrero
- Jasmine Gatlin, 40, New Orleans
- Malcolm Richards, 39, New Orleans
- Kendrick Isom, 52, Vacherie
- Juan D. Gomez, 41, Kenner
- Tracey Rourke, 56, Gretna
- Paul Cordes III, 30, New Orleans
According to Kenner police, six suspects in the investigation are still at large.
- Thadis Misso II, 34, Union, Mississippi
- Dwayne Lewis, 43, Bridge City
- Leonardo Hernandez, 27, Weslaco, Texas
- Lloyd Allen, 32, Prairieville
- Baylee “Sabrina” Dawn Hogan, 27, Houston
- Russell Kyle Rouse, 37, Brunswick, Georgia
The 10 arrested individuals face indecent behavior with a juvenile and computer-aided solicitation of a minor charges. The six wanted individuals have outstanding warrants for those same offenses, officials said.
Police chief’s statement
“Every time we conduct one of these operations, we think we have seen it all. Bringing your own 2-year-old child to a meeting you believe is for sexual activity with a 15-year-old is beyond disturbing. Parents, we are trying our best to take these predators down, but we need your help. Please monitor your children on devices. They will thank you one day,” Kenner Police Chief Keith Conley said.

title: Eddington school board member arrested on new charges

Eddington school board member arrested on new charges
Authorities have arrested an Eddington school board member on new drug charges; she had been out on bail in connection with her infant's reported overdose.
Eddington school board member arrested on new charges
Authorities have arrested an Eddington school board member on new drug charges; she had been out on bail in connection with her infant's reported overdose.
Authorities arrested an Eddington woman Wednesday who was out on bail in connection with an infant's reported overdose.
According to the Penobscot County Sheriff's Office, 36-year-old Brittany Wood is accused of possessing illegal drugs and trying to destroy potential evidence during a traffic stop on Sunday, Nov. 8.
She faces charges of unlawful possession of scheduled drugs, falsifying physical evidence and violating conditions of release.
The sheriff's office said deputies made several unsuccessful attempts to have Wood voluntarily surrender before obtaining an arrest warrant.
Wood had been free on bail in a separate case involving her 9-month-old child, who officials said overdosed in May and tested positive for cocaine and fentanyl. Wood was indicted in October on charges related to the May incident.
Her attorney said in court that Wood had been on vacation and did not know about an arrest warrant until she saw news reports. The defense also said she was on her way to turn herself in when she was arrested.
Wood remains on RSU 63 School Board
Wood represents Eddington on the RSU 63 School Board. Board Chair Rachel Downs confirmed to Maine's Total Coverage that Wood remains an elected member.
The district will continue to follow applicable district policies and Maine law, including 20-A M.R.S. § 1474, which outlines the circumstances under which a vacancy on a regional school unit board may be declared," said Downs, who declined to offer additional comments, calling it a pending law enforcement matter.
Eddington Town Manager Shawna Hinkley told WABI-TV earlier this year that there is no recall process for RSU 63 board members. Under the district's absenteeism policy, a member who misses three consecutive meetings is removed. Wood missed two consecutive meetings after the July warrant and attended the third after being released on bail.

title: $50 million investment brings upgrades to Maine state parks
text:
CASCO, Maine (WMTW) - A $50 million investment is funding upgrades and improvements at state parks across Maine.
State officials celebrated the investment Thursday at Sebago Lake State Park in Casco, where they cut the ribbon on a new day-use entrance station.
The funding comes from Gov. Janet Mills’ Maine Jobs and Recovery Plan, which uses federal money allocated through the American Rescue Plan Act.
Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Commissioner Amanda Beal said the funding has allowed staff to take on multiple projects at parks across the state.
“Being able to access such a sizeable amount of resources really allowed our staff to focus on doing multiple projects in parks across the state,” Beal said.
State officials say the improvements are intended to support park operations, enhance the visitor experience and protect Maine’s natural resources for years to come.

title: Project Wellness Aims to Bring Hygiene Essentials into Local Schools
text:
A new initiative has made its way into schools across Lincoln County, bringing free hygiene kits to students.

title: Why are gas prices dropping and how low will they go?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Why are gas prices dropping and how low will they go?
Experts say several factors are driving the downward trend.
Why are gas prices dropping and how low will they go?
Experts say several factors are driving the downward trend.
The national average for regular gasoline dropped below $4 per gallon this week for the first time since July, according to AAA.
The $3.94 average as of Wednesday afternoon was 18 cents lower than last week and more than 40 cents lower than a month ago, according to an analysis by our Get the Facts Data Team.
Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, predicts prices could fall to between $3.65 and $3.75 by Thanksgiving. Despite the drop, that would still be the highest fuel prices on record for the holiday, according to De Haan.
It comes after major midterm election losses for Republicans that party leaders have, at least in part, blamed on economic pain.
"Specifically, people really honed in on the price for fuel in this country," Senate Republican Leader John Thune told reporters on Tuesday. "I think that had a big impact on our candidates."
De Haan said a range of factors are driving the post-election drop, including typical seasonal trends.
"Americans are driving less as temperatures get colder. The switch over to cheaper winter gasoline is making the cost of fuel less," De Haan said.
Other factors include increasing oil traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and President Donald Trump's recent comments downplaying the likelihood of a military escalation in Iran.
"Iran, militarily, is effectively over. We're just keeping it the status quo," Trump said during a press briefing on Monday. 
Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries have also contributed to elevated fuel prices. Following U.S. mediated talks this week, Russia and Ukraine agreed to a prisoner exchange, but no major breakthroughs were announced on a longer-term deal to stop the fighting. The Trump administration's peace efforts continue as U.S. envoys are expected to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"Until there's some sort of definitive end to these two geopolitical situations, gas prices will likely remain elevated," De Haan said.

title: Meta removes Russell Brand's accounts after rape, sexual assault sentencing
text:
Meta removes Russell Brand's accounts after rape, sexual assault sentencing
Russell Brand's Meta accounts were disabled on Wednesday following his sentence earlier in the week.
Brand was sentenced Monday to 10½ years in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others during a time when his bawdy behavior was indulged and celebrated during his rise to stardom. 
A jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Related video above: Comedian, actor Russell Brand charged with rape and sexual assault
Brand’s team announced the Meta ban on his X account on Wednesday. The post read, “There never was a Russell Brand, according to @Meta. Thank God for @elonmusk. Stay tuned.”
He has over 10 million followers on X, whose owner, Elon Musk, has questioned the British justice system.
Brand had more than 6 million followers on Facebook and nearly 5 million on Instagram, according to an article from The New York Times.
The New York Times reported that a Meta spokesman told the news outlet in an email that the accounts were disabled because its policies do not allow accounts "owned by a convicted sex offender, convicted of offenses related to the sexual abuse of children or adults." The policy also states that includes accounts "owned by a Designated Entity or run on their behalf.
His YouTube account, with more than 6 million subscribers, is still active. A YouTube spokesman declined to comment to The New York Times on whether the former star's conviction would affect the status of his account on the platform.
According to British website GOV.UK, "Prisoners are not allowed to have access to social networking websites," while they are in custody.
The New York Times and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Obituary: William Byron Cheever
text:
HARPSWELL – William Byron Cheever, 77, left the side of his loving family to begin his next Great Adventure on Nov. 5, 2026, from his home in Harpswell. Born Oct. 11, 1949, in Michigan, to parents Marjorie and Markham Cheever, William cultivated a life of exploration by becoming a jack of all trades and a master of many. He liked his comforts simple but his world vast and loved learning languages so he could charm old ladies and grocers alike across the globe. William lived in many places, settling in Virginia before eventually retiring to Harpswell, Maine where he had “never made more friends in his entire life.” His life in Vacationland was marked with gardening, frequent outings with his dog Gina, and performing his songs and stories for friends and neighbors at open mic nights. He had careers spanning from sommelier and the hospitality industry to computer systems analyst. As a father and husband, he shared the best parts of himself. He was a travel partner to his wife of 42 years, Lee, taught the joys of community and service to his son Mark, and shared his boundless creativity in music and writing with his daughter Emily. They will think of him every time they pass a vintage guitar shop, or when an exorbitant dinner bill hits the table, or whenever there’s a moment of silliness to be had. He is survived by his brother Paul Cheever and family in Sydney, Australia, daughter-in-law Kristen and grandchildren Duncan and Adelin in Concord, N.H., and son-in-law Andrew and granddaughter Cecelia in Los Angeles, Calif.
In lieu of flowers, the family requests that you spend a peaceful moment by a fire (extra points given if you are also drinking a nice glass of Beaujolais), and that you give all dogs (good or bad) an extra biscuit in William’s honor. Memorial contributions can be expressed to the Midcoast Hunger
Prevention Program.

Author to discuss emotional effects of long-term caregiving at Rockland library
text:
Caregiver advocate, speaker and author of “Neither Wife nor Widow” Dale Ruth Sherburne will lead a discussion from 6-7:30 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 19, via Zoom and in the Community Room at Rockland Public Library.
Drawing from 20 years of caring for her husband with early-onset dementia, Sherburne’s work explores the unspoken emotional realities of long-term caregiving, such as guilt, resentment and grief. Favorably reviewed in the Journal of Applied Gerontology (February 2026) and by Kirkus Book Review (December 2025), Sherburne’s book and presentations aim to normalize these difficult emotions. She advocates for greater support and resources for caregivers, emphasizing the need for increased awareness among healthcare professionals to address these critical emotional aspects of care.
Contact Jeannie at [email protected] with questions or for the Zoom link. All are welcome to attend. The Rockland Public Library is located at 80 Union St.
